Nidānavaggaṭīkā

The Subcommentary on the Chapter on Causation

1. Nidānasaṃyuttaṃ

1. The Connected Discourses on Causation

1. Buddhavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Buddha

1. Paṭiccasamuppādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. An Explanation of the Discourse on Dependent Origination

1. Dutiyasuttādīnipi [V 2.0001][M 2.0001] paṭiccasamuppādavaseneva desitānīti āha “paṭhamaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasutta”nti. Tatrāti padaṃ ye desakālā idha viharaṇakiriyāya visesanabhāvena vuttā, tesaṃ paridīpananti dassento “yaṃ samayaṃ…pe… dīpetī”ti āha. Taṃ-saddo hi vuttassa atthassa paṭiniddeso, tasmā idha desassa kālassa vā paṭiniddeso bhavituṃ arahati, na aññassa. Ayaṃ tāva tatrasaddassa paṭiniddesabhāve atthavibhāvanā. Yasmā pana īdisesu ṭhānesu tatrasaddo dhammadesanāvisiṭṭhaṃ desaṃ kālañca vibhāveti, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle”ti[V 2.0002]. Tena tatrāti yattha bhagavā dhammadesanatthaṃ bhikkhū ālapi abhāsi, tādise dese, kāle vāti attho. Na hītiādinā tamevatthaṃ samattheti.

1. Because the second sutta and others were also taught by way of dependent origination, he said: 'the first discourse on dependent origination.' To show that the word 'tatra' (therein) is an explanation of those places and times mentioned here as a qualification of the act of dwelling, he said: 'at what time...pe...he clarifies.' For the word 'taṃ' (that) is a reference to what has been said; therefore, here it can be a reference to the place or time, not to anything else. This, for a start, is the explanation of the meaning of the word 'tatra' in its referential sense. But since in such instances the word 'tatra' clarifies the place and time specified for the Dhamma teaching, it was said: 'or in a place and time suitable for speaking.' By this, the meaning of 'tatra' is: in such a place or at such a time where the Blessed One addressed and spoke to the bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. By means of 'Not indeed,' etc., he supports that very meaning.

Nanu ca yattha ṭhito bhagavā “akālo kho tāvā”tiādinā bāhiyassa dhammadesanaṃ paṭikkhipi, tattheva antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova tassa dhammaṃ [M 2.0002] desesīti? Saccametaṃ. Adesetabbakāle adesanāya hi idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ. Tenāha “akālo kho tāvā”ti. Yaṃ pana tattha vuttaṃ “antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā”ti, tampi tassa akālabhāvasseva pariyāyena dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa hi tadā addhānaparissamena rūpakāye akammaññatā ahosi, balavapītivegena nāmakāye. Tadubhayassa vūpasamaṃ āgamento papañcaparihāratthaṃ bhagavā “akālo kho”ti pariyāyena paṭikkhipi. Adesetabbadese adesanāya pana udāharaṇaṃ “atha kho bhagavā maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi, vihārato nikkhamitvā vihārapacchāyāyaṃ paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti evamādikaṃ idha ādisaddena saṅgahitaṃ. “Sa kho so bhikkhave bālo idha pāpāni kammāni karitvā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 3.248) padapūraṇamatte kho-saddo, “dukkhaṃ kho agāravo viharati appatisso”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.21) avadhāraṇe, “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.31) ādikālatthe, vākyārambheti attho. Tattha padapūraṇena vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ kataṃ hoti, ādikālatthena vākyassa upaññāsamattaṃ, avadhāraṇatthena pana niyamadassanaṃ. “Tasmā āmantesi evā”ti āmantane niyamo dassito hotīti.

"But is it not the case that the Blessed One, standing right there where he had rejected Bāhiya's request for a Dhamma teaching with the words 'It is not the time now,' then, while still standing in the middle of the street, taught him the Dhamma?" That is true. For this is an example of not teaching at an unsuitable time for teaching. Hence he said, 'It is not the time now.' And what was said there, 'we have entered among the houses,' that too was said to show indirectly that it was an unsuitable time. For at that time, on account of fatigue from the journey, there was unwieldiness in his material body, and on account of the powerful impact of joy, in his mental body. Awaiting the subsiding of both and in order to avoid proliferation, the Blessed One indirectly rejected him, saying, 'It is not the time now.' An example of not teaching in an unsuitable place is included here by the word 'etc.,' as in: 'Then the Blessed One, having stepped off the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree,' and 'having left the monastery, he sat down on a seat prepared in the shade behind the monastery.' In passages such as, 'That foolish man, bhikkhus, having done evil deeds here...' (MN 129), the particle 'kho' is merely a verse-filler. In phrases like, 'Indeed, one dwells painfully without reverence, without deference...' (AN 4:21), it serves for emphasis. In statements like, 'To what extent, friend, when the Teacher is dwelling in seclusion, do his disciples not train in conformity with his seclusion?' (MN 5), it is in the sense of commencement, that is, the start of a sentence. Therein, by filling the verse, it serves merely as a verbal embellishment; by the sense of commencement, it is merely the introduction of the sentence; but by the sense of emphasis, it is the showing of a determination. Thus, in 'Therefore, he addressed them,' a determination regarding the addressing is shown.

“Bhagavāti lokagarudīpana”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu pubbe “bhagavā”ti padaṃ vuttanti? Yadipi pubbe vuttaṃ, taṃ pana yathāvuttaṭṭhāne viharaṇakiriyāya kattuvisesadassanaparaṃ, na āmantanakiriyāya, idha pana āmantanakiriyāya, tasmā tadatthaṃ puna bhagavāti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti. Tassatthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavāti lokagarudīpana”nti āha. Kathāsavanayuttapuggalavacananti vakkhamānāya paṭiccasamuppādadesanāya savanayogyapuggalavacanaṃ. Catūsupi parisāsu bhikkhū eva edisānaṃ desanānaṃ visesena bhājanabhūtāti sātisayena sāsanasampaṭiggāhakabhāvadassanatthaṃ idha bhikkhugahaṇanti dassetvā idāni saddatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”ti āha. Tattha bhikkhakoti bhikkhūti bhikkhanasīlattā bhikkhanadhammattā bhikkhūti attho. Bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti buddhādīhipi ajjhupagataṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ uñchācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā anuṭṭhitattā bhikkhu. Yo hi koci appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so kasigorakkhādīhi [V 2.0003][M 2.0003] jīvikakappanaṃ hitvā liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā bhikkhu. Parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā vā vihāramajjhe kājabhattaṃ bhuñjamānopi bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāya ussāhajātattā vā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhūti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

"Why is it said, 'The Blessed One, an exposition of the Teacher of the world'? Was not the term 'Blessed One' already stated before?" Although it was stated before, that was for the purpose of showing the distinction of the agent of the act of dwelling, not for the act of addressing. Here, however, it is for the act of addressing; therefore, to convey that meaning, the term 'Blessed One' is stated again in the Pāli. To show its meaning, he said, 'The Blessed One, an exposition of the Teacher of the world.' 'A statement about persons suitable for hearing the talk' means a statement about persons fit to hear the discourse on dependent origination that is about to be spoken. To show that among the four assemblies, bhikkhus are especially the vessels for such teachings, and thus to show their superior status as receptors of the dispensation, the word 'bhikkhus' is used here. Now, to show the meaning of the word, he says, 'Moreover.' Herein, 'bhikkhu' means one who begs: the meaning is that they are bhikkhus because of their habit of begging and their nature of begging. 'One who has undertaken the alms-round': one is a bhikkhu because one has undertaken and practices the alms-round and gleaning, which was also undertaken by the Buddhas and others. For whoever, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, having given up a livelihood from farming, cattle-herding, etc., is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the alms-round by the mere acceptance of the emblem. Or, because his livelihood is dependent on others, even while eating gruel and rice in the middle of the monastery, he has undertaken the alms-round and is thus a bhikkhu. Or, because he has generated enthusiasm for the going forth by relying on the eating of morsels of almsfood, he is a bhikkhu. In this way the meaning should be understood here.

Ādinā nayenāti “bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu, bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhu, bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhikkhū”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 509) āgatanayena. Ñāpaneti avabodhane, paṭivedaneti attho. Bhikkhanasīlatā, na kasivāṇijjādīhi jīvanasīlatā. Bhikkhanadhammatā “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhantī”ti (jā. 1.7.59) evaṃ vuttabhikkhanasabhāvatā, na yācanākohaññasabhāvatā. Bhikkhane sādhukāritā “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”ti (dha. pa. 168) vacanaṃ anussaritvā tattha appamajjatā. Atha vā sīlaṃ nāma pakatisabhāvo. Idha pana tathādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammoti vataṃ. Apare pana “sīlaṃ nāma vatavasena samādānaṃ. Dhammo nāma paveṇi-āgataṃ cārittaṃ. Sādhukāritā sakkaccakāritā ādarakiriyā”ti vaṇṇenti.

By the method that comes in the Vibhaṅga, beginning with: 'A bhikkhu is a wearer of patched-up rags; a bhikkhu is one who breaks up evil, unwholesome states; a bhikkhu is so called because of the brokenness of evil, unwholesome states' (Vibh 244). 'Ñāpana' is in the sense of causing to know, that is, causing to penetrate. The habit of begging, not the habit of living by farming, trade, and so forth. The nature of begging, that is, the nature of begging spoken of thus: 'The noble ones stand with a purpose' (Ja 131), not the nature of begging with deceit. Good practice in begging is being heedful therein, having recollected the saying: 'One should arise and not be heedless' (Dhp 168). Alternatively, 'sīla' is natural disposition, but here it is resolve. 'Dhamma' is a vow. But others explain: 'Sīla is an undertaking by way of a vow. Dhamma is traditional conduct. Good practice is acting carefully, acting with respect.'

Hīnādhikajanasevitavuttinti ye bhikkhubhāve ṭhitāpi jātimadādivasena uddhatā unnaḷā, ye ca gihibhāve paresu atthikabhāvampi anupagatatāya bhikkhācariyaṃ paramakāpaññaṃ maññanti, tesaṃ ubhayesampi yathākkamaṃ “bhikkhavo”ti vacanena hīnajanehi daliddehi paramakāpaññataṃ pattehi parakulesu bhikkhācariyāya jīvikaṃ kappentehi sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatabhāvaniggahaṃ karoti, adhikajanehi uḷārabhogakhattiyakulādito pabbajitehi buddhādīhi ājīvasodhanatthaṃ sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento dīnabhāvaniggahaṃ karotīti yojetabbaṃ. Yasmā “bhikkhavo”ti vacanaṃ āmantanabhāvato abhimukhīkaraṇaṃ, pakaraṇato sāmatthiyato ca sussūsājananaṃ, sakkaccasavanamanasikāraniyojanañca hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “bhikkhavoti iminā”tiādimāha.

'The livelihood practiced by inferior and superior people': This refers to those who, though established in the state of a bhikkhu, are haughty and arrogant on account of conceit of birth and the like; and to those who, while in the household state, not having had to be suppliants to others, consider the alms-round to be the utmost misery. For both of these groups respectively, by the word 'bhikkhus,' he makes known the livelihood practiced by inferior people—the poor who have reached extreme misery and make a living by going for alms among other families—thereby subduing arrogance. And he makes known the livelihood practiced by superior people—the Buddha and others who have gone forth from eminent, wealthy families such as the Khattiyas in order to purify their livelihood—thereby subduing dejection. This is how it should be connected. Because the word 'bhikkhus,' by being an address, brings them face to face, and by its context and capacity it generates a desire to listen and enjoins them to listen attentively and reflect carefully, therefore, to show that meaning, he said: 'By this word "bhikkhus"...' etc.

Tattha sādhukaṃ manasikārepīti sādhukaṃ savane sādhukaṃ manasikāre ca. Kathaṃ pavattitā savanādayo sādhukaṃ pavattitā hontīti? “Addhā imāya [M 2.0004] paṭipattiyā sakalasāsanasampatti hatthagatā bhavissatī”ti ādaragāravayogena kathādīsu aparibhavādinā ca. Vuttañhi “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Na kathaṃ paribhoti, na kathikaṃ paribhoti, na attānaṃ paribhoti[V 2.0004], avikkhittacitto dhammaṃ suṇāti ekaggacitto, yoniso ca manasi karoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammatta”nti (a. ni. 5.151). Tenāha “sādhukaṃ manasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampattī”ti. Sāsanasampatti nāma sīlādinipphatti. Paṭhamaṃ uppannattā adhigamavasena. Satthucariyānuvidhāyakattā sīlādiguṇānuṭṭhānena. Tiṇṇaṃ yānānaṃ vasena anudhammapaṭipattisambhavato sakalasāsanapaṭiggāhakattā.

Therein, 'in careful attention' means in careful listening and in careful attention. How do listening and so on, when they occur, occur carefully? By applying respect and reverence, thinking, 'Surely by this practice the entire accomplishment of the dispensation will come to hand,' and by not disparaging the talk, etc. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a listener of the true Dhamma is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. What five? He does not disparage the talk, he does not disparage the speaker, he does not disparage himself, he listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted and one-pointed mind, and he attends wisely. Bhikkhus, endowed with these five qualities, a listener of the true Dhamma is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states' (AN 5.151). Hence he said: 'For the accomplishment of the dispensation depends on careful attention.' 'Accomplishment of the dispensation' means the achievement of virtue and so on. Because of arising first by way of attainment. Because of conforming to the Teacher's conduct by practicing the qualities of virtue, etc. Because of being receptors of the entire dispensation, since the practice in accordance with the Dhamma is possible by means of the three vehicles.

Santikattāti samīpabhāvato. Santikāvacarattāti sabbakālaṃ saṃvuttibhāvato. Yathānusiṭṭhanti anusāsaniyānurūpaṃ, anusāsaniṃ anavasesato paṭiggahetvāti attho. Ekacce bhikkhūti ye paṭiccasamuppādadhamme desanāpasutā, te. Pubbe “sabbaparisasādhāraṇā hi bhagavato dhammadesanā”tiādinā bhikkhūnaṃ eva āmantanakāraṇaṃ dassetvā idāni bhikkhū āmantetvā dhammadesanāya payojanaṃ dassetuṃ kimatthaṃ pana bhagavāti codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha aññaṃ cintentāti aññavihitā. Vikkhittacittāti asamāhitacittā. Dhammaṃ paccavekkhantāti hiyyo tato paradivasesu vā sutadhammaṃ pati manasā avekkhantā. Bhikkhū āmantetvā dhamme desiyamāne ādito paṭṭhāya desanaṃ sallakkhetuṃ sakkotīti imamevatthaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “te anāmantetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Being near” means because of proximity. “Because of always being in the vicinity” means because of constant association. “As instructed” means in accordance with the instruction; that is, having accepted the instruction completely, without omission. “Certain bhikkhus” refers to those devoted to the teaching on the Dhamma of dependent origination. Previously, after it was shown by such statements as “the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies” why he addressed the bhikkhus, now, to show the purpose of teaching the Dhamma after addressing them, the objection is raised: “For what purpose then does the Blessed One...?” Here, “thinking of something else” means having minds directed elsewhere. “With scattered minds” means with unconcentrated minds. “Reflecting on the Dhamma” means mentally reviewing the Dhamma heard the previous day or on prior days. The words “Without addressing them,” etc., were said to show, by way of contrast, this very point: that when the bhikkhus are addressed and the Dhamma is taught, they are able to pay proper attention to the teaching from the beginning.

Bhikkhavoti ca sandhivasena i-kāralopo daṭṭhabbo “bhikkhavo itī”ti, ayañhi itisaddo hetuparisamāpanādipadatthavipariyāyapakārāvadhāraṇanidassanādianekatthapabhedo. Tathā hesa “ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘rūpa’nti vuccatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hetumhi dissati, “tasmātiha me, bhikkhave, dhammadāyādā bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) parisamāpane, “iti vā evarūpā visūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.13) ādiatthe “māgaṇḍiyoti tassa brāhmaṇassa saṅkhā samaññā paññatti [M 2.0005] vohāro nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanaṃ abhilāpo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 73, 75) padatthavipariyāye, “iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito. Saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.124) pakāre, “atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti ce vadeyya, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīya”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.96) avadhāraṇe, “sabbamatthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, sabbaṃ natthīti ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) nidassane[V 2.0005]. Idhāpi nidassane eva daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhavoti āmantanākāro tamesa iti-saddo nidasseti “bhikkhavoti āmantesī”ti. Iminā nayena bhaddantetiādīsupi yathārahaṃ itisaddassa attho veditabbo.

The elision of the i-vowel in “bhikkhavo'ti” should be understood as due to sandhi, from “bhikkhavo iti.” This particle “iti” has many different meanings, such as cause, conclusion, enumeration, paraphrase, manner, determination, and illustration. For instance, it is found in the sense of cause in: “It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called 'form'” (SN 22.79); in the sense of conclusion in: “Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things” (MN 3); in the sense of enumeration in: “...he abstains from visiting such shows, and so on” (DN 1); in the sense of paraphrase in: “ ‘Māgaṇḍiya’—this is the reckoning, designation, concept, term, convention, name, act of naming, appellation, expression, phrasing, and utterance for that brahmin” (Mnd 1.15); in the sense of manner in: “Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is beset by fear, the wise one is free from fear” (MN 129); in the sense of determination in: “ ‘Is there aging-and-death with this as condition?’—when asked thus, Ānanda, one should say, ‘There is’” (DN 15); and in the sense of illustration in: “ ‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, this is one extreme. ‘Nothing exists,’ this is the second extreme” (SN 12.15). Here too, it should be understood as illustration. The particle “iti” illustrates the form of address “bhikkhavo,” demonstrating that he addressed them, “Bhikkhus!” In this way, the meaning of the particle “iti” in cases such as “bhaddante'ti” should be understood as is appropriate.

Pubbe “bhagavā āmantesī”ti vuttattā bhagavato paccassosunti idha bhagavatoti sāmivacanaṃ āmantanameva sambandhīantaraṃ apekkhatīti iminā adhippāyena “bhagavato āmantanaṃ paṭiassosu”nti vuttaṃ. Bhagavatoti idaṃ pana paṭissavasambandhena sampadānavacanaṃ. Ettāvatā yaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitanti sambandho. Etthāha – kimatthaṃ pana dhammavinayasaṅgahe kariyamāne nidānavacanaṃ, nanu bhagavatā bhāsitavacanasseva saṅgaho kātabboti? Vuccate – desanāya ṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakanimittaparisāpadesehi upanibandhitvā ṭhapitā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā hoti asammosadhammā saddheyyā ca, desakālakattusotunimittehi upanibandho viya vohāravinicchayo. Teneva cāyasmatā mahākassapena “paṭiccasamuppādasuttaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā desādipucchāsu katāsu tāsaṃ vissajjanaṃ karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena “evaṃ me suta”nti āyasmatā ānandena imassa suttassa nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ.

Since it was said previously, “the Blessed One addressed,” and then “they responded to the Blessed One,” the genitive “bhagavato” (of the Blessed One) requires another related term, namely “address.” With this intention it was said, “they responded to the Blessed One's address.” This word “bhagavato,” however, is a dative in connection with the response. Thus far the connection is that the introduction, adorned with the specifications of time, place, speaker, assembly, and occasion, has been spoken. Here one might ask: When a collection of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being made, what is the purpose of the introductory statement? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One be collected? It is said: For the purpose of establishing the teaching's stability, freedom from confusion, and credibility. For a teaching that is established by being connected with the specifications of time, place, speaker, occasion, and assembly becomes long-lasting, a Dhamma free from confusion, and credible, just like a legal decision that is connected with the speaker, time, agent, listener, and occasion. For this very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked, “Friend Ānanda, where was the Discourse on Dependent Origination spoken?” and when questions about the place and other details were asked, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, in answering those questions, spoke the introduction to this discourse, beginning, “Thus have I heard.”

Apica satthu sampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubbaracanānumānāgamatakkābhāvato sammāsambuddhabhāvasiddhi. Na hi sammāsambuddhassa [M 2.0006] pubbaracanādīhi attho atthi, sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya ekappamāṇattā ca ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasatthusāvakānurodhābhāvato khīṇāsavattasiddhi. Na hi sabbaso khīṇāsavassa te sambhavantīti suvisuddhā cassa parānuggahappavatti, evaṃ desakasaṃkilesabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhisīlasampadādūsakānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ accantābhāvasaṃsūcakehi ñāṇasampadāpahānasampadābhibyañjanakehi ca saṃbuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi, tato eva ca antarāyikaniyyānikadhammesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo attahitaparahitapaṭipatti ca nidānavacanena pakāsitā hoti, tattha tattha sampattaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato, idha pana mūladvayavasena antadvayarahitassa tisandhikālabandhassa catubbidhanayasaṅkhepagambhīrabhāvayuttassa paṭiccasamuppādassa bodhiyā nidassanato cāti yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “satthu sampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Further, the introduction is spoken to proclaim the Teacher’s accomplishment. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the attainment of the state of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is established by the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, or reasoning. Indeed, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has no need for prior composition and the like, since his knowledge proceeds unimpeded in regard to everything and is of a single measure toward all knowable things. Likewise, the attainment of the state of one whose taints are destroyed is established by the absence of a “teacher's fist,” of stinginess regarding the Dhamma, and of the need to comply with a teacher or disciples. For such things do not arise at all in one whose taints are completely destroyed; thus his activity of benefiting others is perfectly pure. In this way, the first two kinds of confidence are established by the states of a Buddha that indicate the utter absence of ignorance and craving—which are defilements of the teacher and corrupt the accomplishment of view and virtue—and which manifest the accomplishment of knowledge and the accomplishment of relinquishment, revealing the pure state of a Buddha. Then, from the establishment of the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and liberating phenomena, the latter two kinds of confidence are established. Thus, the Blessed One’s possession of the fourfold confidence and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others are revealed through the introductory discourse, by its illuminating the teaching of the Dhamma with spontaneous eloquence suited to the occasion, according to the inclination of the assembly present. Here, however, it is to be connected with its being the introduction to the awakening to dependent origination—which is profound in its fourfold method, free from the two extremes by way of the two roots, and bound by the three periods of time. Therefore, it is said: “The introduction is spoken to proclaim the Teacher’s accomplishment.”

Tathā [V 2.0006] sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa hi bhagavato natthi niratthikā pavatti, attahitatthā vā, tasmā paresaṃ eva atthāya pavattasabbakiriyassa sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ yathāpavattaṃ vuccamānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsanaṃ, na kabbaracanā. Tayidaṃ satthucaritaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesehi saddhiṃ tattha tattha nidānavacanehi yathārahaṃ pakāsīyati, idha pana dvādasapadikapaccayākāravibhāvanena tena. Tena vuttaṃ “sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Likewise, the introductory statement is spoken to proclaim the accomplishment of the Dispensation. For the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by knowledge and compassion, there is no activity without purpose, nor for his own welfare. Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, all of whose activity proceeds only for the sake of others, are called the Dispensation when spoken of as they occurred—in the sense of an instruction for beings according to what is fitting, with respect to the benefit in this life, the benefit in future lives, and the ultimate benefit—and not as poetic composition. This conduct of the Teacher is appropriately revealed here and there through introductory statements, along with the specifications of time, place, speaker, and assembly. Here, however, it is revealed through the analysis of the twelve-linked causal process. Therefore, it is said: “The introductory statement is spoken to proclaim the accomplishment of the Dispensation.”

Apica satthu pamāṇabhāvappakāsanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ, tañcassa pamāṇabhāvadassanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena “bhagavā”ti ca iminā padena vibhāvitanti veditabbaṃ. “Bhagavā”ti ca iminā tathāgatassa rāgadosamohādi-sabbasaṃkilesamaladuccaritādidosappahānadīpanena vacanena anaññasādhāraṇasuparisuddhañāṇakaruṇādiguṇavisesayogaparidīpanena tato eva sabbasattuttamabhāvadīpanena ayamattho sabbathā pakāsito hotīti. Idamettha nidānavacane payojananidassanaṃ.

Further, the introductory statement is made to show that the Dispensation is the standard by proclaiming that the Teacher is the standard. And this showing that he is the standard should be understood as being clarified by the word “Bhagavā” in accordance with the method explained below. For by this word “Bhagavā”—which illuminates the Tathāgata's abandonment of all defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all stains of misconduct; which illuminates his possession of unique, supremely purified qualities such as knowledge and compassion; and thereby reveals his supreme status among all beings—this meaning is fully explained in every way. This is the demonstration of the purpose in this introductory statement.

Nikkhittassāti [M 2.0007] desitassa. Desanāpi hi desetabbassa sīlādiatthassa vineyyasantānesu nikkhipanato “nikkhepo”ti vuccatīti “suttanikkhepaṃ tāva vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hotī”ti sāmaññato bhagavato desanāya samuṭṭhānassa vibhāgaṃ dassetvā “etthāyaṃ desanā evaṃsamuṭṭhānā”ti desanāya samuṭṭhāne dassite suttassa sammadeva nidānaparijānanena vaṇṇanāya suviññeyyattā vuttaṃ. Tato heṭṭhā “kasmā bhagavatā paṭiccasamuppādavaseneva desanā āraddhā”ti kenaci codanāya katāya “parajjhāsayoyaṃ suttanikkhepo”ti parihāro sukathito hoti. Tattha yathā anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttantāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādipadhānanayena soḷasavidhataṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ attajjhāsayādisuttanikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvanti āha “cattāro hi suttanikkhepā”ti. Ettha ca yathā attajjhāsayassa aṭṭhuppattiyā ca parajjhāsayapucchāhi saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati “attajjhāsayo ca parajjhāsayo ca, attajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, attajjhāsayo ca parajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko cā”ti ajjhāsayapucchānusandhisambhavato, evaṃ yadipi aṭṭhuppattiyā ajjhāsayenapi saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati, attajjhāsayādīhi pana purato ṭhitehi aṭṭhuppattiyā saṃsaggo natthīti. Nayidha niravaseso vitthāranayo sambhavatīti “cattāro hi suttanikkhepā”ti [V 2.0007] vuttaṃ. Tadantogadhattā vā sambhavantānaṃ sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepavasena cattārova dassitā, tathādassanañcettha ayaṃ saṃsaggabhedo gahetabboti.

“Of what is laid down” means of what is taught. For teaching is also called “a laying down” because it lays down the meaning of virtue, etc., that is to be taught in the mental continuities of those to be trained. Thus, it is said: “First, having considered the laying down of the discourse, what is being spoken becomes clear.” Having shown in general the division of the origin of the Blessed One's teaching, when the origins of the teaching are shown by stating, “Here, this teaching has such an origin,” it is said that the exposition of the discourse becomes easy to understand through a correct understanding of its basis. Then, further on, when an objection is raised by someone, “Why did the Blessed One begin the teaching specifically by way of dependent origination?” the reply is well stated: “This laying down of a discourse is due to another's disposition.” Herein, just as the discourses, though of many hundreds and thousands of kinds, do not go beyond sixteen types according to the principal method concerning what is on the side of defilement, etc., so too, by way of the laying down of a discourse based on one's own disposition, etc., they are of four kinds. Thus he says: “For there are four ways of laying down a discourse.” And here, just as a combination is possible of one's own disposition with an occasion and with another's disposition and questions—since there is a possible connection of dispositions and questions, as in: “one's own disposition and another's disposition”; “one's own disposition and a question-based one”; “one's own disposition, another's disposition, and a question-based one”; “an occasion and another's disposition”; “an occasion and a question-based one”; “an occasion, another's disposition, and a question-based one”—so too, although a combination of an occasion with a disposition is possible, there is no combination of an occasion with one's own disposition, etc., when these are placed first. An exhaustive detailed method is not possible here; thus it is said: “For there are four ways of laying down a discourse.” Or, because the remaining possible ways of laying down are included within them, only four are shown as the root ways of laying down. And in showing them thus, this distinction of combinations should be understood.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – nikkhipīyatīti nikkhepo, suttaṃ eva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Atha vā nikkhipanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi kāraṇabhūtoti attajjhāsayo. Attano ajjhāsayo etassāti vā attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayepi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vasena pavattadhammo etassa atthīti, pucchāvasiko. Suttadesanāya vatthubhūtassa atthassa uppatti atthuppatti, atthuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppatti, sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Atha vā nikkhipīyati [M 2.0008] suttaṃ etenāti suttanikkhepo, attajjhāsayādi eva. Etasmiṃ pana atthavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo. Paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo. Pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitvā ñātabbo attho. Tassa pucchāvasena pavattaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasikaṃ, tadeva nikkhepasaddāpekkhāya pulliṅgavasena “pucchāvasiko”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā aṭṭhuppatti eva aṭṭhuppattikoti evampettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, this is the word-meaning: “It is laid down,” thus it is a laying down (nikkhepo); the discourse itself is the laying down, hence suttanikkhepo. Or, the act of laying down is a laying down; the laying down of the discourse is suttanikkhepo, meaning the teaching of the discourse. One's own disposition is attajjhāsayo. Because that exists for one as a cause, it is attajjhāsayo. Or, “one's own disposition” belongs to this, thus attajjhāsayo. This same method applies to another's disposition (parajjhāsayo). The Dhamma that proceeds by way of a question exists for this one, thus pucchāvasiko (question-based). The arising of a matter that is the basis for the teaching of a discourse is atthuppatti. Attha-uppatti is just aṭṭhuppatti. Because that exists for this one, it is aṭṭhuppattiko (occasion-based). Or, “the discourse is laid down by this,” thus suttanikkhepo, which is just one's own disposition, etc. In this alternative meaning, one's own disposition is attajjhāsayo. The disposition of others is parajjhāsayo. “It is asked,” thus it is a question (pucchā); the meaning to be known after asking. The statement of those who receive the Dhamma that proceeds by way of a question is pucchāvasikaṃ; this very word, with reference to the word nikkhepa, is stated in the masculine gender as pucchāvasiko. Similarly, aṭṭhuppatti itself is aṭṭhuppattiko. Thus the meaning here should be understood.

Apicettha paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇanirapekkhattā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ suttanikkhepabhāvo yutto kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva dhammatantiṭhapanatthaṃ pavattitadesanattā. Parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ desanāpavattihetubhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattitānaṃ kathaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ anavarodho, pucchāvasikaaṭṭhuppattikānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattitānaṃ kathaṃ parajjhāsaye anavarodhoti? Na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinimuttasseva suttadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattibhāvena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi brahmajāladhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇaāmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ “aṭṭhuppattī”ti vuccati. Paresaṃ pucchaṃ vinā ajjhāsayaṃ eva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasena eva desito pucchāvasikoti pākaṭovāyamatthoti. Attano ajjhāsayeneva katheti dhammatantiṭhapanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dasabalasuttantahārakoti dasabalavagge anupubbena nikkhittānaṃ suttānaṃ āvali, tathā candopamahārakādayo.

Moreover, herein, since one's own disposition is independent of such causes as the maturation of others' faculties, it is proper for it to be a separate way of laying down a discourse, because the teaching is delivered solely out of one's own disposition for the purpose of establishing the tradition of the Dhamma. But in the case of [discourses] based on another's disposition and those based on questions, which proceed when the dispositions and questions of others have arisen as the cause for the teaching to be delivered, how are they not included under 'occasion'? Or in the case of [discourses] that are question-based and occasion-based, which proceed in accordance with another's disposition, how are they not included under 'another's disposition'? This should not be objected to. For the arising of a reason for teaching a discourse is taken as being an 'occasion' only when it is free from the prompting, questioning, etc., of others; hence the separate treatment of those [discourses] due to another's disposition and those that are question-based. Thus, the occasion for the teaching of the Brahmajāla Sutta, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, etc.—the arising of praise and blame, material gain, etc.—is called an 'occasion.' A [discourse] taught taking only the disposition of others as the occasion, without a question, is [one based on] another's disposition. One taught only by way of a question is question-based. This meaning is clear. It should be seen that one speaks solely out of one's own disposition for the purpose of establishing the tradition of the Dhamma. 'The synopsis of the Dasabala Suttanta' is the series of suttas laid down in sequence in the Dasabala Vagga; similarly the Candopama and other synopses.

Vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā saddhindriyādayo. Ajjhāsayanti adhimuttiṃ. Khantinti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiṃ. Mananti cittaṃ. Abhinīhāranti paṇidhānaṃ. Bujjhanabhāvanti bujjhanasabhāvaṃ, paṭivijjhanākāraṃ vā.

The dhammas that ripen liberation are the faculties beginning with faith. Ajjhāsaya means resolve. Khanti means the acceptance through scrutinizing a view. Mana means mind. Abhinīhāra means aspiration. Bujjhanabhāva means the nature of understanding, or the mode of penetration.

Ugghaṭitaññūti [V 2.0008] ugghaṭanaṃ nāma ñāṇugghaṭanaṃ, ñāṇena ugghaṭitamatte eva dhammaṃ jānātīti attho. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Uddesādīhi netabboti neyyo. Byañjanapadaṃ paramaṃ assāti padaparamo. Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāradhammassa uddese udāhaṭamatte eva. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamāyogo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena saṃkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ [M 2.0009] pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo “ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ saṃkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho puggalo “vipañcitaññū”ti vuccati. Uddesatoti uddesahetu, uddisantassa uddisāpentassa vāti attho, “uddisato”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Paripucchatoti paripucchantassa. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti anukkamena arahattappatti hoti. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti tena attabhāvena maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā antamaso jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ puggalo byañjanapadameva paramaṃ katvā ṭhitattā “padaparamo”ti vuccati.

One of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū): the unfolding is the unfolding of knowledge; the meaning is that one understands the Dhamma as soon as it is unfolded by knowledge. One of extensive understanding (vipañcitaññū) is one who understands the meaning only when it is elaborated. One who is to be led by summaries, etc., is a person to be guided (neyyo). One for whom the letter and the word are the highest is a padaparama. "At the very time of utterance" means as soon as the summary of the uttered Dhamma has been uttered. Breakthrough to the Dhamma (dhammābhisamayo) is the full comprehension together with knowledge of the Dhamma of the Four Truths. This is said: a person who is capable of grasping arahantship by directing their knowledge in accordance with a teaching being laid down by way of a concise summary, in the manner of "the four establishments of mindfulness," etc., is called an ugghaṭitaññū. This is said: a person who is capable of reaching arahantship when the meaning is being analyzed in detail after a concise summary has been laid down, is called a vipañcitaññū. "Because of the summary" means because of the summary, whether of one who recites or of one who causes recitation; this is the meaning. The reading uddisato also has this same meaning. "Of one who questions thoroughly" means of one who questions thoroughly. "There is a gradual breakthrough to the Dhamma" means there is a gradual attainment of arahantship. "There is no breakthrough to the Dhamma in that life" means that with that personal existence one is not able to produce the path or the fruit, or even jhāna or insight. This is said: this person, because they stand having made the letter and the word the highest, is called a padaparama.

Ekacarāti vivekābhiratiyā ekavihārino. Dvicarāti dve ekajjhāsayā hutvā ñāṇacariyādivasena vicarantā. Esa nayo sesesu. Sattasuññatāpakāsanena suññataṃ. Tato eva saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ. “Paresaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā idaṃ suttaṃ ārabhī”ti vatvā te pana “pare”ti vuttapuggalā aparikammikā suparisodhitapubbabhāgapaṭipadā cāti duvidhā, tadubhayesu satthu paṭipattiṃ upamāmukhena pakāsento yathā hītiādimāha. Rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti likhanavasena na uppādeti. Akatābhinivesanti vipassanābhāvanāya akatānuyogaṃ. Sīla…pe… sampadāyāti asamādinnasīlaṃ sīlasampadāya, suparisuddhasīlaṃ samādhisampadāya, anujukatadiṭṭhijukammaṃ diṭṭhisampadāya yojentoti yojanā.

"Ekacarā" means those who dwell alone, delighting in seclusion. "Dvicarā" means two who, having a single disposition, wander by way of the practice of knowledge, etc. This method applies to the rest. By the exposition of the emptiness of beings, emptiness. From that itself, it is gentle and subtle. Having said, "The Blessed One began this discourse by way of the disposition of others," those persons called "others" are of two kinds: those without preliminary preparation and those whose preliminary course of practice has been thoroughly purified. To show the Teacher's practice towards both by way of a simile, he said, "Just as...," etc. "He does not produce a form" means he does not produce it by way of drawing. "Akatābhinivesaṃ" means not having undertaken the development of insight. "Virtue... accomplishment" means: the connection is that one applies unundertaken virtue to the accomplishment in virtue, thoroughly purified virtue to the accomplishment in concentration, and the straightening of one's view to the accomplishment in view.

Yanti yaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ sandhāya. Sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Diṭṭhi cāti kammassakatādiṭṭhi ceva kammapathasammādiṭṭhi ca. Tividhenāti ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā ajjhattabahiddhāti evaṃ visayabhāvato tippakārena. Yathāvuttadiṭṭhivisuddhiyā visesapaccayaṃ sīlaṃyeva bhāvanāya adhiṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāyā”ti.

"Yaṃ" refers to the preliminary course of practice. "Sīlaṃ" means the fourfold purification virtue. "Diṭṭhi ca" means both the view of the ownership of kamma and the right view of the paths of kamma. "Tividhena" means in three ways, because of being an objective domain in this way: internally, externally, and both internally and externally. Virtue itself is the special condition for the aforesaid purification of view and the basis for development; thus it is said: "Relying on virtue, established in virtue."

Sudhantasuvaṇṇaṃ apagatasabbakāḷakaṃ. Caturassādidhoto suparimajjitamaṇikkhandho. Paccayadhammānaṃ avijjādīnaṃ tassa tassa paccayuppannassa hetupaccayādibhāvo paccayākāro. So pana atthato [M 2.0010] avijjā evāti [V 2.0009] āha “paṭiccasamuppādanti paccayākāra”nti. Tenāha “paccayākāro hī”tiādi.

Well-smelted gold from which all dross has been removed. A block of gem, washed and well-polished on its four sides, etc. The mode of conditionality is the state of being a root-condition, etc., for each dependently arisen phenomenon on the part of the conditioning phenomena, ignorance, etc. But since this, in meaning, is just ignorance, he said: "Dependent origination is the mode of conditionality." For that reason he said, "For the mode of conditionality...," etc.

Kāmaṃ vo-saddo padaparaṭṭhito paṭiyogīatthavisesavācako, nāmaparabhūto pana taṃ taṃ kattukammakaraṇādisādhanavisiṭṭhameva pabodheti, hi-nipātaparabhūto pana vacanālaṅkāramattamevāti āha “voti…pe… dissatī”ti. Taṃdesananti tassa paṭiccasamuppādassa desanaṃ. Sā hi idha ta-saddena paccāmasīyati. “Suṇāthā”ti sotaviññeyyatāvacanato na kevalaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo.

The word 'vo', when placed after a word, expresses a specific meaning as a correlative; but when it follows a noun, it indicates something specified by this or that means of accomplishment, such as agent, object, or instrument. And when it follows the particle 'hi', it is a mere embellishment of speech. Thus it is said: 'vo...pe... is seen.' 'Taṃdesanaṃ' means the teaching of that dependent origination. For here, that teaching is referred to by the word 'ta'. Because the word 'Listen' refers to what is cognizable by the ear, it is not only dependent origination that is meant.

Ekatthametaṃ padaṃ ka-saddena padavaḍḍhanamattassa katattā, tasmā sādhusaddassa kato atthuddhāro sādhukasaddassapi kato eva hotīti adhippāyo. Sādhu bhanteti yācāmahaṃ bhanteti ayamettha atthoti āha “āyācane”ti. Puna sādhu bhanteti evaṃ bhanteti ayamettha atthoti āha “sampaṭicchane”ti. Sādhu sādhūti aho ahoti ayamettha atthoti vuttaṃ “sampahaṃsane”ti. Sādhu dhammarucīti puññakāmo sundaroti attho. Paññāṇavāti paññavā. Addubbhoti adūsako. Daḷhīkammeti thirīkaraṇe sakkaccakiriyāyaṃ. Āṇattiyanti āṇāpane. “Suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti hi vutte sādhukasaddena savanamanasikārānaṃ sakkaccakiriyā viya tadāṇāpanampi vuttaṃ hoti. Āyācanatthatā viya cassa āṇāpanatthatā veditabbā.

This word has the same meaning, since the suffix 'ka' is added merely to lengthen the word. Therefore, the extraction of meaning made for the word 'sādhu' is also made for the word 'sādhuka'; this is the intention. When one says, 'Sādhu, bhante,' the meaning here is 'I request, bhante'; thus he says 'in the sense of requesting.' Again, when one says, 'Sādhu, bhante,' the meaning here is 'So be it, bhante'; thus he says 'in the sense of accepting.' 'Sādhu, sādhu' means 'Excellent! Excellent!'; this is the meaning stated as 'in the sense of rejoicing.' 'Sādhu dhammarucī' means 'one who desires merit, who is good.' 'Paññāṇavā' means 'wise.' 'Addubbho' means 'harmless.' 'Daḷhīkamme' means 'in strengthening,' 'in acting carefully.' 'Āṇattiyaṃ' means 'in commanding.' For when it is said, 'Listen carefully, attend closely,' the word 'sādhukaṃ' expresses the careful performance of listening and attending, as well as the command to do so. And its meaning of commanding should be understood just like its meaning of requesting.

Idānettha evaṃ yojanā veditabbāti sambandho. Sotindriyavikkhepanivāraṇaṃ savane niyojanavasena kiriyantarapaṭisedhanabhāvato, sotaṃ odahathāti hi attho. Manindriyavikkhepanivāraṇaṃ aññacintāpaṭisedhanato. Purimanti “suṇāthā”ti padaṃ. Etthāti “suṇātha, manasi karothā”ti padadvaye, etasmiṃ vā adhikāre. Byañjanavipallāsaggāhanivāraṇaṃ sotadvāre vikkhepapaṭibāhakattā. Na hi yāthāvato suṇantassa saddato vipallāsaggāho hoti. Atthavipallāsaggāhanivāraṇaṃ manindriyavikkhepapaṭibāhakattā. Na hi sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ upadhārentassa atthavipallāsaggāho hoti. Dhammassavane niyojeti “suṇāthā”ti vidahanato. Dhāraṇūpaparikkhāsūti ettha upaparikkhaggahaṇeneva tulanatīraṇādike diṭṭhiyā ca suppaṭivedhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sabyañjanoti ettha yathādhippetamatthaṃ byañjayatīti byañjanaṃ, sabhāvanirutti. Saha byañjanehīti [M 2.0011] sabyañjano, byañjanasampannoti attho. Araṇīyato upagantabbato attho, catupārisuddhisīlādiko. Saha atthenāti sāttho, atthasampannoti attho. Dhammagambhīrotiādīsu dhammo nāma tanti. Desanā nāma tassā manasā vavatthapitāya tantiyā desanā kathanaṃ. Attho nāma [V 2.0010] tantiyā attho. Paṭivedho nāma tantiyā tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Yasmā cete dhammadesanāatthapaṭivedhā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāḷhā alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca, tasmā gambhīrā. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmā ayaṃ dhammo…pe… sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti.

Now, the construction here should be understood thus—this is the connection. The prevention of the distraction of the ear-faculty is due to its engagement in listening, which consists in the preclusion of other activities; for the meaning is 'give ear.' The prevention of the distraction of the mind-faculty is due to the preclusion of other thoughts. The former is the word 'Listen.' 'Here' means in these two words, 'Listen, attend closely,' or in this section. The prevention of grasping the letter with distortion is because the ear-door obstructs distraction. For one who listens correctly does not grasp the sound with distortion. The prevention of grasping the meaning with distortion is because the mind-faculty obstructs distraction. For one who carefully considers the Dhamma does not grasp the meaning with distortion. He engages one in listening to the Dhamma by the injunction 'Listen.' In 'retention and examination,' by the taking up of 'examination' one includes comparison, judgment, and the like, as well as the thorough penetration of the view. In 'with its phrasing,' 'phrasing' (byañjana) is what expresses the intended meaning; it is a natural expression. 'Together with its phrasing' means endowed with phrasing; this is the meaning. The meaning derives from its being faultless and approachable, referring to the fourfold purification virtue and so on. 'Together with its meaning' means endowed with meaning; this is the meaning. In 'profound in Dhamma,' etc., 'Dhamma' means the textual framework. 'Teaching' means the exposition of that mentally determined textual framework. 'Meaning' means the meaning of the textual framework. 'Penetration' means the true understanding of both the textual framework and its meaning. Because these—the teaching of the Dhamma, its meaning, and its penetration—are for those of dull wisdom like the great ocean with its sharks and so on, hard to fathom and with no footing to be found, they are therefore profound. Hence it is said: 'Because this Dhamma is... attend to it carefully.'

Ettha ca paṭivedhassa dukkarabhāvato dhammatthānaṃ desanāñāṇassa dukkarabhāvato desanāya dukkhogāhatā, paṭivedhassa pana uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā tabbisayañāṇuppattiyā ca dukkarabhāvato dukkhogāhatā veditabbā. Desanaṃ nāma uddisanaṃ saṅkhepadassanasadisaṃ. Tathā hi vibhaṅgasutte “desessāmī”ti vatvā puna “bhāsissāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassa niddisanaṃ bhāsananti idhādhippetanti āha “vitthāratopi naṃ bhāsissāmīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Paribyattaṃ kathanaṃ vā bhāsanaṃ.

And here, the teaching is hard to fathom because penetration is difficult and because the knowledge for teaching the meanings of the Dhamma is difficult. Furthermore, its being hard to fathom should be understood as due to the impossibility of producing penetration and the difficulty of the arising of knowledge concerning its domain. 'Teaching' (desanā) means a statement of headings, similar to a concise exposition. For so in the Vibhaṅga Sutta, having said 'I will teach,' it is then said 'I will speak.' The detailed explanation of that is 'speaking'; this is what is intended here. Thus he says: 'It is said, "I will speak of it in detail."' Or 'speaking' is a clear statement.

Sāḷikāyiva nigghosoti sāḷikāya ālāpo viya madhuro kaṇṇasukho pemanīyo. Paṭibhānaṃ saddo. Udīrayīti uccārīyati, vuccatīti attho. Evaṃ vutte ussāhajātāti evaṃ “suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti vutte “na kira satthā saṅkhepeneva desessati, vitthārenapi bhāsissatī”ti sañjātussāhā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā.

'A voice like a myna bird's' means like the call of a myna bird: sweet, pleasant to the ear, and lovely. Eloquence is the sound. 'He uttered' means it is uttered, it is spoken; this is the meaning. 'When this was said, they became enthusiastic' means: when it was said, 'Listen carefully, attend closely, I will speak,' they became enthusiastic, joyful, and glad, thinking: 'It seems the Teacher will not teach only in brief but will also speak in detail.'

Katamoti tassa padassa sāmaññato pucchābhāvo ñāyati, na visesatoti tassa pucchāvisesabhāvaṃ kathento “kathetukamyatāpucchā”ti vatvā teneva pasaṅgena mahāniddese āgatā sabbāpi pucchā atthuddhāranayena dasseti “pañcavidhā hi pucchā”tiādinā. Tattha adiṭṭhaṃ joteti etāyāti adiṭṭhajotanā. Diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandīyati etāyāti diṭṭhasaṃsandanā. Saṃsandanañcettha sākacchāvasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ. Vimatiṃ chindati etāyāti vimaticchedanā. Anumatiyā pucchanaṃ anumatipucchā. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave”tiādipucchāya hi “kā tumhākaṃ anumatī”ti anumati pucchitā hoti. Kathetukamyatā kathetukamyatāya.

Regarding the word 'Which?': that it is a question is known in general, but not in particular. Therefore, explaining its nature as a specific kind of question, he says it is 'a question out of a desire to speak.' And in that connection, by the method of extracting the meaning, he shows all the questions that occur in the Mahāniddesa, beginning with: 'For there are five kinds of questions.' Therein, 'that by which one illuminates the unseen' is a question illuminating the unseen. 'That by which one compares the seen' is a question comparing the seen. And here comparing means making a decision by way of discussion. 'That by which one cuts off doubt' is a question cutting off doubt. A question for approval is a question of approval. For by a question such as 'What do you think, monks?' approval is asked, as in 'What is your approval?' A question out of a desire to speak is so called because of a desire to speak.

Lakkhaṇanti [M 2.0012] ñātuṃ pucchito yo koci sabhāvo. Aññātanti yena kenaci ñāṇena aññātabhāvamāha. Adiṭṭhanti dassanabhūtena ñāṇena cakkhunā viya na diṭṭhataṃ. Atulitanti “ettakaṃ ida”nti tulanabhūtena ñāṇena na tulitataṃ. Atīritanti tīraṇabhūtena ñāṇena akatañāṇakiriyāsamāpanataṃ. Avibhūtanti ñāṇassa apākaṭabhāvaṃ. Avibhāvitanti ñāṇena apākaṭīkatabhāvaṃ.

'Characteristic' means any nature about which one asks in order to know. 'Unknown' refers to the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge. 'Unseen' means not being seen by the knowledge that is vision, like the eye. 'Unweighed' means not being weighed by the knowledge that is weighing, as in 'it is this much.' 'Unjudged' means the non-completion of the act of knowing by the knowledge that is judgment. 'Unmanifest' means the state of being unmanifest to knowledge. 'Unclarified' means the state of not having been made clear by knowledge.

Pañcasu [V 2.0011] pucchāsu yā buddhānaṃ sabbato na santi, tā dassetvā idhādhippetapucchaṃ nigametuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. Yadi paṭiccasamuppādo paccayākāro, atha kasmā bhagavatā paṭiccasamuppādadesanāya saṅkhārādayo paccayuppannā kathitāti āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Paccayuppannampi katheti paccayuppannadassanena paccayadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvassa kathitabhāvato. Āhāravaggassātiādi “paccayākāro paṭiccasamuppādo”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sambhavantī”ti pāḷiyaṃ parato vuttaṃ kiriyāpadaṃ ānetvā yojeti, aññathā saṅkhārā kiṃ katāti vā karontīti vā na ñāyeyya. Pavattiyā anulomato “avijjāpaccayā”tiādikā anulomapaṭiccasamuppādakathā.

Having shown which of the five kinds of questions are in no way applicable to the Buddhas, the passage beginning 'Therein' was stated in order to conclude with the question intended here. That is easy to understand. If dependent origination is the mode of conditionality, then why in his teaching on dependent origination did the Blessed One speak of formations and so on, which are dependently arisen? To this he says, 'And here,' etc. He also speaks of the dependently arisen because by showing the dependently arisen, the fact that the conditioning phenomena are conditions is stated. The section on nutriment and so on was stated to show that 'dependent origination is the mode of conditionality.' He brings in the verb 'arise' (sambhavanti), which is stated later in the Pāli text, and construes it here; otherwise it would not be known what the formations have done or are doing. The exposition of dependent origination in forward order, 'with ignorance as condition,' etc., is in accordance with the process of occurrence.

“Avijjāya tvevā”tiādikā pana tassa vilomato paṭilomakathā. Accantameva saṅkhāre virajjati etenāti virāgo, maggo. Asesanirodhāti asesetvā nirodhā samucchindanā. Evaṃ nirodhānanti evaṃ anuppādanirodhena niruddhānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhā. Iti avijjādīnaṃ nirodhavacanena arahattaṃ vadati. Sakalassāti anavasesassa. Sattavirahitassāti paraparikappitajīvarahitassa. Vinivattetvāti anuppādanirodhadassanavasena viparivattetvā.

But the passage beginning 'From the utter fading away and cessation of ignorance...' is the exposition in reverse order. 'Dispassion' (virāgo) is that by which one becomes utterly dispassionate towards formations; it is the path. 'Cessation without remainder' means cessation without anything left over, an extirpation. 'From the cessation' means from the cessation of formations that have ceased by way of cessation through non-arising. Thus, by speaking of the cessation of ignorance and so on, he speaks of arahantship. 'Of the whole' means without remainder. 'Devoid of a being' means devoid of a soul imagined by others. 'Having turned back' means having turned around by way of seeing cessation through non-arising.

Attamanāti pītisomanassena gahitacittā. Tathābhūtā ca haṭṭhacittā nāma hontīti āha “tuṭṭhacittā”ti. “Tassa vacanaṃ abhinanditabba”nti ettha abhinandanasaddo anumodanattho. “Abhinanditvā”ti ettha sampaṭicchanattho. Idha pana ubhayatthopi vaṭṭatīti āha “anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu cā”ti.

'Pleased' means with minds seized by rapture and mental joy. And those who are so are called 'joyful-minded,' hence he says 'with gladdened minds.' In 'his word is to be rejoiced in,' the word 'rejoicing' has the sense of appreciating. In 'having rejoiced,' it has the sense of accepting. But here it is valid in both senses, thus he says: 'they both appreciated and accepted.'

Paṭiccasamuppādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta is concluded.

2. Vibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta

2. Dutiyepīti [M 2.0013] dutiyasuttepi. Pi-saddena tadaññesu suttesupīti attho. “Visuddhimagge vuttā evā”ti vatvāpi tadekadesaṃ idha viniyogakkhamaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti mūlaṃ. Vitthāradesananti “vibhajissāmī”ti padassa atthassa dassanavasena pavattaṃ vibhaṅgadesanaṃ. Uddesadesanā paṭhamasutte anulomadesanāsadisāva. Puna vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ dassentoti “iti kho, bhikkhave”tiādinā pavattiṃ nivattiñca dassento. Paṭhamaṃ uddesavasena vibhajanavasena vivaṭṭaṃ dassitaṃ, tato eva byatirekanayena vivaṭṭampi dassitameva hotīti punaggahaṇaṃ.

2. In the second as well: this means in the second sutta. By the word 'pi' (also), the meaning is 'in other suttas as well.' Although it was said, 'It is just as stated in the Visuddhimagga,' the passage beginning 'Just as...' was stated to show a portion of that suitable for application here. The canon (tanti) is the root text (mūlaṃ). The detailed exposition is the analytical exposition that proceeds by way of showing the meaning of the phrase, 'I will analyze.' The summary exposition is just like the direct exposition in the first sutta. Again, showing the round and its unwinding: this means showing occurrence and cessation with the passage beginning, 'Thus, bhikkhus....' First, the unwinding is shown by way of summary and analysis; then, by the negative method, the unwinding is also shown. Hence the repetition.

Tesaṃ [V 2.0012] tesaṃ sattānanti idaṃ kiñci pakārato anāmasitvā sabbepi satte sāmaññato byāpetvā gahaṇanti āha “saṅkhepato…pe… niddeso”ti. Gatijātivasenāti pañcagativasena, tatthāpi ekekāya gatiyā khattiyādibhummadevādihatthiādijātivasena ca. “Cittaṃ mano”tiādīsu viya kiccavisesaṃ, “mānasa”ntiādīsu viya samāne atthe saddavisesaṃ, “paṇḍara”ntiādīsu viya guṇavisesaṃ, “cetasikaṃ hadaya”ntiādīsu viya nissayavisesaṃ, “cittassa ṭhitī”tiādīsu viya aññassa avatthābhāvavisesaṃ, “alubbhanā”tiādīsu viya aññassa kiriyābhāvavisesaṃ, “alubbhitatta”ntiādīsu viya aññassa abhāvatāvisesanti evamādikaṃ anapekkhitvā dhammamattaṃ vā dīpanā sabhāvaniddeso. Jiṇṇassa jīraṇavasena pavattanākāro jīraṇatāti āha “ākāraniddeso”ti.

'Of those various beings'—this refers to grasping all beings in general without specifying any particular manner, as stated: 'In brief... the exposition.' 'By way of destiny and birth' means through the five destinies, and within each destiny, by birth as khattiyas, earth-deities, elephants, etc. Without regard for such distinctions as: a specific function, as in 'mind, thought'; a specific word with the same meaning, as in 'mental'; a specific quality, as in 'white'; a specific support, as in 'mental, heart'; a specific state of another, as in 'the stability of mind'; a specific state of action of another, as in 'non-greed'; or a specific state of non-existence of another, as in 'the state of non-greed'—the explanation of the mere phenomenon is the 'exposition of intrinsic nature.' The mode of occurrence by way of the aging of what has aged is 'aging'; thus, this is called the 'exposition of mode.'

Kālātikkame kiccaniddesāti kalalakālato pabhuti purimarūpānaṃ jarāpattakkhaṇe uppajjamānāni pacchimarūpāni paripakkarūpānurūpāni pariṇatapariṇatāni uppajjantīti anukkamena supariṇatarūpānaṃ paripākakāle uppajjamānāni khaṇḍiccādisabhāvāni uppajjantīti “khaṇḍicca”ntiādayo kālātikkame jarāya kiccaniddesā. Pakatiniddesāti phalavipaccanapakatiyā niddesā, jarāya vā pāpuṇitabbaphalameva pakati, tassā niddesā, na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarāti udakādigatamaggesu tiṇarukkhasaṃbhaggatādayo viya paripākagatamaggasaṅkhātesu paripuṇṇarūpesu labbhamānā khaṇḍiccādayo jarāya gatamaggāicceva veditabbā, na jarāti.

The exposition of function in the passing of time: From the time of the embryo onward, when earlier material forms reach the moment of aging, later material forms arise in conformity with the ripened material forms, successively transformed. In due course, at the time of the ripening of well-matured material forms, states such as brokenness of teeth arise. Thus 'brokenness of teeth,' etc., are expositions of the function of aging in the passing of time. The exposition of nature is the exposition of the nature of the ripening of fruit; or, nature is simply the fruit to be attained by aging, and this is its exposition. Brokenness of teeth and so on are not aging itself. Just as the breaking up of grass and trees is found on paths gone over by water, so brokenness of teeth and so on, found in fully perfected material forms—which are reckoned as paths gone over by ripening—should be understood only as paths gone over by aging, not as aging itself.

Yasmā [M 2.0014] jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, indriyāni jajjarāni hontīti āyuhānādayo pakatiniddesā, tasmā vuttaṃ “pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā”ti. Tenāha “imehi panā”tiādi.

Because for one who has reached old age the life span diminishes and the faculties become decrepit, 'decline of the life span' and so on are expositions of nature. Therefore it was said: 'The last two are expositions of nature.' For that reason he said: 'But by these...' and so on.

Aviññāyamānantarattā avīcijarā maṇiādīsu mandadasakādīsu ekekadasakesu ca khaṇe khaṇe jiṇṇavikārādīnaṃ duviññeyyattā. Tato aññesūti maṇiādito aññesu ahicchattakādīsu, pāṇīnaṃ ekabhavapariyāpanne sakalaāyusmiṃ gahitataruṇayuvājarākālesu, ekadvittidivasātikkamesu pupphādīsu vāti attho. Tattha hi jarāvisesassa suviññeyyattā savīcijarā nāma.

Aging is without interval (avīcijarā) because its uninterruptedness is not discerned, and because in things like gems, and in each of the dull decades and so on, the decay and alteration from moment to moment is difficult to discern. 'In others than those' means: in things other than gems, such as mushrooms; or in living beings whose entire life span is comprised in a single existence, during the periods taken as youth, adulthood, and old age; or in flowers and so on after one, two, or three days have passed. This is the meaning. For in these cases, because the specific nature of aging is easy to discern, it is called 'aging with interval' (savīcijarā).

Cavanakavasenāti cavanakānaṃ khandhānaṃ vasena. Ekacatupañcakkhandhāya cutiyā cavanameva cavanatāti āha “bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassana”nti, pāḷiyaṃ “cutī”ti vuttassa maraṇassa sabhāvadassananti [V 2.0013] attho. Bhaṅguppatti bhijjamānatā. Tena “bhedo”ti iminā khandhānaṃ bhijjamānatā bhedasamaṅgitā vuttāti dasseti. Ṭhānābhāvaparidīpananti kenacipi ākārena avaṭṭhānābhāvadīpanaṃ. Ghaṭassevāti hi visadisūdāharaṇaṃ. Yathā ghaṭe bhinne kapālādiavayavaseso labbhati, na evaṃ cutikkhandhesu bhaṅgesu, na koci viseso tiṭṭhatīti dassetuṃ “antaradhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇanti maccusaññitaṃ maraṇaṃ. “Kālamaraṇa”nti vadanti. Santānassa accantasamucchedabhūtaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ maraṇaṃ samucchedamaraṇaṃ. Ādi-saddena khaṇikamaraṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa kiriyāti antakassa kiriyā, yā loke vuccati “maccū”ti, maraṇanti attho. Cavanakālo eva vā anatikkamanīyattā visesena kāloti vuttoti tassa kiriyā atthato cutikkhandhānaṃ bhedapavattiyeva. “Maccu maraṇa”nti vā ettha samāsaṃ akatvā yo “maccū”ti vuccati bhedo, tameva maraṇaṃ “pāṇacāgo”ti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'By way of what is ceasing' means by way of the aggregates that are ceasing. For the ceasing that has one, four, or five aggregates, ceasing itself is the act of ceasing. Thus it is said: 'the indication of the characteristic by a word expressing a state.' The meaning is the showing of the intrinsic nature of the death that is called 'ceasing' in the Pāli text. The arising of breaking is the state of being broken. Thereby he shows that by this word 'breaking,' the state of the aggregates' being broken, their being endowed with breaking, is stated. 'Illumination of the absence of standing' means the illumination of the absence of remaining in any way. 'Like a pot' is a dissimilar example. For just as when a pot is broken a remainder of parts such as shards is found, it is not so when the ceasing aggregates break up. To show that no part remains, the word 'disappearance' was used. 'Death reckoned as maccu' means death designated as maccu. They call it 'timely death.' The death of the destroyers of cankers, which is the utter cutting off of the continuity, is 'death by cutting off.' By the word 'etc.,' momentary death is included. 'Its action' means the action of the Ender, which is called 'maccu' in the world; the meaning is death. Or, the time of ceasing itself, because it is unavoidable, is especially called 'time'; thus its action is, in meaning, just the occurrence of the breaking of the ceasing aggregates. Or, in 'maccu, death,' without making a compound, the breaking that is called 'maccu' is itself death, that is, 'the abandoning of life'; thus the meaning should be understood here.

Catuvokāravasenāti catuvokārabhavavasena. Tattha hi rūpakāyasaññito kaḷevaro natthi, yaṃ nikkhipeyya. Kiñcāpi ekavokārabhavepi kaḷevaranikkhepo natthi, rūpakāyassa pana tattha atthitāmattaṃ gahetvā “ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo”ti vutto. Catuvokāravasena cāti ca-saddena “sesadvayavasena khandhānaṃ bhedo”ti imamatthaṃ dasseti sabbattheva khandhabhedasabbhāvato. Sesadvayavasenāti [M 2.0015] sesabhavadvayavaseneva kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Yadipi ekavokārabhave rūpakāyo vijjati, kaḷevaranikkhepo pana natthīti “kaḷevarassa sabbhāvato”icceva vuttaṃ. Yasmā manussādīsu kaḷevaranikkhepo atthi, tasmā manussādīsu kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti yojanā. Kaḷevaraṃ nikkhipīyati etenāti maraṇaṃ kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Ekato katvāti ekajjhaṃ katvā, ekajjhaṃ gahaṇamattena.

'By way of the four-constituent' means by way of the four-constituent existence. For there, there is no corpse designated as a material body that one could lay down. Although in the one-constituent existence too there is no laying down of a corpse, yet taking just the mere existence of a material body there, it is said: 'the laying down of the corpse by way of the one-constituent existence.' 'And by way of the four-constituent existence': by the word 'and' he shows this meaning: 'the breaking up of the aggregates by way of the remaining two,' because the breaking up of the aggregates exists in all cases. 'By way of the remaining two' means the laying down of the corpse is only by way of the remaining two kinds of existence. Although in the one-constituent existence a material body is found, there is no laying down of a corpse; thus it was said, 'because of the existence of a corpse.' Because among humans and so on there is the laying down of a corpse, therefore the connection is: 'the laying down of the corpse among humans and so on.' A corpse is laid down by means of this; thus death is 'the laying down of the corpse.' 'Having made one' means having made into one, by the mere act of grasping as one.

Jāyanaṭṭhenātiādi āyatanavasena yonivasena ca dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā pariyādiyitvā jātiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “kattubhāvavasena padadvayaṃ vutta”nti vadanti. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ jāti sañjātī”ti pana kattari sāminiddesassa katattā ubhayatthāpi bhāvaniddeso. Sampuṇṇā jāti sañjāti. Pākaṭā nibbatti abhinibbatti. Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ…pe… abhinibbattīti sattavasena pavattattā vohāradesanā.

The passage beginning 'In the sense of being born' was stated to show birth by repeatedly encompassing all beings with the two terms, by way of the sense bases and by way of the womb. Some, however, say that the two terms are stated by way of the state of being an agent. But since in 'the birth, arising of those various beings,' the agent is indicated in the possessive case, in both places it is an exposition of a state. Complete birth is arising. Manifest production is complete production. 'Of those various beings... complete production': because this proceeds by way of beings, it is a conventional exposition.

Tatra tatrāti ekacatuvokārabhavesu dvinnaṃ sesarūpadhātuyaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjamānānaṃ pañcannaṃ, kāmadhātuyaṃ vikalāvikalindriyānaṃ vasena sattannaṃ navannaṃ dasannaṃ puna dasannaṃ ekādasannañca [V 2.0014] āyatanānaṃ vasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Santatiyanti yena kammunā khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo, tena abhisaṅkhatasantatiyaṃ. Tañca kho paṭisandhikkhaṇavasena veditabbaṃ.

'There and there': the inclusion by way of sense bases should be understood as follows: five arise at the moment of rebirth-linking in the one- and four-constituent existences; two in the remaining form realm; and in the desire realm, according to whether the faculties are deficient or not deficient, there are seven, nine, ten, again ten, and eleven. 'In the continuity' means in the continuity conditioned by that kamma through which the appearance of the aggregates occurs. And this should be understood by way of the moment of rebirth-linking.

Kammaṃyeva kammabhavo “bhavati etasmā upapattibhavo”ti katvā. Kammena niyyāditaattabhāvupapattivasena bhavatīti bhavo, tathā tathā nibbattavipāko kaṭattārūpañca. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “bhavatīti katvā bhavo”ti upapattibhavassa vakkhamānattā “kammaṃ phalavohārena bhavoti vutta”nti kathitaṃ.

Kamma itself is kamma-becoming, because 'from this, rebirth-becoming comes to be.' It is 'becoming' because it comes to be by way of the production of an individual existence handed over by kamma; it is the resultant-consciousness that has arisen in such and such a way and the material form produced by kamma. In the commentary, however, since rebirth-becoming is about to be explained with 'it comes to be, thus it is becoming,' it is stated that 'kamma is called becoming by way of metaphorical usage for the result.'

Upādiyanti sattā daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhanti etena kilesakāmena. Na kevalaṃ idha karaṇasādhanameva, atha kho kattusādhanampi labbhatīti vuttaṃ “sayaṃ vā”ti. Tanti vatthukāmaṃ. Kāmo ca so kāmanaṭṭhena, upādānañca bhusamādānaṭṭhenāti kāmupādānaṃ. Etanti kāmupādānapadaṃ. Puna etanti kāmupādānasaṅkhātaṃ.

'They cling': beings grasp with a firm grasp by means of this, that is, by sensual craving which is a defilement. Not only is the instrumental derivation found here, but the agentive derivation is also found; thus it is said: 'or by oneself.' 'That' refers to sensual pleasure as an object. And that is 'desire' in the sense of desiring, and 'clinging' in the sense of firm grasping; thus it is 'clinging to sensual pleasures.' 'This' means the term 'clinging to sensual pleasures.' Again, 'this' means that which is reckoned as 'clinging to sensual pleasures.'

Sassato [M 2.0016] attāti idaṃ purimadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyamānaṃ uttaradiṭṭhiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā esā diṭṭhi daḷhīkaraṇavasena purimaṃ uttarā upādiyati, evaṃ “natthi dinna”ntiādikāpīti. Attaggahaṇaṃ pana “attavādupādāna”nti idaṃ na diṭṭhupādānadassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Loko cāti attaggahaṇavinimuttaggahaṇaṃ diṭṭhupādānabhūtaṃ idha purimadiṭṭhiuttaradiṭṭhivacanehi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'The self is eternal': this is said to show a subsequent view that clings to a former view. Just as this view, by way of reinforcement, as a subsequent view clings to a former one, so too do views such as 'There is nothing given.' However, the grasping of a self, that is, 'clinging to a doctrine of self,' should be understood as not being an illustration of clinging to views. 'And the world': the grasping that is free from the grasping of a self, which constitutes clinging to views, should be understood as being expressed here by the words 'former view' and 'subsequent view.'

Yena micchābhinivesena gosīlagovatādiṃ samādiyati ceva anutiṭṭhati ca, so gosīlagovatādīnīti adhippetāni. Tenāha “gosīla…pe… sayameva upādānānī”ti. Abhinivesatoti abhinivesanato.

The wrong adherence by which one undertakes and practices cow-practice, cow-observance, and the like—that adherence is what is intended. Hence it is said: 'cow-practice... etc. ... are themselves clingings.' 'By adherence' means because of adhering.

Attavādupādānanti “attā”ti vādassa paññāpanassa gahaṇassa kāraṇabhūtā diṭṭhīti attho. Attavādamattamevāti attassa abhāvā “attā”ti idaṃ vacanamattameva. Upādiyanti daḷhaṃ gaṇhanti.

Clinging to the doctrine of self means: the view that is the cause for the doctrine, the proclaiming, and the grasping of 'a self.' 'Merely the doctrine of self' means: since there is no self, this 'self' is merely a word. 'They cling' means they grasp firmly.

Cakkhudvārādīsu pavattāyāti idaṃ taṇhāya rūpataṇhādibhāvassa kāraṇavacanaṃ chadvārārammaṇikadhammānaṃ paṭiniyatārammaṇattā. Javanavīthiyā pavattāyāti idaṃ tassā pavattiṭṭhānadassanaṃ. Sabhāveneva uṭṭhātuṃ asakkontassa veḷu viya nissayo ahutvā olumbhakabhāvena bhāvo upādānassa paccayabhāvato ārammaṇampi taṃsadisaṃ vuttaṃ. Rūpeti visaye [V 2.0015] bhummaṃ. Sā tividhā hotīti sambandho. Kāmataṇhā kāmassādabhāvena pavattiyā. Evaṃ assādentīti sassatadiṭṭhiyā sahajātanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatādipaccayabhūtāya saṃsaṭṭhattā niccadhuvasassatābhinivesamukhena assādentī. Bhavasahagatā taṇhā bhavataṇhā. Bhavati tiṭṭhati sabbakālanti hi bhavadiṭṭhi bhavo uttarapadalopena, bhavassādavasena pavattiyā ca. Iminā nayena vibhavataṇhāti ettha attho veditabbo. Vibhavati ucchijjati vinassatīti evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhi vibhavo uttarapadalopena. Evaṃ tāni aṭṭhārasāti yā cha kāmataṇhā, cha bhavataṇhā, cha vibhavataṇhā vuttā, etāni aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni taṇhāpaccayo. Ajjhattanti sakasantatiyaṃ. Bahiddhāti tato bahiddhā. Atītārammaṇāni vā hontu itarārammaṇāni vā, sayaṃ pana atītāni chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. “Aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritānī”tiādinā [M 2.0017] sambandho. Idāni aparenapi pakārena aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni dassetuṃ “ajjhattikassā”tiādimāha. Tattha ajjhattikassāti ajjhattikakhandhapañcakaṃ. Upayogatthe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Upādāyāti gahetvā. Asmīti hotīti yadetaṃ ajjhattikaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena samudāyaggāhato asmīti gāho hoti, tasmiṃ satīti attho. Idha pana rūpādiārammaṇavasena attho veditabbo. Itthamasmīti hotīti khattiyādīsu “idaṃpakāro aha”nti evaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena hotīti attho. Idaṃ tāva anupanidhāya gahaṇaṃ.

'Arisen in the eye-door, etc.': this phrase states the cause for craving's becoming craving for forms, etc., because phenomena related to the six doors have specific objects. 'Arisen in the cognitive series of impulsion': this shows its place of occurrence. Like a bamboo that cannot stand by its own nature, it is not a support but exists by way of depending; and because it is a condition for clinging, its object too is said to be of a similar nature. In the word 'form' (`rūpe`), the locative case is used in the sense of a sphere. 'It is threefold'—this is the connection. Craving for sensual pleasures is so called because it occurs by way of enjoying sensual pleasures. 'Thus delighting': because it is associated with eternalist view—which is a condition for it as conascence, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, etc.—it delights by way of adherence to what is permanent, stable, and eternal. Craving accompanied by the view of existence is craving for existence. For the view of existence (`bhavadiṭṭhi`) is the view that something 'exists, remains for all time'; `bhavo` is used for this with the elision of the final member of the compound, and also because it occurs by way of enjoying existence. In this way, the meaning of 'craving for non-existence' should be understood. The view that occurs as 'it ceases to exist, it is annihilated, it perishes' is `vibhava`, with the elision of the final member. Thus those eighteen—that is, the six cravings for sensual pleasures, six cravings for existence, and six cravings for non-existence that have been mentioned—these eighteen proliferations of craving are the condition 'craving.' 'Internal' means in one's own continuity. 'External' means outside of that. Whether they have past objects or other objects, the proliferations of craving that are themselves past are thirty-six. This same method applies to the other two terms. The connection is with the text 'one hundred and eight proliferations of craving,' etc. Now, to show the one hundred and eight proliferations of craving by another method, it says 'of the internal,' etc. Therein, 'of the internal' means the five internal aggregates. For this is the genitive case in the sense of relation. 'Having clung to' means having grasped. 'There is "I am"' means: when, with respect to the five internal aggregates, there arises the grasp 'I am' from a collective grasp through craving, conceit, and views. Here, however, the meaning should be understood by way of objects such as form, etc. 'There is "I am thus"' means: with regard to khattiyas, etc., it occurs through craving, conceit, and views as 'I am of this kind.' This, for a start, is grasping without comparison.

Evamādīnīti ādi-saddena “evamasmi, aññathāsmi, ahaṃ bhavissaṃ, itthaṃ bhavissaṃ, evaṃ bhavissaṃ, aññathā bhavissaṃ, asasmi, satasmi, ahaṃ siyaṃ, itthaṃ siyaṃ, evaṃ siyaṃ, aññathā siyaṃ, apāhaṃ siyaṃ, apāhaṃ itthaṃ siyaṃ, apāhaṃ evaṃ siyaṃ, apāhaṃ aññathā siya”nti etesaṃ saṅgaho. Upanidhāya gahaṇampi duvidhaṃ samato asamato vāti taṃ dassetuṃ “evamasmi, aññathāsmī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Tattha evamasmīti idaṃ samato upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ, yathā ayaṃ khattiyo, evaṃ ahamasmīti attho. Aññathāsmīti idaṃ pana asamato gahaṇaṃ, yathāyaṃ khattiyo tato aññathā ahaṃ hīno vā adhiko vāti attho. Imāni tāva paccuppannavasena cattāri taṇhāvicaritāni. Bhavissantiādīni pana cattāri anāgatavasena vuttāni, tesaṃ purimacatukke vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Asasmīti sassato asmi, niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Satasmīti asassato asmi, aniccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti imāni dve sassatucchedavasena vuttāni. Ito parāni siyantiādīni cattāri saṃsayaparivitakkavasena vuttāni, tāni purimacatukke vuttanayena atthato veditabbāni. Apāhaṃ siyantiādīni pana cattāri [V 2.0016] “api nāmāhaṃ bhaveyya”nti evaṃ patthanākappanavasena vuttāni, tānipi purimacatukke vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Evametesu –

'And so on': by the word 'etc.' (`ādi`), the following are included: 'I am thus,' 'I am otherwise,' 'I will be,' 'I will be thus,' 'I will be like this,' 'I will be otherwise,' 'I am eternal' (`asasmi`), 'I am non-eternal' (`satasmi`), 'I might be,' 'I might be thus,' 'I might be like this,' 'I might be otherwise,' 'May I be,' 'May I be thus,' 'May I be like this,' 'May I be otherwise.' Grasping by comparison is also twofold, as equal or unequal; to show this, 'I am thus' and 'I am otherwise' are stated. Herein, 'I am thus' is grasping by comparison as equal; the meaning is, 'Just as this khattiya is, so am I.' 'I am otherwise,' however, is grasping by comparison as unequal; the meaning is, 'I am otherwise than this khattiya, that is, inferior or superior.' These, for a start, are four proliferations of craving by way of the present. But the four beginning with 'I will be' are stated by way of the future, and their meaning should be understood by the same method stated for the first tetrad. 'Asasmi' means 'I am eternal'; this is a term for the permanent. 'Satasmi' means 'I am non-eternal'; this is a term for the impermanent. Thus these two are stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism. The four after this, beginning with 'I might be,' are stated by way of doubt and perplexity; their meaning should be understood according to the method stated for the first tetrad. The four beginning with 'May I be' (`apāhaṃ siyaṃ`), however, are stated in the sense of wishing and aspiring, as 'Oh, may I exist!'; they too should be understood by the same method as the first tetrad. Thus, among these—

Dve diṭṭhisīsā cattāro, suddhasīsā sīsamūlakā;

Tayo tayoti etāni, aṭṭhārasa vibhāvaye.
