But for him, even for an annihilationist, the theory is that so long as it is not annihilated, it exists; how much more so for an eternalist. ‘Actual’ means existing. ‘Accomplished’ means produced. The theory is that there is nothing more to be produced for it now. ‘With this as condition, this comes to be’ means: with this nutriment of consciousness as condition, this mentality-and-materiality comes to be. Again, ‘with this as condition, this comes to be’ means: with this mentality-and-materiality as condition, this sixfold sense base comes to be. Since the Blessed One has spoken thus in many places, he has come to the conclusion that this is merely a formation generated from a condition. ‘By that too’ means even by him who has come to that conclusion. ‘Having made it a single block’ means having made it so that there is no opportunity for a question. ‘Mounted on the teaching’ means that from the term ‘sixfold sense base’ onwards, the teaching has indeed mounted the track of dependent origination with the words, ‘With the sixfold sense base as condition, contact.’ ‘That very one’ means having taken just the term ‘sixfold sense base.’ ‘Avoiding’ means turning away from the round of rebirth. ‘He said thus’ means: when it was taught in this way with the words, ‘But of the six…,’ he said this: ‘the person to be trained understands.’ ‘The nutriment of consciousness is for the generation of a new existence in the future’: since it has been taught thus as the condition and root cause for a future existence from a past existence, it is said: ‘Between consciousness and mentality-and-materiality there is one link.’ It should be seen that by this taking up of consciousness, the taking up of volitional-formation consciousness is also accomplished.

Moḷiyaphaggunasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Moḷiyaphagguna Sutta is concluded.

3. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins

13. Ye paccayasamavāye tenattabhāvena saccāni paṭivijjhituṃ samatthā, te bāhirakaliṅge ṭhitāpi teneva tattha samatthatāyogena bhāvinaṃ samitabāhitapāpataṃ apekkhitvā samaṇasammatāyeva brāhmaṇasammatāyevāti [V 2.0031] te nivattetuṃ “saccāni paṭivijjhituṃ asamatthā”ti vuttaṃ. Dukkhasaccavasenāti dukkhaariyasaccavasena. Aññathā kathaṃ bāhirakāpi jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhanti na jānanti. Saccadesanābhāvato “saha taṇhāyā”ti vuttanti keci. Taṃ na suṭṭhu. Yasmā tattha tattha bhave paṭhamābhinibbatti, idha jātīti adhippetā, sā ca taṇhā eva santānena, taṇheva sā jāti. Jarāmaraṇañcettha pākaṭameva adhippetaṃ, na khaṇikaṃ, tasmā sataṇhā eva jātijarāmaraṇassa samudayoti bhūtakathanametaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samudayasaccavasena na jānantīti yojanā. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Sabbapadesūti yattha taṇhā visesanabhāvena vattabbā, tesu sabbapadesu. Yena samannāgatattā puggalo paramatthato samaṇo brāhmaṇoti vuccati, taṃ sāmaññaṃ brahmaññañcāti āha “ariya…pe… brahmaññañcā”ti. Yena hi pavattinimittena samaṇa-saddo brāhmaṇa-saddo ca sake atthe niruḷho, tassa vasena abhinnopi veneyyajjhāsayato dvidhā katvā vattuṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ “ubhayatthāpī”ti. Ekādasasu ṭhānesu cattāri saccāni kathesi avijjāsamudayassa anuddhaṭattā.

13. Those who are capable of penetrating the truths by their own nature through a convergence of conditions, even while standing in an external sect, are indeed considered ascetics and brahmins in consideration of their future state of having calmed and banished evil. To exclude them, it was said: 'They are incapable of penetrating the truths.' By way of the truth of suffering: that is, by way of the noble truth of suffering. Otherwise, how could even outsiders not know that aging and death are suffering? Some say it was said 'with craving' because of the absence of a teaching on the truths. That is not correct. For in whatever existence there is a first arising, that is what is meant here by birth; and that birth, by way of continuity, is just craving—craving itself is that birth. And here aging and death are meant in their manifest sense, not the momentary one. Therefore, this should be seen as a statement of fact that craving itself is the origin of birth, aging, and death. The construction is: 'they do not know by way of the truth of the origin.' This is the method in the remaining passages too. In all passages: that is, in all those passages where craving is to be stated as a qualifier. That on account of which a person is said to be an ascetic or a brahmin in the ultimate sense, that is asceticism and brahminhood. Thus he says: 'the noble...pe... and brahminhood.' For by the conventional indicator through which the terms 'ascetic' and 'brahmin' have become established in their respective meanings, though it is undifferentiated, it can be spoken of in two ways according to the disposition of the trainee. Thus it is said: 'in both cases.' In eleven places he taught the four truths because the origin of ignorance had not been extracted.

Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta is concluded.

4. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta

14. Ime [M 2.0036] dhamme katame dhammeti ca ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena “imesaṃ dhammānaṃ katamesaṃ dhammāna”nti imesaṃ padānaṃ saṅgaho. Etāni hi padāni jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvena vuttāni imissā desanāya papañcabhūtānīti āha “ettakaṃ papañcaṃ katvā kathitaṃ, desanaṃ…pe… ajjhāsayenā”ti. Iminā tāneva jarāmaraṇādīni gahetvā puggalajjhāsayavasena ādito “ime dhamme”tiādinā sabbapadasādhāraṇato desanā āraddhā. Yathānulomasāsanañhi suttantadesanā, na yathādhammasāsananti.

14. Herein, in 'These phenomena, what phenomena?', the particle 'iti' has the sense of 'and so on.' Thereby there is the inclusion of these words: 'of these phenomena, of what phenomena?' For these words, spoken in a general way of aging-and-death and so on, have become a proliferation of this teaching. Thus he says: 'Having made this much proliferation, the teaching ...pe... according to the disposition.' By this, having taken just that aging-and-death and so on, the teaching was begun from the start with 'these phenomena,' etc., as common to all the terms, in accordance with the person's disposition. For a Suttanta teaching is a teaching that follows the sequence, not a teaching that follows the phenomena.

Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta is concluded.

5. Kaccānagottasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse to Kaccānagotta

15. Yasmā idha jānantāpi “sammādiṭṭhī”ti vadanti ajānantāpi bāhirakāpi sāsanikāpi anussavādivasenapi attapaccakkhenapi, tasmā taṃ bahūnaṃ vacanaṃ upādāya āmeḍitavasena “sammādiṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti, bhante, vuccatī”ti āha. Tathāniddiṭṭhatādassanatthaṃ hissa ayaṃ āmeḍitapayogo. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – “aparehipi sammādiṭṭhīti vuccati, sā [V 2.0032] panāyaṃ evaṃ vuccamānā atthañca lakkhaṇañca upādāya kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, sammādiṭṭhi hotī”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sammādiṭṭhī”ti vacane yasmā viññū eva pamāṇaṃ, na aviññū, tasmā “yaṃ paṇḍitā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dve avayavā assāti dvayaṃ, duvidhaṃ diṭṭhigāhavatthu, dvayaṃ diṭṭhigāhavasena nissito apassitoti dvayanissito. Tenāha “dve koṭṭhāse nissito”ti. Yāya diṭṭhiyā “sabboyaṃ loko atthi vijjati sabbakālaṃ upalabbhatī”ti diṭṭhigatiko gaṇhāti, sā diṭṭhi atthitā, sā eva sadā sabbakālaṃ loko atthīti pavattagāhatāya sassato, taṃ sassataṃ. Yāya diṭṭhiyā “sabboyaṃ loko natthi na hoti ucchijjatī”ti diṭṭhigatiko gaṇhāti, sā diṭṭhi natthitā, sā eva ucchijjatīti uppannagāhatāya ucchedo, taṃ ucchedaṃ. Loko [M 2.0037] nāma saṅkhāraloko tamhi gahetabbato. Sammappaññāyāti aviparītapaññāya yathābhūtapaññāya. Tenāha “savipassanā maggapaññā”ti. Nibbattesu dhammesūti yathā paccayuppannesu rūpārūpadhammesu. Paññāyante svevāti santānanibandhanavasena paññāyamānesu eva. Yā natthīti yā ucchedadiṭṭhi tattha tattheva sattānaṃ ucchijjanato vinassanato koci ṭhito nāma satto dhammo vā natthīti saṅkhāraloke uppajjeyya. “Natthi sattā opapātikā”ti pavattamānāpi micchādiṭṭhi tathāpavattasaṅkhārārammaṇāva. Sā na hotīti kammāvijjātaṇhādibhedaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca saṅkhāralokassa samudayanibbattiṃ sammappaññāya passato, sā ucchedadiṭṭhi, na hoti, nappavattati avicchedena saṅkhārānaṃ nibbattidassanato. Lokanirodhanti saṅkhāralokassa khaṇikanirodhaṃ. Tenāha “saṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅga”nti. Yā atthīti hetuphalasambandhena pavattamānassa santānānupacchedassa ekattaggahaṇena saṅkhāraloke yā sassatadiṭṭhi sabbakālaṃ loko atthīti uppajjeyya. Sā na hotīti uppannuppannānaṃ nirodhassa navanavānañca uppādassa dassanato, sā sassatadiṭṭhi na hoti.

15. Because here both those who know and those who do not know, both outsiders and adherents of the teaching, speak of 'right view' on the basis of hearsay and the like, and by personal experience, therefore, taking up the speech of the many, he spoke by way of repetition, saying: '“Right view, right view,” venerable sir, it is said.' This use of repetition is for the purpose of showing that it is designated in such a way. This is the intention here: 'By others too it is called “right view.” But this, being so called, to what extent, venerable sir, is it right view, with respect to its meaning and characteristic?' In the commentary, however, concerning the words 'right view,' since the wise are the standard, not the unwise, it is therefore said: 'what the wise,' etc. It has two parts, thus it is a duality; a twofold basis for the adherence to views. One who relies on this duality by way of adherence to views, not seeing, is 'one who relies on the duality.' Hence he says: 'relying on two portions.' The view by which one with a theoretical view grasps, 'This whole world exists, it is real, it is found at all times,' that view is existence-view. That very view, because of its adherence to the idea that the world always exists at all times, is eternalism. The view by which one with a theoretical view grasps, 'This whole world does not exist, it is not, it is annihilated,' that view is non-existence-view. That very view, because of its adherence to the idea that what has arisen is annihilated, is annihilationism. 'World' means the world of formations, because that is what is to be grasped therein. 'With right wisdom' means with non-perverted wisdom, with wisdom of things as they have come to be. Hence he says: 'path-wisdom together with insight.' 'In arisen phenomena' means: in material and immaterial phenomena that have arisen from conditions. 'Just as they are being cognized' means: just as they are being cognized by way of being bound to the continuity. 'That which is not': that is, the annihilationist view that might arise in the world of formations, to the effect that 'since beings are annihilated and perish right here and there, there is no being or phenomenon that remains.' Even the wrong view that proceeds as 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings' has for its object formations that proceed in such a way. 'That does not occur': For one who sees with right wisdom the origination and production of the world of formations as dependent on conditions of different kinds such as kamma, ignorance, and craving, that annihilationist view does not occur, it does not proceed, because one sees the uninterrupted production of formations. 'The cessation of the world' means the momentary cessation of the world of formations. Hence he says: 'the breakup of formations.' 'That which is': that is, the eternalist view that might arise in the world of formations, to the effect that 'the world exists at all times,' by grasping as a unity the non-interruption of the continuity that proceeds through the connection of cause and effect. 'That does not occur': because one sees the cessation of what has repeatedly arisen and the arising of what is ever new, that eternalist view does not occur.

Loko samudeti etasmāti lokasamudayoti āha “anulomapaccayākāra”nti. Paccayadhammānañhi attano phalassa paccayabhāvo anulomapaccayākāro. Paṭilomaṃ paccayākāranti ānetvā sambandho. Taṃtaṃhetunirodhato taṃtaṃphalanirodho hi paṭilomapaccayākāro. Yo hi avijjādīnaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ hetuādipaccayabhāvo, so nippariyāyato lokasamudayo. Paccayuppannassa saṅkhārādikassa. Anucchedaṃ passatoti anucchedadassanassa hetu. Ayampīti na kevalaṃ khaṇato udayavayanīharaṇanayo, atha kho paccayato udayavayanīharaṇanayopi.

'The world originates from this, thus it is the origin of the world.' Thus he says: 'the forward order of conditionality.' For the state of being a condition for its own fruit on the part of conditional phenomena is the forward order of conditionality. The connection is made by bringing in 'the reverse order of conditionality.' For the cessation of each particular fruit from the cessation of each particular cause is the reverse order of conditionality. For whatever is the state of being a cause-condition, etc., for the conditional phenomena such as ignorance, etc., that, without alternative, is the origin of the world—of the conditionally arisen formations, etc. 'Because one sees non-annihilation': this is the reason for seeing non-annihilation. 'This too': not only the method of deducing arising and passing away by way of moments, but also the method of deducing arising and passing away by way of conditions.

Upagamanaṭṭhena taṇhāva upayo. Tathā diṭṭhupayo. Eseva nayoti iminā upayehi upādānādīnaṃ anatthantarataṃ atidisati. Tathā ca pana tesu duvidhatā upādīyati. Nanu ca cattāri [V 2.0033] upādānāni aññattha vuttānīti? Saccaṃ vuttāni, tāni ca kho atthato dve evāti idha evaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ “ahaṃ mama”nti ayathānukkamena vuttaṃ, yathānukkamaṃyeva pana attho veditabbo. Ādi-saddena paroparassa subhaṃ asubhantiādīnañca saṅgaho veditabbo. Te dhammeti tebhūmakadhamme. Vinivisantīti [M 2.0038] virūpaṃ nivisanti, abhinivisantīti attho. Tāhīti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi. Vinibaddhoti virūpaṃ vimuccituṃ vā appadānavasena niyametvā baddho.

In the sense of approaching, craving itself is an approach. Similarly, view is an approach. By 'this is the method,' he indicates the non-difference in meaning of clinging, etc., from the approaches. And yet a twofoldness is assumed in them. But were not four kinds of clinging spoken of elsewhere? True, they were spoken of, but since in meaning they are just two, it is stated thus here. Though 'I' and 'mine' are stated out of sequence, the meaning should be understood as being in sequence. By the word 'etc.' the inclusion of 'the beautiful and the ugly for oneself and others,' etc., should be understood. 'Those phenomena' means the phenomena of the three planes. 'They settle on them wrongly' means they settle on them in a distorted way; the meaning is, they adhere to them. 'By them' means by craving and view. 'Bound wrongly' means bound in a distorted way, or bound by being constrained through non-release, being hard to be freed from.

“Abhiniveso”ti upayupādānānaṃ pavattiākāraviseso vuttoti āha “tañcāyanti tañca upayupādāna”nti. Cittassāti akusalacittassa. Patiṭṭhānabhūtanti ādhārabhūtaṃ. Dosamohavasenapi akusalacittappavatti taṇhādiṭṭhābhinivesūpanissayā evāti taṇhādiṭṭhiyo akusalassa cittassa adhiṭṭhānanti vuttā. Tasminti akusalacitte. Abhinivisantīti “etaṃ mama, eso me attā”tiādinā abhinivesanaṃ pavattenti. Anusentīti thāmagatā hutvā appahānabhāvena anusenti. Tadubhayanti taṇhādiṭṭhidvayaṃ. Na upagacchatīti “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā taṇhādiṭṭhigatiyā na upasaṅkamati na allīyati. Na upādiyatīti na daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti. Na adhiṭṭhātīti na taṇhādiṭṭhigāhena adhiṭṭhāya pavattati. Attaniyagāho nāma sati attagāhe hotīti vuttaṃ “attā me”ti. Idaṃ dukkhaggahaṇaṃ upādānakkhandhāpassayaṃ tabbinimuttassa dukkhassa abhāvāti vuttaṃ “dukkhamevāti pañcupādānakkhandhamattamevā”ti. “Saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 1.120; 3.373; vibha. 190) hi vuttaṃ. Kaṅkhaṃ na karotīti saṃsayaṃ na uppādeti sabbaso vicikicchāya samucchindanato.

“Adherence” is said to be a specific mode of the process of approach and clinging; thus he says: “that which is approach-and-clinging.” “Of the mind”: that is, of the unwholesome mind. “As a foundation”: meaning as a support. Even when an unwholesome mind arises through the influence of hatred and delusion, its arising is dependently supported by adherence to craving and views; thus craving and views are called the “basis” of the unwholesome mind. In that unwholesome mind, “they adhere,” meaning they engage in adherence with such thoughts as “this is mine, this is my self,” and so on. “They lie dormant”: having become strong, they lie dormant in the sense of not being abandoned. “Both”: the pair of craving and views. “One does not approach”: one does not draw near to or get stuck in the course of craving and views with such thoughts as “this is mine.” “One does not cling”: one does not grasp it tightly. “One does not resolve”: one does not persist by resolving on the grasp of craving and views. The grasp of what is “mine” occurs when there is the grasp of self; thus it is said “my self.” This grasping of suffering is based on the aggregates subject to clinging, because there is no suffering apart from them; thus it is said: “is only suffering, merely the five aggregates subject to clinging.” For it is said: “In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering” (Dī. Ni. 2.387; Ma. Ni. 1.120; 3.373; Vibh. 190). “One does not have perplexity”: one does not give rise to doubt, because of having completely cut off uncertainty.

Na parappaccayenāti parassa asaddahanena. Missakasammādiṭṭhiṃ āhāti nāmarūpaparicchedato paṭṭhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā vuttattā lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ avoca. Nikūṭantoti nihīnanto. Nihīnapariyāyo hi ayaṃ nikūṭa-saddo. Tenāha “lāmakanto”ti. Paṭhamakanti ca garahāyaṃ ka-saddo. Sabbaṃ natthīti yathāsaṅkhataṃ bhaṅguppattiyā natthi eva, sabbaṃ natthi ucchijjati vinassatīti adhippāyo. Sabbamatthīti ca yathā asaṅkhataṃ atthi vijjati, sabbakālaṃ upalabbhatīti adhippāyo. Sabbanti cettha sakkāyasabbaṃ veditabbaṃ “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) viya. Tañhi pariññāñāṇānaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ. Iti-saddo nidassane. Kiṃ nidasseti? Atthi-saddena vuttaṃ. “Atthita”nti niccataṃ. Sassataggāho hi idha paṭhamo antoti adhippeto. Ucchedaggāho dutiyoti tadubhayavinimuttā ca idappaccayatā. Ettha ca uppannanirodhakathanato sassatataṃ, nirujjhantānaṃ asati [M 2.0039] nibbānappattiyaṃ yathāpaccayaṃ punūpagamanakathanato [V 2.0034] ucchedatañca anupagamma majjhimena bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti idappaccayatānayena. Tena vuttaṃ “ete…pe… ante”tiādi.

“Not through another's report”: by not believing another. “He spoke of mixed right view”: because right view has been spoken of starting from the determination of name-and-form, he spoke of a right view that is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. “A vile end”: a low end. For this word nikūṭa is a term for what is low. Thus he says, “a base end.” And “the first one”: the suffix -ka is used here in a pejorative sense. “All does not exist”: the meaning is that just as what is conditioned does not exist on account of its arising and breaking up, so everything does not exist, it is annihilated, it perishes. “And all exists”: the meaning is that just as the unconditioned exists, is found, so it is found at all times. And here, “all” should be understood as the allness of personal identity, as in such suttas as “The Root of All Things” (MN 1). For that is a condition for the knowledges of full understanding. The word “iti” is for illustration. What does it illustrate? What is said by the word “exists.” “Existence” means permanence. For here the grasp of eternalism is intended as the first extreme. The grasp of annihilationism is the second. And what is liberated from both is this-conditionality. And here, without approaching eternalism—from the statement about what has arisen ceasing—and without approaching annihilationism—from the statement about those who are ceasing, in the absence of the attainment of Nibbāna, re-approaching existence according to conditions—the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma by the middle way, by the method of this-conditionality. Thus it is said: “these …pe… extremes,” and so on.

Kaccānagottasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kaccānagotta Sutta is finished.

6. Dhammakathikasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta

16. Nibbindanatthāyāti nibbidānupassanāpaṭilābhāya. Sā hi jarāmaraṇasīsena vuttesu saṅkhatadhammesu nibbindanākārena pavattati. Virajjanatthāyāti virāgānupassanāpaṭilābhāya. Sīlato paṭṭhāyāti vivaṭṭasannissitasīlasamādānato paṭṭhāya. Sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato vivaṭṭasannissitasīle patiṭṭhito upāsakopi pageva catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhito bhikkhu sammāpaṭipanno nāma. Tenāha “yāva arahattamaggā paṭipannoti veditabbo”ti. Nibbānadhammassāti nibbānāvahassa ariyassa maggassa. Anurūpasabhāvabhūtanti nibbānādhigamassa anucchavikasabhāvabhūtaṃ. Nibbidāti iminā vuṭṭhānagāminipariyosānaṃ vipassanaṃ vadati. Virāgā nirodhāti padadvayena ariyamaggaṃ, itarena phalaṃ. Etthāti imasmiṃ sutte. Ekena nayenāti paṭhamena nayena. Tattha hi bhagavā tena bhikkhunā dhammakathikalakkhaṇaṃ pucchito taṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā vissajjesi. Yo hi vipassanaṃ maggaṃ anupādāvimuttiṃ pāpetvā kathetuṃ sakkoti, so ekantadhammakathiko. Tenāha “dhammakathikassa pucchā kathitā”ti. Dvīhīti dutiyatatiyanayehi. Tanti pucchaṃ. Visesetvāti visiṭṭhaṃ katvā. Yathāpucchitamattameva akathetvā apucchitampi atthaṃ dassento dhammānudhammapaṭipattiṃ anupādāya vimuttisaṅkhātaṃ visesaṃ pāpetvā. Bhagavā hi appaṃ yācito bahuṃ dento uḷārapuriso viya dhammakathikalakkhaṇaṃ pucchito paṭiccasamuppādamukhena tañceva tato ca uttariṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipattiṃ anupādāvimuttañca vissajjesi. Tattha “nibbidāya…pe… dhammaṃ desetī”ti iminā dhammadesanaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ katvā dassesi. “Nirodhāya paṭipanno hotī”ti iminā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ, “anupādāvimutto hotī”ti iminā desanaṃ asekkhabhāgiyaṃ katvā dassesi. Tenāha “sekkhāsekkhabhūmiyo niddiṭṭhā”ti.

16. “For the purpose of disenchantment”: for the attainment of the contemplation of disenchantment. For that contemplation proceeds in the mode of disenchantment in regard to conditioned things that are spoken of with aging-and-death as their heading. “For the purpose of dispassion”: for the attainment of the contemplation of dispassion. “Starting from virtue”: starting from the undertaking of virtue that is supportive of turning away. A lay follower who is endowed with the factors of stream-entry and established in virtue supportive of turning away is called one who is practicing rightly, to say nothing of a bhikkhu established in the fourfold purification virtue. Thus he says: “He should be understood as one practicing up to the path of arahantship.” “Of the Dhamma of Nibbāna”: of the noble path that leads to Nibbāna. “Having a corresponding nature”: having a nature suitable for the attainment of Nibbāna. By “disenchantment” he speaks of insight that culminates in the path of emergence. By the two terms “dispassion” and “cessation,” the noble path is indicated; by the other, the fruit. “Here”: in this sutta. “In one way”: by the first method. For there, when asked by that bhikkhu about the characteristic of a Dhamma-teacher, the Blessed One answered after bringing the matter to its culmination. For one who is able to teach by leading others to insight, the path, and liberation without clinging is a Dhamma-teacher in the ultimate sense. Thus he says: “The question about the Dhamma-teacher has been answered.” “By two”: by the second and third methods. “That”: the question. “Having made it special”: having made it distinct. Not speaking merely on what was asked, but showing a meaning that was not asked, he led to the distinction called liberation without clinging by means of the practice in accordance with the Dhamma. For the Blessed One, like a magnificent person who gives much when asked for little, when asked about the characteristic of a Dhamma-teacher, answered by way of dependent origination about that very thing and, going beyond that, about the practice in accordance with the Dhamma and liberation without clinging. There, by the words “He teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment …pe…,” he showed the Dhamma teaching as partaking of the state of good dispositions; by the words “He is practicing for cessation,” as partaking of the state of penetration; and by the words “He is liberated without clinging,” he showed the teaching as partaking of the state of the non-trainee. Thus he says: “The stages of the trainee and the non-trainee have been pointed out.”

Dhammakathikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta is finished.

7. Acelakassapasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta

17. Liṅgena [M 2.0040] acelakoti pabbajitaliṅgena acelako. Tena acelakacaraṇena acelo, na [V 2.0035] niccelatāmattenāti dasseti. Nāmenāti gottanāmena kassapoti. Deseti pavedeti saṃsayavigamanaṃ etenāti deso, nicchayahetūti āha “kiñcideva desa”ntiādi. So hi saṃsayavigamanaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ. Okāsanti avasaṃsandanapadesaṃ. Tenāha “khaṇaṃ kāla”nti. Antaragharaṃ antonivesanaṃ. Antare gharāni etassāti antaragharaṃ, antogāmo. Yadākaṅkhasīti yaṃ ākaṅkhasi. Iti bhagavā sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāreti. Tenāha “yaṃ icchasī”ti. Yadākaṅkhasīti yaṃ ākaṅkhasi, kassapa, tikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipantopi pucchasi, yaṃ ākaṅkhasi, tameva pucchāti attho.

17. “A naked ascetic by the mark” means a naked ascetic by the mark of one who has gone forth. This shows that he is a naked ascetic by that practice, not merely by being without clothes. “By name” means Kassapa by clan name. “He teaches” (deseti), he makes known. “Teaching” (deso) is that by which doubt is dispelled; it is the cause of certainty, thus it is said, “a certain teaching,” and so on. For that dispels doubt; that is the reason. “Opportunity” (okāsaṃ) means a place without obstruction. Thus he says, “a moment, a time.” “Inside a house” (antaragharaṃ) means within a dwelling. The derivation of antaragharaṃ is ‘houses are within it,’ meaning ‘within a village.’ “When you wish” (yadākaṅkhasi) means “whatever you desire.” Thus, the Blessed One invites with the invitation of an omniscient one. Thus he says, “whatever you wish.” “When you wish” (yadākaṅkhasi) means: “Whatever you desire, Kassapa—though having been refused three times, you still ask—ask that very thing you desire.” This is the meaning.

“Yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipī”ti vuttattā “tatiyampi kho”tiādinā pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ. So pana nayavasena saṃkhittoti daṭṭhabbo. Yena kāraṇena bhagavā acelakassa tikkhattuṃ yācāpetvā cassa pañhaṃ kathesi, taṃ dassetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādimāha. Gāravajananatthaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipi tañca dhammassa sussūsāya. Dhammagarukā hi buddhā bhagavanto. Sattānaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno yāvatatiyaṃ yācāpetīti vibhattivipariṇāmavasena sādhāraṇato padaṃ yojetvā puna “ettakena kālenā”ti kassapassa vasena yojetabbaṃ.

Since it is said, “he refused up to the third time,” the reading should be “for the third time,” and so on. But this should be seen as an abridgement for the sake of the method. To show the reason why the Blessed One answered the naked ascetic’s question only after making him ask three times, he said, “but why,” and so on. He refused up to the third time to generate respect and a desire to listen attentively to the Dhamma. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, revere the Dhamma. The phrase, “Awaiting the maturation of beings’ knowledge, he makes one ask up to the third time,” should be construed generally, by way of changing the case endings, and then again, the phrase “in this much time” should be construed in relation to Kassapa.

Māti paṭisedhe nipāto. Bhaṇīti punavacanavasena kiriyāpadaṃ vadati. Mā evaṃ bhaṇi, kathesīti attho. “Iti bhagavā avocā”ti pana saṅgītikāravacanaṃ. Sayaṃkataṃ dukkhanti purisassa uppajjamānadukkhaṃ, tena kataṃ nāma tassa kāraṇassa pubbe teneva kammassa upacitattāti ayaṃ nayo anavajjo. Diṭṭhigatiko pana pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ niccaṃ kārakavedakalakkhaṇaṃ attānaṃ parikappetvā tassa vasena “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti pucchatīti bhagavā “mā heva”nti avoca, tenāha “sayaṃkataṃ dukkhanti vattuṃ na vaṭṭatī”tiādi. Ettha ca yadi bāhirakehi parikappito attā nāma koci atthi, so ca nicco, tassa nibbikāratāya, purimarūpāvijahanato kassaci visesādhānassa kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ahitato nivattanatthaṃ, hite ca vattanatthaṃ upadeso ca nippayojano siyā [M 2.0041] attavādino. Kathaṃ vā so upadeso pavattīyati? Vikārābhāvato. Evañca attano ajaṭākāsassa viya dānādikiriyā hiṃsādikiriyā ca na sambhavati, tathā sukhassa dukkhassa ca anubhavanabandho eva attavādino na yujjati kammabandhābhāvato. Jātiādīnañca asambhavato kuto vimokkho. Atha pana “dhammamattaṃ tassa uppajjati ceva vinassati ca. Yassa vasenāyaṃ kiriyāvohāro”ti vadeyya, evampi purimarūpāvijahanena avaṭṭhitassa attano dhammamattanti na sakkā sambhāvetuṃ. Te vā panassa dhammā avatthābhūtā, tato aññe vā siyuṃ anaññe vā. Yadi [V 2.0036] aññe, na tāhi tassa uppannāhipi koci viseso atthi. Yo hi karoti paṭisaṃvedeti cavati upapajjati cāti icchitaṃ, tasmā tadattho eva yathāvuttadoso. Kiñca dhammakappanāpi niratthikā siyā. Atha anaññe, uppādavināsavantīhi avatthāhi anaññassa attano tāsaṃ viya uppādavināsasambhavato kuto niccatāvakāso. Tāsampi vā attano viya niccatāpattīti bandhavimokkhānaṃ asambhavo evāti na yujjatevāyaṃ attavādo. Tenāha “attā nāma koci dukkhassa kārako natthīti dīpetī”ti. Paratoti “paraṃkataṃ dukkha”ntiādike parasmiṃ tividhepi naye. Adhiccasamuppannanti adhicca yadicchāya kiñci kāraṇaṃ kassaci vā pubbaṃ vinā samuppannaṃ. Tenāha “akāraṇena yadicchāya uppanna”nti. Kasmā evamāhāti evaṃ vakkhamānoti adhippāyo. Assāti acelassa. Ayanti bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sodhentoti sayaṃ visuddhaṃ katvā pucchitamatthaṃ eva attano pucchāya suddhiṃ dassento. Laddhiyā “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti micchāgahaṇassa paṭisedhanatthāya.

The particle 'mā' is used for prohibition. 'Bhaṇīti' refers to the verb of speaking, in the sense of repeating a statement. 'Mā evaṃ bhaṇi' means 'do not speak thus,' implying 'do not say that.' 'Thus the Blessed One said' is the statement of the compilers of the Council. 'Self-made suffering' refers to the suffering that arises in a person, named as such because its cause, kamma, was accumulated by that very person in the past—this reasoning is faultless. However, one holding wrong views, imagining a self detached from the five aggregates—permanent, characterized as a doer and experiencer—asks, 'Is suffering self-made?' The Blessed One replied, 'Do not say so,' hence it is said, 'It is not proper to say "self-made suffering."' Here, if some externalists conceive of a self as existing and permanent, due to its unchanging nature and its not abandoning a previous form, it would be impossible to effect any special state for it. Thus, for turning away from what is unbeneficial and engaging in what is beneficial, the teaching would be pointless for those who advocate a self. How could such teaching function? Due to the absence of change. Just as for unentangled space, actions like giving or harming cannot occur, so too the connection of experiencing pleasure and pain is not tenable for an advocate of a self, due to the absence of a connection to kamma. And since birth, etc., cannot occur, how could liberation be possible? If one were to say, 'Only phenomena arise and cease for it, through which this designation of action occurs,' even then, for a self that is established by not abandoning its previous form, it is not possible to conceive of it as 'mere phenomena.' Those phenomena of it are either its states, or they could be other or not other. If other, then even when they arise, there is no special quality for it. For it is desired that it is this self which acts, experiences, passes away, and is reborn; therefore, for that very reason, the aforementioned fault applies. Moreover, even the postulation of phenomena would be meaningless. If not other, then for a self that is not other than those states which possess arising and ceasing, there would be the possibility of arising and ceasing for it just as for them. Whence the opportunity for permanence? Or if those phenomena too were to attain permanence like it, then bondage and liberation would be impossible—thus, this doctrine of self is untenable. Therefore, he clarifies, 'There is no agent whatsoever who is the maker of suffering.' Regarding 'by another': in the threefold method concerning 'another' in such phrases as 'suffering made by another,' and so on. 'Arisen by chance' (adhiccasamuppannaṃ) means arisen arbitrarily, without any cause or prior condition. Hence it is said, 'arisen without cause, arbitrarily.' 'Why is it said thus?' The meaning is that it will be explained in this way. 'Assāti' refers to the naked ascetic. 'Ayanti'—this refers to the Blessed One. 'Sodhentoti' means showing the purity of his own question by having himself purified the meaning to be asked. 'Laddhiyā'—to reject the wrong grasp of 'self-made suffering.'

So karotīti so kammaṃ karoti. So paṭisaṃvedayatīti kārakavedakānaṃ anaññattadassanaparaṃ etaṃ, na pana kammakiriyāphalānaṃ paṭisaṃvedanānaṃ samānakālatādassanaparaṃ. Itīti nidassanatthe nipāto. Khoti avadhāraṇe. “So evā”ti dassito. Aniyatādesā hi ete nipātā. Āditoti bhummatthe nissakkavacananti āha “ādimhiyevā”ti. “Sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhiyā pageva “so karoti, so paṭisaṃvedayatī”ti saññācittavipallāsā bhavanti. Saññāvipallāsato hi cittavipallāso, cittavipallāsato diṭṭhivipallāso, tenāha “evaṃ sati pacchā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhanti ayaṃ laddhi hotī”ti. Evaṃ [M 2.0042] sati saññācittavipallāsānaṃ brūhito micchābhiniveso, yadidaṃ “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhi. Tasmā paṭinissajjetuṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigatanti dasseti. Tenāha bhagavā “sayaṃkataṃ…pe… etaṃ paretī”ti. Vaṭṭadukkhaṃ adhippetaṃ avisesato atthīti ca vuttattā. Sassataṃ sassatagāhaṃ dīpeti paresaṃ pakāseti, tathābhūto ca sassataṃ daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhātīti. Tassāti diṭṭhigatikassa. Taṃ “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ viparītadassanaṃ. Etaṃ sassataggahaṇaṃ. Pareti upeti. Tenāha “kārakañca…pe… attho”ti. Ekameva gaṇhantanti satipi vatthubhede ayoniso uppajjanena ekameva katvā gaṇhantaṃ.

'He acts' means he performs kamma. 'He experiences'—this is to show the non-difference of the doer and the experiencer, but not to show the simultaneity of the performance of the action and the experiencing of its results. 'Iti' is a particle indicating illustration. 'Kho' is for emphasis. 'So eva' (he himself) is shown. Indeed, these particles have variable application. 'Ādito' is an ablative used in the sense of the locative, hence it is said 'right from the beginning.' Even before the view 'suffering is self-made,' perceptions and thoughts become perverted as 'he acts, he experiences.' For from the perversion of perception comes the perversion of mind, and from the perversion of mind comes the perversion of view. Therefore, it is said, 'When this is so, the view later arises that suffering is self-made.' When this is so, wrong adherence, which is the view 'suffering is self-made,' grows from the perversions of perception and mind. Therefore, it is shown that one should abandon this evil wrong view. Hence, the Blessed One said, 'self-made... this he approaches.' And because it was said that the suffering of the round exists without distinction, this is what is intended. He approaches eternalism. This clarifies the grasp of eternalism; he proclaims it to others, and being such, he takes up a firm grasp of eternalism. 'Tassa' refers to the holder of the wrong view. That view, which proceeds as 'suffering is self-made,' is a perverted view. This is the grasp of eternalism. 'Pareti' means he approaches. Hence it is said, 'the doer... the meaning.' 'They grasp only one' means that even when there is a difference in the basis, due to its unwise arising, they grasp it as one.

Idha “ādimhiyevā”ti pade. “Paraṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhiyā pagevātiādinā hettha vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Ayañhettha yojanā – “paraṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhiyā pageva añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedayatīti saññācittavipallāsā bhavantīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva [V 2.0037] yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ satīti evaṃ muduke ucchedavipallāse paṭhamuppanne sati pacchā “paraṃkataṃ dukkha”nti ayaṃ laddhi hotīti sambandho. Kārakoti kammassa kārako. Tena katanti kammakārakena kataṃ. Kammunā hi phalassa vohāro abhedopacārakattā. Evanti diṭṭhisahagatā vedanā sātasabhāvā kilesapariḷāhādinā saparissayā saupāyāsā, evaṃ. “Pageva itare”ti vuttavedanāya abhitunnassa viddhassa. “Vuttanayena yojetabba”nti vatvā taṃ yojanaṃ dassento “tatrāya”ntiādimāha. Ucchedanti sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ, vibhavanti attho. Asato hi vināsāsambhavato atthibhāvanibandhano ucchedo. Yathā hetuphalabhāvena pavattamānānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ satipi ekasantānapariyāpannānaṃ bhinnasantatipatitehi visese hetuphalānaṃ paramatthato avinābhāvattā bhinnasantānapatitānaṃ viya accantabhedasanniṭṭhānena nānattanayassa micchāgahaṇaṃ ucchedābhinivesassa kāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ hetuphalabhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ vijjamānepi sabhāvabhede ekasantatipariyāpannatāya ekattanayena accantābhedagahaṇampi kāraṇamevāti dassetuṃ “sattassā”ti vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ. Santānavasena hi vattamānesu khandhesu ghanavinibbhogābhāvena ekattagahaṇanibandhano sattaggāho, sattassa ca atthibhāvaggāhanibandhano ucchedaggāho, yāvāyaṃ attā na [M 2.0043] ucchijjati, tāvāyaṃ vijjatiyevāti gahaṇato nirudayavināso idha ucchedoti adhippetoti “uccheda”nti vuttaṃ. Visesena nāso vināso, abhāvo. So pana maṃsacakkhupaññācakkhūnaṃ dassanapathātikkamoyeva hotīti vuttaṃ “adassana”nti. Adassane hi nāsasaddo loke niruḷhoti. Sabhāvavigamo sabhāvāpagamo vibhavo. Yo hi nirudayavināsena ucchijjati, na so attano sabhāvena tiṭṭhati.

Here, in the phrase 'in the beginning itself,' the meaning should be understood according to the method stated below, beginning with 'before the view “suffering is made by another.”' This is the construction here: The view 'suffering is made by another' arises from the distortions of perception and mind that 'one person acts while another experiences.' All this should be construed according to the method previously stated. This being so, when such a subtle annihilationist distortion has first arisen, this view 'suffering is made by another' arises afterwards; this is the connection. 'Kāraka' means the doer of an action. 'Done by that' means done by the doer of the action. For the result is designated by the action due to a figurative identification. 'Thus' refers to feeling accompanied by wrong view, which is pleasant by nature but is fraught with peril and distress because of the fever of defilements, and so on. 'Before the others' refers to one who is tormented and pierced by the aforementioned feeling. Having said, 'It should be construed by the stated method,' he shows that construction, saying, 'Therein, this…,' etc. 'Annihilation' means the cutting off, the destruction of an existing being; 'non-existence' is the meaning. For since the destruction of what is non-existent is impossible, annihilation is based on the state of existence. Just as the wrong grasp of the principle of diversity—by establishing an absolute difference between cause and effect as if they fall into different continuities, though they are ultimately inseparable—is a cause for adherence to annihilationism, so too, to show that the grasp of absolute identity by the principle of unity is also a cause, 'of a being' was said in the Pāli. For in regard to the aggregates occurring as a continuum, the grasp of a 'being' is based on the grasp of unity due to the absence of a clear separation of the mass. And the grasp of annihilation is based on the grasp of that being's existence, from the notion, 'So long as this self is not annihilated, it exists.' Thus, destruction without re-arising is intended here by 'annihilation'; therefore 'annihilation' is said. 'Destruction' (vināso) is destruction (nāso) in a special sense, non-existence. But since this is just the transcending of the range of vision of the physical eye and the wisdom eye, it is called 'disappearance.' For in the world the word 'destruction' is established for what has disappeared. 'Vibhava' is the departure of intrinsic nature, the removal of intrinsic nature. For what is annihilated by destruction without re-arising does not remain with its own intrinsic nature.

Ete teti vā ye ime tayā “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti ca puṭṭhena mayā “so karoti, so paṭisaṃvedayatī”tiādinā, “añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedayatī”tiādinā ca paṭikkhittā sassatucchedasaṅkhātā antā, te ubho anteti yojanā. Atha vā ete teti yattha puthū aññatitthiyā anupacitañāṇasambhāratāya paramagambhīraṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ suññataṃ appajānantā sassatucchede nimuggā sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na visahanti, ete te ubho ante anupagammāti yojanā. Desetīti paṭhamaṃ tāva anaññasādhāraṇe paṭipattidhamme ñāṇānubhāvena majjhimāya paṭipadāya ṭhito, karuṇānubhāvena desanādhamme majjhimāya paṭipadāya ṭhito dhammaṃ deseti. Ettha hīti hi-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā kāraṇato…pe… niddiṭṭho, tasmā majjhimāya paṭipadāya ṭhito dhammaṃ desetīti yojanā. Kāraṇato phalaṃ dīpitanti yojanā, abhidheyyānurūpañhi liṅgavacanāni honti. Assāti phalassa. Na koci kārako vā vedako vā niddiṭṭho, aññadatthu paṭikkhitto hetuphalamattatādassanato kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhagahaṇatoti. Ettāvatāti “ete [V 2.0038] te, kassapa…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti ettakena tāva padena. Sesapañhāti “sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkha”ntiādikā sesā cattāro pañhā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, natthi dukkha”nti pañho pāḷiyaṃ sarūpeneva paṭikkhittoti na uddhato. Paṭisedhitā hontīti tatiyapañho, tāva paṭhamadutiyapañhapaṭikkhepeneva paṭikkhitto, so hi pañho visuṃ visuṃ paṭikkhepena ekajjhaṃ paṭikkhepena ca. Tenāha “ubho…pe… paṭikkhitto”ti. Ettha ca yassa attā kārako vedako vā icchito, tena vipariṇāmadhammo attā anuññāto hoti. Tathā ca sati anupubbadhammappavattiyā rūpādidhammānaṃ viya[M 2.0044], sukhādidhammānaṃ viya cassa paccayāyattavuttitāya uppādavantatā āpajjati. Uppāde ca sati avassaṃbhāvī nirodhoti anavakāsā niccatāti. Tassa “sayaṃkata”nti paṭhamapañhapaṭikkhepo pacchā ce attano niruḷhassa samudayo hotīti pubbe viya anena bhavitabbaṃ, pubbe viya vā pacchāpi. Sesapañhāti tatiyapañhādayo. Tatiyapañho paṭikkhittoti evañca tatiyapañho paṭikkhitto veditabbo – “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā satataṃ samitaṃ paccayāyattassa dīpanena dukkhassa adhiccasamuppannatā paṭikkhittā, tato eva tassa ajānanañca paṭikkhittaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.39-40; mahāva. 1; udā. 1).

'These two': The construction is: These are the two extremes, called eternalism and annihilationism, which were rejected by me with such statements as 'he acts, he experiences' and 'one acts, another experiences,' when I was asked by you about 'suffering is self-made.' Or, the construction is: 'Without approaching these two extremes'—those extremes in which many adherents of other sects, because they have not accumulated the provisions of knowledge and do not understand the supremely profound, fine, subtle emptiness, are sunk in eternalism and annihilationism, unable to lift their heads. 'He teaches': First, established in the middle way of practice by the power of his unique knowledge, and established in the middle way of teaching by the power of his compassion, he teaches the Dhamma. 'Herein, for': The word 'for' (hi) has the sense of a reason. The construction is: 'Because for the reason… indicated, therefore he teaches the Dhamma established in the middle way.' The construction is: 'The result is explained from the cause,' for gender and number conform to what is to be expressed. 'Of this' means of the result. No doer or experiencer is indicated; on the contrary, they are rejected by showing that there are only cause and effect, by the mere grasp of the aggregate of suffering. 'By this much' means by this much of the text: 'These two, Kassapa… the cessation of this entire aggregate of suffering comes to be.' 'The remaining questions' means the remaining four questions beginning with 'Is suffering both self-made and made by another?' In the commentary, however, the question 'But, Master Gotama, is there no suffering?' is rejected in the Pāli itself in terms of its very form, so it is not taken up. 'They are refuted': The third question is refuted by the very refutation of the first and second questions, for that question is refuted both by refuting them separately and by refuting them together. Hence he said, 'Both… refuted.' Here, for one who holds that the self is a doer or experiencer, a self subject to change is thereby admitted. If so, because of the sequential occurrence of phenomena, its dependence on conditions and its liability to arising would follow, just as for material phenomena and for feelings of pleasure and so on. And when there is arising, cessation is inevitable; thus there is no room for permanence. For him, the refutation of the first question, 'Is it self-made?', is that if what had ceased for him were to arise again later, it would have to be as it was before; or as it was before, so it would be later. 'The remaining questions' means the third question and so on. 'The third question is refuted': And the third question should be understood to be refuted thus: by constantly showing the conditionality of suffering with the statement 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be,' etc., the accidental origination of suffering is refuted, and thereby ignorance of it is also refuted. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering' (MN 115; SN 12:35–36; Mv I 1.1; Ud 1.1).

Yaṃ parivāsaṃ samādiyitvā parivasatīti yojanā. Vacanasiliṭṭhatāvasenāti “bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ labheyyaṃ upasampada”nti yācantena tena vuttavacanasiliṭṭhatāvasena. Gāmappavesanādīnīti ādi-saddena nātidivāpaṭikkamanaṃ, navesiyādigocaratā, sabrahmacārīnaṃ kiccesu dakkhatādi, uddesādīsu tibbacchandatā, titthiyānaṃ avaṇṇabhaṇane attamanatā, buddhādīnaṃ avaṇṇabhaṇane anattamanatā, titthiyānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇane anattamanatā, buddhādīnaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇane attamanatāti (mahāva. 87) imesaṃ saṅgaho. Aṭṭha vattānīti imāni aṭṭha titthiyavattāni pūrentena. Ettha ca nātikālena gāmappavesanā tattha visuddhakāyavacīsamācārena piṇḍāya caritvā nātidivāpaṭikkamananti idamekaṃ vattaṃ.

'Having undertaken the probation, he observes it' is the construction. 'By the express wording' means by the express wording of the one who requested, 'May I receive the going forth and the higher ordination in the Blessed One’s presence.' 'Entering the village, etc.': The word 'etc.' includes not returning too late, behaving as if one were new, skill in the duties of fellow monastics, keen desire for recitations and so on, delight in speaking ill of adherents of other sects, displeasure in speaking ill of the Buddha and others, displeasure in praising adherents of other sects, and delight in praising the Buddha and others (Mahāvagga 87). These are included. 'The eight duties': by fulfilling these eight duties for adherents of other sects. Herein, entering the village not too early, wandering for alms there with purified bodily and verbal conduct, and not returning too late in the day—this is one duty.

Ayamettha pāṭhoti etasmiṃ kassapasutte ayaṃ pāṭho. Aññatthāti sīhanādasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 1.402-403). Ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvāti yathā suvaṇṇaṃ nighaṃsitvā adhikaraṇiyā koṭṭetvā niddosameva gayhati, evaṃ parivāsavattacaraṇena ghaṃsitvā suddhabhāvavīmaṃsanena koṭṭetvā suddho eva aññatitthiyapubbo idha gayhati. Tibbacchandatanti sāsanaṃ anupavisitvā brahmacariyavāse tibbacchandataṃ daḷhatarābhirucitaṃ. Aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesīti nāmagottena apākaṭaṃ [V 2.0039] ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpesi ehibhikkhuupasampadāya upanissayābhāvato. Gaṇe nisīditvāti bhikkhū attano santike pattāsanavasena gaṇe nisīditvā.

'This is the reading here' means this is the reading in this Kassapa Sutta. 'Elsewhere' means in the Sīhanāda Sutta and others (Dī. Ni. 1.402–403). 'Having rubbed and hammered': Just as gold is accepted as flawless only after being rubbed on a touchstone and hammered, so here a former adherent of another sect is accepted as pure only after being rubbed by the observance of the duties of probation and hammered by the examination of his state of purity. 'With keen desire' means with keen desire and very firm inclination for living the holy life after having entered the Dispensation. 'He addressed a certain monk': He commanded a certain monk, not specified by name and clan, because there was no basis for the 'Come, monk' ordination. 'Having sat in the assembly': The monks having sat in the assembly in his presence by way of the seats they had obtained.

Acelakassapasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta is finished.

8. Timbarukasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta

18. Yasmā [M 2.0045] timbaruko “vedanā attā. Attāva vedayatī”ti evaṃladdhiko, tasmā tāya laddhiyā “sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti vadati, taṃ paṭisaṃharituṃ bhagavā “sā vedanā”tiādiṃ avoca. Tenāha “sā vedanātiādi sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhanti laddhiyā nisedhanatthaṃ vutta”nti. Etthāpīti imasmimpi sutte. Tatrāti yaṃ vuttaṃ “sā vedanā…pe… sukhadukkha”nti, tasmiṃ pāṭhe. Ādimhiyevāti ettha bhummavacanena “ādito”ti to-saddo na nissakkavacane. Eva-kārena kho-saddo avadhāraṇeti dasseti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ anantarasutte vuttameva. Tattha pana “vedanāto añño attā, vedanāya kārako”ti laddhikassa diṭṭhigatikassa vādo paṭikkhitto, idha “vedanā attā”ti evaṃladdhikassāti ayameva viseso. Tenāha “evañhi sati vedanāya eva vedanā katā hotī”tiādi. Imissāti yāya vedanāya sukhadukkhaṃ kataṃ, imissā. Pubbepīti sassatākārato pubbepi. Purimañhi atthanti anantarasutte vuttaṃ atthaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyanti porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Tanti purimasutte vuttamatthaṃ. Assāti imassa suttassa. Yasmā timbaruko “vedanāva attā”ti gaṇhāti, tasmā vuttaṃ “ahaṃ sā vedanā…pe… na vadāmī”ti.

18. Because Timbaruka is one who holds the view, 'Feeling is the self; the self itself feels,' he therefore says, in accordance with that view, 'Pleasure and pain are self-made.' To retract that, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning 'That feeling....' Therefore it is said: 'The passage beginning "That feeling..." was spoken for the purpose of negating the view that "pleasure and pain are self-made."' Here too: in this very sutta. There: in that passage which states, 'That feeling...pleasure and pain.' As to ādimhiyeva (in the very beginning): here, the suffix -to (as in ādito) is used in the locative sense, not in the ablative sense. The particle eva indicates that the particle kho is for emphasis. Whatever should be said here has already been said in the immediately preceding sutta. There, however, the thesis of one holding the view 'the self is other than feeling, it is the agent of feeling,' or of one who has gone to a speculative view, is refuted; here it is the view 'feeling is the self' that is refuted—this is the only difference. Hence it is said: 'For if this were so, feeling would be made by feeling itself,' etc. By this: by this feeling by which pleasure and pain are made. Previously too: previously also in the manner of eternalism. The former meaning: the meaning stated in the immediately preceding sutta. In the commentary: in the ancient commentary. That: the meaning stated in the previous sutta. Of this: of this sutta. Because Timbaruka holds that 'feeling itself is the self,' it is therefore said: 'I do not say, "I am that feeling..."'

Aññā vedanātiādīsupi yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ anantarasutte vuttanayameva. Kārakavedanāti kattubhūtavedanā. Vedanāsukhadukkhanti vedanābhūtasukhadukkhaṃ kathitaṃ, na vaṭṭasukhadukkhaṃ. “Vipākasukhadukkhameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ “sayaṃkataṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”ntiādivacanato.

Regarding 'another feeling,' etc., whatever should be said is in the same way as was stated in the immediately preceding sutta. Feeling as the doer: feeling that has become the agent. Pleasure and pain that are feeling: pleasure and pain that have become feeling are spoken of, not the pleasure and pain of the round of existence. It is said, 'Only resultant pleasure and pain pertain to the round,' based on the statement 'pleasure and pain are self-made,' etc.

Timbarukasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta is concluded.

9. Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Fool and the Wise Person

19. Avijjā nīvaraṇā bhavādi-ādīnavassa nivāritapaṭicchādikā etassāti avijjānīvaraṇo, avijjāya nivutoti āha “avijjāya nivāritassā”ti. Ayaṃ kāyoti bālassa appahīnakilesassa paccuppannaṃ attabhāvaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā avijjāya paṭicchāditādīnave ayāthāvadassanavasena [V 2.0040] taṇhāya paṭiladdhacittassa taṃtaṃbhavūpagā saṅkhārā saṅkharīyanti. Tehi [M 2.0046] ca attabhāvassa abhinibbatti, tasmā ayañca avijjāya kāyo nibbattoti. Assāti bālassa. Ayaṃ atthoti “ayaṃ kāyo nāmarūpanti ca vutto”ti attho dīpetabbo upādānakkhandhasaḷāyatanasaṅgahato tesaṃ dhammānaṃ. Evametaṃ dvayanti evaṃ avijjāya nivāritattā, taṇhāya ca saṃyuttattā evaṃ saparasantānagatasaviññāṇakakāyasaṅkhātaṃ dvayaṃ hoti. Aññatthāti suttantaresu. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-45; 4.60-61; kathā. 465, 467) ajjhattikabāhirāyatanāni bhinditvā cakkhurūpādidvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā, idha pana abhinditvā cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā “dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso”ti, tasmā mahādvayaṃ nāma kiretaṃ anavasesato ajjhattikabāhirāyatanānaṃ gahitattā. Ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanānīti etthāpi hi saḷāyatanāni saṅgahitāneva. Phassakāraṇānīti phassapavattiyā paccayāni. Yehīti hetudassanamattanti āha “yehi kāraṇabhūtehī”ti. Phasso eva phusanakicco, na phassāyatanānīti vuttaṃ “phassena phuṭṭho”ti. Paripuṇṇavasenāti avekallavasena. Aparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ hīnāni phassassa kāraṇāni honti, tesaṃ viyāti “etesaṃ vā aññatarenā”ti vuttaṃ. Kāyanibbattanādimhīti saviññāṇakassa kāyassa nibbattanaṃ kāyanibbattanaṃ, kāyo vā nibbattati etenāti kāyanibbattanaṃ, kilesābhisaṅkhārā. Ādisaddena phassasaḷāyatanādisaṅgaho. Adhikaṃ payasati payuñjati etenāti adhippayāso, visesakāraṇanti āha “adhikapayogo”ti.

19. Ignorance (avijjā) is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa) because for him it obstructs and conceals the dangers of existence, etc.; hence he is avijjānīvaraṇo (one with the hindrance of ignorance). Because he is veiled by ignorance, the text says 'for one veiled by ignorance.' As to 'this body': for the fool whose defilements are unabandoned, who cherishes his present individual existence with its dangers concealed by ignorance, and who, through not seeing things as they really are, has a mind acquired by craving—for him, formations leading to this or that state of existence are generated. And by them the individual existence is generated. Therefore this body, too, is produced by ignorance. Of him: of the fool. This is the meaning: the meaning of 'this body is also called name-and-form' should be explained by the inclusion of those phenomena within the aggregates of clinging and the six sense bases. Thus this duality: thus, because of being veiled by ignorance and yoked by craving, this duality, designated as the conscious body belonging to one's own and others' continuities, comes to be. Elsewhere: in other suttas. By way of the passage beginning, 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact' (MN 18, etc.), the internal and external sense bases are analyzed, and eye-contact and so on are spoken of as dependent on the pairs of eye and form, etc. Here, however, without analyzing them, eye-contact and so on are spoken of as 'contact dependent on the duality,' that is, on the six internal and external sense bases. Therefore, this is indeed called the 'great duality' because the internal and external sense bases are included without remainder. As to 'internal and external sense bases': here too the six sense bases are indeed included. The causes of contact: the conditions for the occurrence of contact. By which: this merely indicates the cause; thus it says, 'by which causal factors.' Contact itself has the function of impinging, not the sense bases of contact; thus it is said 'touched by contact.' By way of completeness: by way of non-deficiency. For deficient sense bases, the causes of contact are inferior; in contrast to them, it is said, 'or by any one of these.' In the production of the body, etc.: the production of the conscious body is kāyanibbattanaṃ. Or, the body is produced by this, thus kāyanibbattanaṃ refers to the defilements and formations. The word 'etc.' includes contact, the six sense bases, and so on. That by which one strives and exerts oneself more is adhippayāso (intention); it is a special cause, hence it says 'additional exertion.'

Bhagavā amhākaṃ uppādakabhāvena mūlabhāvena bhagavaṃmūlakā. Ime dhammāti ime kāraṇadhammā. Yehi mayaṃ bālapaṇḍitānaṃ samānepi kāyanibbattanādimhi visesaṃ jāneyyāma, tenāha “pubbe kassapasammāsambuddhena uppāditā”tiādi. Ājānāmāti abhimukhaṃ paccakkhato jānāma. Paṭivijjhāmāti tasseva vevacanaṃ, adhigacchāmāti attho. Netāti amhākaṃ santāne pāpetā. Vinetāti yathā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso hoti, evaṃ visesato netā, tadaṅgavinayādivasena vā vinetā. Anunetāti anurūpaṃ netā. Antarantarā yathādhammapaññattiyā paññāpitānaṃ dhammānaṃ anurūpato dassanaṃ hotīti āha “yathāsabhāvato [M 2.0047] …pe… dassetā”ti. Āpāthaṃ upagacchantānaṃ bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā dhammā. Tenāha “catubhūmakadhammā”tiādi. Paṭisarati paṭivijjhatīti paṭisaraṇaṃ, tasmā paṭivijjhanavasena bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Tenāha “api cā”tiādi. Phasso āgacchatīti [V 2.0041] paṭivijjhanakavasena phasso ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, āpāthaṃ āgacchantoyeva so atthato “ahaṃ kinnāmo”ti nāmaṃ pucchanto viya, bhagavā cassa nāmaṃ karonto viya hotīti vuttaṃ “ahaṃ bhagavā”tiādi. Upaṭṭhātūti ñāṇassa paccupaṭṭhātu. Bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātūti bhagavato eva bhāgo hotu, bhagavāva naṃ attano bhāgaṃ katvā vissajjetūti attho, bhagavato bhāgo yadidaṃ dhammassa akkhānaṃ, amhākaṃ pana savanaṃ bhāgoti ayamettha adhippāyo. Evañhi saddalakkhaṇena sameti. Keci pana paṭibhātūti atthaṃ vadanti ñāṇena dissatu desīyatūti vā attho. Tenāha “tumheyeva no kathetvā dethāti attho”ti.

The Blessed One is our originator, our root; thus the phenomena have the Blessed One as their root. These phenomena means these causal phenomena. By which we may know the distinction between the fool and the wise person even when the production of their bodies and so on is similar; therefore it says, 'previously generated by the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa,' and so on. We know means we know directly, from personal experience. We penetrate is a synonym for the same; the meaning is 'we attain.' He leads means he causes it to be attained in our own continuity. He trains means he leads in a special way so that the special knowledge and vision of the noble ones arises; or he trains by way of momentary discipline and so on. He guides suitably means he leads fittingly. From time to time, in accordance with the Dhamma as proclaimed, there is a seeing that conforms to the phenomena proclaimed; thus it says, 'he shows... according to their real nature.' For those who come within range, the Blessed One is the refuge, the place of resort; thus the phenomena have the Blessed One as their refuge. Therefore it is said, 'the phenomena of the four planes,' and so on. One resorts to, one penetrates: this is refuge. Therefore, by way of penetration, the Blessed One is their refuge; thus they have the Blessed One as their refuge. Therefore it is said, 'Moreover,' and so on. Contact comes means by way of penetration, contact comes into the range of knowledge. As it comes into range, it is as if it were asking its name, 'What is my name?' and the Blessed One is as if giving it a name; thus it is said, 'I am the Blessed One,' and so on. Let it be present means let it be present to knowledge. Let it be manifest only to the Blessed One means let it be the Blessed One's portion. Let the Blessed One make it his portion and explain it—this is the meaning. The Blessed One's portion is this, the exposition of the Dhamma, while our portion is the hearing—this is the intention here. For thus it accords with the characteristic of the word. Some, however, say the meaning of 'let it be manifest' is 'let it be seen by knowledge' or 'let it be taught.' Therefore it is said: 'The meaning is, "You yourselves should speak and give it to us."'

Bālassa paṇḍitassa ca kāyassa nibbattiyā paccayabhūtā avijjā ca taṇhā ca. Tenāha “kammaṃ…pe… niruddhā”ti. Javāpetvāti gahitajavanaṃ katvā, yathā paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ samatthaṃ hoti, evaṃ katvā. Yadi niruddhā, kathaṃ appahīnāti vuttanti āha “yathā panā”tiādi. Bhavati hi taṃsadisepi tabbohāro yathā “sā eva tittirī, tāneva osadhāni, tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti ca. Dukkhakkhayāyāti tadatthavisesanatthanti āha “khayatthāyā”ti. Paṭisandhikāyanti paṭisandhigahaṇapubbakaṃ kāyaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ “bālenā”ti karaṇavacanaṃ nissakketi āha “bālato”ti. Bhāvinā saha paṭisandhinā sappaṭisandhiko. Yo pana ekantato tenattabhāvena arahattaṃ pattuṃ bhabbo, so bhāvinā paṭisandhinā “appaṭisandhiko”ti, tato visesanatthaṃ “sappaṭisandhiko”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, so ca yāva ariyabhūmiṃ na okkamati, tāva bāladhammasamaṅgī evāti katvā “sabbopi puthujjano bālo”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi “appaṭisandhiko khīṇāsavo paṇḍito”ti khīṇāsava-saddena appaṭisandhiko visesito. Yadi evaṃ sekkhā kathanti āha “sotāpannā”tiādi. Te hi sikhāpattapaṇḍiccabhāvalakkhaṇābhāvato paṇḍitāti na vattabbā khīṇāsavā viya, balavatarānaṃ [M 2.0048] pana bāladhammānaṃ pahīnattā bālātipi na vattabbā puthujjanā viya. Bhajiyamānā pana catusaccasampaṭivedhaṃ upādāya paṇḍitapakkhaṃ bhajanti, na bālapakkhaṃ vuttakāraṇenāti.

For both the fool and the wise person, ignorance and craving are the conditions for the production of the body. Hence it is said: 'Kamma... have ceased.' Having made it impel means having made the impulsion that has been grasped, having made it so that it is able to draw forth rebirth-linking. If they have ceased, how is it said that they are 'not abandoned'? It is explained by the passage beginning: 'But just as....' For the same designation is used for something similar, as in: 'that same partridge,' 'those same medicinal herbs,' and 'by the residual result of that same kamma.' For the destruction of suffering: this is to specify the purpose; thus it says, 'for the purpose of destruction.' The body with rebirth-linking means the body that is preceded by the grasping of rebirth-linking. In the Pāli text, it explains the instrumental 'by the fool' (bālena) with the ablative 'from the fool' (bālato). One who has a future rebirth-linking is 'one with rebirth-linking' (sappaṭisandhiko). But one who is definitely able to attain arahantship in that very existence is called 'one without rebirth-linking' (appaṭisandhiko) in regard to a future rebirth-linking. To distinguish from that, 'one with rebirth-linking' is said. Although this is said, so long as one has not entered the noble plane, one is still endowed with the qualities of a fool. For this reason it is said, 'Every ordinary person is a fool.' For thus, in the phrase 'the wise one is the taintless one, who is without rebirth-linking,' the term 'one without rebirth-linking' is qualified by the word 'taintless one' (khīṇāsavo). If so, what about the trainees? It is said: 'The stream-enterer,' and so on. For they should not be called 'wise' like the taintless ones, because they lack the characteristic of having reached the summit of wisdom; but nor should they be called 'fools' like ordinary people, because the stronger qualities of a fool have been abandoned. But when analyzed, on account of their penetration of the Four Noble Truths, they belong to the side of the wise, not to the side of the fool, for the reason stated.

Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on the Fool and the Wise Person is concluded.

10. Paccayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discourse on Conditions

20. Sabbampi saṅkhataṃ appaṭicca uppannaṃ nāma natthīti paccayadhammopi attano paccayadhammaṃ upādāya paccayuppanno, tathā paccayuppannadhammopi attano paccayuppannaṃ upādāya paccayadhammoti yathārahaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannatā. Yesaṃ vineyyānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādadesanāyeva subodhato [V 2.0042] upaṭṭhāti, tesaṃ vasena suṭṭhu vibhāgaṃ katvā paṭiccasamuppādo desito. Yesaṃ pana vineyyānaṃ tadubhayasmiṃ vibhajja sute eva dhammābhisamayo hoti, te sandhāya bhagavā tadubhayaṃ vibhajja dassento “paṭiccasamuppādañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi paṭiccasamuppanne ca dhamme”ti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhīti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “satthā imasmiṃ sutte”tiādimāha. Paccayassa bhāvo paccayattaṃ, paccayanibbattatā. Asabhāvadhamme na labbhatīti “sabhāvadhamme”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu ca jāti jarā maraṇañca sabhāvadhammo na hoti, yesaṃ pana khandhānaṃ jāti jarā maraṇañca, te eva sabhāvadhammā, atha kasmā desanāya te gahitāti? Nāyaṃ doso, jāti jarā maraṇañhi paccayanibbattānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ vikāramattaṃ, naññesaṃ, tasmā te gahitāti. Uppādā vā tathāgatānanti na vineyyapuggalānaṃ maggaphaluppatti viya jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇuppatti tathāgatuppādāyattā, atha kho sā tathāgatānaṃ uppādepi anuppādepi hotiyeva. Tasmā sā kāmaṃ asaṅkhatā viya dhātu na niccā, tathāpi “sabbakālikā”ti etena jātipaccayato jarāmaraṇuppattīti dasseti. Tenāha “jātiyeva jarāmaraṇassa paccayo”ti. Jātipaccayāti ca jātisaṅkhātapaccayā. Hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ. Ṭhitāva sā dhātu, yāyaṃ idappaccayatā jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayatā tassa byabhicārābhāvato. Idāni na kadāci jāti jarāmaraṇassa paccayo na hoti hotiyevāti jarāmaraṇassa paccayabhāve niyameti. Ubhayenapi yathāvuttassa paccayabhāvo yattha [M 2.0049] hoti, tattha avassaṃbhāvitaṃ dasseti. Tenāha bhagavā “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti. Dvīhi padehi. Tiṭṭhantīti yassa vasena dhammānaṃ ṭhiti, sā idappaccayatā dhammaṭṭhitatā. Dhammeti paccayuppanne dhamme. Niyameti viseseti. Hetugatavisesasamāyogo hi hetuphalassa evaṃ dhammatāniyāmo evāti.

20. There is nothing conditioned that arises without depending on a condition. Even a condition-phenomenon, depending on its own condition-phenomenon, is dependently arisen; likewise, a dependently arisen phenomenon, depending on its own dependently arisen phenomenon, is a condition. Thus, there is the state of being a condition and being dependently arisen for phenomena according to their suitability. For those disciples for whom the teaching on dependent origination is easily understood just as it is, dependent origination is taught with a thorough analysis on their account. But for those disciples who attain the penetration of the Dhamma only when both are analyzed and heard, the Blessed One, referring to them, began this teaching by analyzing and showing both, saying: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena.” To explain this meaning, it is said: “The Teacher in this sutta…,” and so on. The state of a condition is conditionality, being produced by a condition. Because it is not found in phenomena without an intrinsic nature, it is said to be in “phenomena with an intrinsic nature.” But are not birth, aging, and death themselves phenomena without an intrinsic nature? Since the aggregates to which birth, aging, and death belong are indeed phenomena with an intrinsic nature, why then are the former included in the teaching? This is no fault, for birth, aging, and death are merely an alteration of phenomena with an intrinsic nature that are produced by conditions, not of anything else; therefore they are included. “Whether Tathāgatas arise or not”: the arising of aging and death conditioned by birth is not dependent on the arising of Tathāgatas, like the arising of the path and fruit for persons to be trained. Rather, it occurs whether Tathāgatas arise or not. Therefore, though that element is like the unconditioned, it is not permanent. Still, by the phrase “at all times,” it shows that the arising of aging and death is conditioned by birth. Therefore, it is said: “Birth itself is the condition for aging and death.” “Conditioned by birth” means from the condition designated as birth. The ablative case here is in the sense of cause. That element remains stable, which is this specific conditionality—the fact that birth is a condition for aging and death—because of its non-deviation. Now, it is never the case that birth is not a condition for aging and death; it always is. Thus, it determines its state as a condition for aging and death. By both terms, it shows the necessity of the state of being a condition, as stated, wherever it occurs. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “That element remains stable.” With two terms. “They exist” (tiṭṭhanti): that by which the stability of phenomena is maintained is this specific conditionality, the fixed nature of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā). “Phenomena” (dhamme) means dependently arisen phenomena. “Determines” (niyameti) means it specifies. For the specific connection pertaining to the cause is precisely the fixed nature of cause and effect.

Aparo nayo – ṭhitāva sā dhātūti yāyaṃ jarāmaraṇassa idappaccayatā “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti, esā dhātu esa sabhāvo. Tathāgatānaṃ uppādato pubbe uddhañca appaṭivijjhiyamāno, majjhe ca paṭivijjhiyamāno na tathāgatehi uppādito, atha kho sambhavantassa jarāmaraṇassa sabbakālaṃ jātipaccayato sambhavoti ṭhitāva sā dhātu, kevalaṃ pana sayambhuñāṇena abhisambujjhanato “ayaṃ dhammo tathāgatena abhisambuddho”ti pavedanato ca tathāgato “dhammasāmī”ti vuccati, na apubbassa uppādanato. Tena vuttaṃ “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti. Sā eva “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti ettha vipallāsābhāvato evaṃ avabujjhamānassa etassa sabhāvassa, hetuno vā tatheva bhāvato ṭhitatāti dhammaṭṭhitatā, jāti vā jarāmaraṇassa uppādaṭṭhiti pavattaāyūhana-saṃyoga-palibodha-samudaya-hetupaccayaṭṭhitīti taduppādādibhāvenassā ṭhitatā “dhammaṭṭhitatā”ti phalaṃ pati sāmatthiyato hetumeva vadati. Dhārīyati [V 2.0043] paccayehīti vā dhammo, tiṭṭhati tattha tadāyattavuttitāya phalanti ṭhiti, dhammassa ṭhiti dhammaṭṭhiti. Dhammoti vā kāraṇaṃ paccayabhāvena phalassa dhāraṇato, tassa ṭhiti sabhāvo, dhammato ca añño sabhāvo natthīti dhammaṭṭhiti, paccayo. Tenāha “paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 4). Dhammaṭṭhiti eva dhammaṭṭhitatā. Sā eva dhātu “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti imassa sabhāvassa, hetuno vā aññathattābhāvato, “na jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti viññāyamānassa ca tabbhāvābhāvato niyāmatā vavatthitabhāvoti dhammaniyāmatā. Phalassa vā jarāmaraṇassa jātiyā sati sambhavo dhamme hetumhi ṭhitatāti dhammaṭṭhitatā, asati asambhavo dhammaniyāmatāti evaṃ phalena hetuṃ vibhāveti, taṃ “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”tiādinā vuttaṃ. Imesaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayatāsaṅkhātaṃ idappaccayataṃ abhisambujjhati paccakkhakaraṇena [M 2.0050] abhimukhaṃ bujjhati yāthāvato paṭivijjhati, tato eva abhisameti abhimukhaṃ samāgacchati, ādito kathento ācikkhati, uddisatīti attho. Tameva uddesaṃ pariyosāpento deseti. Yathāuddiṭṭhamattaṃ niddisanavasena pakārehi ñāpento paññāpeti. Pakārehi eva patiṭṭhapento paṭṭhapeti. Yathāniddiṭṭhaṃ paṭiniddesavasena vivarati vibhajati. Vivaṭañhi vibhattañca atthaṃ hetūdāharaṇadassanehi pākaṭaṃ karonto uttānīkaroti. Uttānīkaronto tathā paccakkhabhūtaṃ katvā nigamanavasena passathāti cāha.

Another method: 'That element remains stable' (ṭhitāva sā dhātu) refers to the specific conditionality of aging and death, that 'dependent on birth is aging and death'—this is the element, this is its nature. It was not penetrated before the arising of the Tathāgatas, nor after, but it was penetrated by them during their time. It was not originated by the Tathāgatas. Rather, aging and death always arise dependent on birth—thus, that element remains stable. However, it is only through self-awakened knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa) that 'this Dhamma was fully understood by the Tathāgata' and through declaring it that the Tathāgata is called 'the Lord of Dhamma,' not because of originating what did not exist before. Therefore, it is said, 'That element remains stable.' This very fact—'dependent on birth is aging and death'—because there is no distortion in understanding this nature, or because the cause remains in that very state, is called the 'stability of phenomena' (dhammaṭṭhitatā). Or, birth is the arising, persistence, continuity, aggregation, connection, obstruction, origination, causal condition, and stability for aging and death; the stability of this process—its arising and so forth—is called the 'stability of phenomena.' The effect, due to its capability, speaks of the cause itself. Alternatively, 'Dhamma' (dhammo) is what is upheld by conditions, and 'stability' (ṭhiti) is that the effect persists because its existence is dependent on that. The stability of Dhamma is the 'stability of phenomena.' Or, 'Dhamma' means the cause, which sustains the effect by serving as a condition. Its stability is its nature. And since there is no other nature apart from Dhamma, 'stability of phenomena' refers to the condition. Therefore, it is said: 'Wisdom in the comprehension of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (Paṭisambhidāmagga, Mātikā 4). The stability of phenomena itself is the 'stability of phenomena.' This very element—'dependent on birth is aging and death'—because of the unchanging nature of this reality, or because of the absence of any state where 'aging and death are not dependent on birth,' establishes its regulation—this is the 'regularity of phenomena' (dhammaniyāmatā). Alternatively, the effect—aging and death—arises when birth is present, due to the stability of phenomena as the cause. When birth is absent, there is no arising—this is the 'regularity of phenomena.' Thus, the effect distinguishes the cause. This is what is meant by 'That element remains stable,' etc. The conditionality of aging and death, designated as 'specific conditionality' (idappaccayatā), is fully understood through direct realization—it is comprehended face-to-face, penetrated as it truly is. From that, one fully understands—comes face-to-face with it. Beginning to explain, he declares it—this is the meaning of 'recites' (uddisati). Concluding that recitation, he teaches it (deseti). Having merely pointed it out, he makes it known through detailed explanation, revealing it by way of analysis (paññāpeti). Having explained it, he establishes it through modes of clarification (paṭṭhapeti). As explained, he elaborates it by way of detailed exposition, analyzing and distinguishing it (vivarati vibhajati). Making clear and classified the meaning through examples and demonstrations of causes, he makes it evident (uttānīkaroti). Making it evident, he presents it as directly seen, concluding with 'Behold!' (passatha).

Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādīsūti jātiādīnaṃ jarāmaraṇapaccayabhāvesu. Tehi tehi paccayehīti yāvatakehi paccayehi yaṃ phalaṃ uppajjamānārahaṃ, avikalehi teheva tassa uppatti, na ūnādhikehīti. Tenāha “anūnādhikehevā”ti. Yathā taṃ cakkhurūpālokamanasikārehi cakkhuviññāṇassa sambhavoti. Tena taṃtaṃphalanipphādane tassā paccayasāmaggiyā tappakāratā tathatāti vuttāti dasseti. Sāmagginti samodhānaṃ, samavāyanti attho. Asambhavābhāvatoti anuppajjanassa abhāvato. Tathāvidhapaccayasāmaggiyañhi satipi phalassa anuppajjane tassāvitathatā siyā. Aññadhammapaccayehīti aññassa phaladhammassa paccayehi. Aññadhammānuppattitoti tato aññassa phaladhammassa anuppajjanato. Na hi kadāci cakkhurūpālokamanasikārehi sotaviññāṇassa sambhavo atthi. Yadi siyā, tassā sāmaggiyā aññathatā nāma siyā, na cetaṃ atthīti “anaññathatā”ti vuttaṃ. Paccayatoti paccayabhāvato. Paccayasamūhatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatāti tā-saddena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ yathā “devoyeva devatā”ti, idappaccayānaṃ samūho idappaccayatāti samūhattho tāsaddo yathā “janānaṃ samūho janatā”ti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthato veditabba”nti.

'Dependent on birth is aging and death,' and so forth (jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādīsu) refers to birth and so on being the conditions for aging and death. 'By those very conditions' (tehi tehi paccayehi)—by whatever conditions a result is capable of arising, it arises precisely through those, neither more nor fewer. Hence it is said, 'neither deficient nor excessive' (anūnādhikeheva). Just as, for example, eye-consciousness arises from the conditions of eye, form, light, and attention. Thus, in the production of that particular result, the suitability of that assemblage of conditions is called 'suchness' (tathatā). 'Assemblage' (sāmaggi) means coming together, a union—this is the meaning. 'Because of the absence of non-arising' (asambhavābhāvato)—due to the absence of non-production. For if, even when there is an assemblage of conditions of such a kind, the result did not arise, that would be the falsity of those conditions. 'Through conditions of other phenomena' (aññadhammapaccayehi)—through conditions belonging to a different resultant phenomenon. 'Because of the non-arising of other phenomena' (aññadhammānuppattito)—because another resultant phenomenon does not arise from those conditions. For instance, ear-consciousness never arises from the conditions of eye, form, light, and attention. If it did, that assemblage of conditions would be called 'otherwise' (aññathatā). But since this is not the case, it is said to be 'not otherwise' (anaññathatā). 'From conditionality' (paccayatoti)—from the state of being a condition. 'From a collection of conditions' (paccayasamūhatoti)—here too, the same principle applies. The state of being these conditions is this-conditionality (`idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā`); here the word is augmented by the suffix `-tā`, as in `devatā` (deity) from `deva`. Alternatively, `idappaccayatā` means 'a collection of these conditions,' where the suffix `-tā` has a collective meaning, as in `janatā` (populace), a collection of people. To convey this meaning, it is said: 'Here, the characteristic should be understood from the standpoint of grammar' (lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthato veditabbaṃ).

Na [V 2.0044] niccaṃ sassatanti aniccaṃ. Jarāmaraṇaṃ na aniccaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vikārabhāvato anipphannattā, tathāpi “anicca”nti pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Esa nayo saṅkhatādīsupi. Samāgantvā kataṃ sahiteheva paccayehi nibbattetabbato yathāsabhāvaṃ samecca sambhuyya paccayehi katanti saṅkhataṃ[M 2.0051]. Paccayārahaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca na vinā tena sahitasametameva uppannanti paṭiccasamuppannaṃ. Tenāha “paccaye nissāya uppanna”nti. Khayasabhāvanti bhijjanasabhāvaṃ. Vigacchanakasabhāvanti sakabhāvato apagacchanakasabhāvaṃ. Virajjanakasabhāvanti palujjanakasabhāvaṃ. Nirujjhanakasabhāvanti khaṇabhaṅgavasena pabhaṅgusabhāvaṃ. Vuttanayenāti jarāya vuttanayena. Janakappaccayānaṃ kammādīnaṃ. Kiccānubhāvakkhaṇeti ettha kiccānubhāvo nāma yathā pavattamāne paccaye tassa phalaṃ uppajjati, tathā pavatti, evaṃ santassa pavattanakkhaṇe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmiṃ khaṇe paccayo attano phaluppādanaṃ pati byāvaṭo nāma hoti, imasmiṃ khaṇe ye dhammā rūpādayo upalabbhanti tato pubbe, pacchā ca anupalabbhamānā, tesaṃ tato uppatti niddhārīyati, evaṃ jātiyāpi sā niddhāretabbā taṃkhaṇūpaladdhatoti. Yadi evaṃ nippariyāyatova jātiyā kutoci uppatti siddhi, atha kasmā “ekena pariyāyenā”ti vuttanti? Jāyamānadhammānaṃ vikārabhāvena upaladdhabbattā. Yadi nipphannadhammā viya jāti upalabbheyya, nippariyāyatova tassā kutoci uppatti siyā, na cevaṃ upalabbhati, atha kho anipphannattā vikārabhāvena upalabbhati. Tasmā “ekena pariyāyenettha aniccātiādīni yujjantī”ti vuttaṃ. Na pana jarāmaraṇe, janakappaccayānaṃ kiccānubhāvakkhaṇe tassa alabbhanato. Teneva “ettha ca aniccanti…pe… aniccaṃ nāma jāta”nti vuttaṃ.

What is not eternal or lasting is impermanent. Aging and death are not, in the primary sense, impermanent, because they are transformations of conditioned phenomena and are not directly produced; yet they are called 'impermanent' figuratively. This method applies also to 'conditioned' and so forth. What is made by coming together, what is to be produced by conditions acting in concert, and what is made by conditions meeting and combining according to their own nature—this is called 'conditioned' (saṅkhata).
