What arises dependent on conditions, not without them, but only when they are together and combined, is called 'dependently arisen' (paṭiccasamuppanna). Hence it is said, 'arisen in dependence on conditions.' 'Having the nature of decay' means having the nature of breaking apart. 'Having the nature of vanishing' means having the nature of departing from its own state. 'Having the nature of fading away' means having the nature of crumbling. 'Having the nature of cessation' means having a fragile nature due to momentary dissolution. 'By the method stated'—that is, by the method stated regarding aging. Of the generating conditions such as kamma. 'The moment of the function's influence': Here, 'function's influence' means the activity of a condition such that its result arises when the condition is active; this is said to occur at the moment of such activity. This is what is meant: At the moment when a condition is engaged in producing its own result, whatever phenomena such as form are found at that time—but not found before or after—their arising from that is determined. Thus, birth too must be determined as being found at that moment. If, in this way, the arising of birth is established directly from something, then why is it said, 'in one sense'? Because things being born are to be apprehended as a state of change. If birth were to be apprehended like a fully produced phenomenon, its arising from something would be direct. But it is not apprehended in that way; rather, because it is not a fully produced phenomenon, it is apprehended as a state of change. Therefore, it is said, 'here, in one sense, terms like 'impermanent' are applicable.' But this does not apply to aging and death, because at the moment of the generating condition's influence, birth is not found. Hence it is said, 'here, impermanent... what is called impermanent is what is born.'

Savipassanāyāti ettha saha-saddo appadhānabhāvadīpano “samakkhikaṃ, samakasa”ntiādīsu viya. Appadhānabhūtā hi vipassanā, yathābhūtadassanamaggapaññā pajānāti. “Purimaṃ anta”nti vuccamāne paccuppannabhāvassapi gahaṇaṃ siyāti “purimaṃ antaṃ atīta”nti vuttaṃ. Vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañcāti sassatāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”nti atīte attano vijjamānataṃ, adhiccasamuppattiāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “yato pabhuti ahaṃ, tato pubbe na nu kho ahosi”nti atīte attano avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kasmā? Vicikicchāya ākāradvayāvalambanato. Tassā pana atītavatthutāya gahitattā sassatādhiccasamuppattiākāranissitatā dassitā eva. Āsappanaparisappanapavattikaṃ katthacipi appaṭivattihetubhūtaṃ vicikicchaṃ kasmā uppādetīti na vicāretabbametanti dassento āha “kiṃkāraṇanti na vattabba”nti[M 2.0052]. Kāraṇaṃ vā vicikicchāya ayonisomanasikāro, tassa andhabālaputhujjanabhāvo, ariyānaṃ adassāvitā cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jātiliṅgupapattiyoti khattiyabrāhmaṇādijātiṃ, gahaṭṭhapabbajitādiliṅgaṃ, devamanussādiupapattiñca. Nissāyāti upādāya. Tasmiṃ [V 2.0045] kāle yaṃ santānaṃ majjhimaṃ pamāṇaṃ, tena yutto pamāṇiko, tadabhāvato adhikabhāvato vā “appamāṇiko”ti veditabbo. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā. Te hi “kathaṃ nu kho”ti issarena vā brahmunā vā pubbakatena vā ahetuto vā nibbattoti cintetīti vadanti. Ahetuto nibbattikaṅkhāpi hi hetuparāmasanamevāti. Paramparanti pubbāparappavattiṃ. Addhānanti kālādhivacanaṃ, tañca bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañcāti sassatāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhāna”nti anāgate attano vijjamānataṃ, ucchedāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “yasmiñca attabhāve ucchedanakaṅkhā, tato paraṃ nu kho bhavissāmī”ti anāgate attano avijjamānatañca kaṅkhatīti heṭṭhā vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ.

In 'savipassanāyāti,' the word 'saha' indicates a secondary or subordinate aspect, as in 'samakkhikaṃ' (with flies) and 'samakasa' (with mud). For insight is secondary; it is the wisdom of the path, which sees things as they truly are, that understands. When 'the former end' is spoken of, the present state might also be included, hence it is stated, 'the former end is the past.' Regarding 'existence and non-existence': based on the suspicion of eternalism, one wonders, 'Did I exist in the past?' concerning one's own existence in the past. Based on the suspicion of accidental origination, one wonders, 'Before the time I originated, did I not exist?' concerning one's own non-existence in the past. Why? Because doubt relies on taking up these two aspects. But since its object is the past, its reliance on the ideas of eternalism and accidental origination is indeed shown. Why does doubt arise, which is restless, roaming, and in some cases becomes a cause for not turning back? Demonstrating that this should not be investigated, it is said, 'It should not be said, "What is the reason?"' The reason for doubt, however, is unwise attention, the state of being a blind, foolish ordinary person, and not having seen the noble ones—this should be understood. 'Jātiliṅgupapattiyoti' refers to caste such as khattiya or brahmin, status such as householder or renunciant, and rebirth such as a deva or human. 'Nissāyāti' means 'depending on' or 'taking as a basis.' At that time, one is considered 'measured' if the continuum is of medium measure, but due to its absence or excess, one should be understood as 'immeasurable.' 'Kecīti' refers to some teachers of the Sārasamāsa. They say, 'How then?'—one thinks, 'Is it produced by a god, by Brahmā, by a previous action, or without a cause?' For even doubt about uncaused origination is indeed a consideration of causes. 'Paramparanti' means the continuous sequence of before and after. 'Addhānanti' is a word for time, and it should be seen as a word used in the locative sense. Regarding 'existence and non-existence': based on the suspicion of eternalism, one wonders, 'Will I exist in the future?' concerning one's own existence in the future. Based on the suspicion of annihilation, one wonders, 'After this existence, which is subject to the doubt of annihilation, will I then exist?' concerning one's own non-existence in the future. This should be connected in the same way as stated below.

Paccuppannaṃ addhānanti addhāpaccuppannassa idhādhippetattā “paṭisandhimādiṃ katvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ kathaṃ, idaṃ katha”nti pavattanato kathaṃkathā, vicikicchā, sā assa atthīti kathaṃkathī. Tenāha “vicikicchī”ti. Kā ettha cintā? Ummattako viya bālaputhujjanoti paṭikacceva vuttanti adhippāyo. Taṃ mahāmātāya puttaṃ. Muṇḍesunti muṇḍena anicchantaṃ jāgaraṇakāle na sakkāti suttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ kuladhammavasena yathā ekacce kulatāpasā. Rājabhayenāti ca vadanti. Sītibhūtanti idaṃ madhurakabhāvappattiyā kāraṇavacanaṃ. “Setabhūta”ntipi pāṭho, udake ciraṭṭhānena setabhāvaṃ pattanti attho.

The present time is called 'paccuppannaṃ addhāna' because the strictly present moment is intended here; hence, it is said, 'starting from rebirth-linking,' etc. 'How is this? How is that?'—the proliferation of such questioning is 'kathaṃkathā,' which is doubt (vicikicchā). One who has this is a 'kathaṃkathī.' Hence, he is called 'vicikicchī.' What reflection is there on this? The meaning is that it is already stated summarily as being like a madman, an ignorant ordinary person. That refers to the chief minister's son. 'Muṇḍesuṃ' means they shaved his head while he was sleeping, as he was unwilling and it was not possible while he was awake; this was according to family custom, like certain family ascetics. And some say it was due to fear of the king. 'Sītibhūta' is a term stating the reason for having attained a sweet taste. There is also the reading 'setabhūta,' meaning having attained a white color from long exposure in water.

Attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati kaṇṇo viya sūtaputtasaññī, sūtaputtasaññīti sūriyadevaputtassa puttasaññī. Jātiyā vibhāviyamānāya “aha”nti tassa attano parāmasanaṃ sandhāyāha “evampi siyā kaṅkhā”ti. Manussāpi ca rājāno viyāti manussāpi ca keci ekacce rājāno viyāti adhippāyo. Vuttanayameva “saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāyā”tiādinā. Etthāti “kathaṃ nu khosmī”ti pade. Abbhantare jīvoti [M 2.0053] paraparikappitaṃ antarattānaṃ vadati. Soḷasaṃsādīnanti ādi-saddena sarīraparimāṇaaṅguṭṭha-yavaparamāṇuparimāṇatādike saṅgaṇhāti. Sattapaññatti jīvavisayāti diṭṭhigatikānaṃ matimattaṃ, paramatthato pana sā attabhāvavisayāvāti āha “attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhāna”nti. Yatāyaṃ āgato, yattha ca gamissati, taṃ ṭhānanti attho. Sotāpanno adhippeto vicikicchāpahānassa diṭṭhattā. Itarepi tayoti sakadāgāmīādayo avāritā eva. “Ayañca…pe… sudiṭṭhā”ti nippadesato saccasaṃpaṭivedhassa jotitattā.

He doubts his own warrior status like Kaṇṇa, who is designated as a charioteer's son—'designated as a charioteer's son' means designated as the son of the god Sūriya. Regarding birth being defined, referring to his own clinging to 'I,' he says, 'Might there even be doubt in this way?' 'And humans are like kings' means that some humans are like certain kings. The same method as stated applies to 'depending on shape and appearance,' etc. Here—in the phrase, 'How now am I?'—he speaks of the inner soul as an inner self imagined by others. 'The sixteen-fold, etc.'—by the word 'etc.,' it includes measurements like the body's size, a thumb's length, a barley grain's size, an atom's size, and so on. That the concept of a 'being' pertains to a soul is merely the opinion of those holding wrong views; but in an ultimate sense, it pertains to individual existence, so it is said, 'the place of coming, going, and establishment for individual existence.' This means the place from which one has come and to which one will go. A stream-enterer is intended here, because the abandoning of doubt is seen in them. The other three—the once-returner and so on—are also not excluded. 'This one... clearly seen'—because the complete penetration of the truths is illuminated.

Paccayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Paccayasutta is completed.

Āhāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āhāravagga is completed.

3. Dasabalavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers

1. Dasabalasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Powers

21. Paṭhamaṃ [V 2.0046] dutiyasseva saṅkhepo paṭhamasutte saṅkhepavuttassa atthassa vitthāravasena dutiyasuttassa desitattā, tañca pana bhagavā paṭhamasuttaṃ saṅkhepato desesi, dutiyaṃ tato vitthārato. Paṭhamaṃ vā saṃkhittarucīnaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayena saṅkhepato desesi, dutiyaṃ pana attano ruciyā tato vitthārato. Sīhasamānavuttikā hi buddhā bhagavanto, te attano ruciyā kathentā attano thāmaṃ dassentāva kathenti, tasmā dutiyasuttavasena cettha atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma, tasmiṃ saṃvaṇṇite paṭhamaṃ saṃvaṇṇitameva hotīti adhippāyo.

21. The first discourse is a summary of the second, for the second discourse was taught as an expansion of the meaning stated concisely in the first. The Blessed One taught the first discourse concisely, and the second in greater detail than that. Or, he taught the first discourse concisely to suit the inclinations of individuals who prefer conciseness, while he taught the second in greater detail than that, according to his own preference. For the Blessed Buddhas, whose conduct is like that of a lion, teach according to their own preference, demonstrating their own strength as they speak. Therefore, we will provide an explanation of the meaning here based on the second discourse, with the intention that when it is explained, the first is explained as well.

Dasabalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Powers is finished.

2. Dutiyadasabalasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Ten Powers

22. Tatthāti dutiyasutte. Dasahi balehīti dasahi anaññasādhāraṇehi ñāṇabalehi, tāni tathāgatasseva balānīti tathāgatabalānīti vuccanti. Kāmañca tāni ekaccānaṃ sāvakānampi uppajjanti, yādisāni [M 2.0054] pana buddhānaṃ ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇādīni uppajjanti, na tādisāni tadaññesaṃ kadācipi uppajjantīti. Hatthikulānusārenāti vakkhamānahatthikulānusārena. Kāḷāvakanti kulasaddāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso. Esa nayo sesesupi. Pakatihatthikulanti giricaranadicaravanacarādippabhedā gocariyakāḷāvakanāmā sabbāpi balena pākatikā hatthijāti. Dasannaṃ purisānanti thāmamajjhimānaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ. Ekassa tathāgatassa kāyabalanti ānetvā sambandho. Ekassāti ca tathā heṭṭhākathāyaṃ āgatattā desanāsotena vuttaṃ. Nārāyanasaṅghātabalanti ettha nārā vuccanti rasmiyo, tā bahū nānāvidhā ito uppajjantīti nārāyanaṃ, vajiraṃ, tasmā nārāyanasaṅghātabalanti vajirasaṅghātabalanti attho. Tathāgatassa kāyabalanti tathāgatassa pākatikakāyabalaṃ. Saṅgahaṃ na gacchati attano balābhāvato, tato evassa bāhirakatā lāmakatā ca. Tadubhayaṃ panassa kāraṇena dassetuṃ “etañhi nissāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aññanti kāyabalato aññaṃ tato visuṃyeva. Dasasu ṭhānesu dasasu ñātabbaṭṭhānesu. Yāthāvapaṭivedhato sayañca akampayaṃ, puggalañca taṃsamaṅgiṃ neyyesu adhibalaṃ karotīti āha “akampanaṭṭhena upatthambhanaṭṭhena cā”ti.

22. Therein: in the second discourse. With ten powers: with ten unique powers of knowledge; these are called the powers of the Tathāgata because they belong only to the Tathāgata. And although these powers arise in some disciples, they are not of the same kind as those that arise in the Buddhas, such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, etc., which never arise in others at any time. Following the elephant lineage: following the lineage of elephants to be described. Kāḷāvaka: the neuter gender is used here with reference to the word for lineage (kula). This method applies to the rest as well. The natural elephant lineage: all elephant species, distinguished as mountain-roaming, river-roaming, forest-roaming, etc., named Kāḷāvaka of suitable range, are all naturally strong elephant types. The strength of ten men: the strength of ten men of medium vigor. The bodily strength of one Tathāgata is to be brought in and connected. One: as it has come up in the explanation below, it is said in the stream of the teaching. The strength of Nārāyaṇa’s consolidated force: here, 'nārā' are said to be rays; because many diverse rays arise from it, it is called 'nārāyana,' which is a diamond (vajra). Therefore, 'the strength of Nārāyaṇa’s consolidated force' means 'the strength of a diamond's consolidated force.' The bodily strength of the Tathāgata: the natural bodily strength of the Tathāgata. It is not included in the comparison due to its own lack of strength; hence it is external and inferior. To show both of these as the reason, it is said, “relying on this,” etc. Other: other than bodily strength, distinct from it. In ten places: in ten knowable instances. By penetrating things as they are, he himself is unshakable and makes the person endowed with this knowledge exceedingly strong among those to be guided. Therefore, it is said, “by the meaning of unshakableness and by the meaning of support.”

Ṭhānañca [V 2.0047] ṭhānatoti kāraṇañca kāraṇato. Kāraṇañhi yasmā phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttitāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā “ṭhāna”nti vuccati. Vipariyāyena aṭṭhānanti akāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ bhagavā yena ñāṇena ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ, ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ na hetū na paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhānanti pajānāti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “ṭhānañca…pe… jānanaṃ eka”nti. Kammasamādānānanti kammaṃ samādiyitvā katānaṃ kusalākusalakammānaṃ, kammaññeva vā kammasamādānaṃ. Ṭhānaso hetusoti paccayato ca hetuto ca. Tattha gatiupadhikālapayogā vipākassa ṭhānaṃ, kammaṃ hetu. Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadājānananti sabbagatigāminiyā agatigāminiyā ca paṭipadāya maggassa jānanaṃ, bahūsupi manussesu ekameva pāṇaṃ hanantesu “imassa cetanā nirayagāminī bhavissati, imassa tiracchānayonigāminī”ti iminā nayena ekavatthusmimpi kusalākusalacetanāsaṅkhātānaṃ paṭipattīnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvajānanaṃ[M 2.0055]. Anekadhātunānādhātulokajānananti cakkhudhātuādīhi kāmadhātuādīhi vā bahudhātuno, tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ viparītatāya nānappakāradhātuno khandhāyatanadhātulokassa jānanaṃ. Parasattānanti paresaṃ sattānaṃ. Nānādhimuttikatājānananti hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvassa jānanaṃ. Tesaṃyevāti parasattānaṃyeva. Indriyaparopariyattajānananti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvassa aparabhāvassa vuddhiyā ceva hāniyā ca jānanaṃ. Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ, “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ, savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ, paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnañca navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesavodānavuṭṭhānajānananti hānabhāgiyassa, visesabhāgiyassa “vodānampi vuṭṭhānaṃ, tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti (vibha. 828) evaṃ vuttapaguṇajjhānassa ceva bhavaṅgaphalasamāpattīnañca jānanaṃ. Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimañhi paguṇajjhānaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā vodānampi “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Bhavaṅgena pana sabbajhānehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Phalasamāpattiyā nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhānameva sandhāya “tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Pubbenivāsajānananti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena nivuṭṭhakkhandhānaṃ jānanaṃ. Cutūpapātajānananti sattānaṃ cutiyā upapattiyā ca yāthāvato jānanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Āsavakkhayajānanaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇanti attho. Yattha panetāni vitthārato āgatāni saṃvaṇṇitāni, tāni dassento “abhidhamme panā”tiādimāha.

As to `the possible as a cause`: this means a cause from the standpoint of being a cause. Because the fruit stands dependent on the cause, it arises and continues due to that dependence; therefore it is called 'the possible.' Conversely, the impossible should be understood as a non-cause. The Blessed One comprehends both with his knowledge: whatever phenomena are causes and conditions for the arising of certain phenomena, that is their possibility; whatever phenomena are not causes and conditions for the arising of certain phenomena, that is their impossibility. Referring to this, it is said: 'The possible and... the knowing is one.' The undertaking of kamma: the wholesome and unwholesome kammas performed by undertaking kamma, or simply kamma itself is the undertaking of kamma. From the standpoint of possibility and cause: from the condition and the cause. Therein, the destination (gati), basis of existence (upadhi), time, and effort are the possibility for the result; the kamma is the cause. The knowledge of the path leading everywhere: the knowledge of the path that leads to all destinations or to no destination. Even among many people killing a single being, knowing the nature of their intentions—'This one's volition will lead to hell, this one's to the animal realm'—thus, in a single instance, knowing the true nature of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action without error. The knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements: the knowledge of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements of the world, which are diverse due to the variety of elements such as the eye-element, etc., or the sense-sphere elements, etc. Of other beings: of other beings. The knowledge of their diverse inclinations: the knowledge of the diverse states of inclinations of beings, whether inferior, etc. Of those same beings: of other beings. The knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties: the knowledge of the growth and decline of the faculties such as faith, etc. Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments: of the four jhānas beginning with the first, the eight liberations such as 'One with form sees forms,' etc., the three concentrations such as those with thought and examination, etc., and the nine successive attainments beginning with the first jhāna attainment. The knowledge of defilement, cleansing, and emergence: the knowledge concerning the proficient jhānas that partake of decline and distinction, and concerning the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the attainment of fruition. For each lower proficient jhāna serves as the proximate cause for the higher one; therefore, cleansing is also called 'emergence.' Emergence from all jhānas, however, occurs through the life-continuum. The phrase 'emergence from this or that concentration' is said with reference to emergence from the attainment of cessation by means of the attainment of fruition. The knowledge of past lives: the knowledge of past abodes through the recollection of past lives, knowing the aggregates that have been lived in. The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings: the accurate knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood as given in the Visuddhimagga. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints: the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, meaning the knowledge of the path. Showing where these are explained and described in detail, he said: 'But in the Abhidhamma...' etc.

Byāmohabhayavasena saraṇapariyesanaṃ sārajjanaṃ sārado, byāmohabhayaṃ. Vigato sārado etassāti [V 2.0048] visārado, tassa bhāvo vesārajjaṃ. Taṃ pana ñāṇasampadaṃ pahānasampadaṃ desanāvisesasampadaṃ khemaṃ nissāya pavattaṃ catubbidhaṃ paccavekkhaṇāñāṇaṃ. Tenāha “catūsu ṭhānesū”tiādi. Catūsūti paraparikappitesu vatthūsu. Paraparikappitesu vā vatthumattesu codanākāraṇesu. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti evaṃ paṭijānantena tayā. Ime dhammāti “idaṃ pañcamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, ayaṃ chaṭṭho upādānakkhandho, idaṃ [M 2.0056] terasamaṃ āyatana”nti veditabbā ime dhammā. Anabhisambuddhā appaṭividdhattāti.

Timidity is bashfulness and the fear of delusion; it is the seeking of refuge on account of fear and delusion. One from whom timidity is gone is called 'confident,' and his state is confidence. That confidence, however, relying on the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of distinction in teaching, and security, arises as fourfold reviewing knowledge. Therefore, it is said, 'in four instances,' etc. 'In four instances' means regarding matters conceived by others, or regarding mere objects conceived by others as grounds for accusation. As for `of you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One`: this means 'by you who claim thus: "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One."' As for `these phenomena`: these phenomena are to be understood through such examples as 'this is the fifth noble truth, this is the sixth clinging-aggregate, this is the thirteenth sense-base.' `Are not fully awakened to`: meaning, not penetrated.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ anabhisambuddhadhammasaṅkhāte codanāvatthusmiṃ. Kocīti samaṇādīhi añño vā yo koci. Saha dhammenāti saha hetunā. “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu viya hetupariyāyo idha dhamma-saddo. Hetūti ca uppattisādhanahetu veditabbo, na kārako sampāpako vā. Nimittanti kāraṇaṃ, taṃ panettha codanāvatthumeva. Na samanupassāmi sammāsambuddhabhāvato. Khemappattoti akhemappattarūpāya codanāya anupaddavaṃ patto niccalabhāvappatto. Vesārajjappattoti visāradabhāvappatto. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – ime āsavāti kāmāsavādīsu ime nāma āsavā na parikkhīṇāti āsavakkhayavacanenettha sabbakilesappahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Na hi so kileso atthi, yo sabbaso āsavesu khīṇesu nappahīyeyya. Antarāyikāti antarāyakarā, saggavimokkhādhigamassa antarāyakarāti attho. Dhammo hi yo saṃkilesato niyyāti, so “niyyāniko”ti vutto. Dhamme niyyante taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo niyyānikoti voharito hotīti tassa paṭikkhipanto “so na niyyātī”ti āha. Kathaṃ pana desanādhammo niyyātīti vuccati? Niyyānatthasamādhānato, so abhedopacārena “niyyātī”ti vutto. Atha vā “dhammo desito”ti ariyadhammassa adhippetattā na koci virodho.

Here, 'in that' refers to the matter of accusation concerning a Dhamma not fully comprehended. 'Someone' means any other person, whether an ascetic or another. 'With the Dhamma' means with the cause. In texts like the Dhammapaṭisambhidā, the term 'Dhamma' here is a synonym for cause. The cause should be understood as the productive cause, not the agent or the accomplisher. 'The sign' means the reason, but here it specifically refers to the matter of accusation. 'I do not perceive' [any ground for accusation] due to the state of being a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. 'Having attained safety' means having reached a state free from the harm of accusations, having attained a stable state. 'Having attained confidence' means having reached a state of assurance. The same method applies to the rest. Here, however, there is a distinction—'these taints' refers to the taints of sensuality, etc., meaning these taints are not yet destroyed. Through the statement of the destruction of the taints, the abandonment of all defilements is stated. For there is no defilement that, when all taints are destroyed, would not be abandoned. 'Obstructive' means causing hindrance—hindering the attainment of heaven and liberation. The Dhamma that leads out from defilement is called 'emancipatory.' When the Dhamma is emancipatory, the person endowed with it is said to be emancipatory. Rejecting this, he says, 'He does not lead out.' But how is the teaching Dhamma said to lead out? Because it accomplishes the purpose of leading out, it is figuratively called 'leading out' by way of non-distinction. Or, because 'the Dhamma has been taught' refers to the noble Dhamma, there is no contradiction.

Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ, asantasanaṭṭhena āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ sabbaññutaṃ. Āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyitāya āsabhā nāma pubbabuddhā. Sabbaññutapaṭijānanavasena abhimukhaṃ gacchanti, catasso vā parisā upasaṅkamantīti āsabhā. Catassopi hi parisā buddhābhimukhā evaṃ tiṭṭhanti, na tiṭṭhanti parammukhā. Idampīti “usabho”ti idampi padaṃ. Tassāti nisabhassa. Yesaṃ baluppādāvaṭṭhānānaṃ vasena usabhassa āsabhaṇṭhānaṃ icchitaṃ, tato sātisayānaṃ eva tesaṃ vasena āsabhaṇṭhānaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci loke upamaṃ nāma buddhaguṇānaṃ nidassanabhāvena vuccati, sabbaṃ taṃ nihīnameva. Tiṭṭhamāno cāti atiṭṭhantopi tiṭṭhamāno eva paṭijānāti nāma. Upagacchatīti anujānāti.

'This of the bull' means 'āsabhaṃ' (bull-like), which is like a bull in the sense of being fearless, signifying the supreme state, omniscience. Because they are established in the bull-like state, past Buddhas are called 'āsabhā.' They go forth by declaring omniscience, or the four assemblies approach them—hence they are called 'āsabhā.' Indeed, all four assemblies stand facing the Buddha; they do not stand with their backs turned. 'This also' refers to the word 'usabha.' 'Of him' means of the bull-like one. The bull-like state is desired on the basis of the arising of strength and steadfastness; it should be understood that for those who are exceedingly superior, their bull-like state is based on these same qualities to an even greater degree. Whatever simile exists in the world spoken as an illustration of the Buddha's qualities, all of it is inferior. 'And while standing' means that even when not standing, he is said to make the claim of standing. 'Approaches' means he approves.

Aṭṭha [V 2.0049][M 2.0057] kho imāti idaṃ vesārajjañāṇassa baladassanaṃ. Yathā hi byattaṃ parisaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viññūnaṃ cittaṃ ārādhanasamatthāya kathāya dhammakathikassa chekabhāvo paññāyati, evaṃ imā aṭṭha parisā patvā satthu vesārajjañāṇassa balaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “parisāsū”ti. Khattiyaparisāti khattiyānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ samūho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Māraparisāti mārakāyikānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ samūho. Mārasadisānaṃ mārānaṃ parisāti māraparisā. Sabbā cetā parisā uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena gahitā. Manussā hi “ettha rājā nisinno”ti vutte pakativacanampi vattuṃ na sakkonti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, evaṃ uggā khattiyaparisā, brāhmaṇā tīsu vedesu kusalā honti, gahapatayo nānāvohāresu ca akkharacintāya ca kusalā, samaṇā sakavādaparavādesu kusalā, tesaṃ majjhe dhammakathākathanaṃ nāma ativiya bhāriyaṃ. Devānaṃ uggabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Amanussoti hi vuttamatte manussānaṃ sakalasarīraṃ kampati, tesaṃ rūpaṃ disvāpi saddaṃ sutvāpi sattā visaññitāpi honti. Evaṃ amanussaparisā uggā. Iti cetā parisā uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena vuttā. Kasmā panettha yāmādiparisā na gahitāti? Bhusaṃ kāmābhigiddhatāya yonisomanasikāravirahato. Yāmādayo hi uḷāruḷāre kāme paṭisevantā tatthābhigiddhatāya dhammassavanāya sabhāvena cittampi na uppādenti, mahābodhisattānaṃ pana buddhānañca ānubhāvena ākaḍḍhiyamānā kadāci nesaṃ payirupāsanādīni karonti tādise mahāsamaye. Teneva hi vimānavatthudesanāpi taṃnimittā bahulā nāhosi. Seṭṭhanādanti kenaci appaṭihatabhāvena uttamanādaṃ. Abhītanādanti vesārajjayogato kutoci nibbhayanādaṃ. Sīhanādasuttenāti khandhiyavagge āgatena sīhanādasuttena. Sahanatoti khamanato. Hananatoti vidhamanato viddhaṃsanato. Yathā vātiādi “sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttassa atthassa viññāpanaṃ.

'These eight' is a demonstration of the power of the knowledge of confidence. Just as the skill of a Dhamma-speaker is recognized when, having entered a competent assembly, he speaks in a way capable of pleasing the minds of the wise, so too, upon reaching these eight assemblies, the power of the Teacher's knowledge of confidence becomes manifest. Hence it is said, 'in assemblies.' 'The assembly of nobles' means a gathering of assembled nobles. This method applies everywhere. 'The assembly of Māra' means a gathering of Māra's host. The assembly of māras similar to Māra is the assembly of Māra. All these assemblies are taken as a demonstration of their formidable state. For when it is said, 'Here sits the king,' people cannot even speak naturally; sweat pours from their armpits. Such is the formidable nature of the assembly of nobles. Brahmins are skilled in the three Vedas, householders are skilled in various affairs and the study of letters, and ascetics are skilled in their own and others' doctrines. To give a Dhamma talk in their midst is an exceedingly weighty task. As for the formidable nature of the gods, there is nothing to be said. At the mere mention of 'non-human,' a person's entire body trembles; upon seeing their form or hearing their sound, beings can even become unconscious. Thus the assembly of non-humans is formidable. In this way, these assemblies are described as a demonstration of their formidable state. Why, then, are the assemblies of Yama and others not included here? Because of their excessive greed for sensual pleasures and their lack of wise attention. The beings of Yama and similar realms, indulging in gross sensual pleasures, are so greedy for them that they do not even naturally give rise to the thought of hearing the Dhamma. Only rarely, drawn by the power of great bodhisattas and Buddhas, do they attend upon them at such great occasions. For this very reason, the teaching on the stories of the mansions was not frequently given on account of them. 'Foremost roar' means a supreme roar, due to being unobstructed by anyone. 'Fearless roar' means a roar free from fear from any quarter, due to the possession of confidence. 'By the Lion’s Roar Sutta' means by the Lion's Roar Sutta that comes in the Khandha Vagga. 'Enduring' is from 'to forbear.' 'Destroying' is from 'to demolish' or 'to shatter.' The phrase 'just as' and so on is an explanation of the meaning stated in brief: 'He roars a roar like a lion’s roar.'

Etanti “brahmacakka”nti etaṃ padaṃ. Paññāpabhāvitanti cirakālaparibhāvitāya pāramitāpaññāya vipassanāpaññāya ca uppāditaṃ. Karuṇāpabhāvitanti “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinayappavattāya mahākaruṇāya uppāditaṃ. Yathā abhinikkhamanato pabhuti mahābodhisattānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamanavirodhinī [M 2.0058] paṭipatti natthi, evaṃ tusitabhavanato niyatabhāvāpattito ca paṭṭhāyāti dutiyatatiyanayā ca gahitā. Phalakkhaṇeti aggaphalakkhaṇe. Paṭivedhaniṭṭhattā arahattamaggañāṇaṃ vajirūpamatāyeva sātisayo paṭivedhoti “phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paṭiladdhassapi desanāñāṇassa kiccanipphatti parassa bujjhanamattena hotīti “aññāsikoṇḍaññassa sotāpatti…pe… phalakkhaṇe pavattanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana yāva parinibbānā desanāñāṇappavatti, tasseva pavattitassa dhammacakkassa ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ [V 2.0050] pavattitacakkassa cakkavattino cakkaratanassa ṭhānaṃ viya. Ubhayampīti pi-saddena lokiyadesanāñāṇassa itarena anaññasādhāraṇatāvasena samānataṃ sampiṇḍeti. Urasi jātatāya uraso sambhūtanti orasaṃ ñāṇaṃ.

'This' refers to the term 'brahmacakka' (Wheel of Brahma). Developed by wisdom—produced by the wisdom of the perfections cultivated over a long time and by the wisdom of insight. Developed by compassion—produced by great compassion arising from the thought, 'Alas, this world has fallen into suffering,' and so forth. Just as for the great bodhisattvas from the time of their renunciation onwards there is no practice opposing the attainment of the noble path, so too from their existence in Tusita and their attainment of a fixed destiny onward—this is understood through the second and third methods. 'At the moment of fruition' means at the supreme moment of fruition. The knowledge of the path of arahantship, due to the completion of penetration and its diamond-like nature, is a supremely excellent penetration—thus it is said, 'arisen at the moment of fruition.' The function of the teaching-knowledge, attained thereby, is fulfilled merely by another's awakening—thus it is said, 'the stream-entry of Āññāsikoṇḍañña... is called the setting in motion at the moment of fruition.' From then until final nibbāna, the process of the teaching-knowledge continues; this should be understood as the standing of the Dhamma wheel that has been set in motion, like the standing of the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch once it has been set in motion. 'Both'—the word 'pi' summarizes the equality of the worldly teaching-knowledge with the other by way of their being unique and not shared by others. 'Born from the breast'—arisen from the breast—thus, the knowledge is innate.

Iti rūpanti ettha iti-saddo anavasesato rūpassa sarūpanidassanatthoti tassa “idaṃ rūpa”nti etena sādhāraṇato ca sarūpanidassanamāha. Ettakaṃ rūpanti etena anavasesato “ito uddhaṃ rūpaṃ natthī”ti nimittassa aññassa abhāvaṃ. Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “ruppanasabhāvañcevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ruppanaṃ sītādivirodhipaccayasamavāye visadisuppatti. Ādi-saddena ajjhattikabāhirādibhedaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Lakkhaṇa…pe… vasenāti kakkhaḷattādilakkhaṇavasena sandhāraṇādirasavasena sampaṭicchanādipaccupaṭṭhānavasena bhūtattayādipadaṭṭhānavasena ca. Evaṃ pariggahitassāti evaṃ sādhāraṇato ca lakkhaṇādito ca pariggahitassa. Avijjāsamudayāti avijjāya uppādā, atthibhāvāti attho. Nirodhavirodhī hi atthibhāvo hoti, tasmā nirodhe asati atthibhāvo hoti, tasmā purimabhave siddhāya avijjāya sati imasmiṃ bhave rūpassa samudayo rūpassa uppādo hotīti attho. Taṇhāsamudayā kammasamudayāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Avijjādīhi ca tīhi atītakālikattā tesaṃ sahakārīkāraṇabhūtaṃ upādānampi gahitamevāti veditabbaṃ. Pavattipaccayesu kabaḷīkāraāhārassa balavatāya, so eva gahito, “āhārasamudayā”ti pana gahitena pavattipaccayatāmattena utucittānipi gahitāneva hontīti dvādasasamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpassa paccayato dassanampi bhavitabbamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nibbattilakkhaṇantiādinā kālavasena [M 2.0059] udayadassanamāha. Tattha bhūtavasena magge udayaṃ passitvā ṭhito idha santativasena anukkamena khaṇavasena passati. Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhoti aggamaggañāṇena avijjāya anuppādanirodhato anāgatassa anuppādanirodho hoti paccayābhāve abhāvato. Paccayanirodhenāti avijjāsaṅkhātassa paccayassa nirodhabhāvena. Taṇhānirodhāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Āhāranirodhāti pavattipaccayassa kabaḷīkārāhārassa abhāvā. Rūpanirodhāti taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa abhāvo hoti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇanti bhavakālavasena hetudvayadassanaṃ. Tasmā taṃ padaṭṭhānavasena pageva passitvā ṭhito idha santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati.

“It is form”: Here, the word ‘iti’ indicates the complete nature of form, showing its own nature both generally and specifically by stating, “This is form.” “Only this much form”: This shows the absence of any other sign beyond this, meaning “There is no form beyond this.” Now, to explain this in detail, it is said: “The nature of being afflicted, etc.” Herein, “being afflicted” refers to the arising of dissimilarity due to the confluence of opposing conditions like cold, etc. The word “etc.” includes internal and external distinctions. By way of characteristics, etc., that is, by way of the characteristic of hardness, etc., by way of the function of supporting, etc., by way of the manifestation of reception, etc., and by way of the proximate cause of the three great elements, etc. “Thus comprehended”: It is comprehended both in its common aspect and by way of its characteristics, etc. “With the arising of ignorance”: This means the arising of ignorance, its existence. For existence is indeed opposed to cessation; therefore, when cessation is absent, existence occurs. Therefore, when ignorance, established in a previous existence, is present, in this existence there is the arising of form, the production of form—this is the meaning. “With the arising of craving, with the arising of kamma”: Here too, the same reasoning applies. It should be understood that clinging, being a cooperative cause of these three (ignorance, etc.) due to their past-time nature, is also included. Among the conditions for continuity, because of the strength of physical nutriment, it alone is taken. But by the mere fact of being a condition for continuity, taken as “with the arising of nutriment,” temperature and mind are also included. Therefore, it should be understood that form can also be seen as conditioned by its twelve origins. “By the characteristic of production, etc.”: Here, the arising is shown by way of time. In this context, one who, having seen the arising by way of the elements on the path, stands here, sees it by way of continuity, gradually, by way of moments. “With the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of form”: Through the knowledge of the highest path, from the non-arising cessation of ignorance, there is a non-arising cessation of future form, due to its absence in the absence of a condition. “By the cessation of conditions”: By the cessation of the condition designated as ignorance. “With the cessation of craving”: Here too, the same reasoning applies. “With the cessation of nutriment”: Due to the absence of physical nutriment, a condition for continuity. “The cessation of form”: This is the absence of form originating from that. The rest should be understood according to the method stated below. “By the characteristic of change”: This is the seeing of the two causes by way of the time of existence. Therefore, one who, having first seen it by way of its proximate cause, stands here, sees it by way of continuity, gradually, by way of moments.

Iti vedanātiādīsupi vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Sukhādibhedanti sukhadukkhaadukkhamasukhādivibhāgaṃ. Rūpasaññādibhedanti rūpasaññā, sadda… gandha… rasa… phoṭṭhabba [V 2.0051]… dhammasaññādivibhāgaṃ. Phassādibhedanti phassacetanāmanasikārādivibhāgaṃ. Lakkhaṇa…pe… vasenāti iṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇādilakkhaṇavasena iṭṭhākārasambhogarasādirasavasena kāyikaassādādipaccupaṭṭhānavasena iṭṭhārammaṇādipadaṭṭhānavasena. “Phuṭṭho vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti, phuṭṭho cetetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.93) vacanato tīsu vedanādīsu khandhesu phassasamudayāti vattabbaṃ. Viññāṇappaccayā nāmarūpa”nti vacanato viññāṇakkhandhe nāmarūpasamudayāti vattabbaṃ. Tesaṃyeva vasenāti “avijjānirodho vedanānirodho”tiādinā tesaṃyeva avijjādīnaṃ vasena yojetabbaṃ.

The meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the case of ‘It is feeling,’ etc. The division into pleasure, etc.: This means the classification into pleasure, pain, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, etc. The division into perception of form, etc.: This means the classification into perception of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, etc. The division into contact, etc.: This means the classification into contact, volition, and attention, etc. By way of characteristics, etc.: This means by way of the characteristic of experiencing the desirable, etc., by way of the function of enjoying the agreeable aspect, etc., by way of the manifestation of bodily pleasure, etc., and by way of the proximate cause of desirable objects, etc. From the statement, ‘When contacted, one feels; when contacted, one perceives; when contacted, one wills’ (SN 4.93), it should be said that in the case of the three aggregates—feeling, etc.—contact is their origin. From the statement, ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form,’ it should be said that in the case of the consciousness aggregate, name-and-form originates. By means of these very things: As in ‘With the cessation of ignorance, feeling ceases,’ etc., it should be connected by means of these very things, ignorance, etc.

Upādānakkhandhānaṃ samudayatthaṅgamavasena titthiyānaṃ avisayopi sappadeso sīhanādo dassito. Idāni nippadeso anulomapaṭilomavasena saṅkhepato vitthārato paccayākāravisayo anaññasādhāraṇo dassīyatīti āha, “ayampi aparo sīhanādo”ti. Tassāti “imasmiṃ satī”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttapaṭiccasamuppādapāḷiyā. Ettha ca “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujhtī”ti avijjādīnaṃ bhāve saṅkhārādīnaṃ bhāvassa, avijjādīnaṃ nirodhe saṅkhārādīnaṃ nirodhassa kathanena purimasmiṃ paccayalakkhaṇe niyamo dassito “imasmiṃ [M 2.0060] sati eva, nāsati, imassa uppādā eva, nānuppādā, nirodhā eva, nānirodhā”ti. Tenedaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ antogadhaniyamaṃ idha paṭiccasamuppādassa vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nirodhoti ca avijjādīnaṃ virāgā vigamena āyatiṃ anuppādo appavatti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā”tiādi. Nirodhavirodhī ca uppādo, yena so uppādanirodhavibhāgena vutto “imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti. Tenetaṃ dasseti “asati nirodhe uppādo nāma, so cettha atthibhāvoti vuccatī”ti. “Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti idameva hi lakkhaṇaṃ. Pariyāyantarena “imassa uppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti vadantena parena purimaṃ visesitaṃ hoti. Tasmā na vattamānaṃyeva sandhāya “imasmiṃ satī”ti vuttaṃ, atha kho maggena anirujjhanasabhāvañcāti viññāyati. Yasmā ca “imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti dvidhāpi uddiṭṭhassa lakkhaṇassa niddesaṃ vadantena bhagavatā “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādinā nirodhova vutto, tasmā natthibhāvopi nirodho evāti natthibhāvaviruddho atthibhāvo anirodhoti dassitaṃ hoti. Tena anirodhasaṅkhātena atthibhāvena uppādaṃ viseseti. Tato idha na kevalaṃ atthibhāvamattaṃ uppādoti attho adhippeto, atha kho anirodhasaṅkhāto atthibhāvo cāti ayamattho vibhāvito hoti. Evametaṃ lakkhaṇadvayavacanaṃ aññamaññaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena sātthakanti veditabbaṃ. Ko panāyaṃ anirodho nāma, yo “atthibhāvo, uppādo”ti ca vuttoti? Appahīnabhāvo ca anibbattitaphalabhāvena [V 2.0052] phaluppādanārahatā cāti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paramatthadīpaniyaṃ udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (udā. aṭṭha. 1). Vuttanayena veditabbo.

The partial lion's roar, which is not the domain of the heretics, has been shown by way of the arising and cessation of the aggregates of clinging. Now, the domain of the modes of conditionality, which is complete and unique, is being shown concisely and in detail, by way of conformity and opposition. Thus, it is said, 'This too is another roar of the lion.' This refers to the Pāli text of dependent origination stated concisely by 'When this exists,' etc. And here, by stating 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases,' the existence of formations, etc., when ignorance, etc., exist, and the cessation of formations, etc., when ignorance, etc., cease, the regularity in the characteristic of conditionality mentioned earlier is shown: 'When this exists, it is thus, not otherwise; with the arising of this, it arises thus, not otherwise; with the cessation of this, it ceases thus, not otherwise.' Therefore, this characteristic, which includes an inherent regularity, should be seen as stated here in dependent origination. And 'cessation' means the non-arising and non-occurrence in the future due to the fading away and disappearance of ignorance, etc. As it is said, 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance...' etc. And arising is opposed to cessation, for which reason it is stated with a division into arising and cessation: 'With the cessation of this, that ceases.' By this, it shows that 'When there is no cessation, what is called arising exists—that is said to be its presence here.' The phrase 'When this exists, that comes to be' is indeed the characteristic itself. By stating it in another way—'With the arising of this, that arises'—the former is specified by the latter. Therefore, 'When this exists' is not stated merely with reference to the present, but rather, it should be understood as indicating the nature of not having been made to cease by the path. And because the Blessed One, while explaining the twofold characteristic stated as 'When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases,' spoke of cessation in the passage 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease...' etc., therefore, absence itself is cessation. Thus, existence, which is opposed to absence, is shown as non-cessation. By this non-cessation, designated as existence, arising is distinguished. Therefore, here, not merely the mere existence is intended as arising, but rather, existence characterized as non-cessation—this meaning is clarified. Thus, this twofold statement of characteristics, mutually qualifying and qualified, should be understood as meaningful. But what is this non-cessation, which is called 'existence' and 'arising'? Briefly, here, it is the state of not being abandoned and the state of being suitable for producing results by not having produced its result. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Paramatthadīpanī, the Udāna Commentary (Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 1).

Pañcakkhandhavibhajanādivasenāti pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ dvādasapadikassa paccayākārassa vibhajanavasena. Imasmiñhi dasabalasutte dhammassa desitākāro pañcakkhandhapaccayākāramatto. Tenāha “pañcakkhandhapaccayākāradhammo”ti. Ācariyamuṭṭhiyā akaraṇena vibhūto, so pana atthato ca saddato ca pihito heṭṭhāmukhajāto vā na hotīti āha “anikujjito”ti. Vivaṭoti vibhāvito. Tenāha “vivaritvā ṭhapito”ti[M 2.0061]. Pakāsitoti ñāṇobhāsena obhāsito ādīpitoti āha “dīpito jotito”ti. Tattha tattha chinnabhinnaṭṭhāne. Sibbitagaṇṭhitanti vākaṃ gahetvā sibbitaṃ, sibbituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṭṭhāne vākena gaṇṭhitañca. Chinnapilotikābhāvena vigatapilotiko dhammo, tassa chinnapilotikassa paṭilomatā chinnabhinnatābhāvenāti dassento “na hetthā”tiādimāha. Nivāsanapārupanaṃ pariggahaṇaṃ. Sayaṃ paṭibhānaṃ kappetvā. Vaḍḍhentā attano samayaṃ. Samaṇakacavaranti samaṇavesadhāraṇavasena samaṇapaṭirūpatāya samaṇānaṃ kacavarabhūtaṃ. Attano rūpapavattiyā karaṇḍaṃ kucchitaṃ dhuttaṃ vāti pavattetīti kāraṇḍavo, dussīlo. Taṃ kāraṇḍavaṃ. Niddhamathāti nīharatha. Kasambunti samaṇakasaṭaṃ. Apakassathāti apakaḍḍhatha nanti attho. Palāpeti palāpasadise. Tathā hi taṇḍulasārarahito dhaññapaṭirūpako thusamattako palāpoti vuccati, evaṃ sīlādisārarahito samaṇapaṭirūpako palāpo viyāti palāpo, dussīlo. Te palāpe. Vāhethāti apanetha. Patissatāti bāḷhasatitāya patissatā hothāti.

“By way of the analysis of the five aggregates, etc.” means by way of the analysis of the twelve-factored dependent origination of the five aggregates of clinging. For in this Discourse on the Ten Powers, the manner in which the Dhamma is taught is limited to the dependent origination of the five aggregates. Therefore it is said: “the Dhamma of the dependent origination of the five aggregates.” It is made manifest by the absence of the teacher’s closed fist; it is not hidden in meaning or word, nor is it turned downwards. Thus it is said: “not overturned.” “Made clear” (vivaṭo) means explained (vibhāvito). Therefore it is said: “laid open and revealed.” “Made manifest” (pakāsito) means illuminated by the light of knowledge, lit up. Thus it is said: “illuminated, made to shine.” “Here and there, in places cut and broken.” “Sewn and knotted” means sewn by taking bark fiber, and knotted with bark fiber in a place where one cannot sew. The Dhamma is free from rags due to the absence of torn rags. To show that the opposite of being like a torn rag is the state of being cut and broken, it is said: “not below,” etc. “The taking up of lower and upper robes” means appropriation. “Having conceived his own inspiration.” “Extending their own doctrine.” “The ascetic’s refuse” means that which is the refuse of ascetics by wearing the guise of an ascetic, by being a mere imitation of ascetics. “A kāraṇḍava” (kāraṇḍavo) means one who, through his own bodily behavior, acts in a despicable or deceitful manner, thus an immoral person. That kāraṇḍava. “Expel” (niddhamatha) means drive out (nīharatha). “Refuse” (kasambu) means the dregs of ascetics. “Remove” (apakassatha) means drag away; this is the meaning. Regarding “chaff” (palāpe): this refers to those who are like chaff. For just as husk, devoid of the essence of rice grains, is mere chaff, a counterfeit of grain, so too is one devoid of the essence of virtue and so on, a counterfeit of an ascetic—thus called “chaff,” an immoral person. Those chaff-like ones. “Drive away” (vāhetha) means remove them. “Be mindful” (patissatā) means be strongly mindful; this is the meaning.

Saddhāya pabbajitenāti rājūpaddavādīhi anupaddutena “evañhi taṃ otiṇṇaṃ jātiādisaṃsārabhayaṃ vijinissāmī”ti vaṭṭanissaraṇatthaṃ āgatāya saddhāya vasena pabbajitena. Ācārakulaputtoti ācārena abhijāto. Tenāha “yato kutocī”tiādi. Jātikulaputtoti jātisampattiyā abhijāto. Viññuppasatthāni aṅgāni sammāpadhāniyaṅgabhāvena, kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhabhāvena vīriyaṃ ārabhantassa tathāpavattavīriyavasena “taco ekaṃ aṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Navasu ṭhānesu samādhātabbanti “kālavasena pañcasu, iriyāpathavasena catūsū”ti evaṃ navasu ṭhānesu vīriyaṃ samādhātabbaṃ pavattetabbaṃ.

“Having gone forth out of faith” (saddhāya pabbajita) means one who has gone forth by means of faith, unafflicted by royal troubles and so forth, having come for the purpose of escaping the round, thinking: “Thus will I conquer the fear of the cycle of existence beset by birth and so on.” “A son of a good family due to conduct” (ācārakulaputta) means one well-born due to conduct. Hence it is said: “from whatever place,” etc. “A son of a good family due to birth” (jātikulaputta) means one well-born due to the excellence of birth. “The praised factors of exertion” (viññuppasatthāni aṅgāni) means by way of being factors of right effort, by being indifferent to body and life, for one who undertakes effort in such a way, due to the exertion that thus occurs, it is said: “the skin is one factor.” The same principle applies to the rest. “In nine places exertion is to be applied” (navasu ṭhānesu samādhātabbaṃ) means “by time in five, by postures in four,” thus in nine places exertion is to be applied and set going.

So dukkhaṃ viharatīti kusītapuggalo niyyānikasāsane vīriyārambhassa akaraṇena sāmaññatthassa anuppattiyā dukkhaṃ viharati. Sakaṃ vā atthaṃ sadatthaṃ ka-kārassa da-kāraṃ katvā[V 2.0053]. Kusītassa atthaparihāyanaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “cha dvārānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nisajjāvasena pīṭhamaddanato pīṭhamaddano, nirassanavacanaṃ tassa, kassacipatthassa adhāraṇato kevalaṃ pīṭhabhārabhūtoti adhippāyo. Aññattha pana “makhamaddano”ti [M 2.0062] vuccati, tattha dānamicchāya paresaṃ makhaṃ passantoti attho. Laṇḍapūrakoti kucchipūraṃ bhuñjitvā vaccakuṭipūrako.

“He dwells in suffering” means the lazy person dwells in suffering because, by not making an effort in the teaching that leads to liberation, he fails to attain the goal of asceticism. Or, his own welfare, ‘sadatthaṃ’, by changing the ‘ka’ sound to ‘da’. To show the root cause of the decline in the lazy person’s welfare, it is said: “the six doors,” etc. “Seat-crusher” (pīṭhamaddano) means one who wears out the seat by sitting continuously; it is a word of contempt for him, the meaning being that he is merely a burden on the seat because he cannot fulfill anyone’s expectations. Elsewhere, however, it is said: “makhamaddano,” meaning he looks upon others’ sacrifices (makhaṃ) desiring gifts. “Laṇḍapūrako” means one who fills his stomach and then fills the latrine.

“Āraddhavīriyo”tiādīsu “kusīto puggalo”ti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo, āsīsāya vasena thomito. Āraddhavīriyeti paggahitavīriye. Pahitatteti nibbānaṃ patipesitacitte. Etena sāvakānaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ satthuvandanānisaṃsañca dassesi.

In the passages beginning with “one of aroused energy,” the meaning should be understood in contrast to what was said about “the lazy person” (kusīto puggalo); here, he is praised by way of aspiration. “Aroused energy” (āraddhavīriya) means one who has exerted energy. “Resolute” (pahitatta) means one whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna. Through this, he shows both the right practice of disciples and the benefits of honoring the Teacher.

Hīnenāti vaṭṭanissitena dhammena. Tenāha “hīnāya saddhāyā”tiādi. Aggenāti seṭṭhena vivaṭṭanissitena dhammena, īsakampi katakālusiyavigataṭṭhena maṇḍaṭṭhena ca pasannampi surādi na pātabbaṃ. Sāsananti pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhalakkhaṇaṃ sāsanaṃ. Pasannaṃ vigatadosamalattā pasādaniyattā ca. Pātabbañca pattena viya sukhena paribhuñjitabbato duccaritasabbakilesakasāvamalapaṅkadosarahitattā ca.

“By the inferior” (hīnena) means by the Dhamma dependent on the round of existence. Hence it is said: “by inferior faith,” etc. “By the superior” (aggena) means by the excellent Dhamma, which is transcendent. Even a small amount of liquor, etc., that is clear and purified, free from any impurity caused by fermentation, should not be drunk. “The teaching” (sāsana) is the teaching characterized by theory, practice, and realization. “Clear” (pasannaṃ) because it is free from the stains of faults and is of a pleasing nature. And it is “to be drunk” (pātabbaṃ) to be enjoyed easily, like drinking from a bowl, because it is devoid of all misconduct, defilements, astringency, impurities, and the mud of faults.

Maṇḍabhūtā bodhipakkhiyadhammadesanāpi desanāmaṇḍo. Tassa ekasseva pana desanāmaṇḍassa paṭiggāhakā suppaṭipannā dosarahitā catasso parisā paṭiggahamaṇḍo. Maggabrahmacariyaṃ taggatikattā sakalopi bodhipakkhiyadhammarāsi brahmacariyamaṇḍo. Tenāha “katamo desanāmaṇḍo”tiādi. Tattha viññātāroti saccānaṃ abhisametāvino. Tathā hi ādito “catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ ācikkhaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pubbabhāge “atthi ayaṃ loko”tiādinā idhalokaparalokagatasammosavigamena pavatto adhimokkhova adhimokkhamaṇḍo. Chaḍḍetvā samucchedavasena vijahitvā. Catubhūmakassa saddhindriyassa adhimokkhamaṇḍena maṇḍabhūtaṃ adhimokkhaṃ. Ādi-saddena “paggahamaṇḍo vīriyindriyaṃ kosajjakasaṭa”ntiādiṃ pāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Etthāti etasmiṃ sāsane, “maṇḍasmi”nti vā vacane. Kāraṇavacanaṃ, tena “satthā sammukhībhūto”ti sammukhabhāvanāyogo nirāsaṅkaphalāvahoti dasseti. Tenāha “asammukhā”tiādi. Pamāṇanti anurūpaṃ bhesajjassa pamāṇaṃ. Uggamananti bhesajjassa vamanaṃ virecanaṃ, tassa vā vasena dosadhātūnaṃ vamanaṃ virecanaṃ. Evamevāti yathā bhesajjamaṇḍaṃ vejjasammukhā nirāsaṅkā pivanti, evameva [M 2.0063] “satthā sammukhībhūto”ti nirāsaṅkā vīriyaṃ katvā, maṇḍapeyya sāsanaṃ pivathāti yojanā. Abhiññāsamāpattipaṭilābhena sānisaṃsā. Maggaphalādhigamanena savaḍḍhi[V 2.0054]. Paratthanti attano diṭṭhānugatiāpattiyā, tathā sammāpaṭipajjantānaṃ paresaṃ atthanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

The teaching on the factors of enlightenment, being the essence, is also the essence of the teaching. For that single essence of the teaching, the four assemblies of well-practiced, faultless recipients form the essence of acceptance. The entire mass of the factors of enlightenment, because it leads to the path and the holy life, is the essence of the holy life. Hence it is said: “What is the essence of the teaching?” etc. Herein, “those who understand” (viññātāro) are those who have attained the truths. For from the beginning, it was said: “the declaration of the four noble truths,” etc. In the preliminary stage, the conviction that arises by removing confusion about this world and the next, with the statement “this world exists,” etc., is itself the essence of conviction. “Having abandoned” (chaḍḍetvā) means having relinquished through complete eradication. The conviction of the faculty of faith pertaining to the four planes is the essence of conviction, being the essence. The word “etc.” (ādi-saddena) includes the remaining passage: “the essence of exertion is the faculty of energy, abandoning the refuse of laziness,” etc. “Here” (ettha) means in this teaching, or in the statement “in the essence.” It is a causal expression; therefore, “the Teacher being present” shows that the practice of being face-to-face bears fruit without doubt. Hence it is said: “not in the presence,” etc. “Measure” (pamāṇaṃ) means the appropriate dose of medicine. “Administration” (uggamanaṃ) means the emetic or purgative of medicine, or through it, the emetic or purgative of the humor elements. “Just so” (evameva) means just as they drink the essence of medicine without doubt in the presence of a physician, so too, “the Teacher being present,” without doubt, having exerted energy, you should drink the teaching that is to be drunk like cream—this is the connection. With the attainment of direct knowledge and meditative absorption, it has benefit. With the realization of the path and fruit, it has growth. “For the sake of others” (parattha) means for the benefit of others who practice rightly, following one’s own observed behavior—thus the meaning here should be understood.

Dutiyadasabalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse on the Ten Powers is concluded.

3. Upanisasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary to the Upanisa Sutta.

23. Jānato passatoti ettha dassanaṃ paññācakkhunāva dassanaṃ adhippetaṃ, na maṃsacakkhunāti āha “dvepi padāni ekatthānī”ti. Evaṃ santepīti padadvayassa ekatthattepi ñāṇalakkhaṇañāṇappabhāvavisayasssa tathādassanabhāvāvirodhanāti attho. Tenāha “jānanalakkhaṇañhi ñāṇa”ntiādi. Ñāṇappabhāvanti ñāṇānubhāvena ñāṇakiccavisayobhāsanti attho. Tenāha “ñāṇena vivaṭṭe dhamme passatī”ti. Jānato passatoti ca jānanadassanamukhena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā pavattāti āha – “ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāyā”tiādi. Jānatoti vā pubbabhāgañāṇena jānato, aparabhāgena ñāṇena passato. Jānatoti vā vatvā na jānanaṃ anussavākāraparivitakkamattavasena idhādhippetaṃ, atha kho rūpāni viya cakkhuviññāṇena rūpādīni tesañca samudayādike paccakkhe katvā dassananti vibhāvetuṃ “passato”ti vuttanti evaṃ vā ettha attho.

23. Here, in 'for one who knows, for one who sees,' seeing is intended as seeing with the eye of wisdom, not with the physical eye; thus it is said: 'Both words have the same meaning.' Even so, even if the two words have the same meaning, there is no contradiction with the fact of seeing thus, which is characterized by knowledge and has the power of knowledge as its object. Hence it is said: 'For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing,' etc. 'The power of knowledge' means that the object of the function of knowledge is illuminated by the power of knowledge. Therefore, it is said: 'He sees the phenomena made clear by knowledge.' And 'for one who knows, for one who sees' indicates that the teaching proceeds with the person as its basis, through the portal of knowing and seeing. Hence it is said: 'Taking the characteristic of knowledge as a basis,' etc. Alternatively, 'for one who knows' refers to knowing with the preliminary-stage knowledge, and 'for one who sees' refers to seeing with the subsequent-stage knowledge. Alternatively, having said 'for one who knows,' knowing is not intended here merely in the sense of hearsay or mere reflection; rather, just as forms are seen by eye-consciousness, so too, to clarify that one sees forms and so on, and their origin, etc., after having made them directly present, the term 'for one who sees' is used. This is the meaning here.

Āsavānaṃ khayanti āsavānaṃ accantappahānaṃ. So pana tesaṃ anuppādanirodho sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvo evāti āha “asamuppādo khīṇākāro natthibhāvo”ti. Āsavakkhayasaddassa khīṇākārādīsu āgataṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “āsavānaṃ khayā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ujumaggānusārinoti kilesavaṅkakāyavaṅkādīnaṃ pahānena ujubhūte savipassanāheṭṭhimamaggadhamme anussarantassa. Yadeva hissa parikkhīṇaṃ. Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ “tato aññā anantarā”ti khayasaṅkhāte aggamagge tappariyāpannameva ñāṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ pana aññā arahattanti. Yadipi gāthāya “khayasmiṃ”icceva vuttaṃ, samucchedavasena pana “āsave [M 2.0064] khīṇe maggo khayo”ti vuccatīti āha “maggo āsavakkhayoti vutto”ti. Samaṇoti samitapāpo adhippeto, so pana khīṇāsavo hotīti. “Āsavānaṃ khayā”ti idha phalaṃ, pariyāyena pana āsavakkhayo maggo, tena pattabbato phalaṃ. Eteneva nibbānassapi āsavakkhayabhāvo vuttoti veditabbo.

'The destruction of the taints' means the utter abandoning of the taints. But their non-arising cessation is their complete and utter non-existence; thus it is said: 'non-arising, the state of being destroyed, non-existence.' To show where the term 'destruction of the taints' is used with meanings such as 'the state of being destroyed,' it is said: 'by the destruction of the taints,' and so on. 'One who follows the straight path' means one who, by abandoning the crookedness of defilements, the crookedness of the body, and so on, recollects the lower path-factors together with insight, which have become straight. Regarding the verse: 'In the destruction, the first knowledge [arises], then immediately after, final knowledge (aññā)'—this means that in the supreme path, which is designated as destruction, the knowledge included therein arises first, and immediately after that comes final knowledge, which is arahantship. Although in the verse it is said simply 'in destruction,' by way of eradication it is said: 'When the taints are destroyed, the path is destruction.' Hence it is stated: 'The path is called the destruction of the taints.' 'An ascetic' (samaṇa) is intended as one who has pacified evil, and he is one whose taints are destroyed. Here, 'by the destruction of the taints' refers to the fruit; but figuratively, the destruction of the taints is the path, because the fruit is to be attained by it. By this it should be understood that Nibbāna, too, is spoken of as the destruction of the taints.

Jānato eva passato evāti evamettha niyamo icchito, na aññathā visesābhāvato aniṭṭhāpannovāti tassa niyamassa phalaṃ dassetuṃ “no ajānato no apassato”ti vuttanti āha [V 2.0055] “yo pana na jānāti, na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho”ti. Iminā khandhānaṃ pariññā āsavakkhayassa ekantikakāraṇanti dasseti. Etenāti “no ajānato, no apassato”ti etena vacanena. Te paṭikkhittāti ke pana teti? “Bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.228) ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.101, 227) evamādivādā. Tesu keci abhijātisaṅkantimattena saṃsārasuddhiṃ paṭijānanti, aññe issarapajāpatikāraṇādivasena. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ saṃsārādīhīti ettheva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimena padadvayenāti “jānato passato”ti iminā padadvayena. Upāyo vutto “āsavakkhayā”ti adhikārato. Imināti “no ajānato, no apassato”ti iminā padadvayena. Anupāyo hoti esa āsavānaṃ khayassa, yadidaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ apariññāti “jānato passato”ti imināva aniyamavacanena anupāyapaṭisedhopi atthato bodhito hotīti. Tameva hi atthato bodhitabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ evaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Only for one who knows, only for one who sees'—thus a rule is intended here, not otherwise; for without this distinction, an undesirable consequence would result. To show the fruit of that rule, it is said: 'Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see,' meaning: 'For one who neither knows nor sees, I do not declare it.' By this, it is shown that the full understanding of the aggregates is the certain cause for the destruction of the taints. By this—by the statement 'not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see'—those [views] are refuted. But who are they? They are proponents of such views as: 'Both the fool and the wise, having run on and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering,' or 'Beings are purified without cause, without condition,' and so on. Among them, some profess purification of the round of rebirths merely through transition of birth-class, others through a cause such as a creator god. All this should be seen as included right here by 'the cycle of existence, etc.' By the first pair of words—'for one who knows, for one who sees'—the means is stated, as 'the destruction of the taints' is the topic. By this—by the pair 'not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see'—it is shown that this is a non-means for the destruction of the taints, namely, the non-understanding of the five aggregates. Thus, by the positive statement 'for one who knows, for one who sees,' the refutation of the non-means is also understood in meaning. Indeed, to clarify this very point, the explanation has been given thus.

Dabbajātikoti dabbarūpo. So hi “drabyo”ti vuccati “drabyaṃ vinassati nādrabya”ntiādīsu. Dabbajātiko vā sārasabhāvo, sāruppasīlācāroti attho. Yathāha “na kho dabba dabbā evaṃ nibbeṭhentī”ti (pārā. 384). Vattasīse ṭhatvāti vattaṃ uttamaṃ dhuraṃ katvā. Yo hi parisuddhājīvo kātuṃ ajānantānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ attano vā vassavātādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ chattādīni karoti, so vattasīse ṭhatvā karoti nāma. Padaṭṭhānaṃ na hotīti na vattabbaṃ nāthakaraṇadhammabhāvena maggaphalādhigamassa upanissayabhāvato. Vuttañhi “yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiccakaraṇīyāni, tattha dakkho hotī”tiādi [M 2.0065] (dī. ni. 3.345). Evaṃ jānatoti evaṃ vejjakammādīnaṃ jānanahetu micchājīvapaccayā kāmāsavādayo āsavā vaḍḍhantiyeva, na pahīyanti. “Evaṃ kho…pe… āsavānaṃ khayo hotī”ti imāya pāḷiyā arahattasseva gahaṇaṃ yuttaṃ phalaggahaṇena hetuno avuttasiddhattā. Tenāha “āsavānaṃ khayante jātattā”ti.

'Of good birth' (dabbajātiko) means of an able nature. For he is called 'drabya' in such phrases as 'a substance (drabya) perishes, not a non-substance,' etc. Alternatively, 'of good birth' means of essential nature, that is, one whose virtue and conduct are suitable. As it is said: 'Indeed, Dabba, the able ones (dabbā) do not explain it thus.' 'Having stood at the head of duty' (vattasīse ṭhatvā) means having made duty the highest yoke. For one who, with a purified livelihood, makes umbrellas and so on to protect himself or his fellow celibates who do not know how to make them from rain, wind, etc., is said to do so having stood at the head of duty. It should not be said, 'It is not a proximate cause,' because it is a decisive support (upanissaya) for the attainment of the path and fruit, by being a condition that provides a refuge. As it is stated: 'In whatever various duties are to be performed for fellow celibates, he is skilled,' etc. 'Knowing thus' means that, because of knowing medical practice and so on, which is a condition for wrong livelihood, the taints such as the taint of sensuality increase; they are not abandoned. By this Pāli passage, 'Thus indeed... there is the destruction of the taints,' it is proper to take it as referring only to arahantship, because by the taking of the fruit, the cause is implicitly established even if unstated. Therefore, it is said: 'because it is born at the end of the destruction of the taints.'

Āgamanaṃ āgamo, taṃ āvahatīti āgamanīyā, pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Khayasminti bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe bhummaṃ, khayeti pana visaye. Tenāha “āsavakkhayasaṅkhāte”ti. Upanisīdati phalaṃ etthāti kāraṇaṃ upanisā. Arahattaphalavimutti ukkaṭṭhaniddesato. Sāti vimutti. Assāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa. Manasmiṃ vivaṭṭanissite pana anantarūpanissayāpi paccayā sambhavantīti “labbhamānavasena paccayabhāvo veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

Coming is arrival (āgamo); that which brings it is 'conducive to arrival' (āgamanīyā), the preliminary practice. 'In destruction' (khayasmiṃ) is the locative of circumstance; but 'in destruction' (khaye) is the locative of sphere. Therefore, it is said: 'designated as the destruction of the taints.' The fruit sits down near this, thus it is a cause, a decisive support (upanisā). Because of the supreme designation of the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. 'That' (sā) refers to liberation. 'Of this' (assa) refers to the reviewing knowledge. But when the mind is reliant on the unrolling, even immediately preceding decisive support conditions are possible. Thus it is said: 'the state of being a condition should be understood in the sense of being obtainable.'

Virajjati [V 2.0056] asesasaṅkhārato etenāti virāgo, maggo. Nibbindati etāyāti nibbidā, balavavipassanā. Tenāha “etenā”tiādi. Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāpi muccitukamyatāpakkhikā evāti adhippāyena “catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. “Yāva maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, tāva taruṇavipassanā”ti hi vacanato upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇato paraṃ balavavipassanā. Rūpārūpadhammānaṃ visesabhūto sāmaññabhūto ca yo yo sabhāvo yathāsabhāvo, tassa jānanaṃ yathāsabhāvajānanaṃ. Tadeva dassanaṃ. Paccakkhakaraṇatthena ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā ca gahitā hoti. Tenāha “taruṇavipassana”ntiādi. Saṅkhāraparicchedeñāṇanti nāmarūpapariggahañāṇaṃ vadati. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ paccayapariggaho dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇantipi vuccati. Nayavipassanādikaṃ anupassanāñāṇaṃ sammasanaṃ. Maggāmaggeñāṇanti maggāmaggaṃ vavatthapetvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ. So hi pādakajjhānasamādhi taruṇavipassanāya paccayo hoti. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5.; 4.99; 5.1071) hi vuttaṃ.

Dispassion (virāga) is so called because one becomes dispassionate towards all formations by means of it; this is the path. Disenchantment (nibbidā) is so called because one becomes disenchanted by it; it is strong insight. Therefore, it is said: 'by this,' and so on. The contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā) is also on the side of the desire for liberation, hence it is called 'a designation for the four knowledges.' For it is said: 'As far as the purification of the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, so far is it immature insight.' Strong insight comes after the knowledge of arising and passing away that is free from corruptions. The knowing of the specific and general nature of material and immaterial phenomena, whatever its inherent nature, is 'knowing things as they really are' (yathāsabhāvajānanaṃ). That itself is vision. By the meaning of direct realization, both full understanding as the known and full understanding by investigation are included. Therefore, it is said: 'immature insight,' and so on. The knowledge that discerns formations (saṅkhāraparicchedañāṇa) refers to the knowledge of discerning name and form. The overcoming of doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa) is also called the knowledge of grasping conditions and the knowledge of the establishment of phenomena. Insight by way of method and so on, the knowledge of contemplation (anupassanāñāṇa), is comprehension (sammasana). The knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇa) is the knowledge that stands having determined what is the path and what is not the path. For that concentration of the foundational absorption is a condition for immature insight. As it is said: 'One who is concentrated understands and sees things as they really are.'

Pubbabhāgasukhanti upacārajjhānasahitasukhaṃ. Daratha paṭippassaddhīti kāmacchandādikilesadarathassa paṭipassambhanaṃ. “Sukhaṃpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmī”ti ettha adhippetasukhaṃ dassetuṃ “appanāpubbabhāgassa sukhassā”ti vuttaṃ. “Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466;3.359; a.ni. 1.3.96) vuttaappanāsukhassa passaddhiyā paccayatte [M 2.0066] vattabbameva natthi. Sukhanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Balavapītīti pharaṇalakkhaṇappattā pīti. Tādisā hi vitakkavicārasukhasamādhīhi laddhappaccayā nīvaraṇaṃ vikkhambhantī taṃnimittaṃ darathaṃ pariḷāhaṃ paṭipassambheti. Tenāha “sā hi darathappassaddhiyā paccayo hotī”ti. Dubbalapītīti taruṇapīti. Tenāha “sā hi balavapītiyā paccayo hotī”ti. Saddhāti ratanattayaguṇānaṃ kammaphalassa ca saddahanavasena pavatto adhimokkho, sā pana yasmā attano visaye punappunaṃ uppajjati, na ekavārameva, tasmā āha “aparāparaṃ uppajjanasaddhā”ti. Yasmā saddahanto saddheyyavatthusmiṃ pamudito hoti, tasmā āha “sā hi dubbalapītiyā paccayo hotī”ti. Dukkhadukkhādibhedassa sabbassapi dukkhassa vaṭṭadukkhantogadhattā tassa ca idhādhippetattā vuttaṃ “dukkhanti vaṭṭadukkha”nti. Jarāmaraṇadukkhanti keci, sokādayo cāti apare. Tadubhayassapi saṅgaṇhanato paṭhamo evattho yutto. Yasmā dukkhappatto kammassa phalāni saddahati, ratanattaye ca pasādaṃ uppādeti, tasmā vuttaṃ “tañhi aparāparasaddhāya paccayo hotī”ti. Yasmā “ācariyānaṃ santike dhammaṃ sutvā pavattidukkha”nti cintayato “ekantato ayaṃ dhammo imassa dukkhassa samatikkamāya hotī”ti saddhā uppajjati. Tenāha “dhammaṃ sutvā tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.191). Savikārāti uppādavikārena savikārā khandhajāti [V 2.0057] jāyanaṭṭhena. Jātiyā pana asati tattha tattha bhave natthi dukkhassa sambhavoti āha “sā hi vaṭṭadukkhassa paccayo”ti. Kammabhavoti kammabhavādiko tividhopi kammabhavo. So hi upapattibhavassa paccayo. Evamādiṃ sandhāyāha “etenupāyenā”ti. Sesapadānīti upādānādipadāni. Anulomañāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāpakkhikattā nibbānaggahaṇena gahitaṃ, gotrabhuñāṇaṃ paṭhamamaggassa āvajjanaṃ. So hi tena vipassanāya kiñci kiñci visesaṭṭhānaṃ kayiratīti taṃ anāmasitvā nibbidūpaniso virāgoti “virāgo”icceva vuttaṃ.

The happiness of the preliminary stage is happiness accompanied by access concentration. The calming of distress is the pacification of the distress of defilements such as sensual desire. Here, to indicate the happiness intended by the statement, 'Bhikkhus, I say that happiness has a supporting condition,' it is said, 'of the happiness of the preliminary stage of absorption.' Regarding the happiness of absorption mentioned in 'With the body calmed, one feels happiness,' there is no need to state that tranquility is its condition. The same principle applies here to the term 'happiness.' Strong rapture is rapture that has reached the characteristic of suffusion. Such rapture, having gained its conditions through applied thought, sustained thought, happiness, and concentration, suppresses the hindrances and pacifies the distress and agitation associated with them. Hence it is said, 'For it is the condition for the calming of distress.' Weak rapture is immature rapture. Therefore, it is said, 'For it is the condition for strong rapture.' Faith is the resolution that arises by trusting in the qualities of the Triple Gem and in kamma and its results. Since it arises repeatedly in its own domain, not just once, it is therefore called 'repeatedly arising faith.' Because one who has faith rejoices in the object of faith, it is therefore said, 'For it is the condition for weak rapture.' Since all suffering, of the various kinds such as suffering due to suffering, is included within the suffering of the round of existence, and that is what is intended here, it is said: 'suffering means the suffering of the round.' Some say it is the suffering of aging and death, while others say it is sorrow and the like. The first interpretation is more appropriate as it encompasses both. Because one who experiences suffering trusts in the results of kamma and generates confidence in the Triple Gem, it is therefore said, 'For it is the condition for repeatedly arising faith.' For when one reflects, 'Having heard the Dhamma from the teachers, there is the suffering of existence,' faith arises with the thought, 'This Dhamma is entirely for the transcendence of this suffering.' Hence it is said, 'Having heard the Dhamma, one acquires faith in the Tathāgata,' and so on. 'Subject to change' (savikārā): the birth of the aggregates is subject to change through the change of arising, in the sense of being born. But when birth is absent, there is no arising of suffering in any existence whatsoever. Therefore, it is said, 'For it is the condition for the suffering of the round.' Kamma-becoming refers to the threefold kamma-becoming, beginning with kamma-becoming itself. It is the condition for rebirth-becoming. Referring to this and so on, it is said, 'By this method.' The remaining terms are clinging and the like. Knowledge of conformity, being on the side of equanimity towards formations, is included by the grasping of Nibbāna. Change-of-lineage knowledge is the adverting towards the first path. For since by that insight some special state is produced, without touching upon that, because dispassion has disenchantment as its proximate cause, it is simply called 'dispassion'.

Kena udakena vidārayitvā gatapadesoti katvā kandaro. Nitambotipi udakassa. Yathā ninnaṃ udakaṃ pavattati, tathā nivattanabhāvena nadīkuñchotipi vuccati. Hemantagimhautuvasena aṭṭha māse pavatto pathavīvivaroti katvā padaro. Khuddikā udakavāhiniyo sākhā viyāti sākhā[M 2.0067], khuddakā sobbhā kusubbhā o-kārassa u-kāraṃ katvā. Evameva khotiādi “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave”tiādinā upanītāya upamāya upameyyena saṃsandananti, taṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ “avijjā pabbatoti daṭṭhabbā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjā ca santānavasena ciraṃtanakālappavattanato pacurajanehi duppajahanato “pabbato”ti vuttā. Lokattayābhibyāpanato abhisandanato ca abhisaṅkhārā meghasadisā. Abhisaṅkhārā meghoti daṭṭhabbāti ānetvā sambandho. Tathā sesapadadvayepi. Viññāṇādivaṭṭaṃ anupavattito paramparapaccayato ca kandarādisadisā. Vimutti ekarasattā, hānivuddhiabhāvato ca sāgarasadisāti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ.

A ravine (kandara) is so called because it is a place where water (kaṃ) has gone, having split (dara) it. A slope (nitambo) is also of water. Just as water flows downward, so, due to its turning nature, it is also called a river bend (nadīkuñchi). A fissure (padaro) is so called because it is an opening in the earth that exists for eight months due to the winter and summer seasons. Small streams of water are like branches (sākhā); small hollows (sobbhā) are called kusubbhā, by changing the 'o' to a 'u'. Just so, to show the connection of the object of comparison with the simile introduced by 'Just as, monks,' and so on, by applying it, it is said: 'Ignorance should be seen as a mountain,' and so on. Therein, ignorance is called a 'mountain' because it proceeds from ancient times through continuity and is difficult for many people to abandon. Volitional formations are like clouds due to their pervading the three worlds and their overflowing. The connection is made by supplying the words, 'Volitional formations should be seen as clouds.' It is similar for the remaining two terms. The round of consciousness and so on is like a ravine and so on because it revolves in sequence and due to its chain of conditions. Liberation is like the ocean due to its single essence and the absence of decrease or increase—thus the connection of the similes.

Tattha yasmā purimasiddhāya avijjāya sati abhisaṅkhārā, nāsati, tasmā te uparipabbate pavattā viya hontīti vuttaṃ “avijjā…pe… vassanaṃ veditabba”nti. Assutavā hītiādi vuttasseva atthassa samatthanaṃ. Taṇhāya abhilāsaṃ katvāti etena sabbassapi abhisaṅkhāravuṭṭhitemanatthaṃ dīpeti. Taṇhā hi “sneho”ti vuttā. Antimabhavikassa antabhavanibbattako abhisaṅkhāro nibbānaṃ na patto, tadantassa bhāgassa nibbānaṃ āhacca ṭhito viya hotīti “mahāsamuddaṃ āhacca ṭhitakālo viyā”ti upamānidassanaṃ kataṃ. Viññāṇādivaṭṭaṃ pūretvāpi imināpi hi antimabhavikasseva viññāṇappavatti dassitā. Sā hi pūritāti vattabbā tato paraṃ viññāṇādivaṭṭasseva abhāvato. Jātassa puggalassa jātipaccayavaṭṭadukkhavedanāya dhammassavanaṃ icchitabbaṃ, taṃ pana yadipi imasmiṃ sutte na āgataṃ, suttantaresu pana āgatamevāti tato āharitvā taṃ vattabbanti dassento “buddhavacanaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Tayidaṃ sāvakabodhisattānaṃ vasenāyaṃ desanāti katvā vuttaṃ. Itaresaṃ pana vasena vuccamānaṃ [V 2.0058] suttantaraggahaṇatthaṃ payojanaṃ natthīti “yā hī”tiādimāha. Pāḷiyā vasena gahitamevāti saṅkhepato vuttaatthassa vitthārato dassanaṃ. Nibbattīti nibbattamānā khandhā gahitāti āha “savikārā”ti. Aniccatālakkhaṇādidīpanato lakkhaṇāhaṭaṃ.
