'Sotassa ariyamaggassa ādito paṭṭhāya paṭipattiadhigamo sotāpatti, tadatthāya tattha patiṭṭhitassa ca aṅgāni sotāpattiyaṅgāni, tadubhayaṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘duvidhaṃ sotāpattiyā aṅga’’nti, sotāpattiatthaṃ aṅganti attho.' Stream-entry is the attainment of the practice starting from the stream of the Noble Path; and the factors established therein for that purpose are the factors of stream-entry. Referring to both, it is said, 'the twofold factor of stream-entry'—meaning the factor for the purpose of stream-entry. 'Yaṃ pubbabhāgeti yaṃ sayaṃ sotāpattimaggaphalapaṭilābhato pubbabhāge tadatthāya saṃvattati.' 'Yaṃ pubbabhāge' refers to what in the prior part conduces to that goal, prior to the attainment of the path and fruit of stream-entry itself. 'Kiṃ pana tanti āha ‘‘sappurisasaṃsevo’’tiādi.' But what is that? It is said: 'association with good people,' etc. 'Sappurisānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyañāṇasaññāṇajātā payirupāsanā, saddhammassavanaṃ catusaccadhammassavanaṃ, yoniso upāyena aniccādito manasi karaṇaṃ yoniso manasikāro, ussukkāpentena dhammassa nibbānassa anudhammapaṭipajjanaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipattīti etāni sotāpattiyā aṅgāni.' The factors of stream-entry are: association with good people like the Buddha, who are born of noble knowledge and understanding; listening to the true Dhamma, which is the listening to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; proper attention, which is attending to impermanence, etc., by means of proper method; and the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, which is the diligent practice of the Dhamma leading to Nibbāna—these are the factors of stream-entry. 'Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sotāpattiaṅganti padaṃ apekkhitvā ‘‘evaṃ āgata’’nti vuttaṃ.' In the commentary, however, with reference to the word 'sotāpattiaṅga', it is said, 'thus it is stated.' 'Ṭhitassa puggalassa aṅgaṃ.' It is a factor of a person who has attained stability. 'Sotāpanno aṅgīyati ñāyati etenāti sotāpannassa aṅgantipi vuccati.' A stream-enterer is marked or known by this, hence it is also called 'the factor of a stream-enterer.' 'Idaṃ pacchā vuttaṃ aṅgaṃ.' This latter factor is mentioned afterward. 'Dosehi ārakāti ariyoti āha ‘‘niddoso’’ti.' Because he is far from defilements, he is noble; hence it is said, 'faultless.' 'Kathaṃ avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayotiādinā kenacipi anupārambhiyattā nirupārambho.' 'How ignorance is a condition for formations,' etc., is irreproachable because it cannot be reproached by anyone. 'Ñāṇaṃ sandhāya ‘‘niddoso’’ti vuttaṃ, paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sandhāya ‘‘nirupārambho’’ti vadanti.' 'Faultless' is said with reference to knowledge, while 'irreproachable' is said with reference to dependent origination. 'Ubhayampi pana sandhāya ubhayaṃ vuttanti apare.' But others say that both are stated with reference to both. 'Paṭiccasamuppādo ettha adhippeto.' Dependent origination is intended here. 'Tathā hi vuttaṃ ‘‘aparāparaṃ uppannāya vipassanāpaññāyā’’ti.' Thus it is said: 'with insight knowledge arising again and again.' 'Na hi maggañāṇaṃ vipassanāpaññāti.' For path-knowledge is not insight knowledge. 'Sammā upāyattā tassa paṭiccasamuppanne yāthāvato ñāyatīti ñāyo, paṭiccasamuppādo.' Because it is a right method, that by which one truly knows in the matter of dependent origination is the 'method' (`ñāyo`); this is dependent origination. 'Ñāṇaṃ pana ñāyati so etenāti ñāyo.' But knowledge is called 'ñāyo' because by this one knows.

Tatthāti niraye. Maggasotanti maggassa sotaṃ. Āpannoti adhigato. Apāyesu uppajjanasaṅkhāto vinipātadhammo etassāti vinipātadhammo, na vinipātadhammo avinipātadhammo. Paraṃ ayananti ativiya savisaye ayitabbaṃ bujjhitabbaṃ. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tenāha “avassaṃ abhisambujjhanako”ti.

'Tatthāti niraye.' 'Therein' means in hell. 'Maggasotanti maggassa sotaṃ.' 'The stream of the path' means the stream of the Path. 'Āpannoti adhigato.' 'Āpanna' means 'attained.' 'Apāyesu uppajjanasaṅkhāto vinipātadhammo etassāti vinipātadhammo, na vinipātadhammo avinipātadhammo.' 'One who has the nature of downfall' means one whose nature is designated as arising in the states of loss; 'one who does not have the nature of downfall' is the opposite. 'Paraṃ ayananti ativiya savisaye ayitabbaṃ bujjhitabbaṃ.' 'Going beyond' means it should be exceedingly gone to and understood within one's own domain. 'Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho.' For indeed, for those verbal roots that have the meaning of 'going,' 'understanding' is also their meaning. 'Tenāha ‘‘avassaṃ abhisambujjhanako’’ti.' Therefore, he said: 'One who will assuredly awaken.'

Pāṇātipātakammakāraṇāti pāṇātipātasaṅkhātassa pāpakammassa karaṇahetu. Veraṃ vuccati virodho, tadeva bhāyitabbato bhayanti āha “bhayaṃ veranti atthato eka”nti. Idaṃ bāhiraṃ veraṃ nāma tassa verassa mūlabhūtato verakārapuggalato bahibhāvattā. Teneva hi tassa verakārapuggalassa uppannaṃ veraṃ sandhāya “idaṃ ajjhattikaveraṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, tannissitassa verassa mūlabhūtā verakārapuggalacetanā uppajjati paharituṃ asamatthassapīti adhippāyo. Na hi nerayikā nirayapālesu [M 2.0086] paṭipaharituṃ sakkonti. Nirayapālassa cetanā uppajjatīti etena “atthi niraye nirayapālā”ti dasseti. Yaṃ panetaṃ bāhiraveranti yamidaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikañca bāhiraṃ veraṃ. Puggalaveranti vuttaṃ attakiccaṃ sādhetuṃ asakkonto kevalaṃ parapuggale uppannamattaṃ veranti katvā. Atthato ekameva “cetasika”nti visesetvā vuttattā. Sesapadesūti “adinnādānapaccayā”tiādinā āgatesu sesakoṭṭhāsesu. Attho bhaggoti attho dhaṃsito[V 2.0074]. Adhigatenāti maggena adhigatena. “Abhigatenā”tipi pāṭho, adhivuttenāti attho. Tenāha “acalappasādenā”ti.

'The reason for the act of killing living beings' means the cause for performing the evil deed designated as killing living beings. 'Hostility' is called opposition; that very thing, because it is to be feared, is fear. Thus it is said, 'fear and hostility are one in meaning.' This is called external hostility because it is external to the person who is the root of that hostility. For this reason, with reference to the hostility that has arisen in that hostile person, it is said, 'this is called internal hostility.' The meaning is that the volition of the hostile person, which is the root of the hostility dependent on that person, arises even in one who is unable to strike back. Indeed, beings in hell cannot strike back at the hell-wardens. That the volition of a hell-warden arises shows that 'there are hell-wardens in hell.' As for 'this external hostility,' it is the external hostility that is both in this present life and in a future life. 'Personal hostility' is so called because one, unable to accomplish one's own task, regards it as merely hostility that has arisen in another person. In meaning, it is indeed one, because it is stated with the specification 'mental.' 'In the remaining passages' means in the other sections introduced by 'due to taking what is not given,' and so on. 'The meaning is destroyed' means the meaning is demolished. 'Attained' means attained by the path. There is also the reading 'abhigatena,' which means 'declared.' Hence it is said, 'with unshakable confidence.'

Pañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Five Hostilities and Fears is concluded.

2. Dutiyapañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Five Hostilities and Fears

42. Bhikkhūnaṃ kathitabhāvamattameva visesoti etena yā satthārā ekaccānaṃ desitadesanā, puna tadaññesaṃ veneyyadamakusalena kālantare teneva desitā, sā dhammasaṃgāhakehi “mā no satthudesanā sampaṭiggahaṃ vinā nassatū”ti visuṃ saṅgahaṃ āropitāti dasseti.

42. “The only distinction is the fact that it was spoken to bhikkhus.” By this it is shown that a teaching taught by the Teacher to some, and taught again by him—skilled in taming the trainable—to others at another time, was placed in a separate collection by the compilers of the Dhamma, thinking: “May our Teacher’s teaching not perish without being received.”

Dutiyapañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse on the Five Hostilities and Fears is concluded.

3. Dukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Suffering

43. Samudayanaṃ samudayo, samudeti etamhāti samudayo, evaṃ ubhinnaṃ samudayānamatthatopi bhedo veditabbo. Paccayāva paccayasamudayo. Āraddhavipassako “imañca imañca paccayasāmaggiṃ paṭicca ime dhammā khaṇe khaṇe uppajjantī”ti passanto “paccayasamudayaṃ passantopi bhikkhu khaṇikasamudayaṃ passatī”ti vutto paccayadassanamukhena nibbattikkhaṇassa dassanato. So pana khaṇe khaṇe saṅkhārānaṃ nibbattiṃ passituṃ āraddho “imehi nāma paccayehi nibbattatī”ti passati. “So khaṇikasamudayaṃ passanto paccayaṃ passatī”ti vadanti. Yasmā pana paccayato saṅkhārānaṃ [M 2.0087] udayaṃ passanto khaṇato tesaṃ udayadassanaṃ hoti, khaṇato etesaṃ udayaṃ passato pageva paccayānaṃ suggahitattā paccayato dassanaṃ sukhena ijjhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “paccayasamudayaṃ passantopī”tiādi. Atthaṅgamadassanepi eseva nayo. Accantatthaṅgamoti appavatti nirodho nibbānanti. Bhedatthaṅgamoti khaṇikanirodho. Tadubhayaṃ pubbabhāge uggahaparipucchādivasena passanto aññatarassa dassane itaradassanampi siddhameva hoti, pubbabhāge ca ārammaṇavasena khayato vayasammasanādikāle bhedatthaṅgamaṃ passanto atirekavasena anussavādito accantaṃ atthaṅgamaṃ passati. Maggakkhaṇe panārammaṇato accantaatthaṅgamaṃ passati, asammohato itarampi passati. Taṃ sandhāyāha “accantatthaṅgamaṃ passantopī”tiādi. Samudayatthaṅgamaṃ nibbattibhedanti samudayasaṅkhātaṃ nibbattiṃ atthaṅgamasaṅkhātaṃ bhedañca. Nissayavasenāti cakkhussa sannissayavasena paccayaṃ katvā. Ārammaṇavasenāti rūpe ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ madhupiṇḍikasuttaṭīkāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phassoti “cakkhu rūpāni [V 2.0075] viññāṇa”nti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati samāgame nibbatti phassoti vuttoti āha “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phasso”ti. Tiṇṇanti ca pākaṭapaccayavasena vuttaṃ, tadaññepi pana manasikārādayo phassapaccayā hontiyeva. Evanti taṇhādīnaṃ asesavirāganirodhakkamena. Bhinnaṃ hotīti anuppādanirodhena niruddhaṃ hoti. Tenāha “appaṭisandhiya”nti.

43. 'Origin' means the arising of things; 'it arises from this,' thus it is an origin. In this way, the distinction in meaning between the two kinds of origin should be understood. The origin from conditions is just the conditions. A meditator who has begun insight, seeing, “These phenomena arise moment by moment dependent on this and that combination of conditions,” is said to be one who, “seeing the origin from conditions, also sees the momentary origin,” because the moment of arising is seen through the seeing of conditions. That meditator, having begun to see the momentary arising of formations, perceives, “They arise from these conditions.” They say, “One who sees the momentary origin sees the conditions.” For when one sees the arising of formations from their conditions, the seeing of their momentary arising occurs. For one who sees their momentary arising, since the conditions have already been well grasped, the seeing from the conditions is easily accomplished. Therefore, it is said, “Even one who sees the origin from conditions…” and so on. This same method applies to the seeing of cessation. 'Complete cessation' means non-occurrence, cessation, Nibbāna. 'Cessation by breaking up' means momentary cessation. In the preliminary stage, one who sees either of these two by way of learning, questioning, etc., also accomplishes the seeing of the other. And in the preliminary stage, by way of the object, at the time of contemplating decay and passing away, while seeing cessation by breaking up, one additionally sees the complete cessation from oral tradition and so on. But at the moment of the path, one sees complete cessation by way of the object; through non-delusion, one sees the other as well. Referring to this, it is said, “Even one who sees the complete cessation…” and so on. 'Origin and cessation' means arising, designated as origin, and breaking up, designated as cessation. 'By way of support' means having made the eye a condition by way of its support. 'By way of object' means having made form an object. Whatever should be said here is to be understood in the way explained in the subcommentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta. 'The coming together of three is contact'—it is said that the meeting, the coming together of these three, namely eye, forms, and consciousness, is the arising of contact. Hence it is stated, 'Contact is the coming together of three.' And 'three' is spoken of in terms of the manifest conditions, but attention and others are also conditions for contact. 'Thus' means by the sequence of the remainderless fading away and cessation of craving and so on. 'It is broken' means it has ceased with the cessation of non-arising. Therefore, it is said, 'without rebirth-linking.'

Dukkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Suffering is concluded.

4. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the World

44. Ayamettha visesoti “ayaṃ lokassā”ti samudayatthaṅgamānaṃ visesadassanaṃ. Ettha catutthasutte tatiyasuttato viseso.

44. Herein, the distinction is this: the seeing of the distinction of the arising and passing away of 'this world.' Here, the fourth discourse is distinct from the third discourse.

Lokasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the World is concluded.

5. Ñātikasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse at Ñātika

45. Aññamaññaṃ [M 2.0088] dvinnaṃ ñātīnaṃ gāmo ñātikoti vuttoti āha “dvinnaṃ ñātakānaṃ gāme”ti. Giñjakā vuccanti iṭṭhakā, giñjakāhi eva kato āvasatho giñjakāvasatho. So kira āvāso yathā sudhāparikammena payojanaṃ natthi, evaṃ iṭṭhakāhi eva cinitvā chādetvā kato. Tādisañhi chadanaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā iṭṭhakāchadanaṃ anuññātaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “iṭṭhakāhi kate mahāpāsāde”ti. Tattha dvārabandhakavāṭaphalakādīni pana dārumayāniyeva. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā vattatīti pariyāyo, kāraṇanti āha “dhammapariyāyanti dhammakāraṇa”nti, pariyattidhammabhūtaṃ visesādhigamassa hetunti attho. Upecca suyyati etthāti upassutīti vuttaṃ “upassutīti upassutiṭṭhāna”nti. Attano kammanti yadatthaṃ tattha gato, taṃ pariveṇasamajjanakiriyaṃ. Pahāyāti akatvā. Evaṃ mahatthañhi vimuttāyatanasīse ṭhatvā suṇantassa mahato atthāya saṃvattati. Ekaṅgaṇaṃ ahosīti sabbaṃ vivaṭaṃ ahosi. Tīsu hi bhavesu saṅkhāragataṃ paccayuppannavasena manasikaroto bhagavato kiñci asesetvā sabbampi taṃ ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ upagacchi. Tena vuttaṃ “yāvabhavaggā ekaṅgaṇaṃ ahosī”ti. Tantivasena tamatthaṃ vācāya nicchārento “vacasā sajjhāyaṃ karonto”ti vutto. Paccayapaccayuppannavasena ca atthaṃ āharitvā tesaṃ nirodhena vivaṭṭassa āhatattā “yathānusandhinā”ti vuttaṃ. Addasa ñāṇacakkhunā.

45. 'The village of two mutual relatives is called Ñātika,' hence it is said, 'in the village of two kinsmen.' 'Giñjakā' are called bricks; a dwelling made solely of bricks is a 'giñjakāvasatha.' It is said that this dwelling was constructed by simply building and covering with bricks, such that there was no need for plasterwork. It was with reference to such a covering that the Blessed One permitted brick roofing. Hence it is said, 'in the great mansion made of bricks.' There, however, the door frames, door leaves, panels, and so on were made of wood. 'It encompasses and proceeds to its own fruit,' thus it is a 'pariyāya,' a cause. It is said, 'a discourse on the Dhamma (dhammapariyāya) means a cause for the Dhamma'; the meaning is that it is a condition for attaining the distinction of the Dhamma that has been learned. 'One approaches and listens here,' thus it is 'upassuti'; it is said, 'upassuti means a listening place.' 'One’s own work' refers to the purpose for which one went there, the activity of sweeping the monastic compound. 'Having abandoned' means not having done it. Indeed, for one listening while standing at the pinnacle of the sphere of liberation, it leads to great benefit. 'It became a single courtyard' means everything was fully revealed. For the Blessed One, who was attending by way of conditions and conditioned phenomena to what has become conditioned in the three existences, everything without exception came into the range of his knowledge. Hence it is said, 'up to the peak of existence, it became a single courtyard.' Expressing that meaning with his voice according to the textual thread, he is said to be 'making a verbal recitation.' And because, having brought forth the meaning by way of conditions and conditioned phenomena, the unconditioned was brought about by their cessation, it is said, 'according to the connection.' He saw with the eye of wisdom.

Manasā [V 2.0076] sajjhāyaṃ karonto “tuṇhībhūtova paguṇaṃ karonto”ti vutto. Padānupadanti padañca anupadañca. Purimañhi padaṃ nāma, tadanantaraṃ anupadaṃ. Ghaṭetvā sambandhaṃ katvā avicchinditvā. Pariyāpuṇātīti ajjhayati. Ādhārappattanti ādhāraṃ cittasantānappattaṃ appamuṭṭhaṃ gatattā ādhārappattaṃ nāma. Kāraṇanissitoti lokuttaradhammassa kāraṇasannissito. Ādibrahmacariyakoti ādibrahmacariyaṃ, tadeva ādibrahmacariyakaṃ. Dhammapariyāyāpekkhāya pulliṅganiddeso. Tīsupi imesūti tatiyacatutthapañcamesu tīsu suttesu.

While reciting mentally, it is said: ‘being silent, one makes it proficient.’ ‘Padānupadaṃ’ means the word and the following word. The preceding is called the word, and that which immediately follows is the following word. ‘Ghaṭetvā sambandhaṃ katvā avicchinditvā’ means having connected, having made a connection, without breaking off. ‘Pariyāpuṇāti’ means he studies. ‘Ādhārappattaṃ’ means it has reached the mind-continuum as a foundation; being unforgotten, it is therefore called ‘attained to a foundation.’ ‘Kāraṇanissito’ means dependent on a cause—dependent on the cause of the supramundane Dhamma. ‘Ādibrahmacariyako’ means the beginning of the holy life; that very thing is ‘belonging to the beginning of the holy life.’ The masculine gender designation is with regard to the exposition of the Dhamma. ‘Among these three’ refers to these three discourses: the third, fourth, and fifth.

Ñātikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse at Ñātika is concluded.

6. Aññatarabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse About a Certain Brahmin

46. Nāmavasenāti [M 2.0089] gottanāmavasena ca kittivasena ca apākaṭo, tasmā “jātivasena brāhmaṇo”ti vuttaṃ.

46. “By name” means by way of clan name and by way of fame, he is obscure; therefore, it is said, “a brahmin by birth.”

Aññatarabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse About a Certain Brahmin is concluded.

7. Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta

47. Evaṃladdhanāmoti “jāṇussoṇī”ti evaṃladdhanāmo rañño santikā adhigatanāmo.

47. “Thus named” means that he was known by the name “Jāṇussoṇi,” a name acquired from the king.

Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta is concluded.

8. Lokāyatikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Materialist Discourse

48. Āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti lokāyataṃ. Na hi taṃ laddhiṃ nissāya sattā puññakiriyāya cittampi uppādenti, kuto payogo, taṃ etassa atthi, tattha vā niyuttoti lokāyatiko. Paṭhamasaddo ādiatthavācakattā jeṭṭhavevacanoti āha “paṭhamaṃ lokāyata”nti. Sādhāraṇavacanopi lokasaddo visiṭṭhavisayo idhādhippetoti āha “bālaputhujjanalokassā”ti. Ittarabhāvena lakuṇḍakabhāvena tassa vipulādibhāvena bālānaṃ upaṭṭhānamattanti dassento “āyataṃ mahanta”ntiādimāha. Parittanti khuddakaṃ. Ekasabhāvanti ekaṃ sabhāvaṃ. Avipariṇāmadhammatāyāti āha “niccasabhāvamevāti pucchatī”ti. Purimasabhāvena nānāsabhāvanti purimasabhāvato bhinnasabhāvaṃ. Pacchā na hotīti pacchā kiñci na hoti sabbaso [V 2.0077] samucchijjanato. Tenāha “ucchedaṃ sandhāya pucchatī”ti. Ekattanti sabbakālaṃ attasambhavaṃ. Tathā ceva gahaṇena dvepi vādā sassatadiṭṭhiyo honti. Natthi na hoti. Puthuttaṃ nānāsabhāvaṃ, ekarūpaṃ na hotīti vā gahaṇena dvepi vādā ucchedadiṭṭhiyoti.

48. ‘Because the world does not strive or exert for future welfare, it is called materialism (lokāyata).’ For beings relying on such a view do not even arouse the mind toward meritorious action—how much less effort? That is his view, or he is devoted to it—thus, a materialist (lokāyatika). The first term (paṭhama), being indicative of the beginning, is a synonym for ‘foremost’; hence it is said ‘first materialism (paṭhamaṃ lokāyata).’ Although a common term, ‘world’ (loka) here is intended to have a specific domain; hence it is said, ‘of the foolish ordinary world (bālaputhujjanaloka).’ To show that it is merely the preoccupation of fools due to its transient and contemptible nature, and its vastness, etc., it is said, ‘vast and great (āyataṃ mahanta),’ and so forth. ‘Limited’ (paritta) means small. ‘Of a single nature (ekasabhāva)’ means of one essence. Regarding its unchanging nature, it is said: ‘he asks whether it is of a permanent nature (niccasabhāva).’ ‘Of a nature different from the former’ means of a nature distinct from the former nature. ‘Later it is not (pacchā na hoti)’ means afterward it is nothing at all, due to being utterly annihilated. Hence it is said, ‘he asks with reference to annihilation (uccheda).’ ‘Unity (ekatta)’ means the existence of a self at all times. And by this interpretation, both views become eternalist views. ‘There is not, it is not (natthi na hoti).’ ‘Diversity (puthutta)’ means manifold nature; or by taking it as ‘it is not of one form (ekarūpaṃ na hoti),’ both views become annihilationist views.

Lokāyatikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta is concluded.

9. Ariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Disciple

49. Saṃsayuppatti [M 2.0090] ākāradassananti “kasmiṃ sati kiṃ hotī”ti kāraṇassa phalassa ca paccāmasanena vinā kevalaṃ idappaccayatāya saṃsayassa uppajjanākāradassanaṃ. Samudayati samudetīti atthoti āha “uppajjatī”ti.

49. ‘Seeing the mode of the arising of doubt’ means showing the mode of the arising of doubt merely through specific conditionality, without considering cause and effect as ‘when this exists, what occurs?’ ‘Samudayati’ has the meaning ‘it originates’ (samudeti), hence it is said, ‘it arises’ (uppajjati).

Ariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Disciple is concluded.

10. Dutiyaariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Noble Disciple

50. Dvepi nayā ekato vuttāti idaṃ “viññāṇe sati nāmarūpaṃ hotī”tiādinā navame vuttassa nayassa “avijjāya sati saṅkhārā hontī”tiādinā dasame vuttanaye antogadhattā. Nānattanti purimato navamato dasamassa nānattaṃ.

50. “Both methods are stated together” means that the method stated in the ninth, beginning with “with consciousness as condition, name-and-form exists,” is included within the method stated in the tenth, beginning with “with ignorance as condition, formations exist.” “Diversity” means the difference of the tenth from the former, the ninth.

Dutiyaariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Noble Disciple is concluded.

Gahapativaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Householder Chapter is concluded.

6. Dukkhavaggo

6. The Chapter on Suffering

1. Parivīmaṃsanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Investigation Sutta

51. Upaparikkhamānoti pavattipavattihetuṃ, nivattinivattihetuñca paritulento. Kuto panetanti? “Sammā dukkhakkhayā”ti vacanato. Na hi sabbadukkhaparivīmaṃsaṃ vinā sammā dukkhakkhayo sambhavati. Kasmātiādinā jarāmaraṇasseva gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Jātiādīnampi [V 2.0078] pavatti dukkhabhāvinīti adhippāyo. Yasmā jarāmaraṇe gahite sati jātipi gahitā hoti, tassā abhāve jarāmaraṇasseva abhāvato. Esa nayo bhavādīsupi. Evaṃ yāva jātidhammo jarāmaraṇe gahite gahitova hoti, jarāmaraṇapadesena tabbikāravanto sabbe tebhūmakā saṅkhārā gahitāti evampi jarāmaraṇaggahaṇena sabbampi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tenāha “tasmiṃ gahite sabbadukkhassa gahitattā”ti. Anekavidhanti bahuvidhaṃ bahukoṭṭhāsaṃ. “Aneka”nti vā pāṭho[M 2.0091]. Anekanti bahulavacanaṃ. Vidhanti khaṇḍiccapāliccādivasena viparītakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Nānappakārakanti tato eva nānappakāraṃ. Nhatvā ṭhitaṃ purisaṃ viyāti bālānaṃ attabhāvassa subhākārena upaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyāha.

51. “Examining” means considering the process of occurrence and its cause, and the process of cessation and its cause. But from where is this derived? From the statement, “for the right destruction of suffering.” For without a complete investigation of all suffering, the right destruction of suffering is not possible. With the question beginning “Why?”, he inquires about the taking up of aging and death alone. The intention is that the occurrence of birth and so forth is also of the nature of suffering. Because when aging and death are taken up, birth is also taken up, since in the absence of that, there is no aging and death. This same method applies to becoming and the rest. Thus, whatever has the nature of birth is taken up when aging and death are taken up. By the term ‘aging and death,’ all conditioned phenomena of the three realms that are subject to those alterations are taken up. Thus, by taking up aging and death, all the suffering of the round of existence is taken up. Therefore, it is said, “because when that is grasped, all suffering is grasped.” “Of many kinds” means diverse, with many sections. Or alternatively, the reading is “aneka.” “Aneka” is a word for “many.” “Kinds” means the various sections such as broken teeth, grey hair, and so forth. “Of various types” means just that, of various sorts. “Like a man who has bathed and stands,” he says with reference to the appearance of the individual existence in a beautiful form to fools.

“Sāruppabhāvenā”ti vuttaṃ, kiṃ sabbathā sāruppabhāvenāti āha “nikkilesatāya parisuddhatāyā”ti. Na hi tassesā asaṅkhatatādibhāvena sadisā. Paṭipannoti paṭimukho abhisaṅkhāramukho hutvā panno adhigato. Anugatanti anucchavikabhāvena gataṃ, yathā ca nibbānassa adhigamo hoti, evaṃ tadanurūpabhāvena gataṃ. Ettha ca pāḷiyaṃ “pajānātī”ti pubbabhāgavasena pajānanā vuttā, “tathā paṭipanno ca hotī”ti niyatavasena. “Aparabhāgavasenā”ti apare. Keci pana “yathā paṭipannassa jarāmaraṇaṃ nirujjhati, tathā paṭipanno”ti vadanti. Padavīmaṃsanā pubbabhāgavasena veditabbā, na maggakkhaṇavasena. Saṅkhāranirodhāyāti ettha nayidaṃ avijjāpaccayasaṅkhāraggahaṇaṃ, atha kho saṅkhatasaṅkhāraggahaṇanti āha “saṅkhāradukkhassa nirodhatthāyā”ti. Tenāha “ettāvatā yāva arahattā desanā kathitā”ti.

It is said, “by its appropriate nature.” Does this mean by its appropriate nature in every way? He said, “by being free from defilements, by being purified.” For it is not similar to that in the nature of the unconditioned, etc. “One who practices” means one who has entered upon it, having become one who faces it, one who faces the formation. “Follows” means gone in a suitable manner; just as the attainment of Nibbāna occurs, so it is gone in a way that corresponds to it. Here in the Pāli text, “he understands” is stated with reference to the preliminary phase of understanding, and “he is one who practices accordingly” is stated with reference to the definitive way. Others say, “with reference to the subsequent phase.” Some, however, say, “as aging and death cease for one who practices accordingly, so he practices.” The examination of the words should be understood with reference to the preliminary phase, not with reference to the moment of the path. Here, in “for the cessation of formations,” this is not the taking of formations conditioned by ignorance, but rather the taking of conditioned formations. Thus, it is said, “for the cessation of the suffering of formations.” Therefore, it is said, “to this extent, the teaching is spoken up to arahantship.”

“Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatī”tiādinā arahattaphalapaccavekkhaṇaṃ, “so sukhañca vedanaṃ vedayatī”tiādinā satatavihārañca dassetvā desanā sabbathāva vaṭṭadesanāto nivattetabbā siyā. Avijjāgatoti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tena evamādikaṃ idaṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭakathanaṃ puna gaṇhāti. Puggalasaddo itarāsaṃ dvinnaṃ pakatīnaṃ vācakoti tato visesetvā gahaṇe paṭhamapakatimeva dassento “purisapuggalo”ti avocāti āha “purisoyeva puggalo”ti. Ubhayenāti purisapuggalaggahaṇena. Sammutiyā avijjamānāya kathā desanā sammutikathā. Paramatthassa kathā desanā paramatthakathā. Tatthāti sammutiparamatthakathāsu, na sammutiparamatthesu. Tenāha “evaṃ pavattā sammutikathā nāmā”tiādi. Tatridaṃ sammutiparamatthānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – yasmiṃ bhinne buddhiyā vā avayavavinibbhoge kate na taṃsamaññā, sā ghaṭapaṭādippabhedā sammuti, tabbipariyāyato paramattho. Na hi kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāve ayaṃ nayo labbhati. Tattha rūpādidhammaṃ [V 2.0079] samūhasantānavasena pavattamānaṃ upādāya “satto”tiādi vohāroti āha “satto naro…pe… sammutikathā nāmā”ti[M 2.0092]. Yasmā rūpādayo paramatthadhammā “khandhā dhātuyo”tiādinā vuccanti, na vohāramattaṃ, tasmā “khandhā…pe… paramatthakathā nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu khandhakathāpi sammutikathāva, sammuti hi saṅketo khandhaṭṭho rāsaṭṭho vā koṭṭhāsaṭṭho vāti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana khandhasamaññā phassādīsu tajjāpaññatti viya paramatthasannissayā tassa āsannatarā puggalasamaññādayo viya na dūreti paramatthasaṅgahatā vuttā. Khandhasīsena vā tadupādānā sabhāvadhammā eva gahitā. Nanu ca sabbepi sabhāvadhammā sammutimukheneva desanaṃ ārohanti, na sammukhenāti sabbāpi desanā sammutidesanāva siyāti? Nayidamevaṃ desetabbadhammavibhāgena desanāvibhāgassa adhippetattā, na ca saddo kenaci pavattinimittena vinā atthaṃ pakāsetīti. Tenāha “paramatthaṃ kathentāpi sammutiṃ amuñcitvāva kathentī”ti. Saccameva aviparītameva kathenti.

By 'one attains final Nibbāna by oneself,' and so on, the reflection on the fruit of Arahantship is shown. By 'he feels a pleasant feeling,' and so on, the constant abiding is shown. The teaching should be entirely diverted from the discourse on the round of existence. In 'avijjāgato,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on'; thereby this discussion of the round of existence and its transcendence takes up such matters again. The term 'puggala' is a designation for the other two natures; therefore, to distinguish it from them, when taking it, by showing only the first nature, he said 'a male person' (purisapuggalo), meaning 'only a male is a person' (purisoyeva puggalo). 'By both' (ubhayena) means by the taking of 'a male person.' A discourse or teaching by means of convention about that which is ultimately non-existent is conventional discourse. A discourse or teaching about the ultimate is ultimate discourse. Therein—that is, in conventional and ultimate discourses, not in conventional and ultimate realities. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus, what is called conventional discourse proceeds,' and so on. Herein is the characteristic of the conventional and the ultimate: That of which the designation no longer applies when it is broken or when its parts are mentally separated, such as a pot or a cloth, is convention. The opposite of this is the ultimate. For this method does not apply to the intrinsic nature of things like hardness, contact, and so on. Therein, based on phenomena such as form, which proceed by way of aggregates and continuity, the usage 'a being,' 'a man'... and so on, is called conventional discourse. Because form and other ultimate phenomena are spoken of as 'aggregates,' 'elements,' and so on—not merely as conventional terms—therefore, it is said, 'aggregates... and so on, is called ultimate discourse.' But is not the discourse on aggregates also conventional discourse? For convention is an agreement, and the meaning of 'aggregate' is 'heap,' 'collection,' or 'part,' is it not? This is true. However, this designation 'aggregate,' like a concept derived from them in the case of contact and so on, is based on the ultimate and is very close to it. It is not distant like the designation 'person' and so on; therefore, it is said to be included in the ultimate. Or, by the heading 'aggregates,' the intrinsic phenomena which are their basis are taken. But do not all intrinsic phenomena enter into a teaching only through the medium of convention, not directly? Would not all teaching then be conventional teaching? This is not so, because the division of teaching is intended by the division of the phenomena to be taught. And a word does not illuminate a meaning without some ground for its application. Therefore, it is said, 'Even when speaking of the ultimate, they speak without abandoning convention.' They speak what is indeed true, what is not distorted.

Sammutīti samaññā. Paramo uttamo atthoti paramattho, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvo. Taṃ paramatthaṃ, sammuti pana lokassa saṅketamattasiddhā. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sammutikathāya saccatāti āha “lokasammutikāraṇa”nti lokasamaññaṃ nissāya pavattanato. Lokasamaññāya hi abhinivesanaṃ vinā paññāpanā ekaccassa sutassa sāvanā viya, na musā anatikkamitabbato tassā. Tenāha bhagavā “janapadaniruttiṃ nābhiniveseyya, samaññaṃ nātidhāveyyā”ti. Dhammānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ. Bhūtalakkhaṇaṃ bhāvassa lakkhaṇaṃ dīpentīti katvā.

'Convention' (sammuti) means designation (samaññā). 'Ultimate meaning' (paramattho) means the highest, supreme meaning; it is the true nature of phenomena as they are. That is the ultimate meaning. Convention, however, is established merely by worldly agreement. If so, how is a conventional discourse true? He says, 'because of worldly convention,' which means because it proceeds depending on worldly designation. For a designation made without insistence on worldly designation is like the hearing of something heard by someone; it is not false, because that designation is not to be transgressed. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'One should not insist on regional expressions, nor should one go beyond conventional usage.' 'Of dhammas' means of intrinsic phenomena. Because they reveal the characteristic of what is real, the characteristic of existence.

Terasacetanābhedanti aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalacetanāpañcarūpāvacarakusalacetanābhedaṃ. Attano santānassa punanato pujjabhavaphalassa abhisaṅkharaṇato puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ. Kammapuññenāti kammabhūtena. Vipākapuññenāti vipākasaṅkhātena. Puññaphalampi hi uttarapadalopena “puñña”nti vuccati “evamidaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu viya. “Apuññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”nti idaṃ “puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”nti ettha vuttanayamevāti na uddhataṃ. Apuññaphalaṃ uttarapadalopena “apuñña”nti vuccati. Saṅkhāranti saṅkhārassa gahitattā “avijjāgatoya”nti iminā saṅkhārassa paccayo gahito, “puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”ntiādinā paccayuppannaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tasmiñca [M 2.0093] gahite nāmarūpādi sabbaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tenāha “dvādasapadiko paccayākāro gahitova hotī”ti.

'The division of thirteen volitions' means the division into the eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and the five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere. It is a 'meritorious formation' because it purifies one's own continuity and because it prepares the fruit of a praiseworthy existence. 'By meritorious kamma' means by that which has become kamma. 'By meritorious result' means by that which is reckoned as result. For the fruit of merit is also called 'merit' by eliding the latter word, as in such cases as 'thus this merit increases.' The phrase 'consciousness partakes of demerit' is not cited here because it follows the same method as that stated in 'consciousness partakes of merit.' The fruit of demerit is called 'demerit' by eliding the latter word. Regarding 'formations': because a formation has been taken, by 'come from ignorance' the condition for the formation is taken; by 'consciousness partakes of merit' and so on, the consciousness that has arisen from a condition is taken. And when that is taken, all such as name-and-form are also taken. Therefore, he says, 'The twelve-limbed dependent origination is indeed taken.'

Vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesena. Tassā hi uppādā sabbaso avijjā pahīnā [V 2.0080] hoti. Paṭhamamevāti idaṃ avijjāpahānavijjuppādānaṃ samānakālatādassanaṃ. Tenāha “yathā panā”tiādi. Padīpujjalenāti padīpujjalanahetunā saheva. Vijjuppādāti vijjuppādahetu, evaṃ satīpi samakālatteti adhippāyo. Na gaṇhātīti “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā na gaṇhāti. Na taṇhāyati na bhāyati taṇhāvuttino abhāvā, tato eva bhayavatthuno ca abhāvā.

'Knowledge' (vijjā) is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, by way of a supreme designation. For with its arising, ignorance is abandoned in every way. 'At the very first' (paṭhamameva): this shows the simultaneity of the abandoning of ignorance and the arising of knowledge. Therefore, he says, 'Just as,' and so on. 'With the lighting of the lamp' means simultaneously with the cause of the lamp's lighting. 'The arising of knowledge' means the cause for the arising of knowledge. Even though this is so, the intention is simultaneity. 'He does not grasp' means he does not grasp in such ways as 'this is mine.' He does not crave, he does not fear, because there is no occurrence of craving, and for that very reason, because there is no basis for fear.

Gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvāti gilitvā viya aññassa avisayaṃ viya karaṇena pariniṭṭhāpetvā. Sāmisasukhassa anekadukkhānubandhabhāvato, sukhābhinandassa dukkhahetubhāvato ca sukhaṃ abhinandantoyeva dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāma aggisantāpasukhaṃ icchanto dhūmadukkhānuññāto viya. Dukkhaṃ patvā sukhaṃ patthanatoti ettha dubbalagahaṇikādayo nidassanabhāvena veditabbā. Te hi yāva sāyanhasamayāpi abhutvā sāyamāsādīni karonto jighacchādiṃ uppādetvā bhuñjanādīni karonti. Sukhassa vipariṇāmadukkhato sukhaṃ abhinandanto dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāmāti yojanā. Keci pana dukkhassa abhāvato vipariṇāmasukhato taṃ sukhaṃ abhinandanto dukkhaṃ abhinandatīti vadanti. Taṃ na, na hi tādisaṃ sukhanimittaṃ koci dukkhaṃ abhinandanto diṭṭho, dukkhahetuṃ pana sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ abhinandanto diṭṭho. Dukkhahetuṃ sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ abhinandanto atthato dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāmāti vuttovāyamattho. Kāyoti pañcadvārakāyo, so pariyanto avasānaṃ etassāti kāyapariyantikaṃ. Tenāha “yāva pañcadvārakāyo pavattati, tāva pavatta”nti. Jīvitapariyantikanti etthāpi eseva nayo.

'Having swallowed and brought to an end' means having brought it to an end by making it, as it were, not the domain of another, as if by swallowing it. Because worldly pleasure is followed by many kinds of suffering, and because delighting in pleasure is a cause of suffering, one who delights in pleasure is said to delight in suffering, like one who desires the pleasure of a fire's heat and thereby consents to the suffering from smoke. Regarding 'having reached suffering, one longs for pleasure,' those with weak digestion and so on should be understood as examples. For they, not having eaten even up to the evening, while preparing their evening meal and so on, arouse hunger and then eat. Because of the suffering due to change in pleasure, one who delights in pleasure is said to delight in suffering. This is the construction. Some, however, say that one delights in suffering by delighting in that pleasure which is pleasure due to change, arising from the absence of suffering. That is not so. For no one is seen delighting in suffering with such a sign of pleasure. But one is seen delighting in worldly pleasure, which is a cause of suffering. One who delights in worldly pleasure, which is a cause of suffering, in effect delights in suffering—this is the meaning that has been stated. 'Body' means the five-door body. That which has this as its limit, its end, is 'body-limited.' Therefore, he says: 'It continues as long as the five-door body continues.' This same method applies also to 'life-limited.'

Pacchā uppajjitvā paṭhamaṃ nirujjhatīti ekasmiṃ attabhāve manodvārikavedanāto pacchā uppajjitvā tato paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati, tato eva siddhamatthaṃ sarūpeneva dassetuṃ “manodvārikavedanā paṭhamaṃ uppajjitvā pacchā nirujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni tameva saṅkhepena vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “sā hī”tiādimāha. Yāva tettiṃsavassāpi paṭhamavayo. Paṇṇāsavassakāleti paṭhamavayato yāva paññāsavassakālā, tāva ṭhitā hotīti [M 2.0094] vuḍḍhihāniyo anupagantvā sarūpeneva ṭhitā hoti. Mandāti mudukā atikhiṇā. Tadāti asītinavutivassakāle. Tathā ciraparivitakkepi. Bhaggā nittejā bhaggavibhaggā dubbalā. Hadayakoṭiṃyevāti cakkhādivatthūsu avattetvā tesaṃ khīṇattā koṭibhūtaṃ hadayavatthuṃyeva. Yāva esā vedanā vattati.

Regarding the statement, 'Having arisen later, it ceases first': in one individual existence, it arises after the mental-door feeling and ceases before it. For that very reason, to demonstrate the established meaning in its own nature, it was said, 'The mental-door feeling, having arisen first, ceases later.' Now, to elaborate on that same point which was stated concisely, it is said, 'For it is...' and so forth. Up to thirty-three years is the first period of life. The period up to fifty years—from the first period of life up to the age of fifty—during that time, it remains stable, meaning it persists without undergoing increase or decrease, maintaining its own nature. 'Weak' (mandā) means soft, very subtle. 'At that time' (tadā) means at the age of eighty or ninety years. Likewise, even in prolonged thinking. 'Broken' (bhaggā) means without energy, broken and feeble. 'Only at the heart-base' (hadayakoṭiṃyeva) means that, due to their depletion, it does not occur in the eye-base and other bases, but only in the heart-base, which is the ultimate point. As long as this feeling occurs.

Vāpiyāti mahātaḷākena. Pañcaudakamaggasampannanti pañcahi udakassa pavisananikkhamanamaggehi yuttaṃ. Tato tato vissandamānaṃ sabbaso puṇṇattā.

'By a pond' (vāpiyā) means by a large reservoir. 'Endowed with five watercourses' (pañcaudakamaggasampanna) means equipped with five paths for the water's entering and exiting. 'Overflowing from here and there' (tato tato vissandamānaṃ) means because it is completely full.

Paṭhamaṃ [V 2.0081] deve vassantetiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Imaṃ vedanaṃ sandhāyāti imaṃ yathāvuttaṃ pariyosānappattaṃ manodvārikavedanaṃ sandhāya.

'First, the gods raining down,' and so forth, is a connection of similes. 'With reference to this feeling' (imaṃ vedanaṃ sandhāya) means with reference to this mental-door feeling, as stated, which has reached its culmination.

Kāyassa bhedāti attabhāvassa vināsato. “Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā”ti pāḷi, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana jīvitapariyādānā uddhanti paduddhāro kato. Paralokavasena agantvā. Vedanānaṃ sītibhāvo nāma saṅkhāradarathapariḷāhabhāvo, so panāyaṃ appavattivasenāti āha “pavatti…pe… bhavissantī”ti. Dhātusarīrānīti aṭṭhikaṅkalasaṅkhātadhātusarīrāni. Sarīrekadese hi sarīrasamaññā.

'The breaking up of the body' (kāyassa bhedā) means from the destruction of individual existence. The Pāli text is 'uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā,' but in the commentary, the word division is made as 'jīvitapariyādānā uddhaṃ.' Not going in the sense of another world. The cooling of feelings means the stilling of the torment and fever of formations, and this is by way of non-occurrence, therefore it is said, 'occurrence... will be.' 'Relic-bodies' (dhātusarīrāni) refer to the relic-bodies designated as skeletons. For a part of the body is indeed designated as 'body'.

Kumbhakārapākāti kumbhakārapākato. Ettha paccatīti pāko, pacanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadeva pācanavasena āvasanti etthāti āvāso, tasmā kumbhakārāvāsato. Avigatavūpasamaṃ saṅkharitaṃ kumbhaṃ uddharitvā ṭhapento chārikāya sati pidhānavasena ṭhapeti. Tathā ṭhapanaṃ pana sandhāya vuttaṃ “paṭisisseyyā”ti. Kumbhassa padesabhūtatāya ābaddhā avayavā “kumbhakapālānī”ti adhippetāni, na chinnabhinnāni. Avayavamukhena hi samudāyo vutto. Tattha kapālasamudāyo hi ghaṭo. Tenāha “mukhavaṭṭiyā ekabaddhānī”ti. Avasisseyyunti vaṇṇavisesauṇhabhāvāpagatā ghaṭakārāneva tiṭṭheyyunti. Āditta…pe… tayo bhavā daṭṭhabbā ekādasahi aggīhi ādittabhāvato. Yathā kumbhakāro kumbhakārāvāsaṃ ādittaṃ paccavekkhati, evaṃ āraddhavipassakopesa bhavattayaṃ rāgādīhi ādittanti āha “kumbhakāro viya yogāvacaro”ti. Nīharaṇadaṇḍako [M 2.0095] viya arahattamaggañāṇaṃ bhavattayapākato nīharaṇato. Samo bhūmibhāgo viya nibbānatalaṃ sabbavisamā nivattanato.

'From the potter's kiln' (kumbhakārapākā) means from the potter's kiln. Here, 'it is baked' (paccati), hence 'kiln' (pāko), the place of baking. That very place, because they dwell there for the purpose of baking, is a dwelling (āvāsa); therefore, 'from the potter's dwelling' (kumbhakārāvāsato). Taking out a pot that has been formed and whose heat has not yet subsided, one places it, covering it with ashes as a lid. Referring to such a placement, it is said, 'would place' (paṭisisseyyā). The parts bound together as portions of the pot are intended by 'potsherds' (kumbhakapālāni), not pieces that are cut and broken. For the whole is spoken of by way of its parts. There, the collection of sherds is the pot. Therefore, it is said, 'bound together as one at the rim' (mukhavaṭṭiyā ekabaddhānī). 'Would remain' (avasisseyyuṃ) means they would remain as mere pot-forms, with their specific color and heat departed. 'Aflame... etc... the three states of existence' should be seen as aflame with the eleven fires. Just as a potter examines the potter's dwelling when it is aflame, so too the meditator with aroused insight sees the three states of existence as aflame with lust and so forth; therefore it is said, 'like the potter, the meditator.' Like a removal stick, the knowledge of the path of arahantship is for removing from the baking of the three states of existence. Like a stretch of level ground, the plane of Nibbāna is so because all unevenness has ceased.

“Ādānanikkhepanato, vayovuddhatthaṅgamato, āhāramayato, utumayato, cittasamuṭṭhānato, kammajato, dhammatārūpato”ti (visuddhi. 2.706) imehi sattahi ākārehi sammasanto rūpasattakaṃ vipassati nāma. “Kalāpato, yamakato, khaṇikato, paṭipāṭito, diṭṭhiugghāṭanato, mānasamugghāṭato, nikantipariyādānato”ti (visuddhi. 2.717) imehi sattahi ākārehi sammasanto arūpasattakaṃ vipassati nāma, tasmā yathāvuttaṃ imaṃ rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakañca nīharitvā vipassantassa. Yadipi arahato attabhāvo sabbabhavehipi uddhaṭo, yāva pana anupādisesaparinibbānaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva tasmimpi sugatibhave ṭhitoyevāti vattabbataṃ labbhatīti “catūhi apāyehi attabhāvaṃ uddharitvā”icceva vuttaṃ. Tenāha “khīṇāsavo panā”tiādi. Tathā ca vakkhati “anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutassa vaṭṭavūpasamo [V 2.0082] veditabbo”ti. Na parinibbāti anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyāti adhippāyo, saupādisesāya pana nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānaṃ arahattappattiyeva. Abhisaṅkhārahetuto hettha pariḷāhavūpasamassa upasamabhāvena adhippetattā uṇhakumbhanibbānanidassanampi na virujjhati. Anupādinnakasarīrānīti utusamuṭṭhānikarūpakalāpe vadanti. Bhikkhaveti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Idaṃ pana vacanaṃ. Anuyogāropanatthanti kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno khīṇāsavo api nu puññābhisaṅkhārādikammaṃ kareyyāti pañhaṃ kātuṃ. Atha vā anuyogāropanatthanti “api nu kho khīṇāsavo bhikkhu puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ vā abhisaṅkhareyyā”tiādinā anuyogaṃ āropetuṃ vuttaṃ, na tāva yathāraddhadesanaṃ niṭṭhāpetunti attho.

'By grasping and releasing, by aging and decay, by being food-born, by being season-born, by arising from the mind, by being kamma-born, by being naturally formed' (Visuddhimagga 2.706)—contemplating in these seven ways is called insight into the material septad. 'By groups, by pairs, by moments, in sequence, by uprooting views, by uprooting conceit, by exhausting craving' (Visuddhimagga 2.717)—contemplating in these seven ways is called insight into the immaterial septad. Therefore, for one who contemplates, having extracted this material septad and immaterial septad as stated—although the individual existence of an Arahant is extracted from all existences, as long as he has not attained Nibbāna with no residue remaining, it can be said that he remains in that happy existence; therefore, it is stated, 'having extracted the individual existence from the four states of misery.' Therefore, he says, 'But for one whose taints are destroyed,' and so forth. And thus it will be said: 'For one who has attained final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining, the cessation of the round should be understood.' The meaning is that he does not attain final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. But final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining is indeed the attainment of Arahantship. Here, because the cessation of fever caused by formations is intended as a calming, the simile of the cooling pot is not contradicted. 'Unappropriated bodies' (anupādinnakasarīrāni)—they speak of the material aggregates arisen from temperature. 'Monks' (bhikkhave)—here, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so forth.' This statement, however, is for the purpose of raising a question: 'While experiencing feeling bounded by the body, would even a monk whose taints are destroyed create meritorious formations and so forth?' Or, 'for the purpose of raising a question' means it is said to propose the inquiry: 'Would a monk whose taints are destroyed create meritorious formations or not?' and so forth, not yet to conclude the teaching as it was begun. This is the meaning.

Paṭisandhiviññāṇe siddhe tasmiṃ bhave uppajjanārahānaṃ viññāṇānaṃ siyā sambhavo, nāsatīti vuttaṃ “viññāṇaṃ paññāyethāti paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti. Sabbaso saṅkhāresu asantesu paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ api nu kho paññāyeyya. Tasmiñhi apaññāyamāne sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ na paññāyeyya. Therānanti “bhikkhave”ti ālapitattherānaṃ[M 2.0096]. Pañhabyākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsati tassa sabbaññutaññāṇena saṃsandanato. Appaññāṇanti appaññāyanaṃ. Ādi-saddena viññāṇe asati nāmarūpassa appaññāṇanti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sanniṭṭhānasaṅkhātanti saddahanākārena pavattasanniṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ. Adhimokkhanti nicchayākāravimokkhaṃ saddhāvimokkhañca. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ “saddahatha metaṃ, bhikkhave”ti. Saddhāsahitañhi nicchayākāravimokkhaṃ sandhāyāha “sanniṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ adhimokkha”nti. Antoti pariyanto. Parito chijjati etthāti paricchedo.

When the rebirth-linking consciousness is established, there can be an arising of consciousnesses fit to arise in that existence; it is not that there is none. Thus it is said: 'Consciousness might be discerned,' meaning 'the rebirth-linking consciousness might be discerned.' If all formations were entirely non-existent, would the rebirth-linking consciousness still be discerned? Indeed, if that were not discerned, no consciousness would be discerned. 'Of the elders' (therānaṃ) refers to those elders addressed as 'bhikkhus.' He praises the answer to the question because it accords with the knowledge of omniscience. 'Non-discerning' (appaññāṇaṃ) means non-discernment. By the word 'etc.', it includes such as 'when consciousness is absent, the non-discerning of name-and-form.' 'Designated as determination' means a determination that proceeds in the manner of faith. 'Adhimokkha' means both liberation by way of certainty and liberation by faith. Therefore, the Pāli text states: 'Believe this, bhikkhus.' For it is with reference to liberation by way of certainty, which is accompanied by faith, that it is said: 'adhimokkha designated as determination.' 'End' (anto) means limit. 'It is cut off all around here,' hence 'boundary' (paricchedo).

Parivīmaṃsanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta is concluded.

2. Upādānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Upādāna Sutta

52. Ārammaṇādibhāvena saṃvattanato upādānānaṃ hitāni upādāniyāni, tesu upādāniyesu. Tenāha “catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ paccayesū”ti. Assādaṃ anupassantassāti asādetabbaṃ micchāñāṇena anupassato. Tadāhāroti soḷasa vā vīsaṃ tiṃsaṃ cattālīsaṃ paññāsaṃ vā āhāro paccayo etassāti tadāhāro. Aggikkhandho viya tayo bhavā ekādasahi aggīhi ādittabhāvato etadeva bhavattayaṃ. Aggi…pe… puthujjano aggikkhandhasadisassa bhavattayassa paribandhanato.

52. Because they lead to clinging by being its objects and so forth, things conducive to the clingings are called 'clinging-objects' (upādāniyāni). Regarding these clinging-objects, it is said: 'in the conditions for the four kinds of clinging.' 'Of one who sees gratification' means of one who sees with wrong knowledge what is to be gratified in. 'That whose nutriment is that'—whether sixteen, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty, that is its nutriment and condition. 'Like a mass of fire'—the three states of existence are this very triple existence, being ignited by the eleven fires. 'Fire…' …an ordinary person, because of being bound to the triple existence which is like a mass of fire.

Kammaṭṭhānassāti [V 2.0083] vipassanākammaṭṭhānassa. Tenāha “tebhūmakadhammesū”ti. Dhammapāsādanti lokuttaradhammapāsādaṃ. So hi accuggataṭṭhena “pāsādo”ti vuccati. Satipaṭṭhānamahāvīthiyaṃ phalakkhaṇe pavattāyāti.

Of the meditation subject means of the insight meditation subject. Hence it is said, 'in the phenomena of the three planes.' 'The mansion of Dhamma' means the supramundane mansion of Dhamma. For it is called 'mansion' because of its highly elevated state. Occurring at the moment of fruition on the great avenue of the establishments of mindfulness.

Upādānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upādāna Sutta is concluded.

3-4. Saṃyojanasuttadvayavaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Fetters

53-54. Mahantavaṭṭappabandhaopammabhāvena telapadīpassa āhatattā “mahantañca vaṭṭikapālaṃ gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Purimanayenevāti purimasmiṃ upādāniyasutte [M 2.0097] vuttanayeneva. Tathā vinetabbānaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena hi imesaṃ suttānaṃ evaṃ vacanaṃ evaṃ desanā. Esa nayo ito paresupi.

53-54. Because the oil lamp is said to be struck, by way of an analogy with a large, continuous wick, the phrase 'taking a large wick-bowl' is stated. 'By the previous method' means by the method stated in the previous Upādāniya Sutta. For these suttas are taught in this way according to the inclinations of the individuals to be trained. This method applies to the following ones as well.

Saṃyojanasuttadvayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Two Discourses on Fetters is concluded.

5-6. Mahārukkhasuttadvayavaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Two Great Tree Discourses

55-56. Ojaṃ abhiharantīti rasaharaṇiyo viya purisassa sarīre rukkhamūlāni rukkhassa pathavīāporase upari āropenti. Tesaṃ tathā āropanaṃ “ojāyā”tiādinā vibhāveti. Hatthasatubbedhamassāti hatthasatubbedho, hatthasataṃ ubbiddhassapi. Etthāti etissaṃ vaṭṭakathāyaṃ. Kammārohananti kammapaccayo.

55-56. 'They draw up nourishment' means: just as the roots of a tree make the essence of earth and water rise upwards for the tree, like the nutrient-carriers in a person's body. Their so making it rise is explained in detail by 'for nourishment,' and so on. 'Of one a hundred hands pierced' means one who is a hundred hands pierced, or also of one who has risen up a hundred hands. 'Here' means in this discourse on the round of existence. 'Ascending by kamma' means the condition of kamma.

Puna etthāti etissaṃ vivaṭṭakathāyaṃ. Vaṭṭadukkhaṃ nāsetukāmassa daḷhaṃ uppannasaṃvegañāṇaṃ sandhāya “kuddālo viyā”ti āha. Tato nibbattitañāṇaṃ samādhipacchiyā ṭhitaṃ nissāya pavattetabbavipassanārambhañāṇaṃ. Rukkhacchedanapharasu viyāti evaṃbhūtassa vipassanā ekantato vaṭṭacchedāya hotiyevāti āha “rukkhassa…pe… manasikarontassa paññā”ti. Tattha kammaṭṭhānanti vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ catubbidhavavatthānavasena vīsati pathavīkoṭṭhāsā, dvādasa āpokoṭṭhāsā, cattāro tejokoṭṭhāsā, cha vāyokoṭṭhāsāti dvecattālīsāya koṭṭhāsesu. Viññāṇassa cāti iti-saddo ādiattho pakārattho ca. Tena bhūtarūpāni viññāṇasampayuttadhamme ca saṅgaṇhāti. Sattasu sappāyesu yassa alabhantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ vibhūtaṃ hutvā na upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāyāha “aññataraṃ sappāya”nti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Again, 'here' means in this discourse on the rolling back of the cycle. Referring to the strongly arisen knowledge of spiritual urgency in one who wishes to destroy the suffering of the cycle, it is said, 'like a mattock.' Then, the knowledge born from that, relying on that which is established with the support of concentration, is the initial knowledge of insight meditation to be cultivated. 'Like an axe for cutting a tree' means that for such a one, insight definitively serves to cut through the cycle of existence; thus it is stated: 'for one who wisely contemplates the tree... the wisdom.' Herein, 'meditation subject' refers to the insight meditation subject. That is in forty-two parts by way of the fourfold determination: twenty parts of earth, twelve parts of water, four parts of fire, and six parts of air. In 'and of consciousness,' the word 'iti' is inclusive and indicative of manner. Thus, it includes the primary material elements and mental states associated with consciousness. Referring to one for whom the meditation subject, not being obtained among the seven suitable conditions, becomes unclear and does not appear, it is said, 'a certain suitable condition.' The rest is easily understood.

Mahārukkhasuttadvayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Two Mahārukkha Suttas is concluded.

7. Taruṇarukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Taruṇarukkha Sutta

57-59. Palimajjeyyāti [V 2.0084][M 2.0098] allakaraṇavasena parito pāḷiṃ bandheyya. Tathā karonto yasmā ca tattha tiṇagacchādīnaṃ mūlasantānaggahaṇena taṃ ṭhānaṃ sodheti nāma, tasmā vuttaṃ “sodheyyā”ti. Paṃsunti assa pavaḍḍhakārakaṃ, āgantukaṃ paṃsunti attho. Dadeyyāti pakkhipeyya. Tenāha “thaddha”ntiādi. Vuttanayenevāti “rukkhaṃ nāsetukāmo puriso viyā”tiādinā pañcamasutte vuttanayena. Aṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva vuttanayattā.

57-59. 'He would plaster' means he would make a border around it by moistening it. By doing so, since he indeed cleanses that place by removing the root-systems of grass and shrubs, it is said: 'he would clear it.' 'Soil' refers to soil that causes it to grow, meaning adventitious soil. 'He would give' means he would cast it in. Hence, it is said: 'firmly,' etc. 'By the stated method' means in the manner explained in the fifth sutta: 'like a man wishing to destroy a tree,' etc. The eighth and ninth are straightforward in meaning, since the explanation follows the method already stated.

Taruṇarukkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Taruṇarukkha Sutta is concluded.

10. Nidānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta

60. Bahuvacanavasenāti kurū nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīvasena “kurū”ti evaṃ bahuvacanavasena. Yattha bhagavato vasanokāsabhūto koci vihāro na hoti, tattha kevalaṃ gocaragāmakittanaṃ nidānakathāya pakati yathā “sakkesu viharati devadahaṃ nāma sakyānaṃ nigamo”ti. “Āyasmā”ti vā “devānaṃ piyo”ti vā bhavanti vā piyasamudāhāro esoti āha “āyasmāti piyavacanameta”nti. Tayidaṃ piyavacanaṃ gāravavasena vuccatīti āha “garuvacanameta”nti. Atidūraṃ accāsannaṃ atisammukhā atipacchato uparivāto unnatappadesoti ime cha nisajjadosā. Nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassaravasena chabbaṇṇānaṃ.

60. By way of the plural: the Kurus were princes of a country, and their dwelling, though a single territory, is by convention referred to in the plural as 'Kurus.' Wherever there is no monastery as a dwelling place for the Blessed One, there is only mention of a village for alms, as is customary in the introductory narrative, such as, 'He dwells among the Sakyans at Devadaha, a town of the Sakyans.' Because there are agreeable forms of address such as 'Venerable' or 'Dear to the gods,' he said, ''Venerable' is an affectionate term.' This affectionate term is spoken out of respect, hence he said, 'It is a respectful term.' Too far, too near, directly in front, directly behind, upwind, or on elevated ground—these are the six faults of sitting. Of the six colors: blue, yellow, red, white, madder, and radiant.

Kulasaṅgahatthāyāti kulānuddayatāvasena kulānuggaṇhanatthāya. Sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ nikkhipanto viya bhikkhāpaṭiggaṇhanena tesaṃ abhivādanādisampaṭicchanena ca puññābhisandassa jananena. Paṭisammajjitvāti antevāsikehi sammaṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ sakkaccakāritāya puna sammajjitvā. Ubhayantato paṭṭhāya majjhanti ādito paṭṭhāya vedanaṃ, jarāmaraṇato paṭṭhāya ca vedanaṃ pāpetvā sammasanamāha. Tikkhattunti “ādito paṭṭhāya anta”ntiādinā [M 2.0099] vuttacaturākārupasaṃhite tayo vāre. Tena dvādasakkhattuṃ sammasanamāha. Amhākaṃ bhagavatā gambhīrabhāveneva kathitattā sesabuddhehipi evameva kathitoti dhammanvaye ṭhatvā vuttaṃ “sabbabuddhehi…pe… kathito”ti.

For the sake of helping families means for the purpose of supporting families out of compassion for them. Like someone depositing a bundle of a thousand, by generating a flow of merit through the acceptance of alms and the receiving of their greetings and so forth. 'Having swept again' means, after having the place swept by his pupils, sweeping it again himself to ensure it was done carefully. 'From both ends to the middle' means he speaks of contemplation, having traced the process to feeling starting from the beginning, and also having traced it to feeling starting from aging and death. 'Three times' refers to three rounds, included in the four aspects described with 'from the beginning to the end.' Thus, he speaks of considering twelve times. Because our Blessed One spoke with profundity, and the other Buddhas also spoke in the same way, it is said, standing in the lineage of the Dhamma: 'By all Buddhas... it was spoken.'

Pamāṇātikkameti aparimāṇatthe “yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.3) viya. Atirekabhāvajotano hi yaṃ yāva-saddo. Tenāha “atigambhīroti attho”ti. Avabhāsati [V 2.0085] khāyati upaṭṭhāti ñāṇassa. Tathā upaṭṭhānañhi sandhāya “dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu esa paṭiccasamuppādo ekantagambhīrova, atha kasmā gambhīrāvabhāsatā jotitāti? Saccametaṃ, ekantagambhīratādassanatthameva panassa gambhīrāvabhāsaggahaṇaṃ, tasmā aññattha labbhamānaṃ cātukoṭikaṃ byatirekamukhena nidassetvā tamevassa ekantagambhīrataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ekaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etaṃ natthīti agambhīro agambhīrāvabhāso cāti etaṃ dvayaṃ natthi. Tena yathādassite cātukoṭike pacchimā ekakoṭi labbhatīti dasseti. Tenāha “ayaṃ hī”tiādi.

It exceeds measure in the sense of being immeasurable, as in the phrase 'as far as this was done by the Blessed One' (Dī. Ni. 1.3). For the word 'yāva' indicates an excessive state. Hence it is said, 'The meaning is extremely profound.' It shines forth, appears, becomes manifest to knowledge. Indeed, with reference to its manifestation, it is said, 'it is seen.' Now, is not this dependent origination entirely profound? Then why is its profound manifestation spoken of? Indeed, it is so, but the speaking of its profound manifestation is solely for the purpose of revealing its utterly profound nature. Therefore, having shown elsewhere, by way of exclusion, the four alternatives, that very utter profundity is elucidated with the words 'for indeed this,' etc. 'This does not exist' means: the non-profound and the non-profound manifestation—this duality does not exist. Thus, he shows that when the four alternatives are presented, the last alternative is obtained. This is indicated by the words 'for indeed this,' etc.

Yehi gambhīrabhāvehi paṭiccasamuppādo “gambhīro”ti vuccati, te catūhi upamāhi ulliṅgento “bhavaggaggahaṇāyā”tiādimāha. Yathā bhavaggaggahaṇatthaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā gahetuṃ na sakkā dūrabhāvato, evaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ avijjādipaccayasambhūtasamudāgatattho pakatiñāṇena gahetuṃ na sakkā. Yathā sineruṃ bhinditvā miñjaṃ pabbatarasaṃ pākatikapurisena nīharituṃ na sakkā, evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādagate dhammatthādike pakatiñāṇena bhinditvā vibhajja paṭivijjhanavasena jānituṃ na sakkā. Yathā mahāsamuddaṃ pakatipurisassa bāhudvayavasena pāraṃ tarituṃ na sakkā. Evaṃ vepullaṭṭhena mahāsamuddasadisaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ pakatiñāṇena desanāvasena pariharituṃ na sakkā. Yathā pathaviṃ parivattetvā pākatikapurisassa pathavojaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ itthaṃ avijjādayo saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayā hontīti tesaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasabhāvo pākatikañāṇena nīharitvā gahetuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ catubbidhagambhīratāvasena catasso upamā yojetabbā. Pākatikañāṇavasena cāyamatthayojanā katā diṭṭhasaccānaṃ tattha paṭivedhasabbhāvato, tathāpi yasmā sāvakānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca tattha sappadesameva [M 2.0100] ñāṇaṃ, buddhānaṃyeva nippadesaṃ. Tasmā vuttaṃ “buddhavisayaṃ pañha”nti.

By those profound aspects by which dependent origination is called "profound," illustrating them with four similes, it is said, "for the sake of grasping the peak of existence," and so on. Just as one cannot reach out with the hand to grasp the peak of existence due to its remoteness, so too the meaning of formations and so on, arising from ignorance as a condition, cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot split open Mount Sineru to extract its marrow or the essence of the mountain, so too the truths and the underlying principles within dependent origination cannot be split open, analyzed, and penetrated by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot cross the great ocean with the strength of both arms, so too dependent origination, vast like the great ocean, cannot be fully comprehended through exposition by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot turn the earth over to extract its essence, so too the nature of dependent origination—how ignorance and so on are conditions for formations and so on—cannot be extracted and grasped by ordinary knowledge. Thus, these four similes should be applied to illustrate the fourfold profundity. This explanation is given in terms of ordinary knowledge, because for those who have seen the truths, penetration thereof exists. However, since the knowledge of disciples and paccekabuddhas in that matter is only partial, while the Buddhas alone possess complete knowledge, therefore, it is said, "a question within the Buddha’s domain."

Māti paṭisedhe nipāto. Svāyaṃ “uttānakuttānako viya khāyatī”ti vacanaṃ sandhāya vuttoti āha “mā bhaṇīti attho”ti. Ussādentoti paññāvasena ukkaṃsantoti attho. Apasādentoti nibbhacchanto, niggaṇhantoti attho. Tenāti mahāpaññabhāvena.

The particle "mā" is a prohibitive particle. This statement is made with reference to the phrase "it appears like something upright and inverted," and means "do not speak." "Ussādento" means encouraging, exalting through wisdom. "Apasādento" means rebuking, restraining. "Tena" refers to his great wisdom.

Tatthāti therassa satipi uttānabhāve paṭiccasamuppādassa aññesaṃ gambhīrabhāve. Subhojanarasapuṭṭhassāti sundarena bhojanarasena positassa. Katayogassāti nibbuddhapayoge kataparicayassa. Mallapāsāṇanti mallehi mahābaleheva khipitabbapāsāṇaṃ. Kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānanti kasmiṃ passe imassa pāsāṇassa garutarapadesoti tassa sallahukabhāvaṃ dīpento vadati.

"There" (tatthāti) refers to the fact that even though for the Elder dependent origination is shallow, for others it is profound. "Filled with the taste of excellent food" (Subhojanarasapuṭṭhassāti) means nourished with delicious food. "One who has done effort" (Katayogassāti) means one who has cultivated familiarity with effort leading to awakening. "A wrestler’s stone" (Mallapāsāṇanti) is a stone to be thrown by wrestlers, that is, by those of great strength. "Where is the heavy spot for this?" (Kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānanti) means "On which side is the heavy part of this stone?" Thus, he speaks, indicating its lightness.

Timirapiṅgaleneva [V 2.0086] dīpenti tassa mahāvipphārabhāvato. Tenāha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Pakkuthatīti pakkuthantaṃ viya parivattati parito vattati. Lakkhaṇavacanañhetaṃ. Piṭṭhiyaṃ sakalikaaṭṭhikā piṭṭhipattaṃ. Kāyūpapannassāti mahatā kāyena upetassa, mahākāyassāti attho. Piñcha vaṭṭīti piñcha kalāpo. Supaṇṇavātanti nāgaggahaṇādīsu pakkhapapphoṭanavasena uppajjanakavātaṃ.

They are shown as dark and tawny due to its great expanse. Hence it is said, "of that one, indeed," etc. "Pakkuthati" means it turns around as if boiling; it revolves all around. This is a descriptive term. On the back, the sakalika bones are the back-plate. "Kāyūpapannassa" means endowed with a great body, that is, one with a massive frame. "Piñcha vaṭṭī" means a bundle of feathers. "Supaṇṇavāta" refers to the wind that arises from the flapping of wings, as in the seizing of nāgas, etc.

“Pubbūpanissayasampattiyā”tiādinā uddiṭṭhakāraṇāni vitthārato vivarituṃ “ito kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha itoti ito bhaddakappato. Satasahassimeti satasahassame. Haṃsavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi jātanagaraṃ. Dhurapattānīti bāhirapattāni, yāni dīghatamāni.

The passage beginning 'ito kira...' is stated to explain in detail the reasons indicated by the phrase beginning 'By the attainment of a previous supporting condition.' Therein, 'ito' means from this fortunate aeon. 'Satasahassime' means in the one hundred thousandth aeon. There was a city named Haṃsavatī, a city of birth. 'Dhurapattāni' means the outer leaves, which are the longest.

Kaniṭṭhabhātāti vemātikabhātā kaniṭṭho yathā amhākaṃ bhagavato nandatthero. Buddhānañhi sahodarā bhātaro nāma na honti. Tattha jeṭṭhā tāva nuppajjanti, kaniṭṭhānaṃ pana asambhavo eva. Bhoganti vibhavaṃ. Upasantoti corajanitasaṅkhobhavūpasamena upasanto janapado.

"Kaniṭṭhabhātā" means a younger brother, a half-brother, like our Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One’s younger brother. For Buddhas, there are no brothers born of the same womb. In their case, elder brothers do not arise, and the birth of younger brothers is simply impossible. "Bhoga" means prosperity. "Upasanto" means the country is at peace, pacified by the calming of the disturbance caused by thieves.

Dve [M 2.0101] sāṭake nivāsetvāti sāṭakadvayameva attano kāyaparihāriyaṃ katvā, itaraṃ sabbasambhāraṃ attanā mocetvā.

"Wearing two garments" means taking only two garments as his body covering, having relinquished all other possessions himself.

Pattaggahaṇatthanti antopakkhittauṇhabhojanattā pattassa aparāparaṃ hatthe parivattentassa sukhena pattaggahaṇatthaṃ. Uttarisāṭakanti attano uttariyaṃ sāṭakaṃ. Etāni pākaṭaṭṭhānānīti etāni yathāvuttāni bhagavato desanāya pākaṭāni buddhe buddhasāvake ca uddissa therassa puññakaraṇaṭṭhānāni, paccekabuddhaṃ pana bodhisattañca uddissa therassa puññakaraṇaṭṭhānāni bahūniyeva.

"The purpose of holding the bowl" is for easily holding the bowl as one passes it from hand to hand because of the hot food placed inside. "Uttarisāṭaka" means his upper garment. "These are evident places" refers to these well-known places, as stated in the Buddha's teaching, for the elder's merit-making directed toward the Buddha and his disciples. However, the places for the elder's merit-making directed toward Paccekabuddhas and Bodhisattas are indeed numerous.

Paṭisandhiṃ gahetvāti amhākaṃ bodhisattassa paṭisandhiggahaṇadivaseyeva paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā.

"Taking rebirth" means taking rebirth on the very day of our Bodhisatta's conception.

Uggahanaṃ pāḷiyā uggaṇhanaṃ, savanaṃ atthasavanaṃ, paripucchanaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu atthaparipucchanaṃ, dhāraṇaṃ pāḷiyā pāḷiatthassa ca citte ṭhapanaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ idha paṭiccasamuppādavasena veditabbaṃ, sabbassapi buddhavacanassa vasenātipi vaṭṭati. Sotāpannānañca…pe… upaṭṭhāti tattha sammohavigamena “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti attapaccakkhavasena upaṭṭhānato[V 2.0087]. Nāmarūpaparicchedoti saha paccayena nāmarūpassa paricchijja avabodho. Catūhīti dhammagambhīrādīhi catūhi gambhīratāhi sabbāpi gambhīratā.

'Uggahana' is learning the Pali text; 'savana' is hearing the meaning; 'paripucchana' is questioning about the meaning at knotty points; and 'dhāraṇa' is establishing the Pali text and its meaning in the mind. All this should be understood here in terms of dependent origination, and indeed, it also applies to all the Buddha's word. And for stream-enterers…it is present through the removal of delusion, by way of direct personal experience, that 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' 'Nāmarūpapariccheda' is understanding by discerning name-and-form together with its conditions. By 'four' is meant all profundity, which comprises the four profundities beginning with the profundity of the Dhamma.

Sāvakehi desitā desanāpi pana satthu eva desanāti āha “mayā dinnanaye ṭhatvā”ti. “Sekkhena nāma nibbānaṃ sabbākārena paṭividdhaṃ na hotī”ti na tassa gambhīratāti tassa gambhīrassa upādānassa gambhīratā viya suṭṭhu diṭṭhā nāma hoti. Tasmā āha “idaṃ nibbānameva gambhīraṃ, paccayākāro pana uttānako jāto”ti. Nibbānañhi sabbepi asekkhā sabbaso paṭivijjhanti nippadesattā, paccayākāraṃ pana sammāsambuddhāyeva anavasesato paṭivijjhanti, na itare. Tasmā paccayavasena “idaṃ aparaddha”nti vuttaṃ theraṃ apasādentena. Tameva hissa anavasesato paṭivedhābhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “atha kasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asatipi dhammato bhede saṃyojanatthaanusayatthavasena pana tesaṃ labbhamānabhedaṃ gahetvā “ime cattāro kilese”ti vuttaṃ. Añño hi tesaṃ bandhanattho, añño thāmagamanaṭṭhoti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Iti imesaṃ kilesānaṃ appahīnattā tathārūpaṃ upanissayasampadaṃ [M 2.0102] abhāvayatova anuttānameva dhammaṃ uttānanti na vattabbamevāti adhippāyo. Cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyānīti idaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ santāne bodhiparipācakadhammānaṃ tikkhamajjhimamudubhāvasiddhakālavisesadassanaṃ, tañca kho mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāyāti vadanti. Etehīti yathāvuttabuddhasāvakaaggasāvakapaccekabuddhasammāsambuddhānaṃ visesādhigamehi. Paccanīkanti paṭikkūlaṃ viruddhaṃ. Sabbathā paccayākārapaṭivedho nāma sammāsambodhiyādhigamo evāti vuttaṃ “paccayākāraṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantassevā”ti. Navahi ākārehīti uppādādīhi navahi paccayākārehi. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.45) –

The teaching delivered by disciples is still the teaching of the Master, hence it is said, 'standing in the method given by me.' It is not that Nibbāna is not fully penetrated by a trainee; its profundity is indeed well seen, like the profundity of deep clinging. Therefore, it is said, 'This Nibbāna itself is profound, but the aspect of conditions has become shallow.' For all Arahants fully penetrate Nibbāna in every way due to its indivisible nature, but only the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones fully comprehend the aspect of conditions completely—others do not. Therefore, regarding conditions, it was said, 'This is a fault,' reproaching the elder. To clarify his lack of complete penetration, it was said, 'But why?' etc. Even though there is no real division in the Dhamma, the division is understood in terms of the fetters and underlying tendencies, hence it was said, 'These four defilements.' For their binding nature is one thing, and their tendency to persist is another. This is the method for the rest as well. Thus, because these defilements are not abandoned, and such a basis of support is not developed, the profound Dhamma should not be called shallow. 'Four, eight, sixteen, or countless'—this refers to the showing of the specific time for the maturation of the qualities ripening for enlightenment, which are sharp, moderate, or mild, in the mental continuum of the great bodhisattas, and they say it begins from the great aspiration. 'By these'—through the special attainments of the Buddha's disciples, chief disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, as previously mentioned. 'Opposed' means repugnant, contradictory. The penetration of the aspect of conditions in every way is indeed the attainment of perfect enlightenment, hence it was said, 'striving to penetrate the aspect of conditions.' 'In nine ways'—by the nine aspects of conditions, such as arising. For this is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.45):—

“Avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṭṭhiti ca pavattaṭṭhiti ca nimittaṭṭhiti ca āyūhanaṭṭhiti ca saṃyogaṭṭhiti ca palibodhaṭṭhiti ca samudayaṭṭhiti ca hetuṭṭhiti ca paccayaṭṭhiti ca, imehi navahākārehi avijjā paccayo, saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā”tiādi.

'For ignorance and formations, there is the state of arising, the state of proceeding, the state of being a sign, the state of accumulation, the state of conjunction, the state of obstruction, the state of origination, the state of being a cause, and the state of being a condition. By these nine aspects, ignorance is a condition, and formations are conditionally arisen,' and so forth.

Tattha navahākārehīti navahi paccayabhāvūpagamanehi ākārehi. Uppajjati etasmā phalanti uppādo, phaluppattiyā kāraṇabhāvo. Sati ca avijjāya saṅkhārā uppajjanti, nāsati, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo hoti. Tathā avijjāya sati saṅkhārā pavattanti ca nimiyanti ca. Yathā ca bhavādīsu khipanti, evaṃ tesaṃ avijjā paccayo hoti, tathā āyūhanti phaluppattiyā ghaṭenti saṃyujjanti attano phalena. Yasmiṃ santāne sayaṃ uppannā, taṃ [V 2.0088] palibundhanti paccayantarasamavāye udayanti uppajjanti, hinoti ca saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ upagacchati. Paṭicca avijjaṃ saṅkhārā ayanti pavattantīti evaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvūpagamanavisesā uppādādayo veditabbāti. Uppādaṭṭhitīti ca tiṭṭhati etenāti ṭhiti, kāraṇaṃ. Uppādo eva ṭhiti uppādaṭhiti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Idañca paccayākāradassanaṃ yathā purimehi mahābodhimūle pavattitaṃ, tathā amhākaṃ bhagavatāpi pavattitanti acchariyavegābhihatā dasasahassilokadhātu saṅkampi sampakampīti dassento “diṭṭhamatte”tiādimāha.

Here, 'by nine modes' means by nine ways of assuming the state of a condition. 'Arises from this'—that is, arising, because it is a causal condition for the arising of the fruit. When ignorance exists, formations arise; when it does not exist, they do not arise. Thus, ignorance is the arising-cause of formations. Moreover, when ignorance exists, formations proceed and are produced. Just as they impel towards existence and so forth, so ignorance is a condition for them; similarly, they strive, exert themselves for the arising of the fruit, and are conjoined with their own fruit. In the continuum where they themselves arise, they obstruct it, and in the combination of other conditions, they emerge and arise; and it impels and undertakes the state of being a cause for formations. 'Dependent on ignorance, formations go on and proceed'—thus, the specific ways of ignorance assuming the state of a cause for formations, such as arising, should be understood. 'Uppādaṭṭhiti' means 'ṭhiti' is that by which something stands, a cause. Arising itself is the state, hence 'the state of arising.' This method applies to the rest as well. And this seeing of the aspect of conditions, just as it was set in motion by the former great ones at the root of the Bodhi tree, so too was it set in motion by our Blessed One. Showing that the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled and shook violently, struck by the force of wonder, he said, 'Just upon seeing,' and so forth.

Etassa dhammassāti etassa paṭiccasamuppādasaññitassa dhammassa. So pana yasmā atthato hetuppabhavānaṃ hetu. Tenāha “etassa paccayadhammassā”ti[M 2.0103]. Jātiādīnaṃ jarāmaraṇapaccayatāyāti attho. Nāmarūpaparicchedo tassa ca paccayapariggaho na paṭhamābhinivesamattena hoti, atha kho tattha aparāparaṃ ñāṇuppattisaññitena anu anu bujjhanena. Tadubhayabhāvaṃ pana dassento “ñātapariññāvasena ananubujjhanā”ti āha. Niccasaññādīnaṃ pajahanavasena pavattamānā vipassanādhamme paṭivijjhati eva nāma hoti paṭipakkhavikkhambhanena tikkhavisadabhāvāpattito, tadadhiṭṭhānabhūtā ca tīraṇapariññā ariyamaggo ca pariññāpahānābhisamayavasena pavattiyā tīraṇappahānapariññāsaṅgaho cāti tadubhayapaṭivedhābhāvaṃ dassento “tīraṇappahānapariññāvasena appaṭivijjhanā”ti āha. Tantaṃ vuccati paṭavīnanatthaṃ tantavāyeti tantaṃ āvañchitvā pasāritasuttavaṭṭitaṃ nīyatīti katvā, taṃ pana tantākulatāya nidassanabhāvena ākulameva gahitanti āha “tantaṃ viya ākulajātā”ti. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassento “yathā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samānetunti pubbenāparaṃ samaṃ katvā ānetuṃ, avisamaṃ ujuṃ kātunti attho. Tantameva vā ākulaṃ tantākulaṃ, tantākulaṃ viya jātā bhūtā tantākulakajātā. Majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ anupagantvā antadvayapakkhandena paccayākāre khalitvā ākulabyākulā honti, teneva antadvayapakkhandena taṃtaṃdiṭṭhiggāhavasena paribbhamantā ujukaṃ dhammaṭṭhititantaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na jānanti. Tenāha “na sakkonti paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātu”nti. Dve bodhisatteti paccekabodhisattamahābodhisatte. Attano dhammatāyāti attano sabhāvena, paropadesena vināti attho. Tattha tattha guḷakajātanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne jātaguḷakaṃ piṇḍisuttaṃ. Tato eva gaṇṭhibaddhanti vuttaṃ. Paccayesu pakkhalitvāti aniccadukkhānattādisabhāvesu paccayadhammesu niccādibhāvavasena pakkhalitvā.
