Paccaye ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontoti tasseva niccādigāhassa avissajjanato paccayadhammanimittaṃ attano dassanaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkonto idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthavasena [V 2.0089] gaṇṭhikajātā hontīti āha “dvāsaṭṭhi…pe… gaṇṭhibaddhā”ti.

By 'this Dhamma' is meant this Dhamma known as dependent origination. Since it is, in essence, the cause of phenomena arisen from causes, it is therefore said, 'of this Dhamma of conditions.' The meaning is that birth and so on are conditions for aging and death. The delineation of name-and-form and the comprehension of its conditions do not occur merely by initial adherence, but rather by the repeated arising of knowledge, by understanding little by little. To show the absence of both, it is said, 'by not understanding by way of comprehension of the known.' When insight proceeds by abandoning perceptions of permanence and so on, it indeed penetrates the Dhamma through the suppression of opposing factors, attaining a state of sharp clarity. The decisive comprehension based on this, and the Noble Path, which occurs by way of the realization of comprehension and abandonment, are also included in the comprehension by discerning and abandonment-comprehension. To show the absence of penetration of both, it is said, 'by not penetrating by way of comprehension by discerning and abandonment-comprehension.' 'Tanta' (thread) is so called because it is drawn out, stretched, and twisted by the weaver for weaving. But that (thread) is taken as an example of tangledness, as something tangled, hence it is said, 'like a tangled mass of threads.' Showing the concisely stated meaning in detail, it is said, 'Just as,' and so forth. 'To make it even' means to bring the earlier and later parts to be equal, to make it not uneven, straight. Or, the tangled thread itself is 'tantākula' (tangled mass), and what is born or has come to be like a tangled mass is called 'tantākulakajāta' (born from a tangled mass). Without following the middle way, by falling into two extremes and stumbling in the aspect of conditions, they become confused and bewildered. Due to clinging to those very extreme views, they wander taking up those various views, and do not know how to penetrate the straight thread of the Dhamma’s stability. Therefore, it is said, 'They cannot make the aspect of conditions straight.' The 'two bodhisattas' refer to the Paccekabodhisatta and the Mahābodhisatta. 'By their own nature' means by their own inherent quality, without instruction from others. 'Here and there, knots are formed' means in this and that place, a ball of thread, a knot, is formed. Hence, it is said, 'bound by knots.' 'Faltering among conditions' means faltering in the nature of conditioned phenomena—impermanent, suffering, and non-self—by perceiving them as permanent and so on. Being unable to straighten his own view regarding the sign of conditioned phenomena due to not abandoning that very perception of permanence and so on, he becomes knotted by way of the bodily knot of adherence to 'this is truth.' Therefore, it is said, 'Sixty-two... bound by knots.'

Ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā sassatadiṭṭhiādi diṭṭhiyo nissitā allīnā, vinanato kulāti itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmassa tantavāyassa [M 2.0104] gaṇṭhikaṃ nāma ākulabhāvena aggato vā mūlato vā duviññeyyāvayavaṃ khalitabandhasuttanti āha “kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasutta”nti. Sakuṇikāti vaṭṭacāṭakasakuṇikā. Sā hi rukkhasākhāsu olambanakulāvakā hoti. Tañhi sā kulāvakaṃ tato tato tiṇahīrādike ānetvā tathā tathā vinandhati, yathā tesaṃ pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ viya aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ vivecetuṃ vā na sakkā. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Tadubhayampīti kulāgaṇṭhikanti vuttaṃ kañjiyasuttaṃ kulāvakañca. Purimanayenevāti “evameva sattā”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva.

Whatever ascetics or brahmins are dependent on and cling to views such as eternalism, etc. A weaver's tangled thread (pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ)—a loosely-tied thread whose parts are difficult to discern from the top or the root due to its tangled nature—is called a 'weaver's knot' (kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ). 'Sakuṇikā' means the vaṭṭacāṭaka bird. For that bird has a hanging nest on tree branches. Indeed, it brings grass, strips of fibre, and the like from various places and weaves its nest in such a way that, like the weaver's tangled thread, it is impossible to bring the top to the top or the root to the root, or to separate them. Therefore, it is said, 'Just as,' and so forth. 'Both of these' refers to the tangled thread called the 'weaver's knot' and the bird's nest. 'By the previous method' means by the method previously stated with 'In the same way, beings,' and so forth.

Kāmaṃ muñjapabbajatiṇāni yathājātānipi dīghabhāvena patitvā araññaṭṭhāne aññamaññaṃ vinandhitvā ākulāni hutvā tiṭṭhanti, tāni pana tathā dubbiveciyāni yathā rajjubhūtānīti dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Indeed, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, and other grasses, though growing naturally long, fall down in the forest, become intertwined with one another, and remain tangled. To show that they are then as difficult to separate as if they had become ropes, it is said, 'Just as...' and so forth. The rest here is to be understood in the same way as stated below.

Apāyoti ayena sukhena, sukhahetunā vā virahito. Dukkhassa gatibhāvatoti apāyikassa dukkhassa pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Sukhasamussayatoti “abbhudayato vinipatitattā”ti virūpaṃ nipatitattā yathā tenattabhāvena sukhasamussayo na hoti, evaṃ nipatitattā. Itaroti saṃsāro nanu “apāya”ntiādinā vuttopi saṃsāro evāti? Saccametaṃ, nirayādīnaṃ pana adhimattadukkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ apāyādiggahaṇaṃ gobalibaddañāyena ayamattho veditabbo. Khandhānañca paṭipāṭīti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ hetuphalabhāvena aparāparuppatti. Abbhocchinnaṃ vattamānāti avicchedena pavattamānā.

Apāya means devoid of aya—that is, happiness, or the cause of happiness. Because it is a destination of suffering means because it is the place where the suffering of the woeful states occurs. Vinipāta (downfall) is so called because of 'having fallen from prosperity'; this means having fallen in a distorted way, in such a way that in that state of existence there is no accumulation of happiness. The other is saṃsāra. But is not saṃsāra itself what is called 'apāya', etc.? This is true. However, the mention of 'apāya', etc., is to show the excessive suffering in hell and similar realms; this meaning should be understood by the maxim of the ox and the bull. 'The sequence of aggregates' means the successive arising of the five aggregates through cause and effect. 'Uninterruptedly occurring' means occurring without cessation.

Taṃ sabbampīti taṃ “apāya”ntiādinā vuttaṃ sabbaṃ apāyadukkhañceva vaṭṭadukkhañca. Mahāsamudde vātakkhittā nāvā viyāti idaṃ paribbhamanaṭṭhānassa mahantabhāvadassanatthañceva paribbhamanassa anavattitadassanatthañca veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

All that means all that was stated beginning with 'apāya,' encompassing both the suffering of the woeful states and the suffering of the round of existence. Like a ship tossed by winds in the great ocean—this should be understood as showing both the vastness of the place of wandering and the unceasing nature of wandering. The rest is to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

Nidānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nidāna Sutta is completed.

Dukkhavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Suffering is completed.

7. Mahāvaggo

7. The Great Chapter

1. Assutavāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse to the Uninstructed

61. “Assutavā”ti [V 2.0090][M 2.0105] sotadvārānusārena upadhāritaṃ, upadhāraṇaṃ vā sutaṃ assa atthīti sutavā, tappaṭikkhepena na sutavāti assutavā. Vā-saddo cāyaṃ pasaṃsāyaṃ, atisayassa vā bodhanako, tasmā yassa pasaṃsitaṃ, atisayena vā sutaṃ atthi, so “sutavā”ti saṃkilesaviddhaṃsanasamattho pariyattidhammaparicayo “taṃ sutvā tathattāya paṭipatti ca sutavā”ti iminā padena pakāsito. Atha vā sotabbayuttaṃ sutvā kattabbanipphattiṃ suṇīti sutavā. Tappaṭikkhepena na sutavāti assutavā. Tenāhu porāṇā “āgamādhigamābhāvā, ñeyyo assutavā itī”ti. Tathā cāha “khandhadhātu…pe… vinicchayarahito”ti. Tattha vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho, tattha paripucchanaṃ paripucchā, kusalehi saha codanāpariharaṇavasena vinicchayassa kāraṇaṃ vinicchayo. Puthūnanti bahūnaṃ. Kilesādīnaṃ kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ paṭisambhidāmagganiddesesu (mahāni. 51, 94) āgatanayena. Andhaputhujjano gahito “nālaṃ nibbinditu”ntiādivacanato. Āsannapaccakkhavācī idaṃ-saddoti āha “imasminti paccuppannapaccakkhakāyaṃ dassetī”ti. Catūsu mahābhūtesu niyuttoti cātumahābhūtiko. Yathā pana mahāmattikāya nibbattaṃ mattikāmayaṃ, evamayaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehi nibbatto “catumahābhūtamayo”ti vuttaṃ. Nibbindeyyāti nibbindanampi āpajjeyya. Nibbindanā nāma ukkaṇṭhanā anabhiratibhāvatoti vuttaṃ “ukkaṇṭheyyā”ti. Virajjeyyāti vītarāgo bhaveyya. Tenāha “na rajjeyyā”ti. Vimucceyyāti idha pana accantāya vimuccanaṃ adhippetanti āha “muccitukāmo bhaveyyā”ti. Catūhi ca rūpajanakapaccayehi āgato cayoti, ācayo, vuddhi. Cayato apakkamoti apacayo, parihāni. Ādānanti gahaṇaṃ, paṭisandhiyā nibbatti. Bhedoti khandhānaṃ bhedo. So hi kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttoti āha “nikkhepananti bhedo”ti.

61. Sutavā (instructed) is one who has suta (hearing), which is what is determined through the ear-door, or is determination itself. By negating that, na sutavā, one is assutavā (uninstructed). And this particle -vā is used in the sense of praise, or to indicate excellence. Therefore, one who has praised or excellent hearing is sutavā. Familiarity with the scriptural teaching, which is capable of destroying defilements, and the practice for the sake of its true nature after having heard it, are revealed by this term sutavā. Alternatively, one is sutavā because, having heard what ought to be heard, one accomplishes what ought to be done. By negating that, one is assutavā. Hence the ancients said: 'Due to the absence of scripture and realization, one should be known as uninstructed.' And thus it is said: 'devoid of discrimination regarding aggregates, elements...' Therein, uggaha (learning) is making it come to the lips; paripucchā (inquiry) is questioning about it; vinicchaya (discrimination) is the cause of discrimination by way of charging and refuting together with the skillful. 'Of the many' means of many. 'Of defilements, etc.' means of the defilement-formations; this should be elaborated according to the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and Niddesa. The blind worldling is meant, from the statement 'incapable of becoming disenchanted,' etc. The word idaṃ ('this') refers to what is near and directly perceived; thus he says, 'in this' points to the body which is present and directly perceived. 'Composed of the four great elements' means connected to the four great elements. Just as what is produced from a great lump of clay is 'earthen', so this, being produced from the four great elements, is called 'made of the four great elements'. 'Might become disenchanted' means one might even experience disenchantment. Disenchantment is aversion, a state of non-delight; thus it is said, 'should become averse'. 'Might become dispassionate' means one should become free from lust. Hence he says, 'should not be impassioned'. 'Might be liberated': here, however, complete liberation is intended; thus he says, 'should desire to be liberated'. 'Accumulation' (caya) is what has come from the four form-producing conditions; it means increase, growth. 'Decline' (apacayo) is a departure from accumulation; it means diminution. 'Taking up' (ādāna) is grasping; the arising at rebirth-linking. 'Breaking apart' (bheda) is the breaking apart of the aggregates. Since that is called the 'laying down' of the corpse, he says, ''laying down' means breaking apart'.

Paññāyantīti pakārato ñāyanti. Rūpaṃ pariggahetuṃ pariggaṇhanavasenapi rūpaṃ ālambituṃ. Ayuttarūpaṃ katvā taṇhādīhi pariggahetuṃ arūpaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ yuttarūpaṃ [M 2.0106] karoti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sappāyabhāvato. Tenāha “kasmā”tiādi. Nikkaḍḍhantoti tato gāhato nīharanto.

'They are discerned' (paññāyanti) means they are known in detail. To comprehend form, and by way of comprehension, to take form as an object. He makes it unsuitable to be grasped by craving and so forth, and makes the formless suitable to be comprehended, because it is conducive for those monks. Therefore, it is said, 'Why?' and so on. 'Drawing out' means leading out from that grasp.

Manāyatanasseva [V 2.0091] nāmaṃ, na samādhipaññattīnaṃ “cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 1.9.9), citto gahapatī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 74) viya. Cittīkātabbabhūtaṃ vatthu etassāti cittavatthu, tassa bhāvo cittavatthutā, tena kāraṇena cittabhāvamāha. Cittagocaratāyāti cittavicittavisayatāya. Sampayuttadhammacittatāyāti rāgādisaddhādisampayuttadhammavasena cittasabhāvattā. Tena cittatāya cittattamāha. Vijānanaṭṭhenāti bujjhanaṭṭhena. Ajjhositanti ajjhosābhūtāya taṇhāya gahitaṃ. Tenāha “taṇhāyā”tiādi. Parāmasitvāti dhammasabhāvaṃ aniccatādiṃ atikkamitvā parato niccādito āmasitvā. Aṭṭhasatanti aṭṭhādhikaṃ sataṃ. Nava mānāti seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā āgatā navavidhamānā. Brahmajāle āgatā sassatavādādayo dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo. Evanti vuttākārena. Yasmā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāhavasena puthujjanena daḷhaggāhaṃ gahitaṃ, tasmā so tattha nibbindituṃ nibbidāñāṇaṃ uppādetuṃ na samattho.

This is a name for the mind-base (manāyatana) itself, not for concepts of concentration, as in 'cultivating mind and wisdom' or 'Citto the householder,' and so on. Cittavatthu (mind-base) is so called because its base (vatthu) has become something to be made into mind (cittīkātabbabhūtaṃ); the state of that is cittavatthutā (mind-baseness). For that reason, it speaks of cittabhāva (mind-nature). 'Because of its range as mind' (cittagocaratāya) means because its objects are manifold and various. 'Because of its mind-nature through associated states' (sampayuttadhammacittatāya) means because of its nature as mind by way of states associated with lust, etc., and faith, etc. Because of that mind-nature, it speaks of 'mind-ness' (cittatta). 'In the sense of cognizing' (vijānanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of knowing (bujhanaṭṭhena). 'Clung to' (ajjhosita) means grasped by craving that has become an obsession. 'Having misapprehended' (parāmasitvā) means having transgressed the true nature of phenomena, such as impermanence, and having grasped it from another perspective, as permanent, and so on. 'One hundred and eight' (aṭṭhasata) means one hundred plus eight. 'Nine conceits' (nava māna) refers to the nine kinds of conceit that arise for one who is better, such as 'I am better,' and so on. The sixty-two views, such as eternalism, etc., found in the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'Thus' means in the manner stated. Because it is firmly grasped by a worldling through the grasp of craving, conceit, and views, they are incapable of becoming disenchanted with it or of arousing the knowledge of disenchantment.

Bhikkhaveti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tena “vara”nti evamādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Idaṃ anusandhivacanaṃ “kasmā āhā”ti kathetukāmatāya kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Tenāha “paṭhamaṃ hī”tiādi. Assutavatā puthujjanena. Tenāti bhagavatā. Ayuttarūpaṃ kataṃ “nibbindeyyā”tiādinā ādīnavassa vibhāvitattā. Arūpe pana tathā ādīnavassa avibhāvitattā vuttaṃ “arūpaṃ pariggahetuṃ yuttarūpa”nti, yuttarūpaṃ viya katanti adhippāyo. Gāhoti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāho. “Nikkhamitvā arūpaṃ gato”ti idaṃ bhagavatā ādīnavaṃ dassetvā rūpe gāho paṭikkhitto, na arūpe, tasmā “kātabbo nu kho so tatthā”ti micchāgaṇhantānaṃ so tato rūpato nikkhamitvā arūpaṃ gato viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tiṭṭhamānanti tiṭṭhantaṃ. “Āpajjitvā viya hotī”ti sabhāvena pavattamānaṃ “paṭhamavaye”tiādinā rūpassa bhedaṃ vayādīhi vibhajitvā dasseti.

'Bhikkhus'—here, the word 'iti' signifies 'and so forth,' hence it includes terms like 'excellent' and so on. This is a connective statement, asking the reason, 'Why did he say this?' with the intention of explaining. Therefore, it is said, 'First, indeed,' and so forth. By the uninstructed ordinary person. 'By him'—that is, by the Blessed One. It was rendered inappropriate by means of 'should become disenchanted,' and so on, because the danger was made clear. However, regarding the formless, since the danger was not made clear in the same way, it is said, 'The formless is appropriate to grasp,' the meaning being that it was done as if appropriate. 'Grasping'—this refers to the grasping of craving, conceit, and views. 'Having emerged, he went to the formless'—this was stated by the Blessed One to show the danger in form, rejecting the grasping of form but not of the formless. Therefore, for those who wrongly assume, 'Should that be done there?'—it is as if, having emerged from that form, one went to the formless, and so it was said. 'Remaining' means that which stands. 'As if having entered'—proceeding by its own nature. By means of 'in the first phase,' and so on, it shows the breaking apart of form by distinguishing it through decay and so forth.

Pādassa uddharaṇeti yathā ṭhapitassa pādassa ukkhipane. Atiharaṇanti yathāuddhataṃ yathāṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā haraṇaṃ. Vītiharaṇanti uddhato [M 2.0107] pādo yathāṭṭhitaṃ pādaṃ yathā na ghaṭṭeti, evaṃ thokaṃ passato pariṇāmetvā haraṇaṃ. Vossajjananti tathā parapādaṃ vītisāretvā bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipanatthaṃ avossajjanaṃ. Sannikkhepananti vossajjetvā bhūmiyaṃ samaṃ nikkhipanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ. Sannirujjhananti nikkhittassa sabbaso nirujjhanaṃ uppīḷanaṃ. Tattha tatthevāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ paṭhamavayādike eva. Avadhāraṇena tesaṃ koṭṭhāsantarasaṅkamanābhāvamāha. Odhīti bhāvo, pabbanti sandhi. Paṭhamavayādayo eva hettha odhi pabbanti ca adhippetā. Paṭapaṭāyantāti “paṭapaṭā”iti [V 2.0092] karontā viya, tena nesaṃ pavattikkhaṇassa ittarataṃ dasseti. Etanti etaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ yathāvuttaṃ tattha tattheva bhijjanaṃ evaṃ vuttappakārameva. Vaṭṭippadesanti vaṭṭiyā pulakaṃ barahaṃ. Tañhi vaṭṭiyā pulakaṃ anatikkamitvāva sā dīpajālā bhijjati. Paveṇisambandhavasenāti santativasena.

'Lifting the foot' means raising the foot from where it was placed. 'Moving forward' means carrying the raised foot beyond the original standing place. 'Moving away' means moving the raised foot so that it does not touch the foot that remains in place, thus turning it slightly to the side and carrying it. 'Releasing' means, after moving the other foot away, releasing it down to place it on the ground. 'Setting down' means, after releasing it, placing it evenly on the ground, establishing it. 'Pressing down' means the complete stopping and pressing of the foot that has been placed. 'There, right there' refers to each of the first ages, and so on. By the emphasis, it states the absence of transition between those sections. 'Odhī' is a limit; 'pabba' is a joint. Here, the first ages and so on are intended as 'odhi' and 'pabba.' 'Paṭapaṭāyantā' means as if making a 'paṭapaṭā' sound, thereby showing the transience of the moment of their occurrence. 'This' refers to this breaking of material phenomena, as described, right there, in the manner stated. 'Vaṭṭippadesa' means a knot on a wick or a joint on a reed. For the flame of a lamp breaks without passing beyond the knot of the wick. 'Due to the connection of the sequence' means due to the continuum.

Rattinti rattiyaṃ. Bhummatthe hetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Evaṃ pana attho na gahetabbo anuppannassa nirodhābhāvato. Purimapaveṇitoti rūpe vuttapaveṇito. Anekāni cittakoṭisatasahassāni uppajjantīti vuttamatthaṃ theravādena dīpetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Aḍḍhacūḷanti thokena ūnaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ, tassa pana upaḍḍhaṃ adhikārato vāhasatassāti viññāyati. “Aḍḍhacuddasa”nti keci, “aḍḍhacatuttha”nti apare. “Sādhikaṃ diyaḍḍhasataṃ vāhā”ti daḷhaṃ katvā vadantīti vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Catunāḷiko tumbo. Mahāraññatāya pavaddhaṃ vanaṃ pavananti āha “pavaneti mahāvane”ti. Tanti paṭhamaṃ gahitasākhaṃ. Ayamatthoti ayaṃ bhūmiṃ anotaritvā ṭhitasākhāya eva gahaṇasaṅkhāto attho. Etadatthameva hi bhagavā “araññe”ti vatvāpi “pavane”ti āha.

'Ratti' means 'in the night.' This is a usage in the locative sense. However, this meaning should not be taken, since what has not arisen cannot cease. 'From the previous sequence' means from the sequence mentioned regarding form. To illuminate by the Theravāda tradition the stated meaning that 'many hundreds of thousands of crores of consciousness-moments arise,' it is said, 'And this was said,' and so forth. 'Aḍḍhacūḷa' means a half that is slightly less; however, that half is understood from the context to be a hundred loads. Some say 'thirteen and a half,' others 'three and a half.' It should be investigated why they state emphatically, 'more than one hundred and fifty loads.' A gourd of four nāḷikas. A forest that has grown to be a great wilderness is called a 'pavana'; hence it is said, 'pavana means in a great forest.' 'That' means the first branch grasped. 'This is the meaning' refers to this meaning designated as the grasping of the very branch on which one stands, without descending to the ground. It is precisely for this meaning that the Blessed One, although having said 'in the wilderness,' also said 'in the forest.'

Araññamahāvanaṃ viyāti araññaṭṭhāne brahāraññe viya. Ārammaṇolambananti ārammaṇassa avalambanaṃ. Na vattabbaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena vinā anuppajjanato. Ekajātiyanti rūpādinīlādiekasabhāvaṃ. “Dissati, bhikkhave, imassa cātumahābhūtikassa kāyassa ācayopi apacayopī”ti vadantena rūpato nīharitvā arūpe gāho patiṭṭhāpito nāma, “varaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano”tiādiṃ vadantena arūpato nīharitvā rūpe gāho patiṭṭhāpito nāma.

'Like a great wilderness-forest' means like a great wilderness in a forest place. 'Leaning on an object' means the dependence on an object. It should not be said that it arises without an object as condition, because of its non-arising. 'Of a single kind' means having a single nature, such as blue and so on among forms and so on. By saying, 'Bhikkhus, the accumulation and decline of this body composed of the four great elements is seen,' grasping is established in the formless, as it were, by withdrawing it from form. By saying, 'Better, bhikkhus, is an uninstructed ordinary person,' and so forth, grasping is established in form, as it were, by withdrawing it from the formless.

Nanti [M 2.0108] gāhaṃ. Ubhayatoti rūpato ca arūpato ca. Harissāmīti nīharissāmi. Parivattetvāti mantaṃ jappitvā. Kaṇṇe dhumetvāti kaṇṇe dhametvā. Assāti visassa. Nimmathetvāti nimmadditvā, nīharitvāti adhippāyo.

'It' means grasping. 'From both' means from form and from the formless. 'I will carry away' means 'I will remove.' 'Having recited' means having chanted a mantra. 'Having smoked into the ear' means having blown into the ear. 'Of it' means of the poison. 'Having churned out' means having crushed, the intention being 'having removed.'

Maggoti lokuttaramaggo. “Nibbinda”nti iminā balavavipassanā kathitā.

'Path' means the supramundane path. By this word 'Become disenchanted,' powerful insight is spoken of.

Assutavāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Assutavā Sutta is concluded.

2. Dutiyaassutavāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Second Assutavā Sutta

62. Paccayabhāvena [V 2.0093] sukhavedanāya hitanti sukhavedaniyaṃ. Tenāha “sukhavedanāya paccaya”nti. Paccayabhāvo ca upanissayakoṭiyā, na sahajātakoṭiyā. Tenāha “nanu cā”tiādi. Javanavedanāyāti javanacittasahagatāya vedanāya. Taṃ sandhāyāti taṃ upanissayapaccayataṃ sandhāya. Etanti etaṃ “sukhavedanāya paccaya”nti vacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Eseva nayoti iminā “nanu ca sotasamphasso sukhavedanāya paccayo na hotī”ti evamādiṃ atidisati. So samphasso jāti uppattiṭṭhānaṃ etassāti tajjātikaṃ, vedayitaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā tassa phassassa anucchavikameva hoti, tasmā tassāruppaṃ tassa phassassa anurūpanti ca attho vutto. Vuttanayenāti “sukhavedanāya paccayo”tiādinā vuttavidhianusārena. Adharāraṇiyaṃ uttarāraṇiyā mantanavasena ghaṭṭanaṃ iva saṅghaṭṭanaṃ phassena yugaggāho, tassa pana ghaṭṭanassa nirantarappavattiyā piṇḍitabhāvo idha samodhānaṃ, na kesañci dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā sahāvaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “saṅghaṭṭanasampiṇḍanenāti attho”ti. Aggicuṇṇoti vipphuliṅgaṃ. Vatthūti cakkhādivatthu visayasaṅghaṭṭanato. Labbhamānova dhammo saṅghaṭṭanaṃ viya gayhatīti vuttaṃ “saṅghaṭṭanaṃ viya phasso”ti. Usmādhātu viya vedanā dukkhasabhāvattā.

62. 'Conducive to pleasant feeling' means beneficial for pleasant feeling by way of being a condition. Therefore, it is said, 'a condition for pleasant feeling.' The state of being a condition is in the category of decisive support, not in the category of co-nascence. Therefore, it is said, 'Is it not?' and so forth. 'For the feeling of impulsion' means for the feeling associated with impulsion-consciousness. 'Referring to that' means referring to that state of being a decisive support condition. 'This' means this statement, 'a condition for pleasant feeling,' was said. By 'This very method,' he applies by extension such passages as, 'Is not ear-contact a condition for pleasant feeling?' and so on. That which has that contact as its birth, its place of origin, is 'born from that,' i.e., what is felt. And since that is indeed suitable for that contact, therefore the meaning is also stated as 'its suitability,' that is, 'corresponding to that contact.' 'By the stated method' means in accordance with the method stated by 'a condition for pleasant feeling,' and so on. Contact is the grasping of a pair. Striking together is like the rubbing of the lower fire-stick with the upper fire-stick by way of churning. But here, the state of being compact due to the continuous occurrence of that rubbing is 'coming together,' not the co-existence of any two or three. Therefore it is said, 'the meaning is by the compacting of the striking together.' 'Fire-powder' means a spark. 'Basis' means the eye-basis and so on, from its striking together with an object. A phenomenon, when being received, is grasped like a striking together; thus it is said, 'contact is like striking together.' Feeling is like the heat element, due to its nature of suffering.

Dutiyaassutavāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Assutavā Sutta is concluded.

3. Puttamaṃsūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sutta on the Simile of the Son's Flesh

63. Vuttanayamevāti [M 2.0109] heṭṭhā āhāravaggassa paṭhamasutte vuttanayameva. Lābhasakkārenāti lābhasakkārasaṅkhātāya aṭṭhuppattiyāti keci. Lābhasakkāre vā aṭṭhuppattiyāti apare. Yo hi lābhasakkāranimittaṃ paccayesu gedhena bhikkhūnaṃ apaccavekkhitaparibhogo jāto, taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ nikkhipi. Yamakamahāmeghoti heṭṭhā olambanaupariuggamanavasena satapaṭalasahassapaṭalo yugaḷamahāmegho.

63. 'The very method stated' means the very method stated below in the first sutta of the Chapter on Food. 'By gain and honor': some say this means 'by the occasion designated as gain and honor.' Others say it means 'by the occasion in the matter of gain and honor.' For when, on account of gain and honor, the use of requisites without reflection arose among the bhikkhus with greed, the Blessed One, having made that the occasion, delivered this discourse. 'The great twin cloud' is a great pair-cloud of a hundred and a thousand layers, by way of hanging down below and rising up above.

Tiṭṭhanti ceva bhagavati katthaci nibaddhavāsaṃ vasante, cārikampi gacchante anubandhanti ca. Bhikkhūnampi yebhuyyena kappasatasahassaṃ tato bhiyyopi pūritadānapāramisañcayattā tadā mahālābhasakkāro uppajjatīti vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassapī”ti. Sakkatoti sakkārappatto. Garukatoti garukārappatto. Mānitoti bahumato manasā piyāyito ca. Pūjitoti mālādipūjāya ceva catupaccayābhipūjāya ca pūjito. Apacitoti apacāyanappatto. Yassa hi cattāro [V 2.0094] paccaye sakkatvā suabhisaṅkhate paṇītapaṇīte upanenti, so sakkato. Yasmiṃ garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā denti, so garukato. Yaṃ manasā piyāyanti bahumaññanti, so bahumato. Yassa sabbametaṃ pūjāvasena karonti, so pūjito. Yassa abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānañjalikammādivasena paramanipaccakāraṃ karonti, so apacito. Bhagavati bhikkhusaṅghe ca loko evaṃ paṭipanno. Tena vuttaṃ “tena kho pana samayena…pe… parikkhārāna”nti (udā. 14; saṃ. ni. 2.70). Lābhaggayasaggappattanti lābhassa ca yasassa ca aggaṃ ukkaṃsaṃ pattaṃ.

They remain with the Blessed One when he dwells settled in one place, and they follow him when he goes on tour. For most monks, due to having accumulated the fulfilled perfection of generosity for a hundred thousand eons or more, at that time great gain and honor arose—hence it is said, 'Thus also for the Sangha of monks.' 'Sakkata' means one who has received honor. 'Garukata' means one who has received reverence. 'Mānita' means one who is highly esteemed and cherished in mind. 'Pūjita' means one who is worshipped with offerings such as garlands and with the four requisites. 'Apacita' means one who has received homage. For one is 'sakkata' to whom they offer the four requisites, having honored him, well-prepared, choice and excellent. One is 'garukata' when they give while establishing a sense of reverence towards him. One is 'bahumata' whom they cherish in mind and greatly esteem. One is 'pūjita' for whom they do all this by way of worship. One is 'apacita' to whom they show the utmost respect by way of salutation, rising, joining hands, and so forth. The world conducts itself thus toward the Blessed One and the Sangha of monks. Therefore, it is said, 'At that time... endowed with the requisites' (Ud. 14; SN 2.70). 'Lābhaggayasaggappatta' means having attained the pinnacle of gain and fame.

Paṭhamāhāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the First Nutriment

Assāti bhagavato. Dhammasabhāvacintāvasena pavattaṃ sahottappañāṇaṃ dhammasaṃvego. Dhuvapaṭisevanaṭṭhānañhetaṃ sattānaṃ, yadidaṃ āhāraparibhogo, tasmā na tattha apaccavekkhaṇamattena pārājikaṃ paññapetuṃ sakkāti adhippāyo. Āhārāti “paccayā”tiādinā pubbe āhāresu vuttavidhiṃ sandhāya āha “āhārā”tiādi. Idāni tattha kattabbaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ sandhāya “heṭṭhā vuttatthamevā”ti vuttaṃ.

“Assa” refers to the Blessed One. The spiritual urgency (dhammasaṃvega), which arises from reflecting on the nature of phenomena, is knowledge accompanied by moral dread. This, namely the consumption of food, is a constant basis for beings to resort to; therefore, the intention is that it is not possible to lay down a pārājika offense merely for not reflecting on it. Regarding “Āhāra,” he says “āhārā” and so on, referring to the method stated previously concerning nutriments by means of “requisites” and so on. Now, referring to the exposition of meaning to be done there, it is said, “The meaning is just as stated below.”

Ādīnavanti [M 2.0110] dosaṃ. Jāyāti bhariyā. Patīti bhattā. Apekkhāsaddā cete pitāputtasaddā viya, pāḷiyaṃ pana ā-kārassa rassattaṃ sānunāsikañca katvā vuttaṃ “jāyampatikā”ti. Sammā phalaṃ vahatīti sambalaṃ, sukhāvahanti attho. Tathā hi taṃ “pathe hitanti pātheyya”nti vuccati. Maggassa kantārapariyāpannattā vuttaṃ “kantārabhūtaṃ magga”nti. Dullabhatāya taṃ udakaṃ tattha tāretīti kantāraṃ, nirudakaṃ mahāvanaṃ. Ruḷhīvasena itarampi mahāvanaṃ tathā vuccatīti āha “corakantāra”ntiādi. Pararājūnaṃ veriādīnañca vasena sappaṭibhayampi araññaṃ ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ “pañcavidha”nti.

‘Ādīnava’ means fault. ‘Jāyā’ means wife. ‘Patī’ means husband. These words are like ‘father’ and ‘son’ in implying dependence; but in the Pāli, the long ‘ā’ is shortened and made nasal, and thus it is said ‘jāyampatikā’. It carries the right fruit, thus it is ‘sambala’ (provisions); the meaning is that it brings happiness. Thus indeed it is called ‘pātheyya’ (provisions) because it is beneficial on the path. Because the path is included in the wilderness, it is said, ‘the path that has become a wilderness.’ It is called ‘kantāra’ (wilderness) because one crosses it with difficulty regarding water; it is a great waterless forest. He says that by convention even other great forests are called thus, for example, ‘a thieves’ wilderness’ and so on. It is said ‘of five kinds’ because even a fearsome forest due to hostile kings and enemies is included here.

Ghanaghanaṭṭhānatoti maṃsassa bahalabahalaṃ thūlathūlaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato. “Tādisañhi maṃsaṃ gahetvā sukkhāpitaṃ vallūraṃ. Sūle āvunitvā pakkamaṃsaṃ sūlamaṃsaṃ. Viraḷacchāyāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu gantuṃ asamattho hutvā. Govatakukkuravatadevatāyācanādīhīti govatakukkuravatādivatacaraṇehi ceva devatāyācanādīhi paṇidhikammehi ca mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhūtaṃ.

‘Ghanaghanaṭṭhānato’ means from the place where the flesh is very thick and dense. Indeed, such flesh, when taken and dried, becomes dried meat. Meat roasted by skewering it on a spit is ‘sūlamaṃsa’ (spit-roasted meat). Being unable to go, they sat in the sparse shade. ‘Govatakukkuravatadevatāyācanādīhi’ means by the observance of vows such as those of cattle and dogs, and by acts of resolve such as prayers to deities, immense suffering was experienced.

Yasmā pana sāsane sammāpaṭipajjantassa bhikkhuno āhāraparibhogassa opammabhāvena tesaṃ jāyampatikānaṃ puttamaṃsaparibhogo idha bhagavatā ānīto, tasmāssa nānākārehi opammattaṃ [V 2.0095] vibhāvetuṃ “tesaṃ so puttamaṃsāhāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sajātimaṃsatāyāti samānajātikamaṃsabhāvena, manussamaṃsabhāvenāti attho. Masussamaṃsañhi kulappasutamanussānaṃ amanuññaṃ hoti aparicitabhāvato gārayhabhāvato ca, tato eva ñātiādimaṃsatāyātiādi vuttaṃ. Taruṇamaṃsatāyātiādi pana sabhāvato anabhisaṅkhārato ca amanuññāti katvā vuttaṃ. Adhūpitatāyāti adhūpitabhāvato. Majjhattabhāveyeva ṭhitā. Tato eva nicchandarāgaparibhoge ṭhitāti vuttaṃ kantārato nittharaṇajjhāsayatāya. Idāni ye ca te anapanītāhāro, na yāvadatthaparibhogo vigatamaccheramalatā sammohābhāvo āyatiṃ tattha patthanābhāvo sannidhikārābhāvo apariccajanamadatthābhāvo ahīḷanā avivādaparibhogo cāti upamāyaṃ labbhamānā pakāravisesā, te tathā nīharitvā upameyye yojetvā dassetuṃ “na [M 2.0111] aṭṭhinhārucammanissitaṭṭhānānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ kāraṇanti taṃ tesaṃ jāyampatīnaṃ yāvadeva kantāranittharaṇatthāya puttamaṃsaparibhogasaṅkhātaṃ kāraṇaṃ.

Since the Blessed One introduced here the consumption of their own child’s flesh by those parents as a simile for the proper use of food by a monk practicing rightly in the Dispensation, therefore, to explain its nature as a simile in various ways, the passage beginning “that food of their child’s flesh” is commenced. Herein, ‘sajātimaṃsatāya’ means by being flesh of the same kind, that is, by being human flesh. For human flesh is disagreeable to well-bred people due to its being unfamiliar and reprehensible; therefore, it is said, ‘by being the flesh of relatives’ and so on. But ‘taruṇamaṃsatāya’ and so on is said considering that it is naturally disagreeable and not deliberately prepared. ‘Adhūpitatāya’ means by not having been smoked. It remains in a neutral state. Therefore, it is said that it remains in consumption free from desire and lust, with the intention of merely crossing the wilderness. Now, those specific characteristics obtained in the simile—namely, food not taken away, not consumed to excess, freedom from the stain of stinginess, absence of delusion, absence of future longing for it, absence of hoarding, absence of selfishly retaining it, not scorning, and consumption without dispute—to extract them thus and apply them to the subject of comparison and show them, it is said, ‘not dependent on bones, sinews, skin,’ and so on. ‘That reason’ means that very reason of those parents, namely, the consumption of their child’s flesh, solely for the purpose of crossing the wilderness.

Nissandapāṭikulyataṃ paccavekkhantopi kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ parivīmaṃsati. Yathā te jāyampatikātiādipi opammasaṃsandanaṃ. “Paribhuñjitabbo āhāro”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Apaṭikkhipitvāti anapanetvā. Vaṭṭakena viya kukkuṭena viya cāti visadisūdāharaṇaṃ. Odhiṃ adassetvāti mahantaggahaṇavasena odhiṃ akatvā. Sīhena viyāti sadisūdāharaṇaṃ. So kira sapadānameva khādati.

Even while reflecting on the repulsiveness of its outflow, he examines physical food. The phrase ‘just as those parents’ and so on is also a connection to the simile. The phrase ‘food should be consumed’ should be brought in and connected. This is the method for the subsequent passages as well. ‘Apaṭikkhipitvā’ means without removing. ‘Like a quail or like a chicken’ are dissimilar examples. ‘Odhiṃ adassetvā’ means without making a boundary by taking a large amount. ‘Like a lion’ is a similar example. For he eats, placing his foot on the prey itself.

Agadhitaamucchitādibhāvena paribhuñjitabbato “amaccharāyitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Abbhantare attā nāma atthīti diṭṭhi attūpaladdhi, taṃsahagatena sammohena attā āhāraṃ paribhuñjatīti. Satisampajaññavasenapīti “asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hotī”ti ettha vuttasatisampajaññavasenapi.

‘Amaccharāyitvā’ (not being miserly) and so on is said because it should be consumed without greed or infatuation. The view that there is a self inside is the perception of self; with the delusion associated with that, one thinks, ‘the self consumes food.’ ‘Satisampajaññavasena’ (by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension) means by means of the mindfulness and clear comprehension stated here: ‘He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting.’

“Aho vata mayaṃ…pe… labheyya”nti patthanaṃ vā, “hiyyo viya…pe… na laddha”nti anusocanaṃ vā akatvāti yojanā.

The construction is: without making a wish such as ‘Oh, may we obtain...’ or a lament such as ‘Unlike yesterday... we have not obtained it.’

“Sannidhiṃ na akaṃsu, bhūmiyaṃ vā nikhaṇiṃsu, agginā vā jhāpayiṃsū”ti na-kāraṃ ānetvā yojanā. Evaṃ sabbattha.

The construction is by supplying the negative particle 'na' (not), resulting in: 'They did not make a hoard, nor did they bury it in the ground, nor did they burn it with fire.' This applies everywhere.

Piṇḍapātaṃ vā ahīḷentena dāyakaṃ vā ahīḷentena paribhuñjitabboti yojanā. Sa pattapāṇīti [V 2.0096] so pattahattho. Nāvajāniyāti na avajāniyā. Atimaññatīti atikkamitvā maññati, avajānātīti attho.

The construction is: one should consume almsfood without scorning the alms or the giver. ‘Sa pattapāṇī’ means he has a bowl in his hand. ‘Nāvajāniya’ means not to despise. ‘Atimaññati’ means he thinks surpassingly, that is, he despises.

“Tīhi pariññāhi pariññāte”ti vatvā tāhi kabaḷīkārāhārassa parijānanavidhiṃ dassento “katha”ntiādimāha. Tattha savatthukavasenāti sasambhāravasena, sabhāvato pana rūpāharaṇaṃ ojamattaṃ hoti. Idañhi kabaḷīkārāhārassa lakkhaṇaṃ. Kāmaṃ rasārammaṇaṃ jivhāpasāde paṭihaññati, tena pana avinābhāvato sampattavisayagāhitāya ca jivhāpasādassa “ojaṭṭhamakarūpaṃ kattha paṭihaññatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassāti jivhāpasādassa[M 2.0112]. Ime dhammāti ime yathāvuttabhūtupādāyadhammā. Tanti rūpakhandhaṃ. Pariggaṇhatoti pariggaṇhantassa. Uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammāti sabbepi ye yathāniddhāritā, tehi sahappavattāva sabbepi ime. Sarasalakkhaṇatoti attano kiccato lakkhaṇato ca. Tesaṃ nāmarūpabhāvena vavatthapitānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ paccayo viññāṇaṃ. “Tassa saṅkhārā tesaṃ avijjā”ti evaṃ uddhaṃ ārohanavasena paccayaṃ. Adhoorohanavasena pana saḷāyatanādike pariyesanto anulomapaṭilomaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati. Saḷāyatanādayopi hi rūpārūpadhammānaṃ yathārahaṃ paccayabhāvena vavatthapetabbāti. Yāthāvato diṭṭhattāti “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito bhiyyo, idaṃ nāmaṃ, ettakaṃ nāmaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti ca yathābhūtaṃ diṭṭhattā. Aniccānupassanā, dukkhānupassanā, anattānupassanā, nibbidānupassanā, virāgānupassanā, nirodhānupassanā, paṭinissaggānupassanāti imāsaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena. Soti kabaḷīkārāhāro. Tilakkhaṇa…pe… saṅkhātāyāti aniccatādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ paṭivijjhanavasena lakkhaṇavantasammasanavasena ca pavattañāṇasaṅkhātāya. Pariññāto hoti anavasesato nāmarūpassa ñātattā tappariyāpannattā ca āhārassa. Tenāha “tasmiṃ yevā”tiādi. Chandarāgāvakaḍḍhanenāti chandarāgassa pajahanena.

Having said, ‘fully understood by three kinds of full understanding,’ he then says ‘how?’ and so on, showing the method of fully understanding edible food by means of those. Herein, ‘savatthukavasena’ means by way of its constituents. But by nature, material nutriment is merely nutritive essence. This is indeed the characteristic of edible food. Although the taste-object strikes the tongue-sensitivity, because of their inseparability and the tongue-sensitivity’s ability to grasp the available object, it is said, ‘Where does the material form with nutritive essence as its eighth component strike?’ ‘Tassa’ refers to the tongue-sensitivity. ‘Ime dhammā’ (these phenomena) means these primary and derived phenomena as stated. ‘Taṃ’ refers to the form aggregate. ‘Pariggaṇhato’ means for one who grasps. ‘Uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammā’ (the arisen phenomena with contact as the fifth) means all these phenomena that arise together with those that have been determined accordingly. ‘Sarasalakkhaṇato’ means by their own function and characteristic. Consciousness is the condition for these five aggregates, which have been distinguished as name-and-form. Thus, by way of ascending, the condition is shown: ‘For that, formations; for them, ignorance.’ But by way of descending, seeking the six sense bases and so on, one sees dependent origination in forward and reverse order. For the six sense bases and so on must also be distinguished according to their appropriate conditioning role among material and immaterial phenomena. ‘Yāthāvato diṭṭhattā’ (because it is seen as it really is) means because it is seen as it truly is, thus: ‘This is form, this much form, no more than this; this is name, this much name, no more than this.’ By means of these seven contemplations: the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of not-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of fading away, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment. ‘So’ refers to edible food. ‘Tilakkhaṇa... saṅkhātāya’ means by the knowledge reckoned as proceeding by way of penetrating the three characteristics—impermanence and so on—and by way of comprehending that which possesses characteristics. It is fully understood because name-and-form is known without remainder and because the nutriment is included in it. Therefore, he says, ‘in that very...’ and so on. ‘Chandarāgāvakaḍḍhanena’ means by the abandoning of desire and lust.

Pañca kāmaguṇā kāraṇabhūtā etassa atthīti pañcakāmaguṇiko. Tenāha “pañcakāmaguṇasambhavo”ti. Ekissā taṇhāya pariññā ekapariññā. Sabbassa pañcakāmaguṇikassa rāgassa pariññā, sabbapariññā. Tadubhayassapi mūlabhūtassa āhārassa pariññā mūlapariññā. Idāni imā tissopi pariññāyo vibhāgena dassetuṃ “yo bhikkhū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Jivhādvāre ekarasataṇhaṃ parijānātīti jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā iti paṭisañcikkhati “yo yamettha raso, so vatthukāmavasena ojaṭṭhamakarūpaṃ hoti jivhāyatanaṃ pasādo. So kiṃ nissito? Catumahābhūtanissito. Taṃsahajāto vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā jīvitindriyanti ime dhammā rūpakkhandho nāma. Yo tasmiṃ rase assādo, ayaṃ rasataṇhā. Taṃsahagatā [V 2.0097] phassādayo dhammā cattāro arūpakkhandhā”tiādivasena. Sabbaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatavasena veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “tena pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññātova hotī”ti. Tattha [M 2.0113] tenāti yo bhikkhu jivhādvāre rasataṇhaṃ parijānāti, tena. Kathaṃ pana ekasmiṃ dvāre taṇhaṃ parijānato pañcasu dvāresu rāgo pariññāto hotīti āha “kasmā”tiādi. Tassāyevāti taṇhāya eva taṇhāsāmaññato ekattanayavasena vuttaṃ. Tatthāti pañcasu dvāresu. Uppajjanatoti rūparāgādibhāvena uppajjanato. Lobho eva hi taṇhāyanaṭṭhena “taṇhā”tipi, rajjanaṭṭhena “rāgo”tipi vuccati. Tenāha “sāyeva hī”tiādi. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ “yathā”tiādinā upamāya sampiṇḍeti. Pañcamagge hanatoti pañcasu maggesu sañcarittaṃ karontena maggagāmino hananto “magge hanato”ti vutto.

One for whom the five strands of sensual pleasure are the cause is called ‘one connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘arising from the five strands of sensual pleasure.’ The full understanding of one craving is single-understanding. The full understanding of all lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is all-understanding. The full understanding of the nutriment that is the root of both is root-understanding. Now, to explain these three kinds of full understanding in detail, the text begins with ‘a monk,’ and so on. He fully understands craving for a single taste at the tongue-door. Having savored a taste with the tongue, he reflects thus: ‘Whatever taste there is here, that, by way of objective sensuality, is the tongue-base, the sensitivity, which is material form with nutritive essence as its eighth component. What is it dependent on? It is dependent on the four great elements. Arisen together with it are color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, and the life faculty—these phenomena are called the form aggregate. The delight in that taste is craving for tastes. Associated with it are contact and other phenomena, which are the four immaterial aggregates,’ and so on. All this should be understood in the way it is presented in the commentary. Therefore, it is said, ‘by that, the lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood.’ Here, ‘by that’ means by the monk who fully understands craving for tastes at the tongue-door. But how is it that by fully understanding craving at one door, lust at the five doors is understood? This is explained with ‘why,’ and so on. ‘Of that very’ means of craving itself; it is spoken of as one by way of the generality of craving. ‘Therein’ refers to the five doors. ‘By arising’ means by arising in the form of lust for forms, and so on. For it is greed itself that is called ‘craving’ in the sense of thirsting, and ‘lust’ in the sense of attachment. Therefore, it is said, ‘that very,’ and so on. Now, the meaning already stated is summarized with the simile beginning with ‘just as.’ ‘Killing on the five paths’ means one who commits robbery on five paths, killing travellers, is called ‘one who kills on the path.’

Sabyañjane piṇḍapātasaññite bhattasamūhe manuññe rūpe rūpasaddādayo labbhanti, tattha pañcakāmaguṇarāgassa sambhavaṃ dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Satisampajaññena pariggahetvāti sabbabhāgiyena kammaṭṭhānaparipālakena pariggahetvā. Nicchandarāgaparibhogenāti maggādhigamasiddhena nicchandarāgaparibhogena paribhutte. Soti kāmaguṇiko rāgo.

In a pleasing mass of food, designated as alms-food, complete with sauces, where forms, sounds, and other sensual objects are found, to show the arising of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, ‘how?’ and so forth is said. ‘Having taken it with mindfulness and clear comprehension’ means having taken it as one who protects the meditation subject in all respects. ‘By partaking without desire and lust’ means when it is partaken of with that partaking free of desire and lust which is accomplished by the attainment of the path. ‘That’ refers to the lust connected with the strands of sensual pleasure.

Tasmiṃ satīti kabaḷīkārāhāre sati. Tassāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa. Uppattitoti uppajjanato. Na hi āhārālābhena jighacchādubbalyaparetassa kāmaparibhogicchā sambhavati. Upanijjhānacittanti rāgavasena aññamaññaṃ olokanacittaṃ.

‘When that exists’ means when there is edible food. ‘Of that’ means of the lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Arising’ means from arising. For indeed, the desire for sensual enjoyment does not arise in one afflicted by hunger and weakness due to lack of food. ‘A mind that contemplates’ means a mind looking upon another with lust.

Natthi taṃ saṃyojananti pañcavidhampi uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tena rāgena…pe… natthī”ti. Tenāti kāmarāgena. Ettakenāti yathāvuttāya desanāya. Kathetuṃ vaṭṭatīti imaṃ paṭhamāhārakathaṃ kathentena dhammakathikena.

‘There is no such fetter’ is said with reference to all five higher fetters. Therefore, he says: ‘By that lust... there is not.’ ‘By that’ means by sensual lust. ‘By so much’ refers to the teaching as stated. ‘It is fitting to speak’ means it is fitting for the Dhamma preacher expounding this first discourse on nutriment to speak.

Paṭhamāhāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the first nutriment.

Dutiyāhāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Second Nutriment

Dutiyeti dutiye āhāre. Uddālitacammāti uppāṭitacammā, sabbaso apanītacammāti attho. Na sakkoti dubbalabhāvato, tathā hi itthī “abalā”ti vuccati. Silākuṭṭādīnanti ādi-saddena iṭṭhakakuṭṭamattikākuṭṭādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Uṇṇanābhīti makkaṭakaṃ. Sarabūti gharagoḷikā[V 2.0098][M 2.0114]. Uccāliṅgapāṇakā nāma lomasā pāṇakā. Ākāsanissitāti ākāsacārino. Luñcitvāti uppāṭetvā.

‘Second’ refers to the second nutriment. ‘With skin flayed’ means with skin torn off, entirely removed; that is the meaning. ‘She cannot’—due to weakness, for a woman is called ‘weak.’ ‘Stone walls, etc.’—the word ‘etc.’ includes brick walls, mud walls, and so on. ‘Spider’ means a spider. ‘Sarabū’ refers to a house lizard. ‘Uccāliṅgapāṇakā’ are hairy creatures. ‘Dependent on the air’ means moving through the sky. ‘Plucking’ means tearing off.

Tisso pariññāti heṭṭhā vuttā ñātapariññādayo tisso pariññā. Tammūlakattāti phassamūlakattā. Desanā yāva arahattā kathitā sabbaso vedanāsu pariññātāsu kilesānaṃ lesassapi abhāvato.

‘Three full understandings’ refers to the three full understandings mentioned previously, namely, full understanding by knowledge and so on. ‘Because it is rooted in that’ means because it is rooted in contact. The teaching is explained up to Arahantship, for when feelings have been fully understood in all respects, not even a trace of the defilements exists.

Dutiyāhāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the second nutriment.

Tatiyāhāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Third Nutriment

Aṅgārakāsunti aṅgārarāsiṃ. Phuṇantīti attano upari sayameva ākirantīti attho. Tenāha “narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā”ti. Narāti purisāti attho, na manussā. Bhayañhi maṃ vindatīti bhayassa vasena karonto bhayaṃ labhati nāma. Santaramānovāti suṭṭhu taramāno eva hutvā. Porisaṃ vuccati purisappamāṇaṃ, tasmā atirekaporisā purisappamāṇato adhikā. Tenāha “pañcaratanappamāṇā”ti. Assāti kāsuyā. Tadabhāveti tesaṃ jālādhūmānaṃ abhāve. Ārakāvassāti ārakā eva assa.

‘A pit of coals’ means a heap of burning embers. ‘Scattering’ means throwing upon oneself; that is the meaning. Therefore, it is said: ‘Men, weeping, with scorched limbs.’ ‘Men’ means males, not humans; that is the meaning. ‘For fear seizes me’ means that one acting under the influence of fear obtains fear. ‘Hastening quickly’ means being one who hastens very swiftly. ‘A man’s length’ is said to be the measure of a man; therefore, ‘exceeding a man’s length’ means more than a man’s measure. Therefore, it is said: ‘five cubits in measure.’ ‘Of it’ means of the pit. ‘In their absence’ means in the absence of those flames and smoke. ‘Far from it’ means it is indeed far from it.

Aṅgārakāsu viya tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ ekādasannaṃ aggīnaṃ vasena mahāpariḷāhato. Jivi…pe… puthujjano tehi aggīhi dahitabbato. Dve bala…pe… kammaṃ anicchantasseva tassa vaṭṭadukkhe pātanato. Āyūhanūpakaḍḍhanānaṃ kālabhedo na cintetabbo ekantabhāvino phalassa nipphāditattāti āha “kammaṃ hī”tiādi.

Like a pit of coals, from the great burning of the round of existence in the three planes by means of the eleven fires. A living being... an ordinary person, because of being burned by those fires. Two powers... because kamma casts one, even against one's will, into the suffering of the round of existence. The difference in time between the accumulation of kamma and its drawing near to fruition should not be pondered, because the fruit, which is certain to be, is produced. Therefore, he said: 'For kamma...' and so on.

Phasse vuttanayenevāti tattha “phasso saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ, idha “manosañcetanā saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vattabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. “Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti vacanato manosañcetanāya taṇhā mūlakāraṇanti āha “taṇhāmūlakattā manosañcetanāyā”ti. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Keci pana yasmā manosañcetanāya phalabhūtaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā uppajjati, tasmā evaṃ vuttanti vadanti.

Regarding contact, it is just as was said. There it was said, 'Contact is the formations aggregate,' but here it should be said, 'Mental volition is the formations aggregate.' The rest is as was said. Because of the statement, 'With craving as a condition, clinging arises; with clinging as a condition, becoming arises,' craving is the root cause of mental volition; hence he says, 'because mental volition has craving as its root.' Therefore, he said, 'For not...' and so on. Some, however, say it is stated thus because craving arises in dependence on feeling, which is the fruit of mental volition.

Tatiyāhāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third nutriment is concluded.

Catutthāhāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Fourth Nutriment.

Aniṭṭhapāpanavasena [V 2.0099][M 2.0115] taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ āgacchatīti āgu, pāpaṃ, taṃ carati sīlenāti āgucārī. Tenāha “pāpacāri”nti.

Because it comes to a person endowed with them by way of the undesirable and evil, it is called 'āgu', that is, evil. One who practices that evil by his conduct is an 'āgucārī'. Therefore, he said, 'one who practices evil'.

Rājā viya kammaṃ paramissarabhāvato. Āgucārī puriso viya…pe… puthujjano dukkhavatthubhāvato. Ādinnappahāravaṇāni tīṇi sattisatāni viya puthujjanassa āturamānamahādukkhapatiṭṭhaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ. Tenāha satti…pe… dukkhanti.

Kamma is like a king, due to its supreme authority. An ordinary person is like a criminal... because of being a basis for suffering. The rebirth-linking consciousness of an ordinary person is like three hundred wounds from spear-blows, a foundation for great suffering and affliction. Therefore, it is said: 'spear... suffering'.

Tammūlakattāti paṭisandhiviññāṇamūlakattā ito paraṃ pavattanāmarūpassa.

'Because it has that as its root' means because rebirth-linking consciousness is the root of the mind-and-matter that occurs thereafter.

Catutthāhāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the fourth nutriment is concluded.

Puttamaṃsūpamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Discourse on the Simile of the Son's Flesh is concluded.

4. Atthirāgasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on Craving for Bones.

64. Catutthe soti lobho. Rañjanavasenāti raṅgajātaṃ viya tassa cittassa anurañjanavasena. Nandanavasenāti sappītikatāya ārammaṇassa abhinandanavasena. Taṇhāyanavasenāti visayakattukāmatāya vasena. Eko eva hi lobho pavattiākāravasena tathā vutto. Patiṭṭhitanti laddhasabhāvaṃ. Tatthāti vaṭṭe. Āhāreti keci. Viññāṇanti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ. Viruḷhanti phalanibbattiyā viruḷhippattaṃ. Tenāha “kammaṃ javāpetvā”tiādi. Tattha javāpetvāti phalaṃ gāhāpetvā. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇañhi attanā sahajātānaṃ sahajātādipaccayehi ceva āhārapaccayena ca paccayo hutvā tassa attano phaluppādane sāmatthiyattā viruḷhippattaṃ. Tenāha “kammaṃ santāne laddhabhāvaṃ viruḷhippattañcassa hotī”ti. Vaṭṭakathā esāti katvā “yatthāti tebhūmakavaṭṭe bhumma”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāti sabbesu. Purimapade etaṃ bhummanti “yattha tatthā”ti āgataṃ etaṃ bhummavacanaṃ purimasmiṃ purimasmiṃ pade visayabhūte. Tañhi ārabbha etaṃ “yattha tatthā”ti bhummavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ vipākavaṭṭeti paccuppanne vipākavaṭṭe. Āyatiṃ vaṭṭahetuke saṅkhāre sandhāya vuttaṃ “yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattī”ti vacanato[M 2.0116]. Punabbhavābhinibbattīti ca paṭisandhi adhippetāti vuttaṃ [V 2.0100] “yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti, atthi tattha āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇa”nti. Jātīti cettha mātukucchito nikkhamanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Yasmiṃ ṭhāneti yasmiṃ kāraṇe sati.

64. In the fourth, 'so' is greed. 'By way of coloring' means by way of coloring that mind as if with dye. 'By way of delighting' means by way of delighting in the object with joy. 'By way of craving' means by way of the desire to make something one's object. Indeed, it is just one greed that is spoken of thus according to its mode of occurrence. 'Established' means having acquired its own nature. 'There' means in the round of existence. Some say 'nutriment.' 'Consciousness' means formational consciousness. 'Grown' means having reached a state of growth for the production of fruit. Hence he said, 'having impelled kamma,' etc. Therein, 'having impelled' means having caused the fruit to be grasped. For formational consciousness, by being a condition for its own co-nascent states through co-nascent and other conditions, and through the nutriment condition, becomes capable of producing its own fruit, having reached a state of growth. Hence he said, 'kamma, having acquired a state in the continuum, has also reached growth for it.' Taking this as the discourse on the round, it is said, '`yattha` means in the round of the three planes, in the locative sense.' '`Sabbattha`' means in all. 'This locative in the preceding phrase' means this locative expression `yattha tatthā` applies to each preceding phrase that is its domain. For with reference to that, this locative expression `yattha tatthā` is stated. 'In this result-round' means in the present result-round. With reference to formations that are a cause for the future round, it is said in accordance with the text, 'where there is future rebirth-production.' And 'rebirth-production' is intended to mean relinking, so it is said, 'where there is future rebirth-production, there is future birth, aging, and death.' Herein, 'birth' is intended to mean emergence from the mother's womb. 'In which place' means 'when which cause exists.'

Kāraṇañcettha saṅkhārā veditabbā. Te hi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā hetū, taṇhāavijjāyo, kālagatiādayo ca kammassa sambhārā. Keci pana kilesavaṭṭakammagatikālā cāti adhippāyena “kālagatiādayo ca kammassa sambhārā”ti vadanti. Taṃtaṃbhavapatthanāya tathā tathā gato tividho bhavova tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Tenāha “yatthāti tebhūmakavaṭṭe”ti. Tathā cāha “sasambhārakakammaṃ bhavesu rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti. Rūpanti attabhāvaṃ.

And here, the cause should be understood as formations. For they are the causes of future rebirth-production, along with craving and ignorance, and the accumulations of kamma such as time, destiny, and so on. Some, however, say 'the accumulations of kamma such as time, destiny, and so on' with the meaning of 'the round of defilements, kamma, destiny, and time.' That threefold becoming itself, which proceeds in this or that way due to the aspiration for this or that existence, is the round of the three planes. Hence, he said, '`yattha` means in the round of the three planes.' And so he said, 'Kamma with its accumulations produces form in existences.' 'Form' means individual existence.

Saṅkhipitvāti tīsu akatvā viññāṇena ekasaṅkhepaṃ katvāti attho. Eko sandhīti eko hetuphalasandhi. Vipākavidhinti saḷāyatanādikaṃ vedanāvasānaṃ vipākavidhiṃ. “Nāmarūpena saddhi”nti padaṃ ānetvā sambandho. Nāmarūpenāti vā sahayoge karaṇavacanaṃ. Idha eko sandhīti eko hetuphalasandhi. Āyatibhavassāti āyatiṃ upapattibhavassa. Tena cettha eko sandhi hetuphalasandhi veditabbo.

'Having summarized' means having made a single summary by means of consciousness, without making it three. 'One connection' means one cause-and-effect connection. 'The result-process' means the result-process from the six sense bases up to feeling. The connection is made by supplying the phrase 'together with mind-and-matter.' Or, 'with mind-and-matter' is an instrumental expressing association. Here, 'one connection' means one cause-and-effect connection. 'Of future becoming' means of future rebirth-becoming. Therefore, here 'one connection' should be understood as a cause-and-effect connection.

Khīṇāsavassa aggamaggādhigamanatova pavattakammassa maggena sahāyavekallassa katattā avijjamānaṃ. Sūriyarasmisamanti tato eva vuttanayeneva appatiṭṭhitasūriyarasmisamaṃ. Sāti rasmi. Kāyādayoti kāyadvārādayo. Katakammanti paccayehi katabhāvaṃ upādāya vuttaṃ, na kammalakkhaṇapattato. Tenāha “kusalākusalaṃ nāma na hotī”ti. Kiriyamatteti avipākadhammattā kāyikādipayogamatte ṭhatvā. Avipākaṃ hoti tesaṃ avipākadhammattā.

For one whose taints are destroyed, from the very attainment of the supreme path, the kamma that occurs is non-existent, because the path has rendered it bereft of a companion. 'Like the sun's rays' means like the unestablished rays of the sun, in the very way stated there. `Sā` is a ray. 'Body, etc.' means the body-door, etc. 'Done kamma' is said with reference to its state of having been done by conditions, not from having attained the characteristic of kamma. Therefore, he said, 'There is no such thing as wholesome or unwholesome.' 'Mere activity' means it remains as mere bodily, etc., effort, because it is a non-result-producing state. It is without result because of their nature as non-result-producing states.

Atthirāgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Atthirāgasutta is concluded.

5. Nagarasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Nagara Sutta.

65. Pañcamasutte “pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā”tiādi heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitamevāti avuttameva saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “nāmarūpe kho satī”ti āraddho[M 2.0117]. Tattha dvādasapadike paṭiccasamuppāde imasmiṃ sutte yāni dve padāni aggahitāni, nesaṃ aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ pucchitvā vissajjetukāmo tesaṃ gahetabbakāraṇaṃ tāva dassento “etthā”tiādimāha. Paccakkhabhūtaṃ paccuppannaṃ bhavaṃ paṭhamaṃ gahetvā tadanantaraṃ anāgatassa “dutiya”nti gahaṇe atīto tatiyo hotīti [V 2.0101] āha “avijjāsaṅkhārā hi tatiyo bhavo”ti. Nanu cettha anāgatassa bhavassa gahaṇaṃ na sambhavati paccuppannabhavavasena abhinivesassa jotitattāti? Saccametaṃ, kāraṇe pana gahite phalaṃ gahitameva hotīti tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apicettha anāgato addhā atthato saṅgahito eva yato “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādinā anāgataddhasaṃgāhitā desanā pavattā, catuvokāravasena viññāṇapaccayā nāmanti viseso atthi. Tasmā “pañcavokāravasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tehīti avijjāsaṅkhārehi ārammaṇabhūtehi. Ayaṃ vipassanāti addhāpaccuppannavasena udayabbayaṃ passantassa pavattavipassanā. Na ghaṭīyatīti na samijjhati. Mahā…pe… abhiniviṭṭhoti na ghaṭane kāraṇamāha, heṭṭhā gahitattā pāṭiyekkaṃ sammasanīyaṃ na hotīti adhippāyo.

65. In the fifth sutta, since 'Before my enlightenment, O monks,' etc., has already been explained below, in order to explain only what has not been said, he began with 'When there is name-and-form...' There, in the twelve-factored dependent origination, regarding the two factors in this sutta that were not taken up, wishing to ask and answer the reason for their not being taken up, he first shows the reason why they should be taken up, saying 'Here,' etc. Having first taken the present becoming, which is directly experienced, and then the taking of the future as 'second,' the past becomes the third. Thus he says, 'For ignorance and formations are the third becoming.' But surely, is not the taking of future becoming impossible here, since adherence by way of present becoming is illuminated? This is true, but it should be seen that it is said thus because when the cause is taken, the result is also taken. Moreover, here the future period is indeed included in meaning, since the teaching that includes the future period proceeds with 'with name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases,' etc. There is the distinction that 'consciousness is a condition for name' is in terms of the four-constituent existence. Therefore it is said, 'in terms of the five-constituent existence.' 'By these' means by ignorance and formations, which have become objects. 'This insight' is the insight that occurs for one who sees arising and passing away by way of the present time. 'It does not fit' means it is not accomplished. He states the reason for the 'not fitting' with 'Greatly... entrenched...'. The meaning is that since it was taken up below, it is not something to be investigated separately.

Adiṭṭhesūti anavabuddhesu. Catusaccassa anubodhena na bhavitabbanti āha “na sakkā buddhena bhavitu”nti. Imināti mahāsattena. Teti avijjāsaṅkhārā. Bhavaupādānataṇhāvasenāti bhavaupādānataṇhādassanavasena. Diṭṭhāva “taṃsahagatā”ti samānayogakkhamattā. Na parabhāgaṃ khaneyya attanā icchitassa gahitattā parabhāge aññassa abhāvato ca. Tenāha “kassaci natthitāyā”ti. Paṭinivattesīti paṭisaṃhari. Paṭinivattane pana kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “tadeta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Abhinnaṭṭhānanti akhaṇitaṭṭhānaṃ.

"Not seen" means not comprehended. Because of not understanding the four truths, one cannot become a Buddha; hence he says, "It is not possible to become a Buddha." "This" refers to the great being. "Those" refers to ignorance and formations. "Due to existence, clinging, and craving" means by way of showing existence, clinging, and craving. "Seen indeed" means "accompanied by that," because of being equally capable. One should not dig into another's share, because what is desired has been taken by oneself, and because there is no share for another. Therefore, he says, "because there is nothing of anyone else's." "Turns back" means retracts. However, to show the reason for retracting, "that is this," etc., was said. "Unbroken place" means an unexcavated place.

Paccayatoti hetuto, saṅkhāratoti attho. “Kimhi nu kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī”tiādinā hetuparamparavasena phalaparamparāya kittamānāya, kimhi nu kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotīti ca vicāraṇāya saṅkhāre kho sati viññāṇassa visesato kāraṇabhūto saṅkhāro aggahito, tato viññāṇaṃ paṭinivattati nāma, na sabbapaccayato. Tenevāha “nāmarūpe kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti. Kiṃ nāma hettha [M 2.0118] sahajātādivaseneva paccayabhūtaṃ adhippetaṃ, na kammūpanissayavasena paccuppannavasena abhinivesassa jotitattā. Ārammaṇatoti avijjāsaṅkhārasaṅkhātaārammaṇato, atītabhavasaṅkhātaārammaṇato. Atītaddhapariyāpannā hi avijjāsaṅkhārā. Tato paṭinivattamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ atītabhavopi paṭinivattati nāma. Ubhayampīti paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ vipassanāviññāṇampi. Nāmarūpaṃ na atikkamatīti paccayabhūtaṃ ārammaṇabhūtañca nāmarūpaṃ na atikkamati tena vinā avattanato. Tenāha “nāmarūpato paraṃ na gacchatī”ti. Viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honteti paṭisandhiviññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honte. Nāmarūpe viññāṇassa paccaye honteti nāmarūpe paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccaye honte. Catuvokārapañcavokārabhavavasena yathārahaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Dvīsupi aññamaññaṃ paccayesu hontesūti [V 2.0102] pana pañcavokārabhavavasena. Ettakenāti evaṃ viññāṇanāmarūpānaṃ aññamaññaṃ upatthambhavasena pavattiyā. Jāyetha vā upapajjetha vāti “satto jāyati upapajjatī”ti samaññā hoti viññāṇanāmarūpavinimuttassa sattapaññattiyā upādānabhūtassa dhammassa abhāvato. Tenāha “ito hī”tiādi. Etadevāti “viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpa”nti etaṃ dvayameva.

"From the condition" means from the cause; the meaning is "from formations." "When what exists does aging-and-death exist?" and so on—by stating the sequence of causes leading to the sequence of results, and by investigating "when what exists does consciousness exist?"—the formation, being the specific cause of consciousness, is not grasped, and therefore consciousness turns back, as it were, but not from all conditions. Hence it is said, "When name-and-form exists, consciousness exists." Here, what is intended is the condition in terms of co-nascence, etc., not in the sense of reliance on past kamma or present existence, due to the indication of clinging. As object—from the object consisting of ignorance-and-formations, from the object consisting of past existence. For ignorance-and-formations belong to the past time. When consciousness turns back from that, past existence also, as it were, turns back. Both—both rebirth-linking consciousness and insight consciousness. "Name-and-form does not transcend"—the name-and-form that is a condition and an object does not transcend, because without it, there is no occurrence. Hence it is said, "It does not go beyond name-and-form." "When consciousness is a condition for name-and-form"—when rebirth-linking consciousness is a condition for name-and-form. "When name-and-form is a condition for consciousness"—when name-and-form is a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness. It should be understood according to the four-constituent and five-constituent existences as appropriate. "In both, they are mutually conditions"—this is in terms of five-constituent existence. "By this much"—thus, by the mutual support of consciousness and name-and-form in their occurrence. "Would be born or arise"—the designation "a being is born, arises" occurs because there is no phenomenon, separate from consciousness and name-and-form, that could be the basis for the concept of a being. Hence it is said, "From this," etc. "This very thing"—"consciousness and name-and-form"—just this pair.

Aparāparacutipaṭisandhīhīti aparāparacutipaṭisandhidīpakehi “cavati, upapajjatī”ti dvīhi padehi. Pañca padānīti “jāyetha vā”tiādīni pañca padāni. Nanu tattha paṭhamatatiyehi catutthapañcamāni atthato abhinnānīti? Saccaṃ, viññāṇanāmarūpānaṃ aparāparuppattidassanatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “aparāparacutipaṭisandhīhī”ti. Ettāvatāti vuttamevatthanti yo “ettāvatā”ti padena pubbe vutto, tameva yathāvuttamatthaṃ “yadida”ntiādinā niyyātento puna vatvā. Anulomapaccayākāravasenāti paccayadhammadassanapubbakapaccayuppannadhammadassanavasena. Paccayadhammānañhi attano paccayuppannassa paccayabhāvo idappaccayatā paccayākāro, so ca “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā vutto saṅkhāruppattiyā anulomanato anulomapaccayākāro, tassa vasena.

"By successive deaths and rebirths" means by the two phrases "passes away" and "is reborn," which illuminate successive deaths and rebirths. The five phrases refer to "may be born," and so on. But are not the first and third, and the fourth and fifth, phrases identical in meaning? Indeed, it is so. This was stated to show the successive arising of consciousness and name-and-form. Hence, it is said, "by successive deaths and rebirths." "By this much" refers to the meaning previously stated by that word, which is now being reiterated and explained with "that is," and so on. "In the manner of the forward order of conditions" means in the way of showing the conditioning phenomena first and then showing the phenomena that arise from those conditions. For the fact that conditioning phenomena are a condition for what arises from them is specific conditionality, the mode of conditionality. And this, as stated by "with ignorance as a condition, formations arise," etc., is the forward order mode of conditionality, as it follows the arising of formations. By means of this.

Āpatoti [M 2.0119] parikhāgataudakato. Dvārasampattiyā tattha vasantānaṃ pavesananiggamanaphāsutāya upabhogaparibhogavatthusampattiyā sarīracittasukhatāya nagarassa manuññatāti vuttaṃ “samantā …pe… ramaṇīya”nti. Pubbe suññabhāvena araññasadisaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ janavāsaṃ karonte nagarassa lakkhaṇappattaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “taṃ aparena samayena iddhañceva assa phītañcā”ti.

"From the water" (āpato) means from the water that has entered the moat. For those dwelling there, the gate's completeness provides ease of entry and exit, the abundance of things to be enjoyed and used, and physical and mental comfort, making the city delightful—thus it is said, "all around... pleasant." Previously, it was like a wilderness due to being uninhabited, but when people settled there, it attained the characteristics of a city—thus it is said, "in time, it became prosperous and flourishing."

“Pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo ca suparisuddho”ti vacanato tīhi viratīhi saddhiṃ pubbabhāgamaggopi aṭṭhaṅgikavohāraṃ laddhuṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ “aṭṭhaṅgikassa vipassanāmaggassā”ti. Vipassanāya ciṇṇanteti vipassanāya sañcaritatāya tattha tattha tāya vipassanāya tīrite pariyesite. Lokuttaramaggadassananti anumānādivasena lokuttaramaggassa dassanaṃ. Tathā hi nibbānanagarassa dassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Diṭṭhakāloti adhigamavasena diṭṭhakālo. Maggaphalavasena uppannā paropaṇṇāsa anavajjadhammā, paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ pana tesaṃ vavatthāpakaṃ. Yāpetvāti carāpetvā.

"Even before, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were thoroughly purified"—from this statement, it is said that the preliminary path, along with the three abstinences, deserves to attain the designation of the eightfold path, as it is said, "of the eightfold path of insight." "Cultivated by insight" (vipassanāya ciṇṇaṃ) means that it is traversed here and there, investigated and sought out by that very insight. "Seeing the supramundane path"—this means seeing the supramundane path by way of inference and the like. Thus, the seeing of the city of Nibbāna should be regarded. "At the time of seeing"—this refers to the time of seeing in terms of attainment. Through the path and fruition, more than fifty blameless states arise, but the reviewing knowledge is what determines them. "Having sustained"—means having caused to continue.

Avattamānakaṭṭhenāti buddhasuññe loke kassaci santāne appavattanatova uppādādivasena vattamānavasena. Tathā hi bhagavā “anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā, asañjātassa sañjanetā”tiādikehi [V 2.0103] thomito. Pubbakehi mahesīhi paṭipanno hi ariyamaggo itarehi antarā kehici avaḷañjitoti vuttaṃ “avaḷañjanaṭṭhena purāṇamaggo”ti. Jhānassādenāti jhānasukhena jhānapītiyā. Subhikkhaṃ paṇītadhammāmatatāya tittiāvahaṃ. Pupphitaṃ upasobhitaṃ. Yāva dasasahassacakkavāḷeti vuttaṃ “ekissā lokadhātuyā”ti paricchinnabuddhakhettattā. Tassa atthitāya hi paricchedo atthi. Etasmiṃ antareti etasmiṃ okāse.

"By the characteristic of non-occurrence" means because it does not occur in the continuity of any being in a world empty of Buddhas, in the sense of being present through arising, etc. Indeed, the Blessed One is praised with phrases like, "He is the producer of the unarisen path, the generator of the ungenerated." The noble path practiced by the ancient great sages was not trodden by others in between, and thus it is said, "The ancient path is characterized by being untrodden." "By the delight of jhāna" means by the bliss and rapture of jhāna. "Abundant" refers to the satisfaction brought by the nectar of the sublime Dhamma. "Flourishing" means adorned. Although it is said "up to ten thousand world-systems," it is also said "within a single world-system" because the Buddha-field is limited. For its existence implies a boundary. "In this interval" means in this space.

Nagarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nagara Sutta is concluded.

6. Sammasasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sammasa Sutta

66. Chaṭṭhe assāti bhagavato. Saṇhasukhumadhammaparidīpanato sukhumā. Tīhi lakkhaṇehi aṅkiyattā tilakkhaṇāhatā, aniccādilakkhaṇaparidīpinīti attho. Ariyadhammādhigamassa upanissayabhūtena hetunā sahetukā. Tihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya pāṭihāriyapaññāya ca atthitāya paññavanto [M 2.0120] na kevalaṃ ajjhattikaaṅgasampattiyeva, bāhiraṅgasampattipi nesamatthīti dassetuṃ “siniddhānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Abbhantaranti ajjhattaṃ. Paccayasammasananti paccayuppannānaṃ paccayavīmaṃsaṃ.

66. In the sixth sutta, 'assa' refers to the Blessed One. It is 'subtle' (sukhumā) because it elucidates the gentle and delicate Dhamma. It is 'marked by the three characteristics' (tilakkhaṇāhatā) because it is stamped with the three characteristics, meaning it elucidates the characteristics of impermanence and so on. It is 'with a cause' (sahetukā) because it has a cause that serves as a foundation for the realization of the noble Dhamma. They are 'endowed with wisdom' (paññavanto) because of the existence of wisdom rooted in triple-rooted rebirth-linking and miraculous wisdom. To show that they possess not only internal accomplishments but also external accomplishments, 'smooth' (siniddhāni) and so on are stated. 'Abbhantara' means internal. 'Paccayasammasana' means the investigation of the conditions of conditionally arisen phenomena.

Ārambhānurūpā anusandhi yathānusandhi. Na gatāti na sampattā. Asambhinnapadanti avomissakapadaṃ, aññattha evaṃ anāgataṃ vākyanti attho. Tenāha “aññattha hi evaṃ vuttaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Evanti “tenahānandā”ti ekavacanaṃ, “suṇātha manasi karothā”ti bahuvacanaṃ katvā vuttaṃ nāma natthīti attho. Keci pana “tenahānandā”ti idhāpi bahuvacanameva katvā paṭhanti “sādhu anuruddhā”tiādīsu viya. Upadhīti adhippetaṃ upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti. Uppajjati uppādakkhaṇaṃ udayaṃ paṭilabhati “pākaṭabhāvo ṭhitiko, attalābho udayo”ti. Nivisati nivesaṃ okāsaṃ paṭilabhati. Ekavārameva hi uppannamattassa dhammassa dubbalattena okāse viya patiṭṭhahanaṃ natthi, punappunaṃ ārammaṇe pavattamānaṃ niviṭṭhaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ nāma hoti. Tenāha “nivisatīti punappunaṃ pavattivasena patiṭṭhahatī”ti.

The connection is in accordance with the beginning, a fitting connection. 'Na gatā' means not attained. 'Asambhinnapada' means an unmixed word; the meaning is that such a statement has not occurred elsewhere. Therefore, it is said, 'Indeed, nowhere else is it said thus.' 'Thus' means that nowhere is it said by making 'tenahānandā' singular and 'suṇātha manasi karothā' plural. Some, however, read 'tenahānandā' even here in the plural, as in 'Good, Anuruddhas,' and so on. 'Upadhi' is that upon which suffering is laid; this is the intended meaning. 'It arises' means it obtains the moment of arising, the origin. 'Manifestation is lasting, the acquisition of self is origin.' 'It settles' means it obtains a dwelling, a foothold. Indeed, a phenomenon that has just arisen, due to its weakness, has no establishment as if in a place; only when it occurs repeatedly in relation to an object does it become settled, established. Therefore, it is said, '“It settles” means it becomes established through repeated occurrence.'

Piyasabhāvanti piyāyitabbajātikaṃ. Madhurasabhāvanti iṭṭhajātikaṃ. Abhiniviṭṭhāti taṇhābhinivesena otiṇṇā. Sampattiyanti bhavasampattiyaṃ. Nimittaggahaṇānusārenāti paṭibimbaggahaṇānusārena. Kaṇṇassa chiddapadesaṃ rajatanāḷikaṃ viya, kaṇṇabaddhaṃ pana pāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya. Tuṅgā uccā dīghā nāsikā tuṅganāsā. Evaṃ laddhavohāraṃ attano ghānaṃ. “Laddhavohārā”ti [V 2.0104] vā pāṭho. Tasmiṃ sati tuṅgā nāsā yesaṃ te tuṅganāsā. Evaṃ laddhavohārā sattā attano ghānanti yojanā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato rattakambalapaṭalaṃ viya. Samphassato mudusiniddhaṃ kiccato siniddhamadhurarasadaṃ. Sālalaṭṭhinti sālakkhandhaṃ.

'Piyasabhāva' means of a nature to be cherished. 'Madhurasabhāva' means of an agreeable nature. 'Abhiniviṭṭhā' means sunk down through the adherence of craving. 'Sampatti' refers to prosperity in existence. 'Nimittaggahaṇānusārena' means in accordance with the grasping of the counterpart sign. Like a silver tube in the ear-hole, or like the thread of a fillet bound at the ear. A prominent, high, long nose is a 'tuṅganāsā'. Thus one's own nose has obtained this designation. Alternatively, the reading is 'laddhavohārā'. In that case, 'tuṅganāsā' are those who have prominent noses. The construction is thus: 'beings who have obtained this designation regarding their own noses.' In color and shape, it is like a piece of red woollen cloth. To the touch, it is soft and smooth; in function, it gives a smooth and sweet taste. 'Sālalaṭṭhi' means the trunk of a sal tree.

Addasaṃsūti passiṃsu. Evaṃ vuttanti “kaṃse”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ adhiṭṭhānavohārena.

'Addasaṃsu' means they saw. 'Evaṃ vuttaṃ' means thus spoken; 'kaṃse' is said thus by way of the convention of determination.

Sampattinti vaṇṇādiguṇaṃ. Ādīnavanti maraṇaggatato.

'Sampatti' refers to the qualities of beauty and so forth. 'Ādīnava' refers to culminating in death.

Sattupānīyenāti sattuṃ pakkhipitvā ālolitapānīyena. Cattāri pānāni viya cattāro maggā taṇhāpipāsāvūpasamanato.

'Sattupānīyena' means with a drink made by putting in flour and stirring. Like four drinks, the four paths are for the allaying of craving and thirst.

Sammasasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sammasa Sutta is concluded.

7. Naḷakalāpīsuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Naḷakalāpī Sutta

67. Sattame [M 2.0121] kasmā pucchatīti mahākoṭṭhikatthero sayaṃ tattha nikkaṅkho samāno kasmā pucchatīti adhippāyo. Ajjhāsayajānanatthanti idampi tassa mahāsāvakassa paracittajānanena appāṭihīraṃ siyā, tena taṃ aparitussanto “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha dve aggasāvakāti sīlādiguṇehi uttamasāvakāti attho, na hi mahākoṭṭhikatthero aggasāvakalakkhaṇappatto, atha kho mahāsāvakalakkhaṇappatto.
