“Of them” means of the courses of action. “Conventionally” means by way of mere designation, based on what is bound to the sense faculties. “In the animal realm, etc.”: by the word “etc.” the ghosts are included. Great blameworthiness occurs due to factors such as the greatness of the effort and the object, because of the strength of the volition arising from those conditions. Even when the aforesaid conditions are reversed, slight or great blameworthiness should be understood by way of the strength of the volition due to the respective conditions. “Of psychic power” means of the psychic power that is the result of kamma, like that of fangs, tusks, and so on.

Methunasamācāresūti sadāraparadāragamanavasena duvidhesu methunasamācāresu. Tepi hīnādhimuttikehi kattabbato kāmā nāma. Micchācāroti gārayhācāro. Gārayhatā cassa ekantanihīnatāyāti āha [M 2.0142] “ekantanindito lāmakācāro”ti asaddhammādhippāyenāti asaddhammasevanādhippāyena. Gottarakkhitāti sagottehi rakkhitā. Dhammarakkhitāti sahadhammehi rakkhitā. Sassāmikā nāma sārakkhā. Yassā gamane daṇḍo ṭhapito, sā saparidaṇḍā. Bhariyabhāvāya dhanena kītā dhanakkītā. Chandena vasatīti chandavāsinī. Bhogatthaṃ vasatīti bhogavāsinī. Paṭatthaṃ vasatīti paṭavāsinī. Udakapattaṃ āmasitvā gahitā odapattakinī. Cumbaṭaṃ apanetvā gahitā obhaṭacumbaṭā. Karamarānītā dhajāhaṭā. Taṅkhaṇikaṃ gahitā muhuttikā. Abhibhavitvā vītikkamo micchācāro mahāsāvajjo, na tathā dvinnaṃ samānacchandatāya. Abhibhavitvā vītikkamane satipi maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsane purimuppannasevanābhisandhipayogābhāvato micchācāro na hoti abhibhuyyamānassāti vadanti. Sevanācitte sati payogābhāvo appamāṇaṃ yebhuyyena itthiyā sevanāpayogassa abhāvato. Tathā sati puretaraṃ sevanācittassa upaṭṭhānepi [V 2.0124] tassā micchācāro na siyā, tathā purisassapi sevanāpayogābhāve. Tasmā attano ruciyā pavattitassa vasena tayo, balakkārena pavattitassa vasena tayoti sabbepi aggahitaggahaṇena “cattāro sambhārā”ti vuttaṃ.

“In sexual conduct”: this refers to the two kinds of sexual conduct, that is, intercourse with one’s own wife and with another’s wife. These too are called “sensual pleasures” because they are to be engaged in by those of base disposition. “Misconduct” means blameworthy conduct. Its blameworthiness is due to its utter baseness; thus it is said: “utterly condemned, a vile practice,” which means with the intention for what is not the Dhamma, that is, with the intention to engage in what is not the Dhamma. “Protected by her clan” means protected by her relatives. “Protected by the Dhamma” means protected by those of the same custom. “One with a husband” means one under protection. She for whom a penalty is established for approaching her is “one with a penalty.” “Bought with wealth” means purchased with wealth to be a wife. “One who cohabits by consent.” “One who cohabits for wealth.” “One who cohabits for a garment.” “A water-pot wife,” one taken after touching a water pot. “One with head-pad removed,” one taken after removing her head-pad. “A female slave” and “a captive.” “A temporary wife,” one taken for a moment. Transgression by overpowering is misconduct of great blame, but not so when there is mutual consent of the two. They say that even when there is transgression by overpowering, for the one being overpowered it is not misconduct, due to the absence of a previously arisen intention and application for intercourse while enduring the act. When there is the intention to engage, the absence of application is of little account, mostly because of the absence of the woman’s application to engage. Similarly, even if the intention to engage arose in her beforehand, it would not be misconduct for her if she does not apply herself, just as for the man if he does not apply himself. Therefore, there are three cases based on proceeding from one’s own liking and three based on proceeding by force; thus, by including what was not included, all are covered when it is said, “there are four components.”

Āsevanamandatāyāti yāya akusalacetanāya samphaṃ palapati, tassā ittarakālatāya pavattiyā anāsevanāti paridubbalā hoti cetanā.

“By weakness of cultivation”: the unwholesome volition with which one chatters idly becomes very weak because it is not cultivated, as it occurs for only a short time.

Upasaggavasena atthavisesavācino dhātusaddāti abhijjhāyatīti padassa parabhaṇḍābhimukhītiādiattho vutto. Tanninnatāyāti tasmiṃ parabhaṇḍe lubbhanavasena ninnatāya. Abhipubbo jhe-saddo lubbhane niruḷhoti daṭṭhabbo. Yassa bhaṇḍaṃ abhijjhāyati, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjātiādinā nayena tattha appasāvajjamahāsāvajjavibhāgo veditabbo. Tenāha “adinnādānaṃ viyā”tiādi. Attano pariṇāmanaṃ cittenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The root words express specific meanings by way of prefixes; thus the meaning of the word “covets” is stated as “being directed towards another’s property,” etc. “Inclination towards that” means inclination towards that property of another by way of greed. The root “jhe” preceded by “abhi” should be seen as established in the sense of greed. The division into slight and great blame should be understood here by the method: “When one covets the property of someone of little virtue, it is of slight blame; of someone of great virtue, it is of great blame,” and so on. Therefore he said: “like taking what is not given,” etc. “Appropriating it for oneself” should be seen as being by mind alone.

Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti yo naṃ uppādeti, yassa uppādeti, tassa sati samavāye hitasukhaṃ vināseti. Aho vatāti iminā yathā abhijjhāne vatthuno ekantato attano pariṇāmanaṃ dassitaṃ[M 2.0143], evamidhāpi vatthuno “aho vatā”ti iminā parassa vināsacintāya ekantato niyamitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Evañhi nesaṃ dāruṇappavattiyā kammapathappavatti.

“It destroys welfare and happiness”: whoever generates it, for whomever it is generated, when there is a conjunction, it destroys their welfare and happiness. By this “Oh, that!”: just as in the case of covetousness the complete appropriation of the object to oneself was shown, so here too, by this “Oh, that!,” the state of being completely determined on the thought of another’s destruction is shown. For thus, through their cruel engagement, the course of action comes to be.

Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvenāti yathātacchagahaṇassa abhāvena aniccādisabhāvassa niccādito gahaṇena. Micchā passatīti vitathaṃ passati. Samphappalāpo viyāti iminā āsevanassa appamahantatāhi micchādiṭṭhiyā appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā. Vatthunoti gahitavatthuno. Gahitākāraviparītatāti micchādiṭṭhiyā gahitākārassa viparītatā. Tathābhāvenāti attano gahitākāreneva tassā diṭṭhiyā, gahitassa vā vatthuno upaṭṭhānaṃ “evametaṃ, na ito aññathā”ti.

“Due to the absence of grasping things as they really are” means due to the absence of grasping what is true, by grasping the nature of impermanence, etc., as permanence, etc. “He sees wrongly” means he sees falsely. “Like idle chatter”: by this is meant that wrong view has slight and great blameworthiness due to the slightness and greatness of its cultivation. “Of the object” means of the object grasped. “The perversion of the mode in which it is grasped” means the perversion of the mode in which it is grasped by wrong view. “By its being so” means the establishment of that view by its own grasped mode, or of the grasped object, as: “This is so, not otherwise.”

Dhammatoti sabhāvato. Koṭṭhāsatoti cittaṅgakoṭṭhāsato, yaṃkoṭṭhāsā honti, tatoti attho. Cetanādhammāvāti cetanāsabhāvā eva. Paṭipāṭiyā sattāti ettha nanu cetanā abhidhamme kammapathesu na vuttāti paṭipāṭiyā sattannaṃ kammapathabhāvo na yuttoti? Na, avacanassa aññahetukattā. Na hi tattha cetanāya akammapathattā kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ, kadāci pana kammapatho [V 2.0125] hoti, na sabbadāti kammapathabhāvassa aniyatattā avacanaṃ. Yadā, panassa kammapathabhāvo hoti, tadā kammapatharāsisaṅgaho na nivārito. Etthāha – yadi cetanāya sabbadā kammapathabhāvābhāvato aniyato kammapathabhāvoti kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ, nanu abhijjhādīnampi kammapathabhāvaṃ appattānaṃ atthitāya aniyato kammapathabhāvoti tesampi kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, kammapathatātaṃsabhāgatāhi tesaṃ tattha vuttattā. Yadi evaṃ cetanāpi tattha vattabbā siyā? Saccametaṃ. Sā pana pāṇātipātādikāti pākaṭo tassā kammapathabhāvoti na vuttā siyā. Cetanāya hi “cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi (a. ni. 6.63; kathā. 539) tividhā, bhikkhave, kāyasañcetanā akusalaṃ kāyakamma”ntiādivacanato (kathā. 539) kammabhāvo pākaṭo. Kammaṃyeva ca sugatiduggatīnaṃ tatthuppajjanakasukhadukkhānañca pathabhāvena pavattaṃ kammapathoti vuccatīti pākaṭo, tassā kammapathabhāvo. Abhijjhādīnaṃ pana cetanāsamīhanabhāvena sucaritaduccaritabhāvo, cetanājanitapiṭṭhivaṭṭakabhāvena sugatiduggatitaduppajjanakasukhadukkhānaṃ [M 2.0144] pathabhāvo cāti, na tathā pākaṭo kammapathabhāvoti, te eva tena sabhāvena dassetuṃ abhidhamme kammapatharāsibhāvena vuttā. Atathājātiyakattā vā cetanā tehi saddhiṃ na vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mūlaṃ patvāti mūladesanaṃ patvā, mūlasabhāvesu dhammesu desiyamānesūti attho.

“By nature” means by its intrinsic nature. “By sections” means by the sections of the constituents of consciousness; whatever sections there are, that is the meaning. “Volitional phenomena” means phenomena that are essentially volitional. Regarding 'sequentially for seven': here one might object, 'Since volition is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma among the courses of action (kammapatha), how can it be proper for the seven volitions to have the nature of a course of action?' This is not so, for its omission has another reason. It is not because volition lacks the nature of a course of action that it is unmentioned in the collection of courses of action; rather, its omission is due to its state as a course of action being indeterminate, since sometimes it is a course of action and sometimes it is not. When, however, it does have the nature of a course of action, its inclusion in the collection of courses of action is not precluded. Here it is said: 'If volition is unmentioned in the collection of courses of action because its state as a course of action is indeterminate, then since covetousness and so on also exist without having attained the state of a course of action, their state as a course of action is also indeterminate, and thus they too should not be mentioned.' This does not follow, because they are mentioned there on account of their partaking in the nature of a course of action. 'If so, shouldn't volition also be mentioned there?' That is true. However, since its nature as a course of action is manifest in regard to killing living beings and so on, it may not have been mentioned. For the nature of volition as kamma is manifest from such statements as: 'Bhikkhus, I say that volition is kamma' (AN 6.63; Kvu 539), and 'Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of bodily volition that are unwholesome bodily kamma…' (Kvu 539). And since kamma itself, by being the path to good and bad destinations and to the pleasure and pain that arise there, is called a 'course of action,' its nature as a course of action is manifest. For covetousness and so on, however, their nature as good and bad conduct is due to their being an endeavor of volition, and their nature as a path to good and bad destinations and to the pleasure and pain that arise there is due to their being a consequence generated by volition. Thus their nature as a course of action is not so manifest. Therefore, to show them as having that nature, they are mentioned in the Abhidhamma as included in the collection of courses of action. Alternatively, it should be understood that volition is not mentioned together with them because it is of a different class. “Having reached the root” means having reached the exposition on the root; that is, when things are being taught in their root-natures.

Adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇanti idaṃ “pañca sikkhāpadā parittārammaṇā evā”ti imāya pāḷiyā virujjhati. Yañhi pāṇātipātādidussīlyassa ārammaṇaṃ, tadeva taṃ veramaṇiyā ārammaṇaṃ. Vītikkamitabbavatthuto eva hi viratīti. “Sattārammaṇa”nti vā sattasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇameva upādāya vuttattā na koci virodho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 714) “yāni sikkhāpadāni ettha ‘sattārammaṇānī’ti vuttāni, tāni yasmā ‘sattoti’ti saṅkhaṃ gate saṅkhāreyeva ārammaṇaṃ karontī”ti. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Visabhāgavatthuno “itthipurisā”ti gahetabbato sattārammaṇotipi eke. “Eko diṭṭho, dve sutā”tiādinā samphappalapane diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena. Tathā abhijjhāti ettha tathā-saddo “diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasenā”ti idampi upasaṃharati, na sattasaṅkhārārammaṇataṃ eva dassanādivasena abhijjhāyanato. “Natthi sattā opapātikā”ti pavattamānāpi micchādiṭṭhi tebhūmakadhammārammaṇā evāti adhippāyena tassā saṅkhārārammaṇatā vuttā. Kathaṃ pana micchādiṭṭhiyā mahaggatappattā dhammā ārammaṇaṃ hontīti? Sādhāraṇato. Natthi sukaṭadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipākoti hi pavattamānāya atthato rūpārūpāvacaradhammāpi gahitāva hontīti.

The statement 'Taking what is not given has a being as its object' contradicts the Pāḷi passage: 'The five training rules have only limited objects.' For the object of immoral conduct such as killing living beings is the very same as the object of the abstinence from it, since abstinence is indeed from the object that is to be transgressed. Or, there is no contradiction because the phrase 'has a being as its object' is stated with reference to having as its object the formations designated as 'a being.' For so it is said in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibh-a 714): 'Those training rules that are here said to "have a being as their object" take as their object only the formations that have come to be designated as "a being."' This same method applies to the subsequent cases. Some say it has a being as its object because an object of a different nature, such as 'women and men,' is to be taken. In the case of frivolous talk, such as 'one was seen, two were heard,' it is by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Similarly, in the case of covetousness, the word 'thus' also includes 'by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized'; it does not only indicate having formations designated as 'a being' as its object, since one covets by way of seeing, etc. Even when wrong view occurs as 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings,' it has as its object only phenomena of the three planes; with this intention, its having formations as its object is stated. But how can phenomena that have reached the sublime state be an object for wrong view? By way of generalization. For when it occurs as 'There is no fruit and result of good and bad kamma,' by meaning, phenomena of the form and formless spheres are also included.

Sukhabahulatāya [V 2.0126] rājāno hasamānāpi “coraṃ ghātethā”ti vadanti, hāso pana tesaṃ aññavisayoti āha “sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā pana nesaṃ dukkhasampayuttāva hotī”ti. Majjhattavedano na hoti, sukhavedanova. Tattha “kāmānaṃ samudayā”tiādinā vedanābhedo veditabbo. Lobhasamuṭṭhāno musāvādo sukhavedano vā siyā majjhattavedano vā, dosasamuṭṭhāno dukkhavedano vāti musāvādo tivedano siyā. Iminā nayena sesesupi yathārahaṃ vedanānaṃ [M 2.0145] “lobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāyā”tiādinā bhedo veditabbo.

Because of an abundance of pleasure, kings, even while laughing, say, 'Execute the thief!' But their laughter pertains to another object. Thus it is said: 'But their conclusive volition is indeed associated with painful feeling.' The laughter is not accompanied by neutral feeling, but only by pleasant feeling. Here, the distinction of feeling should be understood by way of the phrase, 'with the arising of sensual pleasures,' and so on. False speech arisen from greed may be accompanied by pleasant feeling or by neutral feeling; false speech arisen from hatred is accompanied by painful feeling. Thus false speech can be accompanied by the three kinds of feeling. By this method, the distinctions of feelings in the remaining cases should also be understood as appropriate by way of such phrases as, 'greed is the source for the arising of kamma,' and so on.

Pāṇātipāto dosamohavasena dvimūlakoti sampayuttamūlameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tassa hi mūlaṭṭhena upakārabhāvo dosaviseso, nidānamūle pana gayhamāne lobhamohavasenapi vaṭṭati. Sammūḷho āmisakiñjakkhakāmopi hi pāṇaṃ hanati. Tenevāha “lobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāyā”tiādi (a. ni. 3.34). Sesesupi eseva nayo.

The statement that killing living beings is two-rooted, by way of hatred and delusion, is made with reference only to the associated roots. For its helpfulness in the sense of a root is a specific kind of hatred. But when the causal root is taken, it can also occur by way of greed and delusion. For a thoroughly deluded person, desiring some kind of meat, also kills a living being. For that reason it is said: 'Greed is the source for the arising of kamma,' and so on (AN 3.34). This same method applies to the remaining cases.

Asamādinnasīlassa sampattato yathāupaṭṭhitavītikkamitabbavatthuto virati sampattavirati. Samādānena uppannā virati samādānavirati. Kilesānaṃ samucchindanavasena pavattā maggasampayuttā virati samucchedavirati. Kāmañcettha pāḷiyaṃ viratiyova āgatā, sikkhāpadavibhaṅge pana cetanāpi āharitvā dassitāti tadubhayampi gaṇhanto “cetanāpi vaṭṭanti viratiyopī”ti āha.

For one who has not undertaken the moral precepts, the abstinence from an object of transgression that has presented itself on some occasion is abstinence on occasion. Abstinence that has arisen through undertaking the precepts is abstinence by undertaking. Abstinence associated with the path, which proceeds by way of cutting off the defilements, is abstinence by eradication. Although in the Pāḷi text here only the abstinences are given, in the Analysis of the Training Rules volition is also brought in and shown. Therefore, taking both into account, it is said: 'Volition is also applicable, and so are the abstinences.'

Adussīlyārammaṇā jīvitindriyādiārammaṇā kathaṃ dussīlyāni pajahantīti dassetuṃ “yathā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīhi viramaṇavasena pavattanato tadārammaṇabhāveneva tāni pajahanti. Na hi tadeva ārabbha taṃ pajahituṃ sakkā tato anissaṭabhāvato.

To show how the abstinences, which have as their object the life faculty and so on—that is, which have an object that is not an immorality—abandon immoralities, the passage beginning 'But how...' was stated. They abandon those immoralities by proceeding by way of abstaining from killing, etc., and thus by way of having those beings as their object. For it is not possible to abandon an immorality by taking that very immorality as an object, because one is not yet free from it.

Anabhijjhā…pe… viramantassāti abhijjhaṃ pajahantassāti attho. Na hi manoduccaritato virati atthi anabhijjhādīheva tappahānasiddhito.

'Of one refraining from ... non-covetousness...' means of one abandoning covetousness. For there is no abstinence from mental misconduct, since its abandonment is accomplished by non-covetousness and so on themselves.

Pañcasikkhāpadasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Five Training Rules and so on is concluded.

7. Dasaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Factors

113. Micchattasammattavasenāti ettha micchābhāvo micchattaṃ, tathā sammābhāvo sammattaṃ. Tathā tathā pavattā akusalakkhandhāva micchāsati, evaṃ micchāñāṇampi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi ñāṇassa [V 2.0127] micchābhāvo nāma atthi. Tasmā micchāñāṇinoti micchāsaññāṇāti attho, ayoniso pavattacittuppādāti [M 2.0146] adhippāyo. Micchāpaccavekkhaṇenāti micchādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ micchā ayoniso paccavekkhaṇena. Kusalavimuttīti pakatipurisasantarajānanaṃ, guṇaviyuttassa attano sakattani avaṭṭhānanti evamādiṃ akusalapavattiṃ “kusalavimuttī”ti gahetvā ṭhitā micchāvimuttikā. Sammāpaccavekkhaṇāti jhānavimokkhādīsu sammā aviparītaṃ pavattā paccavekkhaṇā.

113. By way of wrongness and rightness: Here, the state of being wrong is wrongness, and similarly, the state of being right is rightness. The unwholesome aggregates that proceed in various ways are wrong mindfulness; similarly, wrong knowledge should be understood. For there is no such thing as a state of wrongness inherent in knowledge itself. Therefore, 'one with wrong knowledge' means one with wrong cognition; the intention is the arising of a mind-state unwisely. 'Wrong reflection' means wrong, unwise reflection on wrong views and the like. Those with wrong liberation are established by taking unwholesome processes—such as the knowledge in the continuum of an ordinary person, and the abiding in one's own selfhood of oneself who is devoid of virtues—to be 'wholesome liberation.' 'Right reflection' means proper, non-perverted reflection that occurs in regard to jhānas, liberations, and the like.

Dasaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Factors is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Chapter is concluded.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter

1. Catudhātusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Elements

114. Patiṭṭhādhātūti sahajātānaṃ dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhābhūtā dhātu. Ābandhanadhātūti nahāniyacuṇṇassa udakaṃ viya sahajātadhammānaṃ ābandhanabhūtā dhātu. Paripācanadhātūti sūriyo phalādīnaṃ viya sahajātadhammānaṃ paripācanabhūtā dhātu. Vitthambhanadhātūti dutiyo viya sahajātadhammānaṃ vitthambhanabhūtā dhātu. Kesādayo vīsati koṭṭhāsā. Ādi-saddena pittādayo santappanādayo uddhaṅgamā vātādayo gahitā. Etāti dhātuyo.

114. The supporting element is the element that serves as the foundation for co-nascent phenomena. The binding element is the element that acts as a bond for co-nascent phenomena, like water with bath powder. The ripening element is the element that causes co-nascent phenomena to mature, like the sun with fruits and so on. The sustaining element is the element that supports co-nascent phenomena, like a pillar. The twenty bodily parts, beginning with the hair. By the word 'and so on,' bile and so on, the heating elements, and the upward-moving winds and so on are included. These are the elements.

Catudhātusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Four Elements is concluded.

2. Pubbesambodhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pubbesambodha Sutta

115. Ayaṃ pathavīdhātuṃ nissāya taṃ ārabbha pavatto assādo. Evaṃ pavattānanti evaṃ kāye pabhāvassa pavedanavaseneva pavattānaṃ. Hutvā abhāvākārenāti pubbe avijjamānā paccayasāmaggiyā hutvā uppajjitvā puna bhaṅgupagamanato uddhaṃ abhāvākārena. Na niccāti aniccā addhuvattā, dhuvaṃ niccaṃ. Paṭipīḷanākārenāti udayabbayavasena abhiṇhaṃ pīḷanākārena [M 2.0147] dukkhaṭṭhena. Sabhāvavigamākārenāti attano sabhāvassa vigacchanākārena. Sabhāvadhammā hi appamattaṃ khaṇaṃ patvā nirujjhanti. Tasmā te “jarāya maraṇena cā”ti dvedhā vipariṇamanti. Tenāha [V 2.0128] “vipariṇāmadhammā”ti. Ādīnaṃ vāti pavattetīti ādīnavo, paramakāpaññatā. Vinīyatīti vūpasamīyati. Accantappahānavasena nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ.

115. This is the gratification that arises dependent on the earth element, taking it as its support. 'Thus arisen' means arisen in this way, merely through the mode of manifesting in the body. 'Having been and then ceasing to exist' means that, not having existed before due to a concurrence of conditions, it arises, and then, upon undergoing dissolution, it exists no more. 'Not permanent' means impermanent, unstable—for what is lasting is eternal. 'In the mode of oppression' means having the characteristic of suffering due to the constant oppression of arising and passing away. 'In the mode of vanishing' means the vanishing of its own intrinsic nature. For things of such a nature, after attaining a brief moment, cease. Therefore, they 'change through aging and death,' transforming in two ways. Hence, it is said, 'subject to change.' Ādīnava (danger) is so called because it sets in motion what is vile; it is the ultimate misery. 'Is removed' means it is pacified. Nissaraṇa (escape) is so called because it is the means by which one escapes through complete abandonment.

Sāyaṃ nipannā sabbarattiṃ khepetvā pāto uṭṭhahāma, māsapuṇṇaghaṭo viya no sarīraṃ nissandābhāvato.

Having lain down in the evening, we spend the whole night and rise in the morning; our body is like a pot that has been full for a month, due to the absence of any outflow.

Phusitamattesupīti udakassa phusitamattesupi.

"Even with a mere sprinkling of water"—meaning even with just a slight sprinkling of water.

Atināmenti kālaṃ. Evaṃ vuttanayena pavattā puggalā etā pathavīdhātuādayo assādenti nāma abhirativasena tattha ākaṅkhuppādanato.

'They pass the time.' Persons who proceed in the manner described are said to relish these elements, the earth element and so on, because longing for them is produced by way of delight.

Abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇenāti aggamaggañāṇena. Rukkho bodhi “bujjhati etthā”ti katvā. Maggo bodhi “bujjhati etenā”ti katvā. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ bodhi sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ bujjhanato. Nibbānaṃ bodhi bujjhitabbato. Tesanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Sāvakapāramīñāṇanti sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ yāthāvato dassanavatthu.

'With surpassing knowledge' means with the knowledge of the highest path. The tree is 'bodhi' because 'one awakens here.' The path is 'bodhi' because 'one awakens by means of this.' Omniscient knowledge is 'bodhi' because of awakening rightly and by oneself to all things. Nibbāna is 'bodhi' because it is to be awakened to. 'Of these' is a genitive of specification. 'The knowledge of the disciple's perfections' means that this knowledge is the basis for seeing things as they really are.

Akuppāti paṭipakkhehi akopetabbo. Kāraṇatoti ariyamaggato. Tato hissa akuppatā. Tenāha “sā hī”tiādī. Ārammaṇatoti nibbānārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇānaṃ lokiyasamāpattīnaṃ abhāvato.

'Unshakable' means because it cannot be shaken by opposing factors. 'By reason' means because of the noble path. For that reason, it is unshakable. Hence, it is said, 'for that,' etc. 'By object' means because of having Nibbāna as object, and because of the absence of mundane attainments that have Nibbāna as object.

Vitthāravasenāti ekekadhātuvasenāti vadanti, ekekissā pana dhātuyā lakkhaṇavibhattidassanavasena. Yanti hetuatthe nipāto, yaṃ nimittanti attho. Assādeti etenāti assādo, taṇhā. Ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā assādoti ettha ayaṃ-saddo “pahānapaṭivedho”ti etthāpi ānetvā sambandhitabbo “ayaṃ pahānapaṭivedho paṭivijjhitabbaṭṭhena samudayasacca”nti. Esa nayo sesasaccesupi. Yāti yathāvuttesu assādo ādīnavo nissaraṇanti imesu tīsu ṭhānesu pavattā [M 2.0148] yā diṭṭhi…pe… yo samādhi, ayaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedho maggasaccanti vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

They speak of it as 'by way of expansion,' meaning 'by way of each element'; that is, by way of showing the characteristics and divisions of each individual element. The particle `yaṃ` is used in the sense of cause; the meaning is 'that which is the reason.' `Assādo` (gratification) is 'that by which one savors'; it is craving. Here, in the phrase 'this is the gratification of the earth element,' the word 'this' should also be brought over and connected with 'the penetration of abandonment,' as in: 'this penetration of abandonment is the truth of the origin in the sense that it is to be penetrated.' This is the method for the remaining truths as well. The view... that concentration, which proceeds in these three instances as stated—gratification, danger, and escape—this is the penetration by development, the truth of the path, and should be connected in the manner stated.

Pubbesambodhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pubbesambodha Sutta is concluded.

3. Acariṃsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Acariṃ Sutta

116. Yathā [V 2.0129] yāvatā nissaraṇapariyesanaṭṭhāne ādīnavapariyesanā, evaṃ yāvatā ādīnavapariyesanaṭṭhāne assādapariyesanā sammāpaṭipannassāti vuttaṃ “acarinti ñāṇacārena acariṃ, anubhavanacārenā”ti.

116. Just as the search for danger is found in the sphere of seeking escape, so too, for one who is practicing rightly, the search for gratification is found in the sphere of seeking danger. Thus it is said: 'I have lived' means 'I have lived by means of the wandering of knowledge and by means of the wandering of experience.'

Acariṃsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Acariṃ Sutta is concluded.

4. Nocedaṃsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nocedaṃ Sutta

117. Nissaṭātiādīni padāni, ādito vuttapaṭisedhenāti “nevā”ti ettha vuttena nakārena. Tenāha “na nissaṭā”tiādi. Vimariyādikatenātiādi ca ettha viharaṇapekkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ. Dutiyanayeti “yato ca kho, bhikkhave”tiādinā vuttanaye. Kilesavaṭṭamariyādāya sabbaso abhāvato nimmariyādikatena cittena. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi. Tīsūti dutiyādīsu tīsu.

117. The words beginning with 'Nissaṭā' (released) are connected from the beginning with the negation 'na', as stated here by the particle 'na' in 'neva'. Therefore, it is said, 'not released,' and so on. And here, in 'vimariyādikatena' (by being without boundaries) and so on, the instrumental case expresses dwelling and observing. The second method is the method stated in the passage beginning, 'But, bhikkhus...' Because the boundary of the cycle of defilements is entirely absent, the mind is made boundless. Therefore, it is said, 'there,' and so on. 'Tīsu' (in the three) refers to the three beginning with the second.

Nocedaṃsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nocedaṃ Sutta is concluded.

5. Ekantadukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ekantadukkha Sutta

118. Ekanteneva dukkhāti avīcimahānirayo viya ekantato dukkhā eva sukhena avomissā. Dukkhena anupatitāti dukkheneva sabbaso upagatā. Dukkhena okkantāti bahiddhā viya antopi dukkhena avakkantā anupaviṭṭhā. Sukhavedanāpaccayatāya imāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ sukhatā viya dukkhavedanāpaccayatāpi veditabbā, saṅkhāradukkhatā pana sabbattha caritā eva[M 2.0149]. Sabbatthāti sabbāsu dhātūsu, sabbaṭṭhānesu vā. Paṭhamaṃ sukhaṃ dassetvāpi pacchā dukkhassa kathitattā “dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ kathita”nti vuttaṃ.

118. 'Utterly suffering' means like the Avīci great hell, which is entirely suffering, unmixed with happiness. 'Assailed by suffering' means completely approached by suffering. 'Invaded by suffering' means that internally, as well as externally, they are invaded and penetrated by suffering. Just as the pleasantness of these elements should be understood as conditioned by pleasant feeling, so too should their painfulness be understood as conditioned by painful feeling. But the suffering of formations is active everywhere. 'Everywhere' means in all elements, or in all places. Although happiness is shown first, because suffering is discussed afterward, it is said, 'the characteristic of suffering has been spoken of.'

Ekantadukkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ekantadukkha Sutta is concluded.

6-10. Abhinandasuttādivaṇṇanā

6–10. Commentary on the Abhinanda Sutta and Others

119-123. Chaṭṭhasattamesu vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vivaṭṭaṃ kathita”nti vuttaṃ[V 2.0130]. Tīsu suttesu. Catusaccamevāti cattāri saccāni samāhaṭāni catusaccanti tesaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahaṇaṃ, niyamo pana tabbinimuttassa paramatthassa abhāvato.

119–123. In the sixth and seventh suttas, the cycle of existence and cessation has been explained. However, in the commentary, it is said, 'cessation has been explained' in the three suttas. 'Only the Four Truths' means that the four truths are gathered together as 'the Four Truths,' hence their collective designation. But this is a definite statement because there is no ultimate reality apart from them.

Abhinandasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Abhinanda Sutta and Similar Texts is concluded.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fourth Chapter is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

The Sāratthappakāsinī, Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya

Dhātusaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Dhātusaṃyutta is concluded.

4. Anamataggasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Anamatagga Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Tiṇakaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Tiṇakaṭṭha Sutta

124. Upasaggo [V 2.0131][M 2.0150] samāsavisaye sasādhanaṃ kiriyaṃ dassetīti vuttaṃ “ñāṇena anugantvāpī”ti. Vassasataṃ vassasahassanti nidassanamattametaṃ, tato bhiyyopi anugantvā anamataggo eva saṃsāro. Agga-saddo idha mariyādavacano, anuddesikañcetaṃ vacananti āha “aparicchinnapubbāparakoṭiko”ti. Aññathā antimabhavikaparicchinnakatavimuttiparipācanīyadhammādīnaṃ vasena aparicchinnapubbāparakoṭi na sakkā vattuṃ. Saṃsaraṇaṃ saṃsāro. Pacchimāpi na paññāyati andhabālānaṃ vasenāti adhippāyo. Tenāha bhagavā “dīgho bālāna saṃsāro”ti (dha. pa. 60). Vemajjheyeva pana sattā saṃsaranti pubbāparakoṭīnaṃ alabbhanīyattā. Attho paritto hoti yathābhūtāvabodhābhāvato. Buddhasamayeti sāsaneti attho. Attho mahā yathābhūtāvabodhisambhavato, atthassa vipulatāya taṃsadisā upamā natthīti parittaṃyeva upamaṃ āharantīti adhippāyo. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ “pāḷiyaṃ hī”tiādinā samattheti. Mātu mātaroti mātu mātāmahiyo. Tassevāti dukkhasseva. Tibbanti dukkhapariyāyoti.

124. It is said that a prefix in a compound indicates an action with its means, as in 'even having attained through knowledge.' A hundred years, a thousand years—this is merely an example; even beyond that, having wandered, saṃsāra is indeed without discoverable beginning. Here, the word 'agga' is a term denoting a limit; and this is a non-designative statement, as it is said: 'with immeasurable past and future limits.' Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of immeasurable past and future limits in terms of the final existence, liberation, and the ripening of the Dhamma conducive to deliverance, etc., which are limited. Wandering is saṃsāra. The meaning is that even the end is not discernible due to the blindness of fools. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Long is the wandering for fools' (Dhp 60). Yet beings wander only in the middle, because the past and future limits cannot be obtained. The meaning is limited because of the absence of understanding things as they truly are. 'In the time of the Buddha' means in the Dispensation. The meaning is vast because it arises from understanding things as they truly are; due to the vastness of the meaning, there is no simile like it, hence the intention is that only a limited simile is given. Now, the meaning that has been stated is supported by 'in the Pāli,' and so on. 'Mother's mother' means maternal grandmothers. 'Of that' refers to suffering. 'Intense' is a term synonymous with suffering.

Tiṇakaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tiṇakaṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

2. Pathavīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pathavī Sutta

125. Mahāpathavinti avisesena anavasesapariyādāyinīti āha “cakkavāḷapariyanta”nti. Parikappavacanañcetaṃ.

125. 'Great earth' means without distinction, encompassing all without remainder, as it says, 'the extent of the world-system.' And this is a descriptive expression.

Pathavīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pathavī Sutta is concluded.

3. Assusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Assu Sutta

126. Kandanaṃ [V 2.0132][M 2.0151] sasaddaṃ, rodanaṃ pana kevalamevāti āha “kandantānanti sasaddaṃ rudamānāna”nti. Pavattanti sandanavasena pavattaṃ. “Sinerurasmīhi paricchinnesū”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “sinerussā”tiādimāha. Maṇimayanti indanīlamaṇimayaṃ. Sinerussa pubbadakkhiṇakoṇasamapadesā “pubbadakkhiṇapassā”ti adhippetā. Tehi nikkhantarajatarasmiyo indanīlarasmiyo ca ekato hutvā. Tāsaṃ rasmīnaṃ antaresūti tāsaṃ catūhi koṇehi nikkhantarasmīnaṃ catūsu antaresu. Cattāroti dakkhiṇādibhedā cattāro mahāsamuddā honti. Viasananti visesena khepanaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “vināsoti attho”ti.

126. 'Kandanaṃ' means with sound, while 'rodanaṃ' means solely crying; hence it is said, 'kandantānaṃ' (crying) means 'sasaddaṃ rudamānānaṃ' (crying with sound). 'Pavattaṃ' refers to what occurs through continuous flowing. The briefly stated meaning in 'limited by the rays of Sineru' is elaborated with 'of Sineru' and so on. 'Maṇimayaṃ' means made of sapphire. The area corresponding to the southeast corner of Mount Sineru is intended by 'the southeast side.' The silver rays and the sapphire rays that have emerged from them combine together. 'In the spaces between those rays' means in the four spaces between the rays emerging from the four corners. 'Four' refers to the four great oceans, differentiated as south and so on. 'Viasana' means especially casting away. What is that? It is said, 'vināso' (destruction) is the meaning.

Assusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Assu Sutta is concluded.

4. Khīrasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Milk

127. Mātuthaññanti pītaṃ mātuyā thanato nibbattakhīraṃ bahutaranti veditabbaṃ.

127. ‘Mother’s milk’ is to be understood as the milk produced from the mother’s breast that has been drunk, and is more abundant.

Khīrasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Milk is concluded.

5. Pabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Mountain

128. “Anamataggassa saṃsārassa dīghatamattā na sukaraṃ nasukara”nti aṭṭhakathāpāṭho. Kathaṃ nacchindatīti kathaṃ na pariyosāpeti, kāyacipi gahaṇatāyāti adhippāyo. Tayo kappāsaṃsūti tayo ekakappāsaṃsū. Yehi naṃ phuṭṭhaṃ, tatopi sukhumataraṃ sāsapamattaṃ khīyeyya pabbataṃ sabbabhāgehi aticiravelaṃ parimajjante.

128. The commentary reading is: ‘Due to the extreme length of beginningless saṃsāra, it is not easy, not easy.’ ‘How does it not cut off?’ means ‘how does it not bring to an end?’; the intention is for the sake of grasping even a body. ‘Three kappāsaṃsū’ means three single kappāsaṃsū. By which it is touched, a mountain would wear away by the measure of a mustard seed, even more finely than that, while being rubbed on all sides for a very long time.

Pabbatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Mountain is concluded.

6. Sāsapasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Mustard Seed

129. Nagaranti [M 2.0152] nagarasaṅkhepena pākārena parikkhittataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Anto pana sabbaso vicittasāsapehi eva puṇṇaṃ, evaṃ cuṇṇikābaddhaṃ. Tenāha “na pana…pe… daṭṭhabba”nti.

129. The term ‘city’ is said with reference to being enclosed by a wall, by way of a concise definition. Inside, however, it is entirely filled with various mustard seeds, packed as if into a powder. Therefore it is said: ‘… it should not be seen …’

Sāsapasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Mustard Seed is concluded.

7. Sāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Disciple

130. Tassa [V 2.0133] ṭhitaṭṭhānatoti bhikkhuno anussaritvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato, tena anussaritassa satasahassakappassa anantarakappato paṭṭhāyāti attho. Evanti vuttappakārena. Cattāropi bhikkhū abhiññālābhino. Cattāri kappasatasahassāni divase divase anussareyyunti parikappanavasena vadanti.

130. ‘From his standing place’ means from the standing place where the monk stood and recollected; the meaning is starting from the eon immediately preceding the hundred thousand eons that he recollected. ‘Thus’ means in the manner stated. All four monks were attainers of higher knowledge. They speak by way of supposition, saying that they could recollect four hundred thousand eons day by day.

Sāvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Disciple is concluded.

8. Gaṅgāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Gaṅgā Discourse

131. Etasmiṃ antareti etasmiṃ pabhavasamuddapadesaparicchinne āyāmato pañcayojanasatike atirekayojanasatike vā ṭhāne.

131. ‘Within this’ means in this place bounded by the region of its source and the ocean, extending five hundred yojanas in length, or an additional hundred yojanas.

Gaṅgāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Gaṅgā Discourse is concluded.

9. Daṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Stick

132. Navame khittoti punappunaṃ khitto. Ekavārañhi khitto mūlādīsu ekeneva nipateyya. Tathā sati adhippeto pātassa aniyamo na nidassito siyā. Tattha ca dhammaṃ suṇantā bhikkhū manussaloke, te sandhāya “asmā lokā”ti āha, tadaññaṃ sandhāya “paraloka”nti. Tassa tassa vā puggalassa yathādhippeto ayaṃ loko, tadañño paraloko.

132. In the ninth discourse, ‘thrown’ means thrown again and again. For if it were thrown just once, it would fall in only one place, among the roots and so on. If that were the case, the intended irregularity of its fall would not be shown. Here, the monks listening to the Dhamma are in the human world; with reference to them, it is said, ‘from this world,’ and with reference to another, ‘to the other world.’ Or, for each particular individual, this is the intended world, and the other is the other world.

Daṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Stick is concluded.

10. Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Individuals

133. Samaṭṭhikāloti [M 2.0153] samena ākārena laddhabbaaṭṭhikālo. Giriparikkhepeti pañcahi girīhi parikkhittattā “giriparikkhepo”ti laddhanāme rājagahe.

133. ‘Samaṭṭhikālo’ is the time for obtaining bones in an even manner. ‘In Giriparikkhepa’ means in Rājagaha, which received the name ‘Giriparikkhepa’ because it is surrounded by five mountains.

Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Individuals is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Duggatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Destitute

134. Duggatanti [V 2.0134] kicchajīvikattā sabbathā dukkhaṃ gataṃ upagataṃ. Tathābhūto pana daliddo varāko nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “daliddaṃ kapaṇa”nti. Hatthapādehīti nidassanamattaṃ, aññehipi sarīrāvayavehi dussaṇṭhānehi upeto durupeto evāti.

134. ‘Destitute’ means one who has gone to, or reached, suffering in every way due to a difficult livelihood. Such a person is called a poor wretch, as it is said: ‘a poor, wretched person.’ ‘With hands and feet’ is merely an illustration; he is indeed poorly endowed, being possessed of other ill-formed bodily parts.

Duggatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Destitute is concluded.

2. Sukhitasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Happy One

135. Sukhitanti sañjātasukhaṃ. Tenāha “sukhasamappita”ntiādi. Susajjitanti sukhumupakaraṇehi sabbathā sajjitaṃ.

135. ‘Happy’ means one for whom happiness has arisen. Therefore it is said: ‘endowed with happiness,’ and so on. ‘Well-equipped’ means equipped in every way with fine accessories.

Sukhitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Happy One is concluded.

3. Tiṃsamattasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Thirty

136. Dhutaṅgasamādānavasena, na araññavāsādimattena. Sasaṃyojanā sabbaso saṃyojanānaṃ appahīnattā, na puthujjanabhāvato. Ekekavaṇṇakālova gahetabboti etena mahiṃsādīnaṃ rassadīghapiṅgalādīsu ekekāneva gahetvā dasseti.

136. By way of undertaking the ascetic practices, not merely by dwelling in the forest and so on. 'With fetters' (sasaṃyojanā) means because the fetters are not completely abandoned, not because of being an ordinary person. By the phrase 'each color should be taken individually,' he shows that regarding buffaloes and so on, one should take each one individually among the short, long, tawny, and so on.

Tiṃsamattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Thirty is concluded.

4-9. Mātusuttādivaṇṇanā

4–9. Commentary on the Discourses on the Mother and so on

137-142. Liṅganiyamena [M 2.0154] ceva cakkavāḷaniyamena cāti “purisānañhi mātugāmakālo, mātugāmānañca purisakālo”ti yathā sattasantāne liṅganiyamo natthi, evaṃ kadāci imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe nibbattanti, kadāci aññatarasminti cakkavāḷaniyamopi natthi. Evameva ṭhite

137–142. By the fixedness of gender and by the fixedness of world-systems—just as there is no fixed rule of gender in the continuum of beings, such that 'for men there is a time of being a woman, and for women a time of being a man,' so also there is no fixed rule of world-systems, that they arise sometimes in this world-system and sometimes in another. When it is established thus:

Cakkavāḷe [V 2.0135] mātugāmakāle namātābhūtapubbo natthītiādinā liṅganiyamena cakkavāḷaniyamo ca veditabbo. Tenāha “tesū”tiādi.

By the statement beginning, 'In a world-system, at a time of being a woman, there is no one who has not previously been a mother,' the fixed rule of gender and the fixed rule of world-systems should be understood. Therefore, he said, 'among them,' and so on.

Mātusuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourses on the Mother and so on is concluded.

10. Vepullapabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Vepulla Mountain

143. Ekaṃ apadānaṃ āharitvā dasseti “evaṃ saṃvegaṃ janetvā bhikkhū visesaṃ pāpessāmī”ti. Catūhena ārohanti catuyojanubbedhattā. Dvinnaṃ buddhānanti kakusandhassa koṇāgamanassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ. “Tivarā rohitassā suppiyā”ti manussānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle samaññā tattha desanāmavasena jātāti veditabbā, yathā etarahi māgadhāti.

143. He brings forth one Apadāna and shows it, thinking: 'Thus, having generated a sense of urgency, I will lead the monks to attain distinction.' They ascend in four days, due to its height of four yojanas. 'Of two Buddhas' means of these two Buddhas: Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana. The names 'Tivarā, Rohitassā, Suppiyā' should be understood as designations for people at that particular time, having arisen there by way of the name of the country, just as now there are the Māgadhans.

Puna vassasatanti paṭhamavassasatato uparivassasataṃ jīvanako nāma manusso natthi. Parihīnasadisaṃ kataṃ desanāya. Vaḍḍhitvāti dasavassāyukabhāvato paṭṭhāya yāva asaṅkhyeyyāyukabhāvā vaḍḍhitvā. “Parihīna”nti vatvā taṃ parihīnabhāvaṃ dassento “katha”ntiādimāha. Yaṃ āyuppamāṇesūti yattakaṃ āyuppamāṇesūti.

The phrase 'again, a hundred years' means that after the first hundred years, there was no human being called Jīvanaka. By the teaching, it was made similar to a decline. The term 'having increased' means having increased from a lifespan of ten years up to a lifespan of incalculable years. Having said 'declined,' to show that state of decline, he said 'how' and so on. The phrase 'as to the measures of life' means 'to whatever extent the measures of life.'

Vepullapabbatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Vepulla Mountain is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

Sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Anamataggasaṃyuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Anamatagga Saṃyutta is concluded.

5. Kassapasaṃyuttaṃ

5. The Kassapa Saṃyutta

1. Santuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Santuṭṭha Sutta

144. Santuṭṭhoti [V 2.0136][M 2.0155] sakena uccāvacena paccayena samameva ca tussanako. Tenāha “itarītarenā”tiādi. Tattha duvidhaṃ itarītaraṃ – pākatikaṃ, ñāṇasañjanitañcāti. Tattha pākatikaṃ paṭikkhipitvā ñāṇasañjanitameva dassento “thūlasukhumā”tiādimāha. Itaraṃ vuccati hīnaṃ paṇītato aññattā. Tathā paṇītampi itaraṃ hīnato aññattā. Apekkhāsaddā hi itarītarāti. Iti yena kenaci hīnena vā paṇītena vā cīvarādipaccayena santussito tathāpavatto alobho itarītarapaccayasantoso, taṃsamaṅgitāya santuṭṭho. Yathālābhaṃ attano lābhānurūpaṃ santoso yathālābhasantoso. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Labbhatīti vā lābho, yo yo lābho yathālābho, tena santoso yathālābhasantoso. Balanti kāyabalaṃ. Sāruppanti bhikkhuno anucchavikatā.

144. 'Content' means one who is equally satisfied with one's own high and low requisites. Therefore, he says, 'with one or the other,' and so on. Herein, 'one or the other' is twofold: natural and produced by knowledge. Herein, rejecting the natural and showing only that produced by knowledge, he says, 'coarse or subtle,' and so on. 'The other' is said of the inferior, because it is different from the excellent. Likewise, the excellent is also 'the other,' because it is different from the inferior. For the words 'one or the other' are relational terms. Thus, being content with any requisite whatsoever, whether inferior or excellent, such as robes and so on—such a practice of non-greed is 'contentment with one or the other requisite'; by being endowed with that, one is 'content.' 'Contentment according to gain' is contentment in conformity with one's own gain. This same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Or, 'gain' is what is obtained; whatever gain there is, is 'according to gain'; contentment with that is 'contentment according to gain.' 'Strength' means bodily strength. 'Suitable' means what is appropriate for a monk.

Yathāladdhato aññassa apatthanā nāma siyā appicchatāya pavattiākāroti tato vinivattitameva santosassa sarūpaṃ dassento “labhantopi na gaṇhātī”ti āha. Taṃ parivattetvāti pakatidubbalādīnaṃ garucīvaraṃ na phāsubhāvāvahaṃ sarīrabādhāvahañca hotīti payojanavasena, nātricchatādivasena parivattetvā. Lahukacīvaraparibhoge santosavirodhi na hotīti āha “lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Mahagghacīvaraṃ bahūni vā cīvarāni labhitvā tāni vissajjetvā aññassa gahaṇaṃ yathāsāruppanaye ṭhitattā na santosavirodhīti āha “tesaṃ…pe… dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Evaṃ sesapaccayesu yathābalayathāsāruppaniddesesu api-saddaggahaṇe adhippāyo veditabbo.

Since not desiring something other than what one has obtained might be a mode of practice due to having few wishes, to show that the nature of contentment is precisely turning away from that, he says, 'Even when obtaining, he does not grasp.' 'Having exchanged it' means that for those who are naturally weak and so on, a heavy robe is not conducive to comfort and causes bodily affliction; thus, it is exchanged for practical reasons, not out of excessive desire or the like. He says that using a light robe does not conflict with contentment: 'Even when getting by with a light one, he remains content.' He says that obtaining an expensive robe or many robes, then giving them away and taking another, does not conflict with contentment because it is established in the principle of suitability: 'Even when wearing them... he remains content.' Similarly, in the explanations of the other requisites according to strength and suitability, the intention behind the inclusion of the word 'even' (api) should be understood.

Pakatīti vācāpakatiādikā. Avasesaniddāya abhibhūtattā paṭibujjhato sahasā pāpakā vitakkā pātubhavantīti.

'Natural' means natural speech and so on. Because one is overcome by residual drowsiness, evil thoughts suddenly arise when one awakens.

Muttaharītakanti [V 2.0137][M 2.0156] gomuttaparibhāvitaṃ, pūtibhāvena vā chaḍḍitattā muttaharītakaṃ. Buddhādīhi vaṇṇitanti “pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya yā pabbajjā”tiādinā sammāsambuddhādīhi pasatthaṃ.

'Muttaharītaka' means that which is steeped in cow's urine; or it is called muttaharītaka because it is discarded due to its foul nature. 'Praised by the Buddha and others' means commended by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha and others, as in 'The going forth is dependent on putrid urine as medicine,' and so on.

Eko ekacco santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ na katheti seyyathāpi āyasmā bākulatthero. Na santuṭṭo hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti seyyathāpi thero upanando sakyaputto. Neva santuṭṭho hoti, na santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti seyyathāpi thero lāḷudāyī. Ayanti āyasmā mahākassapo. Anesananti ayoniso micchājīvavasena paccayapariyesanaṃ. Uttasatīti “kathaṃ nu kho labheyya”nti jātuttāsena uttasati. Tathā paritassati. Ayanti mahākassapatthero. Evaṃ yathāvuttaekaccabhikkhu viya na paritassati, alābhaparittāsena vighātappattiyā na parittāsaṃ āpajjati. Lobhoyeva ārammaṇena saddhiṃ ganthanaṭṭhena bajjhanaṭṭhena gedho lobhagedho. Mucchanti gedhaṃ momūhattabhāvaṃ. Ādīnavanti dosaṃ. Nissaraṇamevāti cīvare idamatthitādassanapubbakaṃ alaggabhāvasaṅkhātaniyyānameva pajānanto. Yathāladdhādīnanti yathāladdhapiṇḍapātādīnaṃ. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

One individual is content but does not speak in praise of contentment, just like the Venerable Elder Bākula. Another is not content, yet speaks in praise of contentment, just like the Elder Upananda the Sakyan. Another is neither content nor speaks in praise of contentment, just like the Elder Lāḷudāyī. This one is the Venerable Mahākassapa. 'Improper seeking' means the seeking of requisites improperly, by way of wrong livelihood. 'He trembles' means he trembles with an anxiety that has arisen, thinking, 'How indeed might I obtain it?' Likewise, he is agitated. This refers to the Elder Mahākassapa. Thus, he is not agitated like that certain monk spoken of; he does not fall into agitation through the affliction caused by fear of not gaining. Greed itself, in the sense of binding and in the sense of fettering to an object, is infatuation; this is the infatuation of greed. 'To be infatuated' means greed, the state of being utterly deluded. 'Danger' means fault. 'The escape' means precisely understanding the release, which is designated as the state of non-attachment, preceded by seeing the lack of substance in a robe. 'Of what is obtained and so on' refers to almsfood obtained and so on. And this is a genitive of specification.

Yathā mahākassapattheroti attanā vattabbaniyāmena vadati, bhagavatā pana vattabbaniyāmena “yathā kassapo bhikkhū”ti bhavitabbaṃ. Kassapena nidassanabhūtena. Kathanaṃ nāma bhāro “mutto moceyya”nti paṭiññānurūpattā. Paṭipattiṃ paripūraṃ katvā pūraṇaṃ bhāro satthu āṇāya sirasā sampaṭicchitabbato.

'Just as the Elder Mahākassapa': he speaks according to the way he himself should speak, but according to the way the Blessed One should speak, it should be 'as Kassapa is among the monks.' Kassapa serves as an example. Speaking is a burden, because it must conform to the declaration, 'Being freed, one should free others.' Fulfilling the practice completely is a burden, because the Teacher's command must be accepted with one's head.

Santuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Santuṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

2. Anottappīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Anottappī Sutta

145. Tena rahitoti tena sammāvāyāmena rahito. Nibbhayoti bhayarahito. Kusalānuppādanampi hi sāvajjameva aññāṇālasiyahetukattā. Sambujjhanatthāyāti ariyamaggehi sambujjhanāya. Yogehi khemaṃ tehi anupaddutattā.

145. 'Devoid of that' means devoid of that right effort. 'Fearless' means devoid of fear. Indeed, the non-arising of skillful qualities is blameworthy because it is caused by ignorance and laziness. 'For the purpose of awakening' means for awakening by means of the noble paths. 'Safety from the yokes' means being unharmed by them.

Manuññavatthunti [M 2.0157] manoramaṃ lobhuppattikāraṇaṃ. Yathā vā tathā vāti subhasukhādivasena. Teti lobhādayo. Anuppannāti veditabbā tathārūpe vatthārammaṇe tathā anuppannapubbattā. Aññathāti vuttanayeneva vatthārammaṇehi ayojetvā gayhamāne. Vatthumhīti upaṭṭhākādicīvarādivatthumhi. Ārammaṇeti manāpiyādibhede ārammaṇe. Tādisena paccayenāti ayonisomanasikārasativossaggādipaccayena[V 2.0138]. Imeti vuttanayena paccayalābhena pacchā uppajjamānā pāḷiyaṃ tathā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ uppajjamānatāya nappahīyanti nāma. Anuppādo hi paramatthato pahānaṃ kathitaṃ, tasmā tattha kathitanayeneva gahetabbanti adhippāyo.

'Pleasing object' means a delightful basis, a cause for the arising of greed. 'In one way or another' means by way of beauty, pleasure, and so on. 'Those' refers to greed and so on. 'Not arisen' should be understood as not having arisen before in such an object-base, because of not having previously arisen in that way. 'Otherwise' means when it is grasped without being applied to the object-bases in the manner described. 'In the object' means in the supporting object such as robes and so on, provided by supporters and so on. 'In the object-base' means in the object-base that has distinctions like pleasantness and so on. 'By such a condition' means by a condition such as unwise attention, lapse of mindfulness, and so on. 'These' refers to those that arise afterward due to obtaining a condition in the manner described; it should be seen that it is said thus in the Pāli text. Thus, because of arising in this way, they are indeed called 'not abandoned.' For non-arising is, in the ultimate sense, said to be abandonment; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood in the way explained there.

Appaṭiladdhāti anuppattiyā. Teti yathāvuttasīlādianavajjadhammā. Paṭiladdhāti adhigatā. “Sīlādidhammā”ti ettha yadi maggaphalānipi gahitāni, atha kasmā “parihānivasenā”ti vuttanti āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Imassa pana sammappadhānassāti catutthassa sammappadhānassa vasena. Ayaṃ desanāti “uppannā me kusalā dhammā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti ayaṃ desanā katā. Dutiyamaggo vā…pe… saṃvatteyyāti idaṃ āyatiṃ sattasu attabhāvesu uppajjamānadukkhasaṅkhātaanatthuppattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Ātāpī ottappī bhabbo sambodhāyā”tiādivacanato “ime cattāro sammappadhānā pubbabhāgavipassanāvasena kathitā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Not attained' means by non-attainment. 'Those' refers to the blameless qualities such as virtue and so on, as mentioned. 'Attained' means realized. If the path and its fruition are also included here in 'qualities such as virtue,' then why is 'in terms of decline' said? He says, 'Here too,' and so on. 'By this right effort' means by way of the fourth right effort. 'This teaching' refers to this teaching given: 'May wholesome states that have arisen in me, while ceasing, not conduce to harm.' Or the second path... etc.... 'would conduce to harm'—this is said with reference to the arising of harm, reckoned as suffering, arising in seven future existences. From the statement, 'ardent, conscientious, capable of awakening,' and so on, it is said, 'these four right efforts are spoken of by way of preliminary insight.'

Anottappīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anottappī Sutta is concluded.

3. Candūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Candūpama Sutta

146. Piyamanāpaniccanavakādiguṇehi cando upamā etesanti candūpamā. Santhavādīni padāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ puna citte kilesādhigamo. Sabbehipi padehi katthaci satte anurodharodhābhāvamāha. Attano pana sommabhāvena mahājanassa piyo manāpo. Yadatthamettha candūpamā āhaṭā, taṃ dassento “eva”ntiādimāha. Na kevalaṃ candūpamatāya ettako eva guṇo, atha kho aññepi santīti te dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evamādīhīti ādi-saddena yathā. Cando [M 2.0158] lokānuggahena ajavīthiādikā nānāvīthiyo paṭipajjati, evaṃ bhikkhu taṃ taṃ disaṃ upagacchati kulānuddayāya. Yathā cando kaṇhapakkhato sukkapakkhaṃ upagacchanto kalāhi vaḍḍhamāno hutvā niccanavo hoti, evaṃ bhikkhu kaṇhapakkhaṃ pahāya sukkapakkhaṃ upagantvā guṇehi vaḍḍhamāno lokassa vā pāmojjapāsaṃsattho niccanavatāya candasamacitto adhunupasampanno viya ca niccanavo hutvā carati.

146. The moon is a comparison for them due to qualities such as being dear, pleasing, and ever-new; hence, 'moon-like.' Words such as 'intimacy' are synonyms for one another. 'Obsession' refers to the defilements taking hold of the mind. By all these terms, he states the absence of adherence and aversion towards any being whatsoever. Yet, by his own gentle nature, he becomes dear and pleasing to the multitude. To show the purpose for which the moon-like comparison is brought here, he says, 'Thus,' and so on. It is not only that he possesses such qualities by being moon-like, but there are others as well—to indicate these, it is said, 'Moreover,' and so forth. By 'etc.' in 'thus etc.' is meant as follows. Just as the moon, for the welfare of the world, traverses various paths such as the zodiac, so too does the monk go to various regions out of compassion for families. And just as the moon, moving from the dark fortnight to the bright fortnight, grows in phases and is always new, so too the monk, abandoning the dark fortnight and entering the bright fortnight, grows in virtues and, with a mind like the moon in its constant newness, becomes a source of joy and praise for the world, living ever-new, like one recently ordained.

Apakassitvāti kilesakāmavatthukāmehi vivecetvā. Taṃ nekkhammābhimukhaṃ kāyacittānaṃ ākaḍḍhanaṃ kāyato apanayanañca hotīti āha “ākaḍḍhitvā apanetvāti attho”ti. Catukkañcettha sambhavatīti taṃ dassetuṃ “yo hi bhikkhū”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Having withdrawn' means having separated from sensual defilements and sensual objects. That is the drawing of body and mind towards renunciation and their physical removal; hence it is said, 'the meaning is "having drawn away and removed."' And here, a fourfold division is possible; to show this, it is said, 'For a monk,' and so on.

Niccanavayāti [V 2.0139] “niccanavakā”icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Ka-saddena hi padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, ka-kārassa ca ya-kārādeso. Evaṃ vicariṃsūti kiñjakkhavasena pariggahābhāvena yathā ime, evaṃ vicariṃsu aññeti anukampamānā.

'Niccanavayā' means 'niccanavakā' indeed. The word is augmented by the syllable 'ka,' and the 'ka' sound is replaced by 'ya.' 'Thus they wandered' means: having compassion for others, they wandered just as these do, without possessions, due to having nothing.

Dvebhātikavatthūti dvebhātikattherapaṭibaddhaṃ vatthuṃ. Appatirūpakaraṇanti bhikkhūnaṃ asāruppakaraṇaṃ. Ādhāyitvāti āropanaṃ ṭhapetvā. Tathāti yathā saṅghamajjhe gaṇamajjhe ca, tathā vuḍḍhatare puggale appatirūpakaraṇaṃ. Evamādīti ādi-saddena antaragharappavesane aññattha ca yathāvuttato aññaṃ asāruppakiriyaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tatthevāti saṅghamajjhe gaṇamajjhe puggalassa ca vuḍḍhassa santike.

'The matter concerning two brothers' means a matter connected with the two brother elders. 'Acting improperly' means behaving in a manner unbecoming for monks. 'Having placed' means having established an accusation. 'Similarly' means just as in the midst of the Sangha or a group, so too behaving improperly towards an elder person. By 'etc.' in 'thus etc.' is meant the inclusion of other unsuitable actions not mentioned, such as entering private quarters and elsewhere. 'Right there' means in the midst of the Sangha, in a group, and in the presence of an elder person.

Yathāvuttesu aññesu ca tesu ṭhānesu. Pāpicchatāpi manopāgabbhiyanti eteneva kodhūpanāhādīnaṃ samudācāro manopāgabbhiyanti dassitaṃ hoti.

In the aforementioned and other such instances. Evil desire is also mental effrontery; by this it is shown that the conduct of anger, resentment, and the like is mental effrontery.

Ekato bhāriyanti piṭṭhipassato onataṃ. Vāyupatthambhanti cittasamuṭṭhānavāyunā upatthambhanaṃ. Anubbejetvā cittanti ānetvā sambandho. Cittassa hi tato anubbejanaṃ tadanunayanaṃ. Tenāha “sampiyāyamāno oloketī”ti. Vāyupatthambhakaṃ gāhāpetvāti kāyaṃ tathā upatthambhakaṃ katvā.

'Burdened on one side' means bent over at the back. 'Wind-supported' means supported by the wind arisen from the mind. 'Without agitating the mind' means bringing it into connection. For the non-agitation of the mind by that is its conciliation. Hence it is said, 'Looking with affection.' 'Having caused the wind-support to be taken' means having made the body supported in that way.

Opammasaṃsandanaṃ [M 2.0159] suviññeyyameva. Kāmagiddhatāya hīnādhimuttiko, avisuddhasīlācāratāya micchāpaṭipanno.

The connection of the simile is indeed easy to understand. Due to greed for sensual pleasures, one is of inferior inclination; due to impure virtue and conduct, one is practicing wrongly.

Aṅgulīhi nikkhantapabhā ākāsasañcalanena diguṇā hutvā ākāse vicariṃsūti āha “yamakavijjutaṃ cārayamāno viyā”ti. “Ākāse pāṇiṃ cālesī”ti padassa aññattha anāgatattā “asambhinnapada”nti vuttaṃ. Attamanoti pītisomanassehi gahitamano. Yañhi cittaṃ anavajjaṃ pītisomanassasahitaṃ, taṃ sasantakaṃ hitasukhāvahattā. Tenāha “sakamano”tiādi. Na domanassena…pe… gahitamano sakacittassa tabbiruddhattā. Purimanayenevāti “idāni yo hīnādhimuttiko”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva.

The light emitted from his fingers, by its movement through the sky, became double and wandered in the sky—thus he said, 'as if displaying twin lightning.' Because the phrase 'he moved his hand in the sky' does not occur elsewhere, it is called 'an unprecedented phrase.' 'Delighted' means a mind seized by joy and gladness. For a mind that is blameless and accompanied by joy and gladness is one's own, since it brings benefit and happiness. Therefore, he said, 'one's own mind,' etc. Not by sorrow... a mind seized... because that is contrary to one's own mind. 'In the same way as before' means in the way previously stated, beginning with 'now, one of inferior inclination,' etc.

Pasannākāranti pasannehi kātabbakiriyaṃ. Taṃ sarūpato dasseti “cīvarādayo paccaye dadeyyu”nti. Tathabhāvāyāti yadatthaṃ bhagavatā dhammo desito, yadatthañca sāsane pabbajjā, tadatthāya[V 2.0140]. Rakkhaṇabhāvanti apāyabhayato ca rakkhaṇajjhāsayaṃ. Candopamādivasenāti ādi-saddena ākāse calitapāṇi viya katthaci alaggatāya parisuddhajjhāsayatā sattesu kāruññanti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

'An expression of faith' means an action to be done by the faithful. This is shown in its own form: 'They should give requisites such as robes, etc.' 'For the attainment of that state' means for the purpose for which the Blessed One taught the Dhamma and for which there is the going forth in the Dispensation. 'The state of protecting' refers to the intention of protecting from the fear of the lower realms. 'By way of the moon simile, etc.'—by the word 'etc.' is included such things as: being unattached anywhere like a hand moving in the sky, purity of intention, and compassion for beings.

Candūpamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Candūpama Sutta is concluded.

4. Kulūpakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta

147. Kulāni upagacchatīti kulūpako. Sandīyatīti sabbaso dīyati, avakhaṇḍīyatīti attho. Sā pana avakhaṇḍiyanā dukkhāpanā aṭṭiyanā hotīti vuttaṃ “aṭṭīyatī”ti. Tenāha bhagavā “so tatonidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī”ti. Vuttanayānusārena heṭṭhā vuttanayassa anusaraṇena.

147. 'One who approaches families' is a family-frequenter. 'Is broken' means is completely torn apart; the meaning is 'is cut off.' That cutting off is painful, a vexation, hence it is said, 'he is vexed.' Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Because of that, he experiences pain and sorrow.' In accordance with the method stated, by following the method mentioned below.

Kulūpakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta is concluded.

5. Jiṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Jiṇṇa Sutta

148. Chinnabhinnaṭṭhāne [M 2.0160] chiddassa aputhulattā aggaḷaṃ adatvāva suttena saṃsibbanamattena aggaḷadānena ca chidde puthule. Nibbasanānīti ciranisevitavasanakiccāni, paribhogajiṇṇānīti attho. Tenāha “pubbe…pe… laddhanāmānī”ti, saññāpubbako vidhi aniccoti “gahapatānī”ti vuttaṃ yathā “vīriya”nti.

148. In a place that is cut and broken, when the hole is not wide, it is mended merely by sewing with a thread without applying a patch; and when the hole is wide, by applying a patch. 'Worn-out garments' means those whose function as garments has been long served; the meaning is, worn out through use. Therefore it is said, 'formerly... obtained names.' The rule preceded by perception is impermanent; thus it is said 'householders' just as 'energy'.

Senāpatinti senāpatibhāvinaṃ, senāpaccārahanti attho. Attano kammenāti attanā kātabbakammena. Soti satthā. Tasminti mahākassapatthere karotīti sambandho. Na karotīti vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “kasmā”tiādimāha. Yadi satthā dhutaṅgāni na vissajjāpetukāmo, atha kasmā “jiṇṇosi dāni tva”ntiādimavocāti āha “yathā panā”tiādi.

'Senāpati' means one who possesses the qualities of a commander; that is, one fit for the office of a commander. 'Attano kammena' means by the work to be done by oneself. 'So' means the Teacher. The connection is with 'in that Mahākassapa Thera, he does.' Explaining the meaning of 'he does not do,' he says, 'Why?' and so on. If the Teacher did not wish to have the ascetic practices relinquished, then why did he say, 'You are now old,' and so forth? He explains this with 'Just as...' and so on.

Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve phāsuvihāraṃ. Amānusikā savanaratīti atikkantamānusikāya araññasadduppattiyā araññehaṃ vasāmīti vivekavāsūpanissayādhīnasaddasavanapaccayā dhammarati uppajjati. Aparoti añño, dutiyoti attho. Tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva ekassa viharaṇaṭṭhāne viharaṇasamaye ca phāsu bhavati cittavivekasambhavato. Tenāha “ekassa ramato vane”ti.

'A pleasant dwelling in this very life' means a comfortable dwelling in this very existence. 'Delight in hearing non-human sounds' means: due to the arising of forest sounds that transcend the human, a delight in the Dhamma arises, conditioned by hearing sounds that are dependent on the support of dwelling in seclusion, with the thought, 'I dwell in the forest.' 'Apara' means another; that is, a second. 'Tattheva' means right there, in that very place of dwelling for one, and at the time of dwelling, comfort arises from the arising of mental seclusion. Therefore, it is said, 'for one delighting alone in the forest.'

Tathāti [V 2.0141] yathā āraññikassa rati, tathā piṇḍapātikassa labbhati diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro. Esa nayo sesesu. Apiṇḍapātikādhīno itarassa visesajotakoti tamevassa visesaṃ dassetuṃ “akālacārī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Tathā' means: just as the forest-dweller has delight, so too the alms-goer obtains a pleasant dwelling in this very life. This is the method for the remaining cases. Because dependence on not being an alms-goer illuminates the distinction of the other, to show that very distinction of his, 'one who goes at the wrong time' and so on is said.

Amhākaṃ salākaṃ gahetvā bhattatthāya gehaṃ anāgacchantassa sattāhaṃ na pātetabbanti sāmikehi dinnattā sattāhaṃ salākaṃ na labhati, na katikavasena. Piṇḍacārikavatte avattanato “yassa cesā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it was given by the owners with the stipulation, 'For one who, having taken our ticket, does not come to the house for a meal, it should not be issued for seven days,' he does not receive the ticket for seven days; this is not by way of a formal agreement. Because of not conducting oneself in the practice of an alms-goer, 'And for whom this...' and so on is said.

Paṭhamataraṃ kātabbaṃ yaṃ, taṃ vattaṃ, itaraṃ paṭivattaṃ. Mahantaṃ vā vattaṃ, khuddakaṃ paṭivattaṃ. Keci “vattapaṭipatti”nti paṭhanti, vattassa karaṇanti attho. Uddharaṇa-atiharaṇa-vītiharaṇavossajjana-sannikkhepana-sannirumbhanānaṃ [M 2.0161] vasena cha koṭṭhāse. Garubhāvenāti thirabhāvena.

That which should be done first is the vatta (duty); the other is the paṭivatta (counter-duty). The great is the vatta, the small is the paṭivatta. Some read 'vattapaṭipatti,' meaning the performance of the vatta. There are six sections by way of lifting up, carrying forth, moving apart, relinquishing, laying down, and hemming in. 'Garubhāvena' means by steadfastness.

“Amukasmiṃ senāsane vasantā bahuṃ vassavāsikaṃ labhantī”ti tathā na vassavāsikaṃ pariyesanto carati vassavāsikasseva aggahaṇato. Tasmā senāsanaphāsukaṃyeva cinteti. Tena bahuparikkhārabhāvena phāsuvihāro natthi parikkhārānaṃ rakkhaṇapaṭijagganādidukkhabahulatāya. Appicchādīnanti appicchasantuṭṭhādīnaṃyeva labbhati diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro.

He does not wander about seeking a rains-residence with the thought, 'Living in such and such a dwelling, they obtain much for the rains-residence,' because he does not grasp at the rains-residence itself. Therefore, he thinks only of a suitable dwelling. Because of having many requisites, there is no comfortable dwelling, due to the abundance of suffering involved in guarding and attending to the requisites. For those with few desires, contentment, and so on, a pleasant dwelling in this very life is indeed obtained.

Jiṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Jiṇṇa Sutta is concluded.

6. Ovādasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta

149. Attano ṭhāneti sabrahmacārīnaṃ ovādakaviññāpakabhāvena attano mahāsāvakaṭṭhāne ṭhapanatthaṃ. Atha vā yasmā “ahaṃ dāni na ciraṃ ṭhassāmi, tathā sāriputtamoggallānā, ayaṃ pana vīsaṃvassatāyuko, ovadanto anusāsanto mamaccayena bhikkhūnaṃ mayā kātabbakiccaṃ karissatī”ti adhippāyena bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tasmā attano ṭhāneti satthārā kātabbaovādadāyakaṭṭhāne. Tenāha “evaṃ panassā”tiādi. Yathāha bhagavā “ovada, kassapa…pe… tvaṃ vā”ti. Dukkhena vattabbā appadakkhiṇaggāhibhāvato. Dubbacabhāvakaraṇehīti kodhūpanāhādīhi. Anusāsaniyā padakkhiṇaggahaṇaṃ nāma anudhammacaraṇaṃ, chinnapaṭipatti katā vāmaggāho nāmāti āha “anusāsani”ntiādi. Atikkamma vadanteti aññamaññaṃ atikkamitvā atimaññitvā vadante. Bahuṃ bhāsissatīti dhammaṃ kathento ko vipulaṃ [V 2.0142] katvā kathessati. Asahitanti pubbenāparaṃ nasahitaṃ hetupamāvirahitaṃ. Amadhuranti na madhuraṃ na kaṇṇasukhaṃ na pemanīyaṃ. Lahuññeva uṭṭhāti appavattanena kūlaṭṭhānaṃ viya tassa kathanaṃ.

149. 'In his own place' means for the purpose of establishing himself in the position of a great disciple by being an advisor and instructor to his fellow monastics. Alternatively, the Blessed One began this teaching with the thought, 'I will not remain long now, nor will Sāriputta and Moggallāna. But this one has a life span of twenty years; by advising and instructing, he will fulfill the duties I must perform for the monks after my passing.' Therefore, 'in his own place' means in the position of one who gives advice, a duty to be performed by the Teacher. Hence it is said, 'Thus, indeed, for him...' and so on. As the Blessed One said, 'Advise, Kassapa… or you…' They are difficult to speak to because they are not receptive to what is right. 'By things that make them difficult to admonish' means by anger, resentment, and so on. Regarding instruction, taking it respectfully is called practicing in accordance with the Dhamma; having cut off the practice is called 'left-handed grasping.' Thus it is said, 'instruction' and so on. 'Speaking by transgressing' means speaking while transgressing against and despising one another. 'He will speak much' means: when teaching the Dhamma, who will speak making it extensive? 'Incoherent' means the latter is not connected with the former, lacking cause and simile. 'Unpleasant' means not sweet, not pleasant to the ear, not endearing. 'It arises lightly' means his speech is like a riverbank with no firm footing.

Ovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta is concluded.

7. Dutiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Second Ovāda Sutta

150. Okappanasaddhāti [M 2.0162] saddheyyavatthuṃ ogāhitvā “evameta”nti kappanasaddhā. Kusaladhammajānanapaññāti anavajjadhammānaṃ sabbaso jānanapaññā. Parihānanti sabbāhi sampattīhi parihānaṃ. Na hi kalyāṇamittarahitassa kāci sampatti nāma atthīti.

150. 'Resolute faith' means faith that, having penetrated a basis for faith, resolves, 'It is so.' 'Wisdom that knows wholesome qualities' means wisdom that knows all blameless qualities completely. 'Decline' means decline from all attainments. For one lacking good friends, there is indeed no attainment whatsoever.

Dutiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Ovāda Sutta is concluded.

8. Tatiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Third Ovāda Sutta

151. Pubbeti paṭhamabodhiyaṃ. Etarahīti tato pacchime kāle. Kāraṇapaṭṭhapaneti kāraṇārambhe. Tesu vuttaguṇayuttesu theresu. Tasminti tasmiṃ yathāvuttaguṇayutte puggale. Evaṃ sakkāre kayiramāneti “bhaddako vatāyaṃ bhikkhū”ti ādarajātehi bhikkhūhi sakkāre kayiramāne. Ime sabrahmacārī. “Ehi bhikkhū”ti taṃ bhikkhuṃ attano mukhābhimukhaṃ karontā vadanti. Yañhi tanti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ upaddavoti vuccati anatthajananato. Patthayati bhajati bajjhatīti patthanā, abhisaṅgoti āha “abhipatthanāti adhimattapatthanā”ti.

151. 'Formerly' means at the first awakening. 'Now' means in the time after that. 'Establishing a reason' means at the commencement of a reason. 'In those' means in those elders endowed with the stated qualities. 'In that' means in that person endowed with the qualities as stated. 'When honor is shown thus' means when honor is shown by monks in whom respect has arisen, saying, 'Indeed, this monk is good!' These are the fellow monastics. They say, 'Come, monk,' making that monk face them. Here, `taṃ` is merely a particle. 'Affliction' is so called because it generates what is not beneficial. `Patthanā` (longing) is so called because one desires, resorts to, and is bound by it. Regarding `abhisaṅga` (clinging), he said: '`Abhipatthanā` means intense longing.'

Tatiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Ovāda Sutta is concluded.

9. Jhānābhiññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Jhānābhiññā Sutta

152. Yāvadevāti iminā samānatthaṃ “yāvade”ti idaṃ padanti āha “yāvade ākaṅkhāmīti yāvadeva icchāmī”ti. Yadicchakaṃ jhānasamāpattīsu vasībhāvadassanatthaṃ tadetaṃ āraddhaṃ. Vitthāritameva, tasmā tattha vitthāritameva gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Āsavānaṃ khayāti āsavānaṃ khayahetu ariyamaggena sabbaso āsavānaṃ khepitattā. Apaccayabhūtanti ārammaṇapaccayabhāvena apaccayabhūtaṃ.

152. The word 'yāvade' is synonymous with 'yāvadeva.' Thus, he said, 'yāvade ākaṅkhāmi' (as much as I wish) means 'yāvadeva icchāmi' (as much as I desire). This has been undertaken to show mastery over the jhānic attainments, according to one's wish. It is indeed elaborated elsewhere; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood in detail from there. 'From the destruction of the taints' means because the taints have been completely destroyed by the noble path, which is the cause for the destruction of the taints. 'Having become unconditioned' means having become unconditioned in the sense of not being an object-condition.

Jhānābhiññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Jhānābhiññā Sutta is concluded.

10. Upassayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Upassaya Sutta

153. Lābhasakkārahetupi [V 2.0143][M 2.0163] ekacce bhikkhū bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantvā bhikkhuniyo ovadanti, evamevaṃ ayaṃ pana thero na lābhasakkārahetu bhikkhunupassayagamanaṃ yācati, atha kasmāti āha “kammaṭṭhānatthikā”tiādi. Eso hi ānandatthero ussukkāpetvā paṭipattiguṇaṃ dassento yasmā tā bhikkhuniyo catusaccakammaṭṭhānikā, tasmā pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayādipakāsaniyā dhammakathāya vipassanāpaṭipattisampadaṃ dassesi. Aniccādilakkhaṇāni ceva udayabbayādike ca sammā dassesi. Hatthena gahetvā viya paccakkhato dassesi. Samādapesīti tattha lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanaṃ samādapesi. Yathā vīthipaṭipanno hutvā pavattati, evaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Samuttejesīti vipassanāya āraddhāya saṅkhārānaṃ udayabbayādīsu upaṭṭhahantesu yathākālaṃ paggahasamupekkhaṇehi bojjhaṅgānaṃ anupavattanena bhāvanāmajjhimavīthiṃ pāpetvā yathā vipassanāñāṇaṃ suppasannaṃ hutvā vahati, evaṃ indriyānaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇena vipassanācittaṃ sammā uttejesi, nibbānavasena vā samādapesi. Sampahaṃsesīti tathā pavattiyamānāya vipassanāya samappavattabhāvanāvasena upari laddhabbabhāvanāvasena cittaṃ sampahaṃsesi, laddhassādavasena suṭṭhu tosesi. Evamettha attho veditabbo.

153. Some monks, for the sake of gain and honor, go to the nuns' quarters and advise the nuns. However, this elder does not ask to go to the nuns' quarters for the sake of gain and honor. Why then? He says, “for the sake of a meditation subject,” and so on. Indeed, this Venerable Ānanda, having made an effort and showing the virtue of practice—because those nuns were practitioners whose meditation subject was the four truths—demonstrated the perfection of insight practice through a discourse on the Dhamma that reveals the arising and passing away, and so on, of the five aggregates of clinging. He correctly showed the characteristics of impermanence, and so on, as well as arising and passing away. He showed it directly, as if taking them by the hand. “He established them” (samādapesi) means he established them in insight meditation with the characteristics as its object.
